stories.title: Max Miller’s Corporate Backers Go Silent on Embattled Congressman
stories.author: Dave Levinthal
stories.summary: Dozens of company and trade group PACs refuse to say whether they’ll ditch — or defend — the Ohio Republican.
stories.content: Corporate PACs have given tens of thousands of dollars toward Rep. Max Miller’s campaign but few responded to NOTUS’ questions about the donations. Tom E. Puskar/AP Dozens of different corporate interests combined to fill Rep. Max Miller’s reelection account with six-figures worth of campaign cash in recent weeks. But now, amid accusations that Miller abused his daughter and now ex-wife — accusations the congressman denies — his business allies are falling silent. Of the more than 35 corporate and trade association political action committees that contributed at least $1, to Miller’s campaign since mid-April, according to Federal Election Commission records , all either ignored or declined to answer questions from NOTUS about their relationship with the Republican lawmaker. Among those questions: Do they continue to support Miller for a third term representing Ohio’s 7th Congressional District? Have they requested refunds of previous donations? Will they give Miller’s campaign money in the future? Among the corporate PACs that wouldn’t openly distance themselves from — or defend — Miller: TD Bank, Citigroup, ConocoPhillips, John Deere & Co., Blue Cross Blue Shield Association, Pfizer, Genentech, Cencora, Altria, Tenaska and Elevance Health. Trade association PACs that are remaining similarly mum on Miller include those of the Allied Pilots Association, Advanced Medical Technology Association, America’s Health Insurance Plans, American Dental Association, American Academy of Sleep Medicine, American Investment Council, American Bankers Association, International Franchise Association, International Council of Shopping Centers, Investment Company Institute, National Apartment Association, National Roofing Contractors Association, National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, Healthcare Distribution Alliance, National Association of Convenience Stores, National Electrical Contractors Association, Ohio Corn and Wheat Growers Association, United Brotherhood of Carpenters and Joiners of America and the Farm Credit Council. Associated General Contractors of America spokesperson Brian Turmail confirmed in an email that his organization’s PAC contributed $2, to Miller’s campaign this spring, but he wouldn’t otherwise comment. Meanwhile, several special interest group PACs also did not respond to repeated inquiries, including the House Conservatives Fund, American Israel Public Affairs Committee and Pakistani American Public Affairs Committee. Miller’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on whether PACs have requested refunds or otherwise communicated their future intentions. Miller says he isn’t dropping out of his race despite the accusations and a call for him to step aside by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), the father of Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Bernie Moreno wrote on X . “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” This week, Miller’s attorney released naked photos of Miller’s young daughter and also revealed her name as part of a cache of documents intended to bolster Miller’s assertions of innocence. The attorney, Aaron Minc, said the release was “completely unintentional and a mistake.” Miller, for his part, told PBS News Hour: “No criminal charge has ever been filed against me. My former wife is engaging in a pattern of reporting incredible, serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence.” Ohio law gives Republicans a deadline of Monday to replace a congressional nominee on the November ballot, meaning Miller would have to abandon his reelection campaign by then in order for the party to nominate someone else. As matters stand, Miller is set to Democrat Brian Poindexter in a race the Cook Political Report scores as “likely Republican.”

stories.title: Chuck Edwards Ends His Reelection Following Harassment Allegations
stories.author: Christa Dutton
stories.summary: The House Ethics Committee had recommended the North Carolina Republican be censured.
stories.content: Bill Clark/AP Rep. Chuck Edwards suspended his campaign for reelection early Wednesday morning following a House Ethics report that cited alleged inappropriate behavior toward two women staffers . “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” he posted on X . “I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support. God bless WNC and America.” The Ethics committee recommended on Monday that the North Carolina Republican be censured and found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces,” according to a committee press release . Edwards was running for reelection in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, one of two competitive districts in the state crucial to both parties’ path to a majority in Congress. Pressure had been building among Republicans to force him out. House Republicans were privately trying to convince Edwards to abandon his reelection bid in light of the House Ethics committee’s report, CNN reported on Tuesday. A source on Capitol Hill told The News & Observer that Sen. Ted Budd (R-North Carolina) asked Edwards to drop out of the race. A spokesperson for Budd told NOTUS on Tuesday that while the senator doesn’t disclose his private conversations, he “finds the House Ethics report deeply concerning.” The spokesperson that Budd "believes Rep. Edwards faces a significant uphill battle in his reelection bid,” pointing to Edwards’ trailing poll numbers and that his opponent is vastly outraising Edwards. Since Edwards withdrew from the race before military and overseas absentee ballots were distributed on Sept. 4, state law says the North Carolina 11th District GOP Executive Committee, which includes the district party’s officers as well as other members, can choose Edwards’ replacement on the ballot. The House Ethics Committee found that Edwards gave the two women staffers “lavish gifts,” including expensive jewelry, designer purses, vacations, guns, and dinners. The report also pointed to instances when Edwards paid for spa trips, talked to staffers about going to D.C. strip clubs, and told one of the staffers not to let his scheduler know about a dinner the two had planned. The committee did not find evidence that Edwards “engaged in sexual activity with or explicitly propositioned any individual under his employ.” The report said that Edwards was aware that his “excessive attention toward the young women had led to rumors and innuendo in the office” and “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate.” Even before news broke about him being the subject of a House Ethics investigation in May, Edwards a competitive challenge from Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer backed by the centrist group Blue Dog Democrats who comes from a family of North Carolina politicians. Ager is one of several Democrats running in red districts that have the backing of House Democrats’ campaign arm through its Red to Blue program. The Cook Political Report changed the district’s rating from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” in June. The state’s other competitive seat is North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, currently held by Democrat Rep. Don Davis.

stories.title: Freedom 250 Sponsors Failed to Disclose Donations — A Potential Lobbying Law Violation
stories.author: Taylor Giorno
stories.summary: Corporate giants such as Lockheed Martin, ExxonMobil and United Health Group could run afoul of the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
stories.content: The President Donald Trump-backed Freedom staged the Great American State Fair — and solicited millions of dollars in corporate contributions. Jacquelyn Martin/AP The Great American State Fair was covered in the logos of dozens of corporate lobbying giants. But most of the event sponsors — including defense contractors Lockheed Martin, GE Aerospace and Northrop Grumman — did not disclose payments to the President Donald Trump-supported event organizer Freedom , in potential violation of federal lobbying law, according to a NOTUS review of federal lobbyist contribution reports due to Congress by last Friday. The Great American State Fair was also “presented by” corporate giants including ExxonMobil, SAP, Exiger, Mosaic and ScottsMiracle-Gro, according to billboards NOTUS photographed around the fair grounds last month. They’re among the almost two-dozen companies, including Palantir, Oracle, UnitedHealth Group and John Deere, listed as “sponsors” on the Freedom website . LockheedMartin.State.Fair ( , AR: 1.78)Only three Freedom corporate sponsors — Chevron, United Airlines and RTX — disclosed financial contributions to the organization as required by the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act. Ethics experts told NOTUS that the other companies should, too. Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act , any entity that lobbies the federal government must file semiannual reports with Congress detailing honorary expenses, event cost payments and donations to political campaigns, presidential inaugurations , presidential libraries and other entities established or controlled by public officials. The law “is certainly not airtight, and certain entities have found ways to try to exploit this law,” Aaron Scherb, a longtime ethics and democracy advocate, told NOTUS. “Nonetheless, it requires full disclosure of political spending when companies are trying to curry favor with an administration and elected officials,” Scherb . “So, companies contributing to Freedom should absolutely be required to disclose their political spending.” Freedom was established by Task Force , which Trump created via executive order . Trump himself is the chair of Freedom . The limited liability corporation is housed within the National Park Foundation, the nonprofit charity arm of the National Park Service, to which companies have previously disclosed donations . “When it comes to other nonprofits, the question is always whether it was created and controlled by Trump,” Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist at the left-leaning nonprofit watchdog Public Citizen, told NOTUS. “But there is little question about Freedom .” The offices of the clerk of the House and secretary of the Senate, which are tasked with processing lobbying disclosures and questioning lobbyists who fail to comply with reporting requirements, did not respond to requests for comment on obligations to disclose contributions to Freedom . The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which is tasked with enforcing compliance, also did not respond to questions. The Wall Street Journal reported that Freedom had raised $50 million from a variety of corporate interests. But the vast majority of these reported contributions — including $2 million from TikTok and $1 million each from Oracle and ExxonMobil — were not separately disclosed in certified federal disclosures, as required by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. As of Tuesday evening, only three companies that both lobby the federal government and contributed money to Freedom disclosed how much they gave to the Trump-backed organization. Oil company Chevron, a presenting sponsor of the Great American State Fair, shelled out $5 million in May, according to federal records first reported by Politico and Sludge . United Airlines disclosed donating $2.5 million in March. And RTX, the defense company formerly known as Raytheon, reported giving $1.5 million in May. Chevron, United Airlines and RTX are among the nearly two-dozen corporate sponsors listed on the Freedom website . “As a proud American company, Chevron is pleased to support celebrations of years of the country's independence,” Bill Turenne, a spokesperson, told NOTUS. United Airlines declined to comment. RTX did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Palantir, one of the companies listed as a sponsor on the website, told NOTUS the company did not donate to Freedom . “Palantir is proud to adhere to all lobbying and donation disclosure requirements, but the company did not make a contribution to Freedom ,” the Palantir spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement. GE Aerospace declined to comment. UnitedHealth Group, John Deere, Lockheed Martin, TikTok, Oracle, ExxonMobil, Northrop Grumman, ScottsMiracle-Gro, Exiger, Mosaic and SAP did not respond to requests for comment from NOTUS. Other companies not listed by Freedom as official partners or sponsors said they did not pay the organization money despite having their corporate logos posted around the Great American State Fair. Axiom Space had an exhibit that included a video and a large astronaut cutout. But Meridyth Moore, a spokesperson for Axiom Space, said the company “was not a paid sponsor.” Axiom.Space ( , AR: 1.78)"That’s it. We provided a cutout image of our spacesuit and a video to be played,” Moore responded when asked for more details about the exhibit. When NOTUS asked if the organizers had allowed Axiom to include the pieces for free, Moore confirmed “no expenditures were spent.” Hillsdale College, a small, Christian liberal arts school in Michigan, also had a branded booth at the Great American State Fair. Emily Davis, a college spokesperson, described Hillsdale as a “partner” but said the college did not donate to Freedom . “The college complies with all reporting obligations. It has not given any monies to the Freedom group,” Davis said. SAP, a business software company, operated a large exhibit at the Great American State Fair, which included a display wall featuring the logos of several client companies alongside QR codes and a rotating digital display detailing some of the brands. SAP.ads.Great.American.State.Fair ( , AR: 1.78)Todd Scott, senior communications manager at Hershey, one of the companies featured in the SAP exhibit, told NOTUS that the chocolate company was not a sponsor and that this was the first he had heard about the company’s logo being on the SAP exhibit at the Great American State Fair. (NOTUS reported on Hershey’s presence at the Great American State Fair in July.) Scott pointed to an article in The Philadelphia Inquirer , where he previously said Hershey was “asked so late in the game” to participate in the Great American State Fair that the company could not logistically participate. Funding for Freedom has often lacked transparency since the group began operating alongside America250 — a separate nonprofit group supporting the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission, which Congress established a ago. Oil company BP, for one, disclosed a $ , contribution to America250 in February, according to its latest contribution report filed last Friday. Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee accused Freedom of diverting funds from America250, including by allegedly giving donors the routing and account numbers for Freedom , according to a report released by the committee last month. Freedom spokesperson Danielle Alvarez previously told NPR that the claims are "categorically false” and a "partisan smear." "Congressional members should be ashamed they are spending countless hours fabricating a report instead of joining Americans in creating an absolutely beautiful celebration," Alvarez told NPR last month. Alvarez did not immediately respond to a NOTUS message following up on questions emailed separately to Freedom .

stories.title: Max Miller Says Mike Johnson Is 'Standing Behind Me'
stories.author: Adora Brown
stories.summary: The Ohio Republican told CNN’s Jake Tapper that all three women who accused him of violence are lying.
stories.content: Rep. Max Miller said he has no plans to drop out of the race before the deadline despite facing growing calls to do so from within his party, including from his former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno. Amanda Andrade-Rhoades/AP Photo Rep. Max Miller said House Speaker Mike Johnson is standing behind him in his bid for reelection, in a Tuesday interview on CNN about allegations of abuse by several women, including his ex-wife. “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else, they're standing behind me. No one has told me to get off the ballot, and that's because they know I can win this seat,” Miller (R-Ohio) told CNN’s Jake Tapper in the 23-minute conversation. Johnson’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether he supports Miller’s reelection campaign. Miller said he has no plans to drop out of the race before the deadline despite facing growing calls to do so from within his party, including from his former father-in-law , Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). The House Ethics Committee has opened a probe into the allegations against Miller after the congressman requested an investigation on Tuesday, saying he thought it would “clear my name.” Tapper pushed Miller on the mounting allegations from Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, who accused the Ohio congressman of domestic abuse and child abuse in court filings, as well as reports from an ex-girlfriend, former White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham, and a Politico report about an alleged incident of violence against a female classmate during high school. When asked if all three women independently lied, Miller said, “Yes, it's very easy.” Miller said his side of the story has been taken out of context in other interviews. He also told Tapper his daughter once said, “I do not want to go to mommy’s” and “I do not feel safe” in audio he recorded. Tapper said the network would not be able to air those recordings, and brought up a police report in which Emily Moreno said their child told her things like, “Daddy kill you,” and “Daddy’s house is scary.” “I wish you could talk to my beautiful baby girl. She can't string together sentences like that. She's 2½ years old. She doesn't have the ability to articulate any of what you just said,” Miller responded, calling the claims an “entire fabrication of the truth.” “You just told me that she had said she was scared to go to mommy’s house, but now you’re saying that she’s not capable of saying, ‘Daddy kill you,’” Tapper rebutted. “It seems like she’s either able to say one but not the other — that doesn’t make sense.” Emily Moreno also accused Miller of using illegal drugs after finding needles in his bedroom. He told CNN they were for testosterone replacement therapy, and that the last time he used illegal drugs was “several years ago.” Miller said that like President Donald Trump — who was reelected despite facing “the most extreme allegations in the world” — he too could win his Ohio reelection campaign in November. “For no second am I going to sit here and continue to be debased by false and baseless allegations and be pushed out of a seat I have worked so hard to represent and done a terrific job for our community,” Miller said. Republicans are nonetheless walking a tightrope in this Ohio race. Miller is set to Democrat Brian Poindexter, a former union ironworker, in November’s election. Poindexter was up by 5 percentage points, and 41% of voters had an unfavorable view of Miller, according to recent polling conducted by a Republican firm that was obtained and reviewed by NOTUS.

stories.title: Rep. Max Miller Demands an Ethics Investigation Into Himself
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The committee said it would review the allegations of domestic abuse, hours after Miller made his unusual request.
stories.content: Complicating matters is the fact that Miller's ex-wife is the daughter of a fellow Republican lawmaker, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images The House Ethics Committee is actively “reviewing allegations” of domestic abuse and illegal drug use against embattled Rep. Max Miller, after he made the unusual move Tuesday of urging the committee to launch an investigation into himself. Miller is facing mounting pressure to step down following allegations of domestic abuse from his ex-wife, who is the daughter of a fellow Republican lawmaker, Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno. “In light of all the renewed interest in my family affairs I am going to file my own paperwork for an ethics investigation into myself to clear my name from these horrific attacks on myself and family,” Miller wrote Tuesday on X. He that he intends to provide the committee with “all necessary documents needed” to conduct a detailed examination. The committee has been hesitant in the past to investigate members of Congress during election years and has a rule barring it from pursuing investigations within 60 days of an election. The committee is unlikely to release any findings by Election Day and would have to reauthorize the probe after a new Congress begins. Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused the congressman of throwing scalding water on her, shoving her against a wall and holding a gun to her head. Miller has denied those allegations and another claim that he caused his daughter’s broken collarbone. Sen. Moreno on Monday called his family’s experience with Miller “truly the seventh circle of hell,” and said his “daughter lives in constant fear of this man.” The Ohio senator put out a lengthy statement over the weekend saying Miller should seek professional help and should not serve in Congress .He’s not the only Republican to call for Miller to step down. “He should resign. He should quit,” Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) told Politico this week. Marshall said the trust he has in Moreno as a “good friend” makes him think the senator’s family is “telling the whole truth and nothing but the truth.” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) also said she agrees with Moreno’s condemnation of Miller. “I don’t know [Miller]. I haven’t read a whole lot about him, but if [Moreno] thinks he ought to resign, I’m supportive of that,” Capito told Politico . While Moreno has stopped short of explicitly calling for Miller to resign, the senator has said he “should not serve in the House of Representatives.” In Miller’s congressional race, recent polling shows him trailing his Democratic challenger, Brian Poindexter. Some senators think it should be left up to voters to decide Miller’s future in Congress. “The best thing is, the public’s going to take him out of office,” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida) told MeidasTouch , responding to a question about whether Miller should resign. When asked if there is a double standard with how Democrats and Republicans handle allegations of misconduct, Scott said it didn’t exist but “everybody should be held accountable.” Miller reaffirmed his plans to seek reelection in a livestream on X on Sunday and denied the allegations of abuse. The congressman also released a trove of files containing court documents, text messages, audio recordings and videos that he says back up his side of the ongoing dispute. Emily Moreno’s legal team subsequently wrote a letter accusing Miller of releasing an image of their daughter that could be considered “child sexual abuse material” as part of that trove. One of Miller’s attorneys took responsibility for sharing the photo. “I am solely responsible for what happened,” attorney Aaron Minc said in a statement to Politico on Tuesday. “I was the only person responsible for assembling, creating, reviewing, adding, deleting, redacting, or making any changes to the information and files that were in this folder.” This is not the first time Miller has allegations of domestic abuse. Miller, who served as a White House aide during President Donald Trump’s first term, dated White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham in . After their relationship ended, Grisham published an opinion piece in The Washington Post describing the abuse she allegedly endured from a former partner who was not named in the piece, but whom Grisham later identified as Miller. He denied the allegations, arguing they coincided with the release of her memoir. Miller sued Grisham for defamation in , and they reached a confidential settlement in . Grisham recently sued Miller and filed for a temporary restraining order on Tuesday, claiming he broke the terms of the settlement by speaking publicly about the case. This story has been updated with the House Ethics Committee’s announcement.

stories.title: How Politicians Living and Dead Play the Stock Market With Campaign Cash
stories.author: Mark Alfred
stories.summary: Opaque investments boost lawmakers’ campaign coffers with little public oversight.
stories.content: Former House Speaker Tom Foley, pictured here in , died in . But his congressional campaign committee is technically active — and still earning money. Laura Patterson/CQ Roll Call via AP Images Former Speaker of the House Tom Foley lost his final bid for reelection in after three decades in office. In , Foley died . But the “Committee to Reelect Tom Foley” — his still-technically active campaign committee — lives on, and it reported earning a small profit this year from several financial investments, including stock in tech giants Microsoft and Meta. Foley’s old committee stands among scores of federal campaign operations that reap the rewards of invested campaign funds, a NOTUS review of federal records indicates. For prolific fundraisers, including current members of Congress, such investments can yield six- or seven-figure windfalls annually, with political figures of all partisan leanings making sometimes lucrative stock and financial gambles using money donors gave their campaigns for election purposes. There are no set limits on the amount of money campaigns can earn by investing donor cash, giving politicians an — although potentially risky — tool for boosting their campaign coffers beyond traditional fundraising methods. Campaign committees’ investments are often secretive, too: Few campaigns report details beyond a dollar figure and their bank or investment house of choice. This leaves voters unable to determine whether a political campaign’s specific investments could potentially conflict with a candidate’s official duties, such as a member of Congress who oversees military matters while investing campaign cash in defense contractor stocks. While members of Congress are notorious for making improperly disclosed personal stock trades while in office, their penchant for using campaign cash to play the markets is far less scrutinized and, often, even more opaque. NOTUS attempted to contact the campaigns of nearly current members of Congress to ask whether they would voluntarily share details about their campaign committees’ specific financial investments. Only five responded, and those who did said their investments were conservative — largely just earning interest from bank accounts. Investors of the 119th Congress It makes sense for candidates with hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of dollars in their campaign accounts to park their cash somewhere where it can accumulate interest over time, if only to defend against inflation . Many federal candidates report steady earnings consistent with conservative investment accounts such as money market funds or certificates of deposit. Rep. Chuck Fleischmann (R-Tennessee), for example, has reported stable monthly yields between $10, and $13, in “bank interest” for the past two years. For over two decades, both Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Minority Leader Chuck Schumer have earned steady interest from the millions of surplus dollars sitting in their campaign accounts. The campaign of Rep. Julia Brownley (D-California) stores its money in a “non-traditional bond fund,” two high-yield bond funds and “short term CDs,” a campaign spokesperson said. For candidates who invest their campaign money more aggressively, many have good months … and bad months. In February, the campaign of Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois) reported a $16, “investment gain.” But in March, he reported a $21, “ investment loss. ” Other lawmakers’ campaign portfolios swing wildly from quarter to quarter. In November , the campaign of Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan) reported $1.9 million in “investment income.” In February , it reported a $1.2 million “loss.” Mounting losses across this election cycle caused his cash on hand to fall more than $1.8 million — a remarkable drop for a campaign already $13.6 million in debt to Thanedar himself. Last quarter, his campaign reported a loss of $ , , which it labeled "Investment Income Loss from a mutual fund." Election House Detroit AP- ( , AR: 1.41)Representatives for Thanedar, who faces a competitive Democratic primary in August, did not respond to a request for comment. In , Thanedar vowed to personally stop trading individual stocks after NOTUS reported that he violated the federal Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act ’s disclosure provision with improperly disclosed personal trades. “Members of Congress should not trade in individual stocks,” Thanedar told NOTUS at the time. “Many of my individual stock purchases I did are from years before I was in Congress. My goal is to get rid of all the individual stocks in my portfolio, but it takes time.” In a single December filing, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, reported more than $1.1 million from "investment account earnings" and another $ , in dividends. Graham’s campaign committee had $2.3 million in remaining cash, with several options for disposing of it . Lindsey Graham AP - ( , AR: 1.50)Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) criticism during the financial crisis for dumping much of his personal stock holdings as markets reeled and Congress prepared relief legislation. Federal filings show his personal campaign, in contrast, was months ahead of the curve, selling its stocks in May and netting $ , in the process. Nowadays, Durbin’s campaign nets about $ a month in basic interest. What’s legal, what’s not The reporting requirements for trading using campaign cash are far less stringent than what lawmakers are obligated to disclose when making financial trades that affect their own personal finances. It's generally easy to spot possible conflicts of interest when lawmakers who have jurisdiction over specific industries buy and sell shares of companies directly affected by their actions. That’s because the STOCK Act requires them to publicly detail and disclose within 45 days any stock, bond or cryptocurrency trade that they make in their personal capacity. That same scrutiny cannot be applied to those lawmakers when they trade using their campaign funds under the current rules. “The current opaque investment income for campaigns conceal potential conflicts of interests from the media and voters, such as campaign investing in the personal business interests of the candidate or candidate’s family,” Public Citizen lobbyist Craig Holman said. “If campaigns are enriching their own pockets or those of political friends, that is information that donors and voters would want to know.” “The requirements also need to be enhanced to provide the full picture of investment income by campaigns, much in the same way as personal financial disclosure requirements placed on officeholders,” Holman said. Some lawmakers fail to even meet the low bar for campaign-finance reporting requirements under the current rules. To the ire of federal regulators, Thanedar repeatedly failed to disclose the financial institution his campaign used to invest donor dollars, prompting several letters to the campaign’s treasurer: Thanedar himself. (The congressman clarified in April that his campaign used LPL Financial.) Where lawmakers’ campaigns do their banking is often a partisan affair. At least 86 incumbent Democrats park their campaign funds at Amalgamated Bank, a unionized and labor-aligned institution that champions accessibility and affordable housing. Republican lawmakers and presidential hopefuls flock to Chain Bridge Bank, founded by former Republican Sen. Peter Fitzgerald. Beyond standard banking, other members employ wealth managers to grow their campaign cash. Janney Montgomery Scott, a Philadelphia-based wealth management firm that predates the Civil War, is particularly popular: In recent years, nearly three-dozen campaign committees have hired the firm, according to NOTUS’ review of FEC records. The campaigns of Reps. Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Pete Aguilar (D-California) and Jim Himes (D-Connecticut) each pay five- or six figures annually to Janney Montgomery Scott in various management or brokerage fees. Each has pulled in six-figure sums this cycle alone via their investments. Torres’ total is nearly $ , . No incumbent Republicans bank with the firm. The campaign of Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-North Carolina) has paid steadily increasing four-figure quarterly fees to Blue Trust, a Christian wealth management firm dedicated to bringing “financial expertise and biblical wisdom together.” Virginia Foxx AP- ( , AR: 1.50)In , Foxx reported $ , in “Realized Capital Gains on Investment” via Blue Trust. (Foxx’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment). Republican Michael Carbonara is the founder of the fintech firm Ibanera, and his tenure as CEO overlapped with the first few months of his bid to represent Florida’s 22nd Congressional District. In that time, his congressional campaign made sizable purchases of Bitcoin and Ethereum through Ibanera, paying thousands of dollars in fees to the company he still ran, according to federal records. Carbonara’s campaign sold the Ethereum stake for $ , in November, a week after stepping down as chief executive, realizing a roughly 80% gain on his investment. Last quarter alone, he reported $1.86 million in cryptocurrency liquidations. Bitcoin’s price, meanwhile, has tumbled . Carbonara did not respond to a request for comment. Roots of campaign investing The practice of political campaigns investing donor dollars has a long history. Two decades before former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-New Jersey) went to prison over a bribery scheme that saw him receive payoffs in cash and gold bars, his campaign spent years trading stocks in various individual companies. Eight of those companies were gold mines — literally. Among them: Glamis Gold, Harmony Gold, Newmont Mining and Goldcorp . Former President Barack Obama’s campaign earned $1.58 million from bank interest alone. In , the presidential campaign committee inherited by then-Vice President Kamala Harris after President Joe Biden dropped out pulled in $1.35 million in interest via Amalgamated Bank. Both were simple cases of campaign cash accumulating interest over time. Trump-aligned PACs Trump 47 Committee and Never Surrender brought in over $1 million in “ interest revenue ” from their Chain Bridge Bank accounts in and , respectively. Other campaigns have taken riskier approaches to their investments. Several Trump administration officials retained their campaign accounts after leaving office, and the old committees continue to net investment gains. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy departed the House in and hasn’t run for elected office since. But his old campaign has earned more than $1 million in unspecified “investment gains” across the past several years, FEC records indicate. Duffy, ever the family man , recently contributed $1 million in campaign funds to Northwoods Future, the super PAC supporting his son-in-law, Michael Alfonso, who is running for Congress in Wisconsin. Perhaps no other former member of Congress has pulled in as much investment income as Trump loyalist Devin Nunes . Devin Nunes AP- ( , AR: 1.50)When he left Congress to oversee Trump’s media venture Truth Social, Nunes had $11 million in his congressional campaign coffers. That figure ballooned to $15.5 million during his time out of office via funds placed with Edward Jones Investments, a remarkable sum that his lawyer told federal regulators could be for “a potential future election.” Last quarter alone, he reported pulling in $1.5 million from his investment account. Nunes’ campaign did not respond to questions about its specific investments. Nunes is one of several former lawmakers teasing a future run to justify his campaign’s continued existence. Tom Byrne, the son of former New Jersey Gov. Brendan Byrne, never made it into elected office despite House and Senate bids over 25 years ago. Over the years, Byrne has mulled another statewide run and has grown his campaign cash in a Charles Schwab account, bringing in over $ , this cycle alone. Now, in his 70s and facing questions from federal regulators, Byrne said he’s still on the lookout for an opportunity, with his campaign telling the FEC : “it is hard to predict when another [statewide] opening may occur but it is an effort to level the playing field versus the number of self-financing statewide candidates in NJ.” Former Rep. Cliff Stearns (R-Florida) is using a similar tactic to keep his campaign operational and collecting interest over a after leaving Congress. Late last year, Stearns, now 85, told federal regulators that he would wind down his committee — with a significant caveat: “We will continue to move to terminate the committee … unless we decide to be a candidate for federal office again.” Former Democratic Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II of Massachusetts, the elder brother of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has maintained his personal campaign committee — “Citizens For Joe Kennedy ” — as a de facto investment vehicle for more than 25 years after leaving office. JosephKennedyII ( , AR: 1.32)As Kennedy racked up “dividend income, interest income, quarterly portfolio appreciation, and capital gains,” the campaign repeatedly assured federal regulators in recent years that any expenses would be “for legal and accounting purposes in connection with keeping the committee open.” The campaign, which did not respond to a request for comment, regularly pulls in hundreds of thousands of dollars annually in investment income. As of July 30, Kennedy’s old committee reported having more than $1.3 million in its account — after earning more than $ , between April 1 and June 30 from investments with Goldman Sachs, according to FEC records . The FEC recommends that the dormant campaign accounts of retired or deceased lawmakers be wound down within six months, but there is no hard rule requiring that deadline to be met. Dormant campaign accounts with surplus cash can, by law, donate the money to charity, transfer it to political party committees, disgorge it to the U.S. Treasury or — as is so often the case — just sit on it. Rep. Tom Lantos (D-California) died while in office in , but it took four years to fully close his committee, which continued to collect interest income across eight bank accounts. The campaign ultimately contributed the proceeds to the Lantos Foundation for Human Rights and Justice — $ , across three donations. Former Rep. John LaFalce (D-New York), who left Congress in , died last year. But his campaign committee lived on with money in its account — until September, when the committee emptied out the remaining $ , and gave it to the nonprofit Community Foundation for Greater Buffalo. As for Foley, the late house speaker from Spokane, Washington, his campaign is managed by his widow and former chief of staff, Heather Foley, who did not respond to a request for comment. Heather.Foley ( , AR: 1.49)Every so often, FEC officials ask her what the campaign intends to do with its cash on hand. And just as often, she replies : “I wrote you previously that I do not intend to spend any of the campaign funds left [after] my husband’s death for personal use.” “As soon as I have accumulated sufficient funds,” she writes, “I intend to give it to the Spokane Parks Foundation.”

stories.title: Author of Democrats’ 2024 Autopsy Releases ‘Missing’ Chapter
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The DNC contends that it never received the document in question.
stories.content: The consequences of President Joe Biden’s decision to run again were not discussed at length in the original -page document released in May. In the newly released chapter, Paul Rivera addresses the former president’s decision. Evan Vucci/AP The author of the Democratic National Committee’s widely panned postelection autopsy report released what he said is an unpublished chapter on Monday, breathing new life into a scandal that threatens to distract the party as it prepares for the closing stretch of the midterms. Paul Rivera, a longtime Democratic consultant, shared the 28-page installment with The New York Times , claiming that the missing document includes questions about President Joe Biden’s decision to run for reelection and addresses frustration that high-earning Democratic elites “drive too much of the decision-making within the ecosystem.” The consequences of Biden’s decision to run again were not discussed at length in the original -page document released in May. In the newly released chapter, Rivera addresses the former president’s decision. “Is there a single point of failure for ? Perhaps it is a decision of the President to seek re-election instead of passing the torch, but Democrats do not have a time machine to go back and change his decision,” Rivera wrote. Rivera told the Times he personally delivered the chapter in a binder to Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin in January. But Martin and other representatives for the DNC disputed that they had ever seen the chapter in question, and that the “missing” chapter could not be located in an extensive search of the committee’s files. “That is false,” Martin wrote in a statement. “The only binder I was working with Paul on was for lessons learned materials. This alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed.” If the DNC had received the chapter in question from Rivera, it “would have released it with the rest of the report,” Martin said. Neither NOTUS nor The New York Times could independently verify either account. The chapter also reviewed Democrats’ declining support from Hispanic, Black, Asian American and Native American voters, and noted that digital consultants had missed the mark with voters. “They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation,” Rivera wrote — though he did not identify anyone by name. Martin said “one of [his] key priorities remains, to hold the consultant-industrial complex accountable,” and that the DNC would have “absolutely” published any “report materials that went after self-enriching consultants,” if the committee had them. “Whether that was a conscious decision on their part to bury the section for the purposes of hiding a paragraph, I don’t know,” Rivera told The New York Times. “That’s a them question. What I can tell you is they had it, and they made a decision not to release it.” After submitting files to the DNC in late , Martin allegedly told Rivera he was disappointed with the quality of his work, and the pair met for a discussion in January. Rivera then compiled a new -page report that he claims included the chapter in question. But Martin said his “work with Paul in January is being misrepresented,” because they only discussed documents that outlined “lessons learned.” “That effort did not include reviewing new report material, only the material the DNC had already received, which is what we released in May,” Martin said. The original report drew a rebuke by Democrats for its failure to address Biden’s impact on the race and Kamala Harris’ subsequent campaign without an official primary process. The report was also missing an executive summary, even though there was an apparent place for one in the first few pages of the report, with an annotation that the section was not provided by the author. The entire report included an annotation in red at the top of every page, saying “this document reflects the views of the author, not the DNC.” The committee in the disclaimer that Rivera did not provide “underlying sourcing, interviews, or supporting data for many of the assertions” contained in the report. Some Democrats thought the original report failed to draw any meaningful conclusions about where the party went wrong in . Rivera sought to address the criticism by releasing a -page independent autopsy report on Aug. 3, called Blue by , that opens with an accounting of the events surrounding the original report. “In late December, the DNC decided to announce it was not releasing a report, and did not release an executive summary. In the ensuing six months, the DNC never asked for a meeting to discuss content, or provided markup or questions to the after-action project team,” Rivera wrote. The timeline appears to conflict with Rivera’s account of his discussions with Martin in January. Blue by did not immediately respond to a request for comment. After the Times released Rivera’s missing chapter, some political analysts said the new document suffers from many of the same problems that plagued the publicly released version of the report. “I think the author of the DNC autopsy is giving himself too much credit,” Nate Silver, a statistician and the founder of FiveThirtyEight.com , wrote on X. “If you actually read the omitted chapter (good of the NYT to include it), it consists largely of boilerplate and clichés and mentions Biden's decision to run only in passing.” Neither the original report nor Rivera’s additional chapter make any mention of Israel or its war in Gaza, a crucial issue that split Democratic voters in the lead-up to the election and continues to be a controversial topic for candidates. Critics of the original report released by the DNC also took issue with the omission of the conflict, but in a statement at the time Martin acknowledged that a number of key issues were left out of the autopsy. “I am not proud of this product; it does not meet my standards, and it won’t meet your standards,” Martin said in May. “I don’t endorse what’s in this report, or what’s left out of it.”

stories.title: Ethics Committee Recommends Censure for Rep. Chuck Edwards Over ‘Inappropriate Conduct’
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: Edwards denies that the conduct was “intended as a sexual or romantic advance.”
stories.content: Among the House Ethics Committee findings was that Rep. Chuck Edwards gave two staffers gifts including designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop, a cellphone and a KitchenAid mixer. Bill Clark/AP The House Ethics Committee recommended censuring Rep. Chuck Edwards on Monday, citing his alleged inappropriate relationships with staffers. “The Committee concluded there was substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces,” the committee wrote in a press release about the North Carolina Republican. The committee’s report found that Edwards “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.” Edwards, 65, who has been married since ,has denied that the alleged conduct “was intended as a sexual or romantic advance.” Sources told NOTUS in May that the House Ethics Committee had launched an investigation into allegations that Edwards had an affair with a former staffer who left the office earlier this year. The staffer was Edwards’ former deputy chief of staff, and she was initially hired as a legislative assistant to Edwards when he was a state senator in . The committee issued a public request in April for anyone to report information about House members or staffers engaging in sexual misconduct. “Shortly after that announcement, the Committee was informed of allegations regarding Representative Edwards’ conduct towards women in his office and began confidentially reviewing the allegations,” the committee wrote in its 25-page report. Edwards was aware that his conduct toward the staffers had generated discussion and “rumors” in his office, according to the report. “Representative Edwards also went beyond norms of professional behavior by giving both women lavish gifts,” the committee wrote. “Both women received numerous gifts from Representative Edwards, including jewelry totaling over $1, , designer purses, guns, shoes, flowers, a laptop and cell phone, KitchenAid mixer, robotic vacuum, vacations, tickets to performances, and one-on-one dinners.” One of the staffers said she felt “obligated to wear” a necklace Edwards gave her, and the congressman told her he was disappointed when she did not wear it. The report catalogues instances of alleged inappropriate conduct with the staffers, including the congressman paying for spa treatments, discussing going to strip clubs in D.C. and directing one of the staffers not to notify Edwards’ scheduler about a dinner the pair had planned. Edwards brought one of the staffers to a holiday event at the White House and told her he wanted the night to be “perfect.” The congressman allegedly pressured the staffer to continue the evening with him and asked her to travel to and from the event in his car with his driver. Edwards told the committee he did not recall pressuring her that evening, but he acknowledged traveling with her to her home in Virginia because he “felt uncomfortable dumping a young lady on the street.” The congressman skipped House votes to decorate a Christmas tree with one of the staffers, according to the committee. He also went to that same staffer’s house to “perform chores like yardwork, pick her up and drop her off for events and activities with his driver.” The committee found that Edwards wrote poems for one of the staffers, “including one that he read at her going away party in the congressional office accompanied by a slideshow, during which he cried.” Multiple staffers testified to the committee that the incident made them feel uncomfortable, and Edwards said he recognized the discomfort among his staff. A censure serves as a public condemnation of a congress member’s behavior. The committee will bring Edwards’ censure recommendation for a vote by the full House. This is the first time the Ethics Committee has recommended censure since it took action against former Rep. Charles Rangel (D-New York) in over improper fundraising, financial disclosures and failing to pay taxes. This story has been updated with more details from the Ethics Committee report.

stories.title: The Struggle of Being a No-Corporate-PAC-Money Democrat
stories.author: Oriana González, Kadia Goba
stories.summary: “I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” one House Democrat said.
stories.content: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told NOTUS that there are “racial and gender dynamics” that come into play in relation to fundraising. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP An increasing number of Democratic candidates are pledging to reject donations from business-linked political action committees in — a promise House Democrats say is easier said than done. “I am deciding whether I'm going to committee or a meeting based on whether I have to meet with individual donors,” one House Democrat, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told NOTUS. “That's fucked up.” Democrats who take funds from corporate super PACs “perform significantly worse” against a Republican candidate compared to Democrats who reject outside PAC money, according to a recent analysis from the progressive think tank Data for Progress . That leaves candidates facing what is likely to be the most expensive midterm election in history with few good options: take money from corporations and alienate the base, or spend all day, every day, dialing individual donors for dollars. But the time constraints attached to calling and meeting individual donors can cut into lawmakers’ legislative responsibilities. Members who spoke to NOTUS say they or their campaign teams spend around 10 to 20 hours a week doing what’s known as “call time.” “That call thing, calling a stranger in California or New York — it kind of sometimes feels a little demoralizing, right?” Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois) told NOTUS. “It’s less community events sometimes, right? Because the truth is that AIPAC, AI, and crypto want nothing more than someone like me to not be here, so if I don’t have enough money in the bank, they will primary me and it’s really hard to beat $30 million,” continued Ramirez, who said she also spends less time with family because of call time. “There are sacrifices.” Rep. Dave Min (D-California), who said he spends 20 hours a week fundraising, split between weekends and little pockets of time while he’s in Washington, said it’s important that members are “seen as above reproach.”“So yes, do I have to work harder? Yes. Do I have to spend Saturdays often fundraising instead of like, hanging out with my family? Yes. But that's a decision I made,” Min . Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told NOTUS that there are “racial and gender dynamics” that come into play in relation to fundraising. “Women and people of color and people who come from different socioeconomic backgrounds don't always come with the personal network of people who have thousands of dollars to give,” she said. Corporate cash has ended in the hands of Democrats, including some who have sworn it off, as NOTUS recently reported . And the difficulties attached to rejecting business-linked money has made it so that some members start accepting it. Rep. Emily Randall (D-Washington) did not take corporate PAC money during her six years in the Washington State Legislature or during her initial bid for Congress. Now, as a freshman House lawmaker, she does. Randall pivoted to accepting cash from corporations immediately after winning her election in . She recalled how she often had to prioritize making calls over knocking on doors when she was a first-time congressional candidate who'd sworn off corporate money. “It was hard,” Randall said. “After the ’24 cycle, I was like, ‘Look, now I'm a safe seat member. My job is to raise as much money as possible to support frontline and Red to Blue members.’ I know what that was like as a member from a tough district in the Legislature, and I want to be a team player that helps make sure that my colleagues can keep their seats and that we can win the seats we have to win.” The first House Democrat who spoke anonymously concurred. Members who pay dues to the caucus’ campaign arm to help vulnerable Democrats are “constantly getting the messages, ‘You need to give your full dues, you need to give your full dues.’ But it’s really hard to pay for your full dues if you don’t take corporate cash.” Veteran and more high-profile Democrats don’t the same issue. Rep. Jim McGovern of Massachusetts made the leap away from taking corporate money in after he was sworn in as the top Democrat on the House Rules Committee. Between January and June of this year, McGovern has amassed more than $ , in contributions. In , the last election cycle he accepted corporate PAC money, he raised over $1.1 million . McGovern, who is often captured giving provocative floor speeches, cited C-SPAN and social media as big drivers for his small-donor contributions, but admitted he has an advantage as a 15-term member with a relatively high profile. “I guess it's harder for a freshman, you know, when you don't have an established platform. People outside your district, you know, may not know you as well,” he said. A second House Democrat who spoke anonymously told NOTUS that while now their campaign operation averages around 10 to 15 hours a week, “as a first-time candidate, I was doing like 40 hours a week because you don't know anybody and you just have to try to connect with other people.” In contrast, Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), a pioneer in the no-corporate-PAC movement, said she spends about two hours a month making fundraising calls, with the bulk of her donations coming from text and email campaigns. But, she , that’s still a hassle. "I hate it,” Jayapal told NOTUS. "I don't like it. I don't think I should like asking people to give me money.” One of the priorities in the Congressional Progressive Caucus’ legislative agenda — especially if Democrats win the majority in November, is to pass legislation to limit super PAC contributions. “There is still a structural problem,” CPC Chair Greg Casar told NOTUS. The legislation, he continued, is “one of the multiple ways that we can eventually just get big money out of politics.” Rep. Summer Lee (D-Pennsylvania), who leads the Abolish Super PACs Act and co-leads other campaign finance reform legislation, said “Corporations recognize that this is a gap, a loophole in the system.” “It does two things: It creates an overreliance on their influence in the first place,” Lee said of corporate money. “It also keeps people out. It keeps working class people out. It keeps women out. It keeps particularly Black women, the folks who are going to have the hardest time fundraising, in the back.” “It is an imbalance that even now members who accept corporate PACs are starting to recognize,” Lee . Democratic lawmakers like Reps. Grace Meng of New York, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Mike Thompson of California, who accept corporate PAC money, are listed as co-sponsors for her bill. The makeup of the district can also have a direct impact on lawmakers’ fundraising ability. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California), who represents the heart of Silicon Valley, touted the need for public financing “so that we reduce that influence” in elections. But he said he sympathizes with his colleagues who do not represent wealthy districts like he does and have a harder time fundraising. “I don't come at it with some pretense that I'm sort of morally superior to my colleagues when I have access to a lot more wealthy donors than they do,” he told NOTUS. For members in House Democratic leadership, this is just part of the job. Rep. Lauren Underwood of Illinois, a recruitment co-chair for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee who does not take corporate money, put it simply: “We always have to make fundraising calls. We always have to go travel and do events. I have to go and literally get the money.” “We are the stars. We are the talent. We have to go get this money to sustain the campaign,” she told NOTUS.

stories.title: Rep. Marcy Kaptur Hospitalized After Hit-and-Run Crash in Ohio
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: A witness says the other driver fled in another vehicle as police report an “active and ongoing” investigation.
stories.content: Rep. Marcy Kaptur was hospitalized after the crash Sunday with non-life-threatening injuries, her office said. Carlos Osorio/AP Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur was hospitalized following a hit-and-run car crash in her home state of Ohio on Sunday morning, according to the Toledo Police Department. The crash occurred around 10:45 a.m. in Toledo, and two people were taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said. It was unclear who the second person was. "This morning Congresswoman Kaptur was a passenger in a vehicle on her way to a church service when the car she was traveling in was struck,” Kaptur’s office wrote in a statement. “She is active, alert, and being treated for non-life threatening injuries.” Toledo police described the investigation as “active and ongoing" and did not immediately say whether any suspect had been apprehended. Local news station WTOL 11 published photos from the scene showing two damaged vehicles. One witness told WTOL that the other driver was picked up by another vehicle and fled shortly after the incident. Kaptur’s colleagues shared messages of support on X. “Tina and I are praying for a quick and full recovery for @RepMarcyKaptur,” Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) wrote . “We hope the person responsible for this reckless act is apprehended quickly and held accountable.” “I'm praying for my colleague @RepMarcyKaptur after her crash this morning,” Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Arizona) posted . “May she be restored to full health in short order.” Kaptur is running for reelection for Ohio’s 9th Congressional District. She is set to former state Rep. Derek Merrin in November. Merrin asked followers to help him in “praying for her speedy recovery.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

stories.title: Sen. Bernie Moreno Says His Ex-Son-In-Law, Rep. Max Miller, ‘Shouldn’t Serve in the House’
stories.author: Jenna Monnin, Reese Gorman
stories.summary: Miller earlier Sunday defended himself in a livestream against domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the senator’s daughter.
stories.content: A screen grab from Max Miller's announcement share on X. X formerly Twitter Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno said Sunday that his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller, should seek professional help and should not serve in Congress, citing allegations of domestic abuse against his daughter and granddaughter. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Moreno wrote on X . “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.” Miller, a fellow Ohio Republican, reaffirmed his plans to seek reelection in a livestream on X earlier Sunday and denied the allegations of abuse from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno. The two-term congressman released files containing court documents, text messages, audio recordings and videos that he says back up his side of the ongoing dispute. “My former wife is engaging in a pattern of reporting incredible, serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence,” Miller said on the livestream. “God bless you all,” Miller said later, directing people to view files he’d shared on Dropbox. “I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November, and I'll be back in the 120th” congressional session. Miller’s Sunday pushback comes as his reelection chances could be dimming. A poll conducted by a Republican firm Wednesday and Thursday and reviewed by NOTUS showed Miller underwater in his district. His Democratic opponent in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, Brian Poindexter, was up 5 percentage points, polling at 44% to Miller’s 39% with 16% undecided. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points. His favorability rating was also down, with 41% of voters viewing him unfavorably and only 25% holding a favorable view. Some 22% were unsure and 12% had never heard of him. Emily Moreno and Miller were married from to . The couple have one daughter. The domestic abuse allegations surfaced in May, complicating Miller’s reelection bid in the midterms that will determine which party controls Congress. “It is shameful that Max Miller decided to go on a bizarre and lie-filled rant about his ex-wife to desperately try to save his political career,” Stefan Mychajliw, a spokesperson for Emily Moreno, wrote in a statement posted after the livestream. “No loving parent would have ever used their daughter as a PR pawn to save their own political career. Miller can lie and spin on X, but he cannot do so under oath in a court of law. We are confident that justice will prevail in court.” Emily Moreno asked the court on Thursday to issue a restraining order against Miller preventing him from contacting her lawyer Andrew Zashin, alleging the congressman had physical and verbal altercations with Zashin. During their marriage, Miller allegedly threw hot or scalding water at Emily Moreno during an argument which caused burns to her body, according to court filings in the legal battle. Emily Moreno also said in court filings that Miller shoved her against a wall during one confrontation and another time held a gun to her head. Miller has denied all of the allegations. “It was horseplay in our kitchen,” Miller said Sunday about the hot water incident. “I sprayed water at her from the sprayer attached to our kitchen sink tap water, which does not reach boiling temperature or scalding.” Mother Jones reported last month that Emily Moreno said she could not rule out the possibility that Miller caused their daughter's broken collarbone due to his alleged history of violence toward her. Miller on Sunday disputed that account. “I had dropped my daughter off with my former wife before that injury was even discovered,” Miller said. “She was not in my care during that time, and when I found out about her injury, I canceled my trip to Florida to be there for her while she recovered.” Sen. Moreno, who told NOTUS last week that “I don’t know” if Miller should be replaced on the ticket, said Sunday on X that he is seriously concerned whenever Miller is watching his grandchild. “He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter,” Bernie Moreno wrote. Miller said Emily Moreno has “struggled with significant mental health challenges,” and he said he believes it has contributed to the allegations against him. Miller’s X account posted a link to Dropbox with a slew of files, though the link was quickly deleted. The congressman blamed the website, and said the files were not made using congressional resources: “Just to be clear: these documents were produced by my personal attorneys and paid for by me directly.” He posted the files again later Sunday morning. Emily Moreno’s comments about Miller aren’t the first allegations of domestic abuse the Ohio congressman has . Miller, who served as an aide to President Donald Trump in his first term, dated White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham in . After their relationship ended, Grisham published an opinion piece in The Washington Post describing abuse she allegedly endured from a former partner who was not named in the piece, but whom Grisham later identified as Miller. He denied the allegations, arguing they coincided with the release of her memoir. Miller sued Grisham for defamation in , and they reached a confidential settlement in . Grisham recently sued Miller, claiming he broke the terms of the settlement by speaking publicly about the case. This story has been updated to include a statement from Emily Moreno's spokesperson and new polling information.

stories.title: George Santos Settles Kalshi Insider Trading Case With the CFTC
stories.author: Torrie Herrington, Kadia Goba
stories.summary: The former lawmaker was accused of betting on whether he would attend President Trump’s State of the Union.
stories.content: George Santos Settles Kalshi Insider Trading Case With the CFTC Anthony Behar/Sipa USA via AP The Commodity Futures Trading Commission announced Friday that it has settled a case involving former Rep. George Santos, who was facing an insider trading investigation by the Justice Department for betting on his own attendance to President Donald Trump’s State of the Union address earlier this year. Santos has agreed to pay a $17, fine and repay the $17, .98 he made on the bet, the CFTC announced. He also is barred from trading on prediction markets for three years. In a statement, Joseph W. Murray, Santos’ attorney, said the former congressman agreed to resolve the CFTC’s inquiry to “put this matter behind him.” Santos admitted to placing the bet in question but maintains that the act does not amount to any wrongdoing, his lawyer . “He chose a prompt, practical resolution rather than protracted, costly litigation, and that choice should not be mistaken for an admission of any wrongdoing, because it is not one,” Murray said. In February — just four months after his sentence for committing wire fraud and aggravated identity theft was commuted by Trump — Santos placed his first bet on Kalshi. The former congressman wagered that he would not be in attendance at the Capitol for the State of the Union address, despite publicly stating he would be there. “I'm going to be there for the State of Union in the gallery, guys,” Santos said in a video he posted on X a day before the address. Santos wasn’t the only person betting on who would be in attendance for the speech; people were placing bets worth millions of dollars on attendees, and Santos’ video confirming his attendance affected those bets. But in the end, he did not show up. “Watching SOTU from an airport tv was not part of the plan! FML,” Santos wrote on X later that day. Santos’ lawyers argue there was no wrongdoing by Santos because he did not hide “his intention to attend, nor his change of plans to not attend the SOTU, from anyone.” “There was absolutely no intent to deceive any person, nor intent to manipulate any market,” Murray said in a statement following the settlement announcement. According to NPR , three people with direct knowledge of Santos’ trades said he misled the public on purpose and profited based on that deception. Two sources told the outlet that when Kalshi detected Santos' trades, it froze his account and referred the case to the CFTC and the DOJ.

stories.title: Sen. Bernie Moreno Doesn't 'Know' if Embattled Rep. Max Miller Should Stay on Ballot
stories.author: Adora Brown
stories.summary: The senator’s daughter accused Miller of domestic violence. Miller denies the allegations, but they’re making his reelection race tighter.
stories.content: “I don’t know,” Moreno told NOTUS when asked if Republicans should replace Miller on the ticket. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio is unsure whether Rep. Max Miller should stay on the ballot in his House district after Miller was accused of domestic violence by his ex-wife — who is also the senator’s daughter. “I don’t know,” Moreno told NOTUS when asked if Republicans should replace Miller on the ticket. Republicans, including Moreno, have said little about the allegations against Miller, even as Miller’s reelection race grows tighter. His seat in Ohio is one of many that could determine which party controls the House next year. On Thursday, Sabato’s Crystal Ball downgraded his seat from “likely Republican” to “ leans Republican .” “While we won’t dignify this baseless attacks by Democrats and their media allies, Senator Moreno will not speak on active litigation involving his family,” Reagan McCarthy, a spokesperson for Moreno, told NOTUS in a statement. Other Republicans have also largely held back from admonishing Miller. When asked on Thursday why he has allowed Miller to stay in the House Republican conference, Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters , “The key word there is ‘allegation,’” and that there’s an investigative process that would need to play out before a member of Congress is removed. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, told an ABC station in Ohio on Wednesday that the allegations are “serious and certainly troubling,” but that “the people of his district are going to have to weigh the facts. They're the ones who decide who they want to represent them." Miller has held the seat since and ran uncontested in May’s primary election. He was a political aide for President Donald Trump during Trump’s first term. Trump endorsed Miller in his first run, when he launched a primary against Republican Rep. Anthony Gonzalez, who voted to impeach the president . He once again gave Miller his “complete and total endorsement” for his reelection in May, adding that the representative “WILL NOT LET YOU DOWN!” in a Truth Social post. A source familiar with the matter told NOTUS that the president has no plans to withdraw his endorsement of Miller in light of the allegations of domestic violence and child abuse. The deadline to replace Miller on the ballot is August 9. Miller did not respond to a request for comment. Emily Moreno, the senator’s daughter, has alleged that Miller abused her and their daughter in court filings and police records obtained by Mother Jones. The couple filed for divorce in , and on Thursday, her lawyers reportedly filed for a new restraining order against her ex-husband. The New York Times reported that in legal filings Emily Moreno had previously accused Miller of burning her by throwing hot water on her body, holding a gun to her head, pushing her hard enough to cause an injury and breaking their daughter’s collarbone. Miller has denied these accusations and called Emily Moreno a woman who “isn’t all there.” Miller has sued Moreno for defamation. The restraining order requested by Emily Moreno’s lawyers on Thursday alleges that Miller “harassed, threatened, and communicated directly” with Moreno’s attorneys and “placed his hands” on one of her lawyers. Some of the allegations that Miller faces go back to his time in the first Trump administration. Stephanie Grisham, a former White House press secretary who dated Miller, published an op-ed in alleging an abusive relationship with a former boyfriend, whom she identified as a White House staffer and someone Trump endorsed for a bid in Congress after she warned the president about the abuse. Miller filed a defamation suit against Grisham in , even though Grisham had avoided including his name. The matter ended in a settlement in , but Grisham filed a lawsuit against Miller in early July after he spoke about her in several interviews, saying the public comments violated a nondisclosure agreement he had signed as part of the settlement. This November, Miller is running against Brian Poindexter, a Democrat and former union ironworker who’s juxtaposing his blue-collar background against Miller’s wealthy upbringing. When Miller ran for reelection in — in a district that overwhelmingly voted for President Donald Trump — he won with only 51% of the vote. In Congress, the Democratic Women’s Caucus is calling for the House Ethics Committee to investigate the allegations against Miller. “Allegations of violence against women and children have to be met with the utmost seriousness,” its members said in a joint statement on Thursday.

stories.title: Letitia James Takes Aim at Prediction Market Kalshi
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: The lawsuit comes amid disputes between the federal government and states over who has jurisdiction to regulate the rapidly growing prediction market industry.
stories.content: Forty-four state attorneys general, including James, signed a letter to the CFTC on Monday asking that the agency “start afresh with its rulemaking and clarify that sports bets and gambling cannot be traded on [designated contract markets], but are instead subject to state law.” Maureen Adarve/STAR MAX/IPx via AP New York Attorney General Letitia James sued prediction market Kalshi in state court on Friday, alleging that the company runs an “illegal gambling operation” without proper state licenses. James’ lawsuit comes amid disputes between an independent federal agency and state governments over who has jurisdiction to regulate the rapidly growing prediction market industry, which includes companies like Kalshi and Polymarket. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction marketplaces, has argued that the companies are “designated contracted markets” that offer event contracts , otherwise known as swaps, that offer odds on yes-no scenarios. State governments have rebutted that argument, contending that the sport contracts offered on prediction markets mirror sports gambling that falls under states’ regulatory purview. Forty-four state attorneys general, including James, signed a letter to the CFTC on Monday asking that the agency “start afresh with its rulemaking and clarify that sports bets and gambling cannot be traded on [designated contract markets], but are instead subject to state law.” James used a similar stance in her lawsuit against Kalshi, accusing the company of circumventing state regulations on sports betting “by offering what is quintessentially wagering under the guise of ‘event contracts’ on a ‘prediction market.’” The lawsuit also accused Kalshi of allowing individuals under the age of 21 to wager on the platform. James’ lawsuit asked a judge to bar Kalshi from operating within the state by offering “contracts relating to sports, culture, elections, and other events” without required licenses. It also asked for Kalshi to pay restitution to consumers, pay a fine equal to three times the gains the company made and forfeit any alleged illegal profits. “New York’s gambling laws protect children from underage betting and help combat gambling addiction,” James said in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “No matter what they call themselves, prediction markets like Kalshi are gambling platforms, plain and simple. By ignoring our laws, Kalshi is running an illegal operation and harming New Yorkers in the process.” The CFTC preemptively requested a temporary restraining order in federal court ahead of James’ lawsuit to stop the state from pursuing civil or criminal enforcement actions against Kalshi while litigation continues. Kalshi and New York were engaged in “ongoing negotiations” on a comprehensive tax proposal prior to the lawsuit, a source familiar with Kalshi’s negotiations told NOTUS. The source said New York did not respond to the proposal “in substance” and then “abandoned” the idea. James’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the tax negotiations. “It's sad to see this type of political theater from the leadership in our own state,” Elisabeth Diana, Kalshi’s head of communications, said in a statement. “States can’t just shut down a federally licensed exchange. This would also hurt New Yorkers, who would be driven offshore. We love New York, we love New Yorkers, and New Yorkers love our product."

stories.title: OPM Director Scott Kupor Publicly Touted Robinhood. He’s Also an Investor.
stories.author: Dave Levinthal
stories.summary: A Kupor spokesperson said government ethics officials didn’t require him to divest his investment in the financial services company.
stories.content: Director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor’s Robinhood stock sales on June 18 are together worth between $1.7 million and $3.5 million, a disclosure document filed with the Office of Government Ethics indicates. Mariam Zuhaib/AP In December, U.S. Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor highlighted a partnership between financial services company Robinhood Markets Inc. and the Trump administration that temporarily places skilled private-sector tech workers in federal government jobs. “We’re doing this in partnership with about 25 of the tech companies that you all know and love — so, you know, Coinbase, Robinhood, Databricks, Snowflake, NVIDIA, xAI, OpenAI,” Kupor told technology news show TBPN in explaining the Trump administration’s “US Tech Force” initiative. Screenshot -07-30 at 8.05.51 PM.png ( , AR: 0.95)What Kupor didn’t say: He has maintained massive personal financial interests in Robinhood. And last month, the OPM director exercised stock call options and sold seven figures worth of his Robinhood shares, according to new federal ethics records reviewed by NOTUS. Kupor’s Robinhood stock sales on June 18 are together worth between $1.7 million and $3.5 million, a disclosure document filed with the Office of Government Ethics indicates.
