Putting a player with career receptions, 11, yards and 74 touchdowns alongside Terry McLaurin ( receptions, 6, yards and 41 touchdowns) makes the receiving unit deep and dangerous. The two veterans will be grouped with promising rookie Antonio Williams, who has had breakout moments during training camp; former first-rounder Treylon Burks; veteran Van Jefferson and a host of other young receivers. Diggs spent the first five seasons of his career with the Vikings before being traded to the Bills in . After four years in Buffalo, Diggs played in Houston before joining the Patriots and reaching last year’s Super Bowl. Diggs has also garnered headlines away from the field. In May, he was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef. He is currently suing a social media influencer who has accused him of sexual assault and facing a civil lawsuit for accusing a former concierge of stealing his Ferrari.

stories.title: On the Right Track
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: People board a Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) train while others wait on the opposite platform at the Metro Center station in Washington, D.C. on March 11, . Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A drop in Metro crime, $1.4 billion for the National Guard and a confusing Nats trade deadline. THE LATEST Crime on Metro has hit a “new historic low.” New crime data released by WMATA shows that Part I crimes — more serious offenses like assaults, robberies and thefts — are down 12% since last year and 61% since . The consistent decreases in crime come from cops, cameras and compassion , says WMATA general manager Randy Clarke . There are more police officers and security guards patrolling stations and buses; 30, cameras are monitoring the system; and low-income riders are offered discounts to help prevent fare evasion. Clarke said Tuesday the drop in crime and increase in ridership have created something of a virtuous cycle for Metro, with safer trains and buses encouraging ridership, and more riders putting more eyes to work. “Not only is [Metro] much safer, it’s much safer for a lot more people,” he said. (Even still, ridership numbers remain below where they were pre-pandemic.) Fare evasion enforcement has been a particular focus for Metro in recent years. Clarke said enforcement on trains increased % from to . Ramped-up enforcement on buses that was launched this year has led to a 1, % spike in citations. Clarke himself has even gotten in on enforcing the rules. He said he recently stopped an older man who tried to get into a Metro station using one of the Kids Ride Free cards that are handed out to schoolchildren in the city. (Note to self: Don’t use your kids’ cards.) Still, there have been snags. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle recently reported that a bureaucratic snafu has led to most fare-evasion citations issued in D.C. being dismissed. Clarke says he wants a regional solution to ensure that fare evasion is prosecuted consistently across the Metro system. President Donald Trump plans to spend $1.4 billion in taxpayer funds keeping the National Guard in D.C. until January , NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez reports . The eye-popping estimate, provided to Sen. Elizabeth Warren ’s office and shared with NOTUS, includes a recently announced $ million contract to keep troops housed through the end of Trump’s term. For context: The D.C. police department’s annual budget for its 3, officers is roughly $ million. National Guard DC AP - ( , AR: 1.50) FROM THE DISTRICT The left-leaning Free D.C. Slate swept up 75% of the seats up for grabs on the D.C. Democratic State Committee, ousting the committee’s more moderate members, The Washington Post reports . JBG Smith — a real estate investment trust with a massive footprint in the DMV — delayed its earnings report after a D.C. Superior Court judge ordered last week that the company pay $ million to a condo association, the Washington Business Journal reports . The condo owners sued in , alleging defects in their building’s elevators, roof, HVAC system, electrical system, exterior walls, parking garage elevators and foundation. JBG Smith has about $2.6 billion in debt and has reported 12 straight quarterly losses. NOTUS previously reported on abysmal conditions at another property it co-owns: The Gale Eckington . FROM MARYLAND Montgomery County’s gun laws are in the Trump administration’s crosshairs. This week, the Justice Department sued the county over a law it says makes it “practically impossible for individuals in the county to go about their daily business while lawfully carrying a firearm.” Late last year, the DOJ similarly filed suit against D.C. over the city’s ban on AR-15 assault rifles. FROM VIRGINIA Virginia’s health department is investigating the state’s first documented case of locally acquired dengue virus. The disease is spread through infected mosquitoes, but officials said the public’s risk of acquiring it is low. PLAN YOUR WEEKEND For Mac, Charlie, Frank, Dennis and Dee: “ SUNNY RAVE ” at Howard Theatre, Friday. For the crafter : Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington, Saturday. For the sneakerhead: SneakerCon at the Washington Convention Center, Saturday and Sunday. For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here . SPORTS Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson breaks down the Commanders’ options at center, as a group of converted guards aims to fill one of the offense’s most important positions. The Nationals took a hybrid approach to the trade deadline , which meant selling key players to add a bunch of new pitchers — a few of whom could help the team this season. But since there was still more selling for the future than buying for the present, the deadline felt familiar to fans who are tired of rooting for a team that keeps trading away some of its best talent every summer, NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty writes . The Freedom IndyCar race taking place in the District this month will be longer than anticipated: Officials announced this week that the race will be extended from laps to so it can hit the -mile mark. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Wings, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Samuel Corum/Sipa USA. One last thing: That $ , home we showed you yesterday is located in D.C.

stories.title: Do the Commanders have a problem at center?
stories.author: Martenzie Johnson
stories.summary: With presumed starter Nick Allegretti sidelined, the position has drawn attention early in camp.
stories.content: Washington's Nick Allegretti, a converted guard, is the presumed starter at center heading into the season. Chris Szagola/AP Things are looking a little dicey at the center of the Commanders’ offensive line. The team’s presumed starter at the center position is actually a converted guard. His backup is also a converted guard. The rookie they drafted in the sixth round of April’s draft — a converted guard. The center they signed earlier this week to fill in due to injuries? You guessed it. As the Commanders make their way through the second week of training camp, the centers have drawn a fair amount of attention. With the offense seeking to rebound from a bottom-10 performance last season, it's unclear what one of the unit’s most important positions will look like next week, let alone next month. Coach Dan Quinn isn’t in panic mode. Despite the absence of starter Nick Allegretti due to a calf strain, Quinn said the offensive line has held up. “Both sides of the line I thought had, you know, advantage here, advantage there, and that's what I'm hoping to see,” he said ahead of practice Tuesday. “If one gets tilted too much to the other, then I'd be more concerned. So I like the back-and-forth, honestly, to say good run here, good blitz there.” Despite Quinn’s optimistic take, there are still plenty of question marks. Allegretti has not practiced since July 29. His backup, Julian Good-Jones, has had an up-and-down run as fill-in with the first team, including one snap that went over Jayden Daniels’ head during team drills on Tuesday. Rookie Matt Gulbin has rolled almost exclusively with the second team, but depth is clearly a concern. The team worked out centers Gus Hartwig, Joe Michalski and Trey Hill on Saturday. Hill, a sixth-round pick by the Bengals in who played guard early in college, was signed the following day. Following Saturday’s and Monday’s practices, guards Timothy McKay and Brandon Coleman and tackle Trent Scott stayed to take snaps with Marcus Mariota. Quinn said all the maneuvering has been aimed at building depth (before Hill’s arrival Gulbin was the only player on the team roster listed as a center), but is also an experiment to see who is capable of handling center responsibilities. “If you can play inside, you want somebody that can play both [center and guard],” Quinn said. “And that's basically kind of the rhythm behind it.” The center position is pivotal to the offense. The job isn’t solely about successfully snapping the ball to the quarterback. Centers are responsible for calling out defensive alignments, coordinating blocking assignments and, of course, handling the defender in front of them. And yet Washington has not had consistency at the position for years. Since , at least 10 players have taken snaps at center for Washington. Last season, the offensive line was just about average in ESPN’s pass- and run-block metrics, and that was before starting center Tyler Biadasz was released in February. Quinn has commended Gulbin for his command of the second unit line. “I think it's just kind of a next-man-up mentality,” Gulbin said. “I have to step up to the plate and make sure the O line's functioning, and I'm getting out calls.” Allegretti has helped coach up Good-Jones and Gulbin from the sideline. Those three, and now Hill, can be seen bouncing ideas and techniques off one another. After practice they often put in extra work with assistant offensive line coach Shane Toub. “I come off the sideline, he's [Allegretti’s] helping me out with ‘Oh, what was this? What was this look?’ We break it down together,” Good-Jones said. “So it's a brotherhood, man. It's a collaborative unit.” Quinn has said he doesn’t expect Allegretti to be out much longer. And even though the seven-year veteran started just one game at center for Washington last season, his teammates, the coaching staff and front office have raved about him. “What stands out to me with Nick is just his leadership, his command, his confidence, the way the guys gravitate to and listen to him,” general manager Adam Peters said at a press conference before camp. “And so that's a big part of it. Knowing what to do, knowing where to go, knowing where to direct the guys, just the calling up in the huddle — it's a big deal.”

stories.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 7)
stories.author: Rebecca Ritzel
stories.summary: The grand opening of Olney Theatre’s expansion, a sitcom-inspired dance party, and a canine competition at the Wharf.
stories.content: Olney Theatre. Photo by Kiati Plooks Photography Thursday “ Woody Guthrie’s American Song ,” Theatre Alliance at Wharf Park Water St. SW, 7:15 p.m., pay what you can One of D.C.’s buzziest theater companies opens a three-month, citywide festival of performances and exhibits celebrating “America's most enduring folk poet and social agitator.” Expect more than a “This Land Is Your Land” sing-along at this outdoor musical revue that addresses America’s turbulent social climate through the lens of Guthrie’s writings and songs. Recommended for fans of Bob Dylan, Pete Seeger and Rhiannon Giddens. Rip! Tear! Collage Exhibit at Eye Street Gallery I St. SE, 6 p.m. free The D.C. Commission on the Arts and Humanities picked “Collage as Critique” as the theme for its annual juried show, which awards grants to artists whose work is chosen for display. More than 20 local artists have work in the exhibit, and three of them will be on hand to lead a workshop on shredding, tearing and ripping up paper, then turning the scraps into art. More to explore: “Apollo 13” blasts off at the Library of Congress’ Movies on the Lawn. Friday “Tosca” at Wolf Trap Trap Road, Vienna, Va., 8 p.m., $39 to $ The Washington National Opera Orchestra — a beleaguered group of veteran musicians who were recently kicked out of the Kennedy Center — will accompany up-and-coming singers on the Wolf Trap stage. The summer company produces one major opera each year, and this season it’s Puccini’s classic about an artist, his muse and the religious zealot police chief out to thwart their star-crossed romance. Husband-and-wife team Ryan and Tonya McKinny, who have vocally opposed President Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover, will direct the production and provide subtext, while José Luis Gómez conducts. “SUNNY RAVE” at the Howard Theatre T St., 10 p.m., $30 New York and Toronto may have “Heated Rivalry” parody musicals, but D.C. has [ checks notes ] a late-night “Always Sunny in Philadelphia” dance party? Yep. That’s a thing. The Philadelphia-based “dj pressed” will spin tunes accompanied by clips from the long-running FX comedy at the Howard Theatre. Come dressed as Mac, Dee or Danny DeVito. More to explore: Country singer Jordan Davis performs a free show for ticketholders after the Nationals game. Saturday Chesapeake DogDocks at The Wharf District Square SW, 10:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., free Come watch Prince, Banana and their canine frenemies play fetch in a 40-foot pool installed outside The Anthem. Billed as the mid-Atlantic’s premiere “aquatic dog performance” club, the Chesapeake DockDogs are hosting their first District competition surrounded by bougie people drinking beer. (Cerveza Pacifico and Tito’s “Vodka for Dog People” are the event sponsors.) Think your pooch might have what it takes to take the big leap next year? The club is organizing a “Youth Day” introductory session in Marriottsville, Md., on Aug. 15, minus the pool and booze. Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington 14th St. S, Arlington, Va., 2:30 to 4 p.m., free Bring your own needles or pick up a free pair at this informal gathering hosted by the Crochet Cart Project. Participants will each contribute a square for a community blanket. That may sound more wholesome than trad-wife Instagram, but the group also aims to spread the joy of crocheting to all communities and help people express “creativity through fibre art.” More to explore: Swing Fling dance convention at the Dulles Hyatt Regency; Sneaker Con at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center. Sunday Summerfest Open House at Olney Theatre Olney-Sandy Spring Road, Olney, Md., 11:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., free Families in the Northern suburbs (and anyone else who loves theater and has a car) are likely to love the grand opening of Olney Theatre Center’s multimillion-dollar expansion project. After two years of construction, the 88-year-old Montgomery County theater has a new lobby, studios and education spaces. More than two-dozen free shows, tours and workshops are on the schedule, while food trucks and a used costume shop are open all day. A gala performance featuring “Younger” star and Tony-winner Sutton Foster caps off the celebration, but tickets have long been sold out. Mandoleers at Lyon Park Community Center N. Fillmore Street, Arlington, Va., 5 p.m., free Since , the Mandoleers have been making music together on instruments that resemble miniature guitars. The ensemble holds a three-day intensive each summer, open to anyone who plays the mandolin, mandola, mandocello, classical guitar or upright bass. It’s unclear how exactly this merry band of musicians will celebrate the Declaration of Independence, but the event culminates with a free community concert called, “America at : We the People, All of Us.” Ernesto Parets conducts. More to explore: Final weekend to see the critically hailed “American Aspirations” exhibit at the Smithsonian Institution Building.

stories.title: The Nationals’ Confusing Trade Deadline
stories.author: Jesse Dougherty
stories.summary: Monday’s trade of pitcher Foster Griffin capped a busy deadline for the Nats, and left fans wondering where the team is headed.
stories.content: The Nationals traded all-star pitcher Foster Griffin as part of their deadline dealing. Nick Wass/AP “Isn’t this trade deadline kind of a mindfuck?” That's how a member of the Nationals’ front office put it to me in late July, a week before Monday’s deadline passed. The Nats weren’t supposed to be so competitive this season — if competitive at all — meaning the decision to buy or sell was expected to be fairly easy, at least up to the tough choice of whether to deal shortstop CJ Abrams. But then they kept winning a tad more than they lost, mostly because of their league-best offense (and very much in spite of their abysmal bullpen). And so somewhere along the line, as a reaction to the team’s surprising record, explosive lineup and obvious lack of pitching, the decision to buy or sell morphed into figuring out the best way to do some of both, which seemed like a shift from what was once a stubborn plan to just use to prepare for the future, not to actually invest any more in … . “Yeah,” I replied, “mindfuck feels right.” Now, on the other side of the deadline, the hybrid approach certainly brought more selling for the future than buying for the present. That was expected, too, especially after the Nats lost five in a row to end last week, which dropped them to 4 ½ back for the National League’s final wild-card spot, now 5 ½ after they lost their sixth straight Monday night. There was, then, a well-reasoned baseball case for most of what the Nationals did in the last 10 days, if not all of it. We’ll get to that in a minute here. But there’s also well-earned frustration for fans who are tired of rooting for a team that believes the best path forward is to trade some of its best players, even when it’s on the outer edge of the playoff race. Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, kept saying Monday evening that he still believes in this club, that it still has an “it factor,” that it could still “go on a heater here soon and put us right back in the mix,” which is why he felt a responsibility to improve the current bullpen while also subtracting from the lineup and a paper-thin starting rotation. Which begged the question of how, if he truly believes in the Nats’ chances of making a run, he justifies trading their most reliable starter, Foster Griffin, for four unproven pitchers. Which, once again, comes down to the heavy tension between now and later while trying to build a sustainable winner. Which gets even more complicated with an ownership group that hasn’t spent anywhere close to real money in free agency — or with pre-free-agency extensions — since . “It's one of the hardest things about my job, balancing the here and now with the future,” Toboni said. “I think every baseball fan that's really, really into it understands it. I think if they're asked, in practice, how do you do that … it becomes a lot more challenging, you know what I mean?” Here are some snippets of how he explained it from there: “ … And so what I try to do is just be real with everyone. Like: ‘Hey, if the goal here is to be good for a long period of time, you only have so many opportunities to make this foundation really strong.’ … “ … but if we pass up those opportunities to create this really strong foundation — live with me for a second on this metaphor — basically we'll be moving into the house without the foundation being totally strong. And it might turn out that two, three years down the line, we might have to move out of the house because the foundation is cracking …” “ … but at the same time, yeah, just speaking from the heart, I believe in the guys in the locker room and I believe in what they can do. And I can see how it would be received as: ‘Hey, you're telling me you believe in this team but then you just shipped out, you know, one of our better pitchers.’ I get that. What I would say is basically it's probably my brain and heart at odds, too. …” “ … we want to make sure this is really stable while at the same time, yeah, when I say that, I hope when Woody hears it or CJ hears it or whoever hears it — Blake — they sense that it's genuine.” Toboni is aware that the fan base is not his only audience, that he has to sell the clubhouse on the long view, too. Woody is James Wood, a 23-year-old who is already one of the best hitters in the sport. CJ is CJ Abrams, the star shortstop who the Nats held onto through the deadline, maintaining an extremely high bar to move him. Blake is Blake Butera, the team’s first-year manager. Over the last week and a half, they’ve said goodbye to Curtis Mead, who had an . on-base-plus-slugging percentage, Luis García Jr., who led the National League in slugging percentage, and Griffin, who made the NL’s All-Star team with a 2.77 ERA at the break. On Monday night, the Nats lost because — wait for it — their pen couldn’t hold a late lead. Wood left after feeling discomfort in his left oblique. The vibes are turning fast. Soon, then, there could be more time to look ahead and analyze what the Nats received for Mead, García and Griffin. The total haul, factoring in a minor league trade that sent outfielder Christian Franklin to the Orioles, included 10 players, nine of them pitchers. The deals included … Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed starter Connelly Early García to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers: Jack Cebert, a starter, plus Ben Grable, Yovanny Cruz and Jake Bird Griffin to the Guardians for left-handed pitchers Will Dion and Josh Hartle; right-handed pitcher Kendeglys Virguez; and outfielder Nick Mitchell And Franklin to the Orioles for right-handed pitcher Joe Glassey As for immediate help, Toboni listed Early, Cruz and Dion as pitchers who could contribute in August and September. Early is working his way back from the injured list, where he landed in July because of elbow pain. Cruz, a flamethrower, is already in the majors. Dion, a soft thrower who gets a lot of chase, appeared in 12 games for the Guardians this year. Bird, 30, has career relief appearances between the Rockies and Yankees. He could also chip in soon as a marginal improvement over one of the Nats’ low-leverage arms. The Mead-Early trade was probably the best example of dealing for now and later, as the Nationals traded from a clear strength (hitting) for five-and-a-half years of a big league starter that Toboni drafted while working in Boston. The García and Griffin trades, while including major league-ready relievers, seemed more focused on stockpiling minor league arms to mold, which should give the Nats a shot at better pitching depth in upcoming years. For Griffin, who is a two-month rental for Cleveland, the Nationals only received one player (Hartle) in the Guardians’ top 25 prospects, at least according to MLB Pipeline. Virguez is already a reliever at 22. With any trade of this nature, the Nats are betting on their player development system. Notably, none of Mead, Griffin or García were penciled in as major contributors to start the year. They signed Griffin to a one-year deal out of Japan, which also means he will be a free agent this fall. Mead was adrift before the season, just released by the White Sox, then had a breakout season under the Nats’ new coaching staff. Much like Mead, García unlocked much more power by improving his pitch selection and pulling the ball in the air more. Through the dispassionate lens of logical roster building, flipping each of them now, at what could be the height of their value, made perfect sense. But for the past four summers, Nats fans have been told to turn away from a shoddy product because there’s a new reliever in the minors with an intriguing fastball. Then, it was Jarlin Susana. Now, it’s Ben Grable, plugged right into an all-too-familiar mind trick of ignoring what you can see to believe in what you can’t just yet. Two things can be true, as Toboni said Monday when describing the conflict between his head and heart: His front office, new to the job, deserves the opportunity to build a foundation without the burden of what happened before they arrived. And yet, after four months of competitive baseball, after what felt like the first warm days of a long overdue spring, it’s fair for D.C. to wonder when this kind of deadline selling will stop. Maybe next July.

stories.title: Won't You Be My Neighborhood Commissioner?
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: A voter casts a ballot at Calvary Episcopal Church in Northeast on primary election day in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 16, . Tom Williams/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Advisory neighborhood commissioners, Montgomery County schools and a NYC-DC crossover. THE LATEST No one is on the ballot for a good chunk of the District’s advisory neighborhood commissioner positions ahead of tomorrow’s nomination deadline . Of ANC positions, 58 had no listed candidates as of Saturday . Though the unpaid position isn’t the flashiest in D.C. politics, ANC commissioners are vital neighborhood voices, advising the government on community issues like local zoning decisions. Some, including Mayor Muriel Bowser , go on to higher office. “I'm not concerned about the vacancies that are on the nominating list, and I probably wouldn't be concerned until after the deadline,” Kent Boese , head of D.C.’s ANC office, told NOTUS. There are fewer vacancies this cycle than there were two years ago , Boese said, and many candidates file right before the deadline or launch write-in campaigns closer to November. The vacancies are an opportunity for advocacy groups like the Washington Area Bicyclist Association. The nonpartisan nonprofit circulated an email this week urging members in empty districts to apply. “We do want to encourage the District to create safe transportation infrastructure, including bike lanes, bus priority projects, and working with the ANCs is a great way to do it,” Seth Grimes , an organizer with WABA, told NOTUS. “Many times vacancies are hard to fill. There are no candidates, and so we thought, well, why not use our database and reach out to people?” WABA has filled nine vacant ANC spots with its members since March , Grimes said. FROM THE DISTRICT President Donald Trump is considering removing U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro from her post, CNN reports . Pirro, a longtime Trump ally, recently angered the president when her office dismissed all charges against David Hearn , the Olympic canoeist who was arrested on suspicion of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool. Pirro’s office said the damage was more likely due to a botched job by the contractor, not widespread vandalism as Trump has repeatedly claimed. On Monday, Trump said Pirro “ folded like an umbrella. ” FROM VIRGINIA Amazon wants to build four data centers on George Washington University’s Ashburn campus, which the company bought this year for $ million, the Loudoun Times-Mirror reports . Amazon got its application in ahead of a fall meeting in which Loudoun County officials will weigh a data center moratorium as they consider how to regulate the industry. FROM MARYLAND Montgomery County redrew its public school boundaries this spring, but the debate didn’t end there. Some parents are suing, saying the plan illegally closes one of the county’s most prestigious high schools, Jeff Barker writes for NOTUS . FROM YOUR FEED tweet attempting to map New York City boroughs onto the DMV made the rounds over the weekend. Our team has some thoughts: “It is genuinely hard to think of a single thing College Park, Maryland, has in common with the Upper West Side. And I say that as a proud Maryland alum.” — Michael Errigo, deputy editor “Comparing Capitol Hill to New Jersey is a choice.” — Shamira Muhammad, D.C. reporter "This is pretty perfect social media content: It plays on D.C.'s occasional insecurities of not being NYC, it makes sweeping generalizations about D.C.'s neighborhoods that miss loads of local nuance, and, despite my best efforts not to, I end up arguing with people about it." — Martin Austermuhle, D.C. reporter WHAT YOU GET FOR $ , Kenyon St Real Estate 2 ( , AR: 1.50) Listed for $ , , this two-bedroom, two-bathroom home features solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and an open-concept living space. Guess where this listing is sold: Maryland Virginia D.C. We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right. SPORTS The MLB trade deadline has officially passed, and the Nats turned out to be both buyers and sellers. After adding an arm last week, Washington made three trades in the 24 hours before Monday’s 6 p.m. deadline. They sent out infielder Luis García Jr., pitcher Foster Griffin and outfielder Christian Franklin. In return they got back eight more pitchers, some of whom are expected to contribute right away. NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty broke down the Garcia deal, calling it both strategically sound and emotionally fraught for fans. Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders’ offensive struggles may have been greatly exaggerated. On Monday in Ashburn, Jayden Daniels got the unit rolling. He completed multiple impressive touchdown passes, and the offensive line held up much better than it did last week. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Real estate photo by Derek & Vee. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was A) D.C. A special shout-out to Carolynn Race, who answered first.

stories.title: Montgomery County Approved New School Boundaries. Parents Won’t Let It End There.
stories.author: Jeff Barker
stories.summary: Some residents are pursuing a legal challenge to the planned closure of the highly rated Wootton High School.
stories.content: Rockville Council member Adam Van Grack. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS A smattering of “Save Wootton” and “It’s Not Over!” yard signs dot neighborhoods surrounding the Rockville, Maryland, high school whose name and student body are due to be transferred in -28 to a new building several miles away. With the Montgomery County Board of Education having approved the shift last spring, the red, white and blue signs — matching the colors of Thomas S. Wootton High School — remain as a defiant statement by residents, some of whom are pursuing a legal challenge to plans they say would illegally close the highly rated, half-century-old school in the Washington suburbs. “It’s such a necessity,” said Rockville Council member Adam Van Grack, whose son attends Wootton. “It’s not a question of if it’s going to be a permanent school again, the only question is when.” A dozen miles away, similar yard signs remain in the neighborhood around the sprawling Silver Spring International Middle School, which area residents fear isn’t in the county’s future plans. “The school gives us an opportunity to greet one another. It gives us a sense of community," said Angie Kronenberg, an attorney who, during the campaign's busiest periods, devoted as many as 30 to 40 hours a week organizing efforts to preserve the school, which is adjacent to Silver Spring’s downtown and home to sought-after Spanish and French immersion programs. Montgomery County, home to Maryland’s largest public school system, completed sweeping boundary studies in March that upended the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International, and redrew boundaries for other schools to account for enrollment shifts, school building conditions and other factors. But the school assignment debates never quite seem over, and in the case of Wootton, parents and community members have lodged complaints over everything from deteriorating building conditions to property values. Boundary shifts stir powerful protective instincts, said Sarah Asson, a senior researcher at the nonprofit research group Education Northwest, often turning parents into activists fighting for what they view as their children's best interests. “These rezonings touch two of the most important things for parents -– their kids’ education and their communities,” Asson said. While parents typically frame their objections around their children's education and their communities, issues regarding image and status are often at play as well, said Genevieve Siegel-Hawley, a professor in Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Education. “There is a lot of anxiety — status anxiety — about securing their kids’ futures through education,” Siegel-Hawley said. DC0A5520 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Real estate values can also be an important, if less openly acknowledged, subtext. Homes assigned to highly regarded schools often command a premium, and some residents worry boundary changes will diminish their property values. Wootton, which has about 1, students, is one of the county’s prestigious, so-called “W” schools along with high-achieving Walt Whitman, Walter Johnson and Winston Churchill. It is not uncommon for families in the more diverse eastern portion of the county, including Silver Spring and Wheaton, to move to the western part so their kids can attend a “W” or the highly rated Bethesda-Chevy Chase High School. “For 20-some years if I had a property in the Wootton school district, I hardly had to say anything about the house. I just said ‘Wootton,’ and it had this magnetic attraction for buyers,” said Kevin Grolig, a real estate agent in the county. If plans to move Wootton remain intact, Grolig estimates that values of homes within walking distance of the school’s current location could drop 15% or more. Wootton remains open for now. An oversized “Wootton Strong” banner hangs from the back of the football field bleachers. But the school, whose former students include actor Thomas Jane, NFL player Trevon Diggs and several members of the rock band O.A.R., was built in and has issues with leaking ceilings, heating and cooling units and mice. On March 26, the county Board of Education voted 7-1 to approve moving Wootton to a new school in Gaithersburg for the -28 school year. Thomas Taylor, the superintendent of Montgomery County Public schools, said a single school could efficiently handle current enrollment and that the old Wootton would be employed as a “holding school” for when other schools are undergoing construction. At the meeting, parents held signs reading “Don’t Close Wootton” and “Vote No,” and some parents chanted “shame” when the vote was complete. “This is not a closure of Thomas S. Wootton High School — this is a move of the school to a new building,” said a Montgomery County Public Schools announcement in February explaining the plan. It said Wootton students “will transition to a state-of-the-art facility” and that the system was responding “to updated enrollment data showing needs can be met more efficiently with the current number of schools.” But critics said importing the school’s name, colors and “Patriots” mascot to a new building won’t make it the real Wootton, but rather a weird facsimile. DC0A5489 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) In April, a nonprofit group composed of Wootton parents, alumni and others filed an administrative appeal with the Maryland State Board of Education challenging the March decision. “At the heart of the appeal is a straightforward question: Can a school board avoid Maryland’s statutory school closure requirements by characterizing a school closure as a ‘relocation?’” the group said in a prepared statement. The case is pending. Montgomery County Public Schools said it could not comment on any litigation. The school system declined to make Taylor available for an interview or answer NOTUS’ questions about possible scenarios for the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International. Rather, Montgomery County Public Schools emailed a statement about the new two-year, elementary and middle school boundary study. The statement said the study will address “system-wide facility capacity, optimize building utilization and evaluate potential school closures or consolidations" with community input. Last year, the county Board of Education declined to pursue Taylor’s recommendation to convert Silver Spring International, whose buildings are in deteriorating condition, into a holding school. While the school wasn’t targeted for closure in the March vote, many parents say the board’s decision to reduce its number of feeder elementary schools has placed the school on an uncertain path because its enrollment will decline. Proponents of maintaining Silver Spring International and Wootton often raise concerns that are difficult to quantify. Some speak nostalgically of the quiet ritual of children being close enough to walk to their neighborhood schools. “That was the number one thing parents were saying to me: ‘Our kids can still walk to school, right?’” said Kronenberg, who helps lead a Silver Spring group called “Save Our Schools.” “We believe our school is still at risk,” Kronenberg said. "We have to keep at it."

stories.title: What $800K Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
stories.content: Derek & Vee A penthouse condo in Columbia Heights. A spacious townhouse in North Bethesda. A cozy and convenient house in Arlington. Here’s what $ , gets you in the District, Maryland and Virginia. (Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com .) D.C. Untitled The Listing: Kenyon St. NW #3 The Price: $ , The Specifics: This two-bedroom, two-bathroom penthouse condo comes in at just over 1, square feet, and features a private rooftop deck in addition to parking spaces for two cars. The home also includes a spacious primary bedroom with a spa-like bath, walk-in shower and dual vanities, according to the listing. The real estate agent also highlights the home’s solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and open-concept living. The Neighborhood: This home is in the heart of Columbia Heights, within a short walk to the neighborhood’s Metro station with access to the Green and Yellow lines. Also nearby are a number of fitness studios and grocery stores, in addition to popular bars and restaurants like Wonderland Ballroom and St. Vincent Wine. The neighborhood itself is densely populated and known for its historic row houses and cultural diversity. Maryland Untitled The Listing: Gloxinia Drive, Rockville The Price: $ , The Specifics: This spacious townhome comes in around 2, square feet, with the real estate agent describing it as “a rare blend of timeless character, effortless open-concept living, and modern peace of mind.” The three-bedroom, five-bathroom home has only had two previous owners, and features a secluded private courtyard. Recent updates in the home include a new roof, new HVAC and new doors, according to the listing. The Neighborhood: The home is in North Bethesda, and is 10-minute drive from the Bethesda Trolley Trail and just five minutes from Pike & Rose, a shopping and entertainment area featuring restaurants, a movie theater and live music venues. It’s also a short drive from the North Bethesda Metro station, with access to D.C. via the Red Line. Virginia Untitled The Listing: 6th St. S., Arlington The Price: $ , The Specifics: This home offers just over 1, square feet of room with three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. The lower level features hardwood floors, while the upper level is carpeted. The basement is unfinished, making it the perfect spot for storage or a workshop. The shaded and spacious backyard features raised gardening beds and a storage shed. The Neighborhood: This Arlington home is located in the Alcova Heights neighborhood, which is known for its proximity to Columbia Pike, connecting Northern Virginia to D.C for a commute the real estate agent describes as “effortless.” The home is also conveniently close to Alcova Heights Park, shopping centers and restaurants.

stories.title: So Long, Luis García Jr. (And Hello to Four New Arms.)
stories.author: Jesse Dougherty
stories.summary: On Sunday, the Nats traded García, their longest-tenured player, to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers.
stories.content: The Nationals have traded first baseman Luis Garcia Jr. to the Yankees. David Zalubowski/AP Photo If every trade is a peek inside a front office’s collective brain, the Nationals’ latest deal — sending Luis García Jr. to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers on Sunday — only furthers what we’d already learned about the new group running the team: They view pitching as a real organizational weakness and are willing to trade controllable bats to change that. And rather than always hunting one or two high-upside prospects in trades, they’re up for swapping established talent for a handful players, which reads as having high confidence in their development process. In this case, the big haul included Jack Cebert, Ben Grable, Yovanny Cruz and Jake Bird. None of them ranked in the Yankees’ top 10 prospects on Baseball America, which slotted Cebert at No. 11, Grable at No. 19 and Cruz at No. 24. Of the four, Cebert is the only starter, a 24-year-old who’s dominated AA in recent weeks. Grable, also 24 and in AA, has an intriguing fastball that’s generated a lot of in-zone whiffs in the minors. Cruz, a 26-year-old with four big league appearances, can run his four-seamer into the triple digits. Bird, 30, has made relief appearances between the Yankees and Rockies and never finished a season with an ERA better than 4.33. Unlike the others, he is no longer a prospect. Each has their flaws, of course, which is why they were part of a four-player package for a high-end platoon player. But the head says this is a definite win for the Nats, especially given their need for pitching — and especially given that García, 26, was treading water before this season and then turned into a valuable trading chip. Instead of cutting him loose, Paul Toboni, the club’s first-year president of baseball operations, made him a full-time first baseman who mostly played against righties. The Yankees, first in the American League wild-card standings, will almost certainly use him in a platoon, too. In plate appearances, García has already set a career high with 23 homers, all but three of them against righties. He also has the best slugging percentage (. ) in the National League. And he’s under team control for another season beyond . So if you’re a Nationals fan, it may feel a bit more complicated for the heart. Signed out of the Dominican Republic in , García was the team’s longest-tenured player, the last on-field link to the best era in the franchise’s short history. Trading him now, as the team is finally on a jagged upswing, can be both strategically sound and emotionally fraught. For five summers, the team has often traded away its most recognizable players, leaving the city starved for reliable connection points. At some point, in theory, the Nats’ short-term ambitions might outweigh the benefits of selling high on a player like García to improve future rosters. That point just isn’t this week. The trade deadline is 6 p.m. Monday. For the last couple months, ever since the Nats’ strong start proved more than a statistical oddity, Toboni has been saying that team performance could affect his deadline approach. Or put another way: If the Nationals kept winning, Toboni seemed willing to bend his long view to the present. At the start of last week, with five games to the deadline, the Nats were 55-53, smack in the middle of the wild-card race. Then they lost five in a row, dropping to 4½ games out of the final wild-card spot with four teams in front of them. Still, despite a crowded, fragile path to the playoffs, Toboni has seemingly sold and bought at the same time. For the Nationals’ first trade of the deadline season, they sent infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, who is on the injured list but could return this month. With the package for García, both Cruz and Bird could immediately contribute to a bullpen that has blown 27 saves. That doesn’t mean the present was the main focus for either of those deals. It does, however, show the front office is interested in addressing short- and long-term needs this summer (and capable of trying both within the same transaction, results pending). Bird was optioned to AAA after the deal was completed Sunday, as was right-handed reliever Riley Cornelio. That indicates that Cruz could join the team ahead of a series opener in Philadelphia on Monday night. The Nats will have to fill García’s and Cornelio’s spots, at a minimum, since they could also make more trades. Abimelec Ortiz, acquired in the five-player return for MacKenzie Gore last winter, is the logical replacement for García, a left-handed first baseman with a compelling offensive profile. If the Nats use him just like García, he’ll pair with Andrés Chaparro in a platoon at first. The offense, still ranked first in runs scored by a good margin, will need some new energy after losing two players (García and Mead) with an OPS over . . And as for what the Nats could do before the deadline, Foster Griffin, their all-star starting pitcher, has attracted a lot of interest. So has shortstop CJ Abrams, though the chances of him moving are far, far lower than the Nationals flipping Griffin for future parts, according to multiple people familiar with the team’s thinking. The market for starting pitchers has thinned in recent days, with Tarik Skubal (Tigers to Dodgers), Luis Castillo (Mariners to White Sox), Freddy Peralta (Mets to Rays) and Kevin Gausman (Blue Jays to Cubs) all off the board. Broadly, those deals have favored the buyers, though a scarcity of front-line arms could now work in the Nationals’ favor. Then D.C. will make a full assessment of Toboni’s first deadline after 6 p.m.

stories.title: A Big, Beautiful Parking Garage
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: A sign of Washington Dulles International Airport station is seen during the opening of new Silver Line Extension at Washington Dulles International Airport, in Chantilly, Va., Nov. 15, . Jose Luis Magana/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Dulles’ new parking deck, Trump’s golden horses and fans at Commanders training camp. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST One of the D.C. area’s biggest attractions may soon be a parking garage. As part of his sweeping $22.5 billion overhaul of Dulles International Airport, President Donald Trump says a new parking deck will be built in front of the historic main terminal with enough space for 32, cars. “It’ll be the largest garage in the world,” he said last week. “It will be beautiful.” What’s unclear is whether Dulles even needs that much parking. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports that a master plan for the airport drawn up by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which manages Dulles, found that the existing 22, parking spots would suffice until at least . But just to be on the safe side, the authority had drawn up plans for a new parking deck — with one-fifth the capacity of what Trump is pledging. There are also unanswered questions about the sheer physical scale of Trump’s garage. As proposed, it could stand some 15 stories tall, towering over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen. With a garage that big, there’s likely to be “all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety,” said local parking expert Bill Boyle . “There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.” FROM THE DISTRICT GoldHorses_Grid.jpg ( , AR: 2.05) Trump’s golden horses have (finally) arrived. In May, NOTUS’ Anna Kramer reported that the National Park Service was re-gilding the four massive horse statues near the Lincoln Memorial with an unusually thick layer of 23.75-karat gold, to the tune of 5 million taxpayer dollars. The Park Service wanted the horses (known as the Arts of War and Arts of Peace) finished in time for the July Fourth festivities, calling it an “immovable deadline” in their justification for handing out a rushed, no-bid contract this spring. But the rush was for naught: Two of the horses were just unveiled last week, and two more are still covered up. The city’s July Fourth crowds got nothing more than some scaffolding and drapes. A high-level aide to D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser is parting ways with the city, marking the first big departure in the waning months of the mayor’s time in office. Lindsey Parker , who joined Bowser’s administration more than a ago and rose to chief of staff, will next take the reins of the Maryland Stadium Authority. It’s a logical move: Parker’s last role in D.C. government was as senior adviser for the Commanders stadium project. A Republican senator wants more patriotism in D.C. schools. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida) has introduced a bill that would require that the U.S. flag be displayed in every classroom in D.C. schools, and mandate that students recite the Pledge of Allegiance at the start of every day. (Parents would be allowed to opt their children out.) Moody said the bill would help “restore pride in our nation” and fight an “outrageous curriculum” that includes lessons on LGBTQ+ history. Critics say this is another unnecessary intrusion into the city’s affairs. Organizers of the popular Cherry Blossom 10-Miler recently warned runners that, starting next year, the race’s “most memorable sections” could be affected or even eliminated by Trump’s planned construction in Memorial Circle and around East Potomac Park. Preservationists are mounting their latest campaign to stop a Trump-led remake of a D.C. building, seeking an injunction to stop the administration from painting the Eisenhower Executive Office Building white, NBC4 reports . TRIVIA In which jurisdiction can you get married without an officiant? D.C. Maryland Virginia Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter. SPORTS Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson was in Ashburn on Saturday for the first of 11 Commanders practices open to fans. Thousands showed up, with some arriving hours ahead of the 8:30 a.m. start time. The session featured a lot of fan service, including a fun segment where the offensive linemen ran pass routes. But the biggest reaction of the day came during the appearances of Hall of Famers Darrell Green and John Riggins, who will have new roles with the franchise this season. The WNBA trade deadline has come and gone , with the Mystics standing pat. Washington will be leaning on the second-youngest roster in league history as it makes a playoff push. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photos by Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS.

stories.title: Let’s Talk About the Massive Parking Garage Trump Wants to Build at Dulles
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle
stories.summary: The 32, -spot deck would surpass both existing parking capacity and what airport officials have said is needed.
stories.content: President Donald Trump unveiled plans to build a parking garage with space for 32, cars at Dulles International Airport. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP It won’t exactly be the eighth wonder of the world, but it will be big — like, Guinness World Records big. That’s what President Donald Trump promised last week when he unveiled plans to build a parking garage with space for 32, cars as part of his sweeping $22.5 billion renovation of Dulles International Airport. “We’re building a massive … parking garage that will be right next to the terminal,” he said as he sat in front of a model of the new airport splayed across the top of the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “It’ll be the largest garage in the world. Thirty-two thousand is big. It will be beautiful.” The new parking deck got less attention than Trump’s announcement that the long-maligned mobile lounges that have shuttled passengers around Dulles since it opened in will be retired. But the detail does speak to many travelers’ annoyances with parking at Dulles, most of which is in satellite lots that require a shuttle to get to and from the main terminal. Still, the big, beautiful deck-to-be stands as one of the Dulles renovation’s most surprising elements, since it would increase the airport’s parking capacity beyond what existing plans say is necessary, would add significant construction and airport operation challenges and would likely tower over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen. Dulles currently has just over 22, parking spots for travelers, half of them in the distant economy lots. (This reporter almost lost track of their car in one of those lots.) While parking capacity fluctuates during the year (and can be viewed on a daily basis here ), the Dulles Master Plan finalized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority in July predicted that the existing number of parking spots available at the airport would suffice until at least . The plan noted that parking demand can fluctuate based on a number of factors, including “rises in gasoline prices could result in the reduced use of private vehicles.” (Gas prices have risen in the U.S. due in part to the ongoing conflict in Iran.) Still, the authority has already started planning to increase capacity to more than 28, spots, most of which would come through the construction of a new parking deck in front of the main terminal building where a surface lot now exists. That three-story deck — to be built between and — would fit 6, cars. During his presentation, Trump seemed to be unaware of those plans. “We have an empty site right directly across the street that nobody wanted to tinker with, which is crazy,” he said. His proposed parking deck — which would go in that same location — would accommodate five times as many cars. But few details exist: The deck wasn’t included in any of the renderings of the new airport that were put out by MWAA and the U.S. Department of Transportation (in fact, the main rendering kept the existing surface lot), and neither agency responded to specific questions about it from NOTUS. The proposal has drawn skeptical reactions from some parking experts, including Bill Boyle, who owns a parking company in D.C. and runs the Washington Parking Association, a trade group. “I looked up the biggest terminal garages in the U.S.,” he told NOTUS. “One is in Seattle and has 13, spots, and the other is in Detroit and has 11, . This would be two-and-half times bigger than those two. That creates all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety. There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.” The world’s biggest parking lot is outside the West Edmonston Mall in Canada; it fits 20, cars in surface lots. Without specifics, it’s impossible to know the actual physical scale of the proposed parking deck. But if MWAA kept to Trump’s pledge that most of it would be above-ground — “People don’t like down underneath,” he said — it could reach up to 15 stories. That would make the parking deck taller than the main terminal, which tops out at 65 feet. It would also likely block most views of the historic terminal itself for passengers arriving by Metro or car, a concern that MWAA was already aware of with its plan for a three-story parking deck in front of the terminal. The master plan says it would address viewshed concerns by raising Saarinen Circle — a traffic circle in front of the terminal — “approximately 11 to 15 feet” above where it is now. Boyle also said that building a record-breaking parking deck while the airport remains in operation would be challenging. “When you build it you’ll have to have cranes, materials and hauling routes,” he said. “You’re building an enormous garage in a constrained space and doing it while everything is functioning around it, and I don’t see anyone addressing that problem.” It’s also unclear what such a parking deck would cost. A February report from the UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies estimated that each above-ground spot in a parking deck in and around Washington, D.C. can cost $29, to build. While that’s below the national average of $52, , it would also mean that Trump’s proposed 32, parking spots could cost more than $ million. (And that price tag would go up if any levels were underground; the UCLA report says that underground spots can cost $40, a piece to construct.) Since November , there has been an alternative for getting to and from Dulles: Metro. The Silver Line station Dulles sees anywhere from 1, to 4, entries per day, depending on the time of year. “Why should we build the world's largest parking garage in the world on an airport we just invested $6B to connect to Metro?” tweeted Virginia Democratic Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell. But Trump has touted the proximity and convenience of his new parking deck. “People will literally be able to park their car and walk 15 yards and be in the terminal,” he said. “It will be a parking garage the likes of which no one has even seen before!” offered one commenter on Reddit, in what could be seen as either a high compliment or a sarcastic criticism.

stories.title: Past Due
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Michael Brice-Saddler, Zara Norman
stories.content: Quarterback Jayden Daniels works out on Day 2 of the Washington Commanders' training camp Thursday. John McDonnell/AP Photo Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: D.C.’s worst landlord, a $ million Metro expansion and the legendary Venus Williams. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST D.C.’s worst landlord is its housing authority. Of all city landlords with unabated violations, DCHA is far and away the biggest offender, with more than 2, violations and more than $2.2 million in associated fines, NOTUS’ Zara Norman reports . “It does not surprise me,” said Megan Browder , a director with Legal Aid D.C. “I think it is partially the size of the portfolio and also a systematic disregard for their mission.” D.C.’s Department of Buildings cannot collect fines from DCHA like it can from other landlords. The agency is responsible for policing its own payments. The housing authority is not the only proprietor with a long list of unresolved violations: More than local landlords owe the city more than $ , each. To better resolve cases, the DOB is shifting its strategy: It’s starting to settle with landlords before heading to adjudication, allowing them to avoid fines if they make immediate fixes. “For me it’s really concerning,” Browder told NOTUS. “I think it just lessens the accountability for landlords to say, ‘Hey, you can kind of just limp along and settle with DOB without any meaningful corrective action.’” DEEP DIVE Fort Myer Construction — a D.C. road-paving titan since — has agreed to settle a lawsuit with Attorney General Brian Schwalb that alleged nearly a of illegal water pollution at the company’s Ward 5 facility. On paper, the $ , penalty might seem like a slap on the wrist. City records show that D.C. has paid Fort Myer more than $1 billion through infrastructure and paving contracts over the past , including more than $ million since the lawsuit was filed in October . But Schwalb’s office says the real victory is the settlement’s operational requirements. Under a three-year consent order announced today, Fort Myer must overhaul its equipment, fix drainage infrastructure and submit to monthly water-quality testing to stop the alleged petroleum and industrial runoff from reaching city waterways. In a statement, Schwalb said the agreement ensures that Fort Myer will make “much-needed and long overdue changes to its equipment and business practices to protect the District, our environment and our residents moving forward.” FROM THE DISTRICT All aboard for the Commanders stadium. Metro has signed a pair of agreements with D.C. to start working on two projects that will be critical for getting fans to and from the new stadium when it opens in . The first is a $ million expansion of the Stadium-Armory station. The second is a new bus rapid transit line — dubbed the Gold Line — that will run from Union Station to the stadium along H Street and Benning Road Northeast. There are only about 8, parking spots planned for the new stadium, so city and team officials are pressing to increase mass transit options. D.C. Public Schools officials told parents Wednesday that sensitive student information, such as names and home addresses, may have been exposed in a data breach, NBC4 reports . A major D.C. law firm’s political action committee told federal regulators that a thief stole multiple political contribution checks from mailboxes in Cleveland Park last year, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports . The embattled chairman of the D.C. Public Service Commission , which regulates utilities including Pepco and Washington Gas, says he is resigning in August . Emile Thompson ’s decision comes ahead of what could have been a contentious fall, especially as the commission has felt the heat over rising electric and gas bills. “Rising energy prices are not attributable to any one agency, group or thing,” Thompson emphasized in his resignation statement. METRO MOMENTS Leyla Adali’s tweet asking locals to share their “worst day in D.C.” caught fire this week. NOTUS asked her why. (Responses have been lightly edited for length and clarity.) What inspired you to start that thread? I was hanging out with my husband and two of our friends — a couple getting married. The groom was not interested in having a bachelor party. We started joking around that he could pick the worst day in D.C. ever. I said we should crowdsource. Were you surprised by some of the responses? There were some frequent offenders. Some answers I hadn’t thought of that I quite liked: David’s Tent (religious tunes on the Mall), the Scientology museum. A lot of people captured the spirit of a bad day in D.C.: It’s hot, humid, you’ve been going to museums for hours, you start to feel ill and run to the nearest food truck. Why do you think this got so much engagement? One thing about Twitter is people love to complain. This summer in D.C., we have the National Guard around, it’s very hot, a lot of locals felt frustrated by [Freedom ]. I also think a lot of the worst things in D.C. have been the worst things for a while. … I think it was that Tom Sietsema reviewed Founding Farmers. I will say, I love D.C. and this was all in the spirit of fun. There are a million ways to have the best day in D.C. Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it . SPORTS “How would you like to play doubles with Venus Williams?” That was the question posed to 22-year-old Russian pro Diana Shnaider on the eve of this week’s D.C. Open. In a last-minute reshuffling, Shnaider was paired with the 46-year-old tennis legend, and the duo played two matches together. As NOTUS’ Dave Sheinin writes , the two players — meeting at opposite ends of their careers — both learned plenty from the experience. Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders’ revamped defense has made a strong first impression through two days of camp. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Braves, 7:15 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Wings, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! stories.title: D.C.’s Worst Landlord Is Its Housing Authority
stories.author: Zara Norman
stories.summary: The Department of Buildings fines the city’s bad landlords. None owe more than the DCHA.
stories.content: The District’s housing authority owes the Department of Buildings more than $2.2 million for over 2, unresolved violations across its properties. Alex Brandon/AP D.C.’s beleaguered housing authority — which has leadership turnover , a cyberattack and a scathing audit this year — is the city’s worst offender when it comes to unresolved housing violations. The District’s housing authority (DCHA) owes D.C.’s Department of Buildings (DOB) more than $2.2 million for over 2, unresolved violations across its properties, per a public DOB dashboard . Some violations date back to . The issue stems in part from the fact that the agency, which owns more than 8, public housing units, polices itself. Unlike private landlords who answer to DOB, by law, DOB cannot do more than issue fines to the housing authority. “If someone calls us up, we’ll go out, we’ll inspect, we will see what’s broken, we’ll create a [notice of infraction], and we will provide it to DCHA. They are supposed to then fix it and tell us,” Keith Parsons, DOB’s director of strategic enforcement, told NOTUS. “There is really no ‘stick,’ by law.” That the housing authority is the District’s worst offender doesn’t surprise Megan Browder, Legal Aid DC’s director for systemic advocacy and law reform. “I think it is partially the size of the portfolio and also a systematic disregard for their mission,” Browder told NOTUS. In , the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development found that DCHA was out of compliance with its annual inspection requirements, inspection outcomes weren’t monitored, and emergency work orders went uncompleted at night due to safety concerns. In , D.C.’s attorney general sued the DCHA for endangering thousands of tenants across 10 of its properties. D.C. has the country’s highest rates of rent nonpayment for low-income tax credit buildings, a fact landlords often point to as an explanation for their inability to make repairs. But DCHA doesn’t have that excuse, Browder said, as their properties are subsidized by the government. “DCHA takes steps to fully abate any infraction within the abatement timeframe listed on the notice and provide proof of abatement to the DOB,” Alison Burdo, a DCHA spokesperson, told NOTUS in a statement. “There may be a delay in updates to DOB’s public database if further clarification between DCHA and DOB is needed.” Some of the violations on the public dashboard are “associated with vacant units currently undergoing modernization or awaiting modernization pending sufficient funding,” Burdo said, and others are for properties DCHA doesn’t own or control but where the agency may have a long-term ground lease for redevelopment. The housing authority is in the middle of a three-year “ recovery plan ” meant to improve the quality of its housing stock and improve work order systems, among other goals. The agency meets monthly with DOB to review any notices of infraction, Burdo said. DHCA is far from the only landlord with an extensive list of outstanding violations. Per DOB’s dashboard , more than 84, housing violations, dating back to , are currently unresolved, with more than $83 million in associated fines. More than landlords owe at least $ , each. Some of the violations — particularly those dating back years — are in active litigation, Parsons said. Others may have already been fixed, but either DOB is waiting for evidence of that abatement or associated fines are tied up in the department’s adjudication process. That adjudication process is why it’s so hard to collect. It starts when DOB issues a notice of infraction after a property inspection, which may also carry a fine. There, the department runs into its first problem: the D.C. Council found in that over half of those infraction notices were sent to the incorrect address. Once a landlord receives a notice, the department must take them through a monthslong appeal and adjudication process administered by the city’s Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) in order to collect any money. “A landlord is entitled to due process,” Browder said. “That does take time, largely because there’s a big backlog at OAH.” Because of that system, each year DOB receives just a fraction of the fines it assessed and abates less than half of violations. In the fiscal year, the department collected $2.6 million in fines, but referred $25 million more to the city’s collections unit. Even as D.C. navigates a tight fiscal era , the DOB argues that the best outcome for the city is not necessarily collecting that $83 million. “Success is making sure the problems are fixed, and the fines are a way to motivate the landlord to do it,” Parsons told NOTUS. “So, if we can get things fixed, that is our goal.” In that spirit, and in line with the council’s recommendations from , the department is shifting its approach. Instead of chasing down every penny owed, the department is trying to settle with landlords for less or no money in order to fix violations sooner. It has set a “very ambitious” goal of resolving 80% of emergency violations within 30 days, and 90 days for non-emergencies, Parsons said. “There’s work to do here, but because we’re timing ourselves now, we are actually orienting operations around trying to move those things more quickly,” he said. The strategy seems to be paying off: DOB’s collection rate for fines increased by 10% from fiscal years to . Last year, fines collected before final order exceeded $1 million for the first time. “We’re doing more outreach. We're doing more talking to people. These options have usually been here, but we’re emphasizing them more,” Parsons said. “If you fix [violations] soon enough, we will just resolve it without fines at all.” Not everyone thinks that’s a win. Browder worries that landlords, some of whom already don’t take the abatement process seriously, won’t be incentivized to make fixes. “For me it’s really concerning,” she told NOTUS. “I think it just lessens the accountability for landlords to say ‘Hey, you can kind of just limp along and settle with DOB without any meaningful corrective action.’” Browder thinks informal settlements could be beneficial for smaller landlords, but that bigger housing providers — especially corporate landlords who own multiple properties under LLCs — should be forced to go through the fine collection process. She is hoping for a more transparent violations dashboard, and a public list of the owners of properties held under LLCs. “DOB enforcement should be the last step before litigation. The landlord should just fix the issue; it shouldn’t get to the point where you have to request DOB,” she said. “If we could figure out who the repeat violators [are], DOB could focus on those folks.”

stories.title: The Commanders’ Defense Has Made a Strong First Impression at Camp
stories.author: Martenzie Johnson
stories.summary: The offense? Not so much.
stories.content: Commanders rookie Sonny Styles has been one of the early standouts at training camp. John McDonnell/AP Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones had a simple message for his unit ahead of Thursday's training camp practice: “They don’t get in the fucking end zone.” Two days into camp, it’s clear Jones’ players have taken heed. The defense has mostly smothered the offense so far, both starters and reserves. Facing a relentless pass rush and suffocating coverage, Washington’s offense has struggled to move the ball, let alone reach the end zone. This defensive unit was slow and aged just a year ago, so the front office went out and signed eight players in free agency, hoping the group could become faster and more versatile. Based on first impressions in Ashburn, that effort appears to be paying off already. “When you look at this roster … the firepower we got, guys coming off the edge, guys all the way on the front seven, guys we got flying around in the back end — the sky's the limit,” veteran safety Will Harris said. It’s hard to decide who or what has stood out most for the defense since training camp kicked off Wednesday. The line and edge rushers, particularly free agent signee Odafe Oweh, have practically moved into the offensive backfield and declared squatter’s rights. Oweh stuffed multiple plays on Day 1 and swatted down a pass from quarterback Jayden Daniels, while fellow linebackers Jordan Magee and K’Lavon Chaisson (another new ) have made their way into the backfield on multiple run plays. Safety Nick Cross (also new) blitzed Daniels at one point to blow up a pass play. “When we put it all together, it’s going to be a masterpiece,” linebacker Frankie Luvu said. “I'm excited for the guys up front — we got some dogs. We holding them back right now because we ain't got the pads on, but when it’s time to let them loose we’ll have a lot of splash plays in the backfield.” In coverage, new cornerbacks Ahkello Witherspoon and Amik Robertson have looked solid. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles — picked seventh overall in large part because of his elite athleticism — has stayed hip-to-hip, stride-for-stride with his assignments like he’s their ballroom dance partner. The defense nabbed two interceptions Thursday, one by undrafted free agent Malik Spencer early in the session and a would-be pick-6 by newly signed corner Rasul Douglas on the final play of the day. During two-minute drills, the defense forced three field goals after stuffing the offense on third down. “We bring in those guys that come in and get after the quarterback,” Daniels said Wednesday about the new defensive linemen. “It's good work on both sides that at the end of the day, that's all camp really is. Building our identity, making sure guys get good work, make each other better.” On the other side of the ball, the offense is going through the growing pains expected of a unit run by a first-time playcaller implementing a new system . The group has looked out of sorts at times. The receivers have been a source of much debate this offseason and that uncertainty hasn’t been quelled in these early days. They have consistently struggled to gain separation. The defense “had a really good day. I'm not afraid to say that,” veteran receiver Terry McLaurin said Thursday. “But, that's camp. There's gonna be back and forth.” You can see the vision that coordinator David Blough has for his unit: lots of pre-snap motion and shifts; quarterbacks alternating from shotgun to under center; plenty of play action to hold the defense. It just hasn’t led to immediate success. Ahead of Wednesday’s practice, coach Dan Quinn said he expected early mistakes from the offense, but hoped to see less and less as camp progresses. “I just wanna see the execution, guys functioning at a high level together,” Quinn said. On Wednesday, there were highlight throws to receivers Antonio Williams, Jaden Bradley and Treylon Burks, who hauled in multiple difficult touchdown catches. (Burks missed Thursday’s practice due to foot soreness.) Tight end Chig Okonkwo found success on back-to-back out routes Thursday while receiver Luke McCaffrey shook free from cornerback Mike Sainristil for an impressive toe-tapping touchdown grab in the back of the end zone. When Daniels or his backups have had time, they’ve made quick and accurate throws. It’s just that those moments have come few and far between. But, as most players have emphasized, it’s only been two practices and the sky has not fallen. “It's just Day 2,” McLaurin said Thursday. “It's good to have guys out there flying around. The juice is what I'm super excited about, the competitiveness. We shake [hands] with guys after practice. I didn't really wanna shake up with anybody because we got beat. That's how I am. But at the end of the day, we're still brothers. We're going back and forth, but we still have ‘Commanders’ across our chest, so that's the main thing.”

stories.title: JLG Holds Court
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Jenny Gathright, Zara Norman
stories.content: DC Council member and Mayoral candidate Janeese Lewis George, 37, campaigns at the Wah Luck House Senior Day Center in Chinatown on May 29. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Janeese Lewis George meets with campaign foes, a veteran sues the National Guard and Dulles Airport gets a makeover. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Oh, to be a fly on the wall in that meeting. Janeese Lewis George , winner of last month’s Democratic mayoral primary, recently met with the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, which was highly critical of her during the hotly contested campaign. The meeting — brokered by the firefighters union, which endorsed her — was part of what Lewis George’s aides do not yet want to call a mayoral transition, but is an effort to lay the groundwork for the significant shift in priorities and policies that will take place if and when she takes office in January. “There is a sense of urgency here,” said Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who has been advising Lewis George’s post-primary efforts. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and any candidate who won with a massive mandate would be champing at the bit to be engaged.” That includes meetings with friends and foes alike to try to find common ground — or at least open channels of communication, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports . Other than the D.C. Police Union, Lewis George recently sat down with a small group from the Greater Washington Partnership, which represents large employers in the region. The business community has been especially concerned about what Lewis George will do in office, though some leaders think it’s best to keep an open mind. “We can’t walk in saying, ‘We don’t like this,’ without saying, ‘This is what success looks like,’” said one local business leader. Lewis George’s aides say they believe winning the primary with 54% of the vote gave her a broad mandate, and they are still focusing on her plans to try to bring down prices of child care and utilities, build more housing and end police cooperation with ICE. DEEP DIVE A veteran alleges that National Guard troops assaulted her outside her D.C. home, and she’s asking for $3 million in damages. Anna King said she was sitting on her front patio, scrolling on her phone, when National Guard troops walked onto the property and violently detained her, restraining her with handcuffs so tight that she tore at least one ligament in her wrist and required surgery. The ACLU of D.C. posted a video of the interaction , which happened in May. King filed a tort claim with the Idaho National Guard and the Defense Department on Wednesday. She has been a vocal critic of the Guard’s presence in the District, and was detained in May over an accusation of assaulting Guard members two days earlier. She was never charged in that case, but has been charged with assault over the incident on her patio. A spokesperson for the Idaho National Guard declined to comment on the specific allegations in King’s tort claim, citing the pending litigation, but said the Guard takes “all allegations of misconduct seriously.” The Defense Department did not provide comment.
