The broader goal here is to give football players a real say in the decisions shaping the name, image and likeness (NIL) era of college sports. And the timing is certainly interesting, too, as a handful of U.S. senators keep pushing the Protect College Sports Act , a bill supported by the NCAA and many conferences but generally loathed by labor groups. It’s impossible to separate any athlete organizing from what’s going on on Capitol Hill , especially with how the possibility of employment and unions plays into most — if not all — of these policy discussions. Just take it from Ernest Cooper, a redshirt senior linebacker at Stanford who was elected by his teammates as one of the leaders for their chapter with the CFBPA. “You see what’s going on in Congress; I think it’s hard when people who can’t relate, or try to say they understand the space, are trying to govern and put rules over you when you don’t have an ambassador at that table to advocate on your behalf,” Cooper said in a phone interview. “They’re trying to determine what’s right for us without talking to us.” Late last week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters he doesn’t expect a floor vote on the Protect College Sports Act before this session ends Aug. 7. And while that doesn’t mean a vote couldn’t happen post-recess, it does raise doubts about its chances of passing through the Senate — let alone the House — despite the legislation being driven by two powerful senators on opposite sides of the aisle: Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas). In June, the bill made it out of the Senate’s commerce committee with a 19-9 vote. To that point, Cruz and Cantwell had a lot of control over its fate, seeing that Cruz is the committee’s chair and Cantwell its ranking member. But now the midterms are closing in. Soon, as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), one of the bill’s co-sponsors, explained recently, focus will shift to campaigning, then to budget negotiations —- at which point the PCSA could run out of time. A major hangup has been opposition from the SEC and Big Ten — the two biggest, richest conferences in college sports — which has led to ongoing negotiations with Cruz and Cantwell, along with Schmitt and Chris Coons (D-Delaware), the last original co-sponsor. Employment is not among the issues they are going back and forth on. But ever since the bill was introduced, including a line about how it is “neutral on, and does nothing to alter, employee or non-employee status for student athletes,” employment has been a complicating factor for Democrats and Republicans, though largely for different reasons. Many Republicans, in the Senate and House, want any sweeping college sports bill to bar athletes from becoming employees. That includes Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), a former D-I football coach who’s been pushing against the PCSA, according to multiple people familiar with his messaging to fellow Republicans. This is also a long-running goal for the NCAA and its schools. On the other side, many pro-labor Democrats believe the bill could stunt future attempts to organize college athletes. Their argument: By giving the NCAA and conferences the antitrust protection needed to regulate compensation, player movement and eligibility without the threat of lawsuits, the PCSA would set rules that should be subject to collective bargaining, like in the NFL, NBA and other pro leagues. Then to take that argument a step further: If the PCSA instituted those rules along with antitrust immunity, labor groups would lose key leverage points. Why would college athletes unionize if they couldn’t negotiate over these issues? Which brings us back to Stanford’s new chapter with the CFBPA. On Capitol Hill, its existence should only strengthen those sentiments on both sides. Again, it’s not an immediate attempt to unionize. But a number of factors will determine whether that’s eventually possible. One, of course, is what happens with the PCSA. Another is the outcome of Johnson vs. NCAA, a federal lawsuit that is seeking employment status for college athletes under the National Labor Relations Act. And another is whether a Democrat wins the White House in , which would almost certainly lead to a more union-friendly National Labor Relations Board. The Dartmouth men’s basketball team began its attempt to unionize when Joe Biden was president. It then withdrew its petition with the NLRB a few weeks before Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “Collective is what you eventually want to get to, one hundred percent,” Cooper, the Stanford linebacker, said of the long-term plan for his team’s chapter and the CFBPA. “You see the NFL and how they have their players association. All I want is for college athletes to not just get what they deserve, but to be protected while playing, too.” The CFBPA is one of a few prominent college athlete labor groups. Others include Athletes.org and the National College Players Association, whose executive director, Ramogi Huma, led the attempt to unionize Northwestern’s football team more than a ago. But the CFBPA, founded by Stahl, is the only group that is solely focused on football players. While Stahl’s ultimate vision is to scale this across the country, a more specific goal is to leverage Stanford’s chapter to get more ACC teams on board. Down the line, he hopes, ACC football players would collectively bargain with the conference over compensation, player safety and so on. If that were to happen, chapter leaders from each program would participate in negotiations. The ACC, meanwhile, has been lobbying hard for the PCSA. The conference’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee recently sent a letter to a handful of senators stumping for the bill. When the NCAA and conferences select athletes to testify for their interests on Capitol Hill, they are usually involved with the advisory committee, which is an NCAA-sponsored program. And this letter, a full-throated endorsement of the PCSA, further illustrates the divide between the big-money sports and everyone else. Of the 28 athletes who signed the letter, none was a football or men’s basketball player. It’s only reason one million why it’s difficult to govern D-I sports with one set of rules — and, to that end, one federal bill. “If there is collective bargaining down the line, it would make sense for football to be the focus,” Cooper said. “It’s just where the most money is.”

stories.title: D.C.’s Disabled Residents Have Dismal Transit Options. Would Waymo Help?
stories.author: Zara Norman
stories.summary: Advocates fear that autonomous vehicles will be allowed to operate in the District without accessibility requirements.
stories.content: The possibility of Waymos in D.C. has already divided the city's disability advocates. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP When Kelly Mack orders a wheelchair-accessible Uber or Lyft, she does so knowing that most rides will cancel on her. Even when Claire Stanley’s rideshare is accepted, some drivers pull up to the curb, see her guide dog and tell her they don’t want her in their car. As members of D.C.’s disability community, both Mack and Stanley are accustomed to “abysmal” experiences getting a ride. But there is a potentially powerful newcomer in the market, one that has already divided disability advocates: Waymo. A bill before the D.C. Council would allow companies to operate a fleet of up to autonomous vehicles in the District. The bill, which received a hearing this month but won’t get a vote until the fall, has its supporters, including some disabled Washingtonians who are excited by the prospect. “There is just something very cool, as an adult who’s never been able to drive, that when you take an AV, you feel that freedom and that autonomy,” Stanley, an advocacy director at the American Council Of The Blind, told NOTUS. But the bill doesn’t require operators to make their vehicles wheelchair-accessible, and that troubles wheelchair users, who say they have no reliable on-demand transportation service in the city. “We support the wider disability community getting their needs met, we just want to widen the scope of what [AV operators are] required to do to meet the needs of all of our community members,” said Heidi Case, a wheelchair user and disability advocate. In theory, D.C. residents with disabilities can use the Metro system, for-hire vehicles or the city’s paratransit service to get around. But the bus and rail aren’t door-to-door services. Rideshare is only reliable in the heart of the city and sometimes refers riders out to taxi services, which struggle with driver shortages and have limited operating hours. City paratransit has to be booked at least a day in advance, and often has multiple stops. “They either pick you up super early, or they get you there super late, or there’s multiple people on paratransit at the same time,” Stanley said. “So, what should be a 20-minute ride suddenly is an hourlong ride.” Mack said she and her husband once had to show up at the airport a full day before their early-morning flight because paratransit couldn’t guarantee they’d have an accessible vehicle available for her to use. WMATA did not respond to a request for comment on how it plans to improve or expand its paratransit service. The limited options are, in part, a product of policy. D.C. green-lit Uber and Lyft’s operations over a ago without mandating those companies provide accessible rides. That was a “big flaw” in that legislation, Jonathan Rogers, executive director of D.C.’s Department of For-Hire Vehicles, told NOTUS. He believes District leaders have an opportunity to do something different this time around. “Instead of just hoping that they will prioritize those issues more than [companies] did when Uber and Lyft came here over a ago, let’s require it,” said Rogers. At a hearing last week, Waymo contended it can’t mandate what the automotive industry doesn’t manufacture. A Tesla spokesperson testified the company is trying to develop a “purpose-built wheelchair-accessible autonomous vehicle.” “We are a technology company. We do not develop our own and manufacture our own vehicles,” testified Waymo spokesperson Matthew Walsh. “We have not been able to identify an electric vehicle platform that is fully wheelchair-accessible while also meeting the very unique specifications that we need to retrofit that vehicle with our technology.” But D.C. requires taxi companies to make 20% of their fleet wheelchair-accessible. Those companies don’t employ drivers directly, and they also don’t own most of the fleet, Rogers said. “It’s a little ironic,” he said. “It’s challenging to provide that service, but taxis are these tiny little small businesses, and they’re in the exact same position as these multinational corporations.” Taxi companies complete about 96% of the city’s wheelchair[accessible rides, Rogers said. In , taxis completed more than , wheelchair-accessible rides. A spokesperson for Waymo told NOTUS the company is “actively assessing how we will provide an additional fleet of wheelchair accessible vehicles alongside our fully autonomous fleet,” should Waymo be allowed to operate here. The company could do what it has done in some of the 11 cities where it operates: partner with local organizations to provide wheelchair-accessible vehicles — though with a human behind the wheel. Private companies aren’t required by law to provide wheelchair-accessible cars, but they cannot discriminate against people with disabilities. A settlement in an ongoing disability discrimination lawsuit between the Equality Rights Center and Uber required the platform to incentivize drivers to provide wheelchair-accessible rides. But D.C. advocates hope they will be given access to autonomous vehicles without getting tied up in court. “I ask you to please require [Waymo] to do it,” Mack testified at the council hearing. “Otherwise, it’s putting the onus on my community to litigate.”

stories.title: What the Nationals' First Deadline Deal Really Means
stories.author: Jesse Dougherty
stories.summary: The Nats traded infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox on Saturday in exchange for pitcher Connelly Early.
stories.content: Pitcher Connelly Early is coming to Washington. Kevin Ng/AP Photo In late March, the Nationals traded a young catcher named Boston Smith for an Australian infielder named Curtis Mead, who had been solidly below-average in career plate appearances — and was just designated for assignment by the White Sox, a team that lost games in . And then late Saturday night, the Nats flipped Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, which was both their first trade deadline deal and a clear self-assessment for the new front office and coaching staff. They are feeling very, very good about the organization’s ability to develop hitting — and particularly power — in the majors and minors. They have every reason to, too, given that Mead went from floating in the ether to having a breakout year, including 17 home runs in less than four months. Players up and down the Nats’ major league roster are also tracking toward career highs in homers, if they aren’t there already. Which is all why it made perfect sense to trade from a position of strength (bats) to improve a glaring weakness (arms). ( ESPN first reported the Mead-Early trade .) Some more top-line details: Early is only 24 and will be under team control for another five years after this one (through ). Mead, 25, is controllable through . Early has been on the injured list since July 1 with left elbow inflammation, which underscores the inherent risk of swapping a hitter for a pitcher who’s never thrown more than innings at any level. But the Nats’ front office is intimately familiar with him, seeing that Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, was a key decision maker when Boston drafted Early in , as was Devin Pearson, now one of Toboni’s assistant general managers in Washington. (Toboni has now done two deals with his former club.) The deadline is Aug. 3, meaning the Nats could just be getting started. Shortstop CJ Abrams is generating real interest, according to multiple people familiar with his market, though it would take a massive return for the Nats to move him while hanging on the edge of the wild-race race. It wouldn’t require nearly as much for them to part with first baseman Luis García Jr. or starter Foster Griffin — though Griffin, an All Star with a 2.68 ERA, is in a higher tier than García, who would be a lefty platoon bat for a contender. And if the Nationals can improve on their 53-52 record over the next week, they could very well seek bullpen help while weighing offers for the players above. If the Mead-Early trade revealed anything about their broader deadline approach, it is that it’s not necessarily a binary choice between buying or selling. Early has allowed a ton of hard contact in 91⅔ innings this season. But he’s still managed a 3.44 ERA while mixing five to six pitches. Advanced metrics love his changeup. His extension, which measures the distance between the rubber and where a pitcher releases the ball, is well above average, a trait the Nats’ front office likes. And with the Red Sox, obvious needs lined up at the perfect time. The Red Sox just ripped off a 15-game winning streak and needed more offense for their playoff push. The Nats, confident they can replicate the process that revived Mead’s career, leaped at the chance to bring in a high-upside pitcher they know well. The Red Sox have the pitching prospects to backfill Early’s spot. The Nats have a handful of intriguing infield prospects, including Brady House, who will join the team Sunday to replace Mead on the active roster (which The Athletic first reported ). That’s the anatomy of a one-for-one trade of young big leaguers. House will be the next test of just how well the Nats can coach up power hitting in the majors, which they’ve done with multiple players now by emphasizing pulling the right pitches in the air. A first-round pick in , House started the year with the Nationals and struggled with contact and pitch selection. When he did connect, he hit the ball hard more often than not, resulting in seven homers in a limited sample. But he also struck out 50 times, nearly a third of this plate appearances, while working only 13 walks. Righties have chewed him up. That’s not to say that House’s next two months should color the assessment of trading Mead for Early. House’s promotion doesn’t mean the Nationals necessarily view him as their third baseman of the future, especially given how they pulled Mead from obscurity to effectively replace House for a few months. But House, who just turned 23, is coming off an encouraging stretch in AAA. And if the major league staff can keep turning him in the right direction, Saturday’s deal will make even more sense.

stories.title: The LeBron James Sixers Really Could Win It All
stories.author: Martenzie Johnson
stories.summary: NBA superteams rarely work out. Here's why this one might be different.
stories.content: LeBron James is headed to Philadelphia. Kyusung Gong/AP Superteams in the modern era of the NBA rarely work out. For a litany of reasons — chemistry, coaching, injury — a collection of stars on one team often doesn’t lead to championships. The Heat did it, sure. The Warriors did it, of course. But for every Heat and Warriors there are many more teamups that end up in failure and dirt being thrown around in the media. So there’s reason to be reluctant to … king the 76ers as next season’s champions simply because LeBron James decided on Friday his “last decision” was to sign with them. But sometimes in basketball the obvious is in front of you. Of course we all should have assumed the Knicks would win the Finals after they kept blowing out all of their Eastern Conference playoff opponents. Of course Victor Wembanyama was going to live up to the hype; he did this before even making it to the NBA. LeBron James — the LeBron James — just joined a team with former MVP Joel Embiid, former Finals MVP Jaylen Brown and two of the more promising young guards in the NBA in Tyrese Maxey and V. J. Edgecombe. What weaknesses does this collection of players have? All five of them are capable of regularly putting up 20 points. Four can regularly give you 30. Three can easily get you 40 or 50 if you absolutely need them to. Oh, and Embiid went for 70 just two years ago. The 76ers’ defense wasn’t great last season (16th in defensive efficiency) but adding Brown to play alongside Edgecombe on the wing and Embiid in the post makes that unit difficult to score on. James isn’t the all-defensive team player he used to be, but he’s who you fear like Michael Myers lurking on a fastbreak layup attempt. The bench lacked scoring (32.4 points per game ranked 27th) but the additions of Dean Wade (5.8 points per game) and Anfernee Simons (14.3) should be enough to hold the second unit afloat. Sure, there’s only one basketball: Brown (3rd) and Embiid (6th) were top 10 in the NBA in usage rate last season; Maxey ranked 27th and James 47th. But when these starting five are on the court you can’t double-team anyone, you can’t sag off of anyone, you can’t zone your way out of those problems. How many lineups in the league have five players who could reasonably take the last shot in a game? I’ll wait. The one thing that can trip these 76ers up is all the testosterone in that locker room. We know James brings a media circus wherever he sets up, not to mention his style of leadership has at times been described as passive-aggressive. Embiid has no problem throwing a teammate under the bus, as he infamously did to Ben Simmons after the playoffs. Brown has publicly bad-mouthed Embiid (“[He] flops. He know it.”) and James’ son (“I don't think Bronny is a pro.”) and overall isn’t afraid to say what’s on his mind. Maxey and Edgecomb may not say as much, but their collective demeanors read: Try me if you want to . Egos or toxicity ruined the -04 and -13 Lakers, the late 2000s Celtics, the -18 Cavaliers, the -22 Nets, and Kevin Durant’s recent stints with the Suns and Rockets. But if no issues arise in the Philadelphia locker room, and if — big if — Embiid is playing healthy ball in April and May next year, this very well could be the year the 76ers finally do it. (And the fact that they built this team not from intentionally losing games to get high draft picks, as they did in the Process era, is certainly not lost on most Philly fans.) We could be looking at the -27 NBA champions being formed in real time.

stories.title: Bowser’s Final Lap
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: Children play in the streams of water in the M Street Water Park in the summer heat on July 20, in Washington, D.C. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Mayor Bowser’s final priorities, a win for ranked-choice voting and a Reddit AMA. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Pools are simple. Politics, less so. That’s the reality Mayor Muriel Bowser is likely to in her final five months in office, and one she indirectly seemed to embrace Thursday when she cut the ribbon on the $6.8 million renovation of the outdoor Rosedale Pool in Ward 7. No one has officially declared her a lame duck, but conversations inside and out of the Wilson Building have shifted from what Bowser is doing to what Janeese Lewis George , her presumptive successor, is promising to do and the challenges she’s likely to . Bowser — a political institution in her own right — just isn’t the center of the political conversation anymore. That’s not to say Bowser is phoning it in. She told NOTUS that she plans to keep hammering home the message that D.C. needs to focus on growing an economy that has been hit hard by sweeping cuts to the once-steady federal workforce. “We worked for 12 years on making sure our finances are robust,” she said. “So our No. 1 issue for the next months, and even for the next mayor, is how do we grow our city? Attract businesses, create jobs, keep D.C. residents, and attract more D.C. residents?” Housing is another priority: This month, Bowser introduced a package of bills touching on everything from eviction timelines to tenant rights in buildings that hit the market. None of this is to say the D.C. Council will heed her words, much less pass her bills. Bowser has had a prickly relationship for years with city lawmakers, many of whom are now looking to what’s next. But where politics may come up short, pools — and other public projects — will remain. D.C. officials tell NOTUS that there are at least 28 planned groundbreakings or ribbon-cuttings planned for the remainder of the year, everything from an expansion of the Southeast Tennis and Learning Center in Ward 8 to the reopening of a brand new Harriet Tubman Elementary School in Ward 1. FROM THE DISTRICT Most D.C. voters ranked two or more candidates in the June 16 Democratic primary, according to a new analysis by FairVote, an elections reform group. Why does that matter? FairVote, which supports the use of ranked-choice voting, says it shows that D.C. voters were able to navigate the system in its inaugural usage. The data also shows that while Lewis George won the Democratic nomination for mayor with 54% of the vote, 71% of voters ranked her in their top three. Want even more nerdy data on the election’s outcomes? Find it here . Understaffing at D.C.’s public safety agencies resulted in a “substantial” $ million spent on overtime last fiscal year, according to a new report from D.C.’s auditor. The family of a 6-year-old boy who nearly drowned at a D.C. summer camp on Monday told City Cast DC that he faces a “long and uncertain” road ahead. Some students who’d been accepted to Howard University say the school unexpectedly unenrolled them for unpaid tuition balances, weeks before move-in. The university acknowledged Thursday it had unenrolled some students, but said families had been notified multiple times about payment deadlines. D.C. homicides have fallen by 37% over the past year, according to preliminary crime data — one of the steepest declines in the country, WTOP reports . FROM MARYLAND The Board of Public Works approved a nearly $85 million contract for a new voting system ahead of the election, Maryland Matters reports . METRO MOMENTS On Fridays, this is your space. We want to feature your photos, your questions, your “only in D.C.” moments. Email us with any of the above: metro@notus.com . SPORTS The Mystics have reached the All-Star break , and there is no longer any doubt that they are contenders, writes NOTUS’ Dave Sheinin . With the trade deadline around the corner, should this young team go all in for a playoff push? Heads up, Nats fans: NOTUS sports reporter Jesse Dougherty will be doing an AMA over at r/nationals at noon today. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals vs. Diamondbacks, 6:45 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.
