stories.title: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA
stories.author: Dave Sheinin
stories.summary: Washington closed the first half of its season with a win over the powerhouse Aces, further proving it is a legitimate contender.
stories.content: Forward Kiki Iriafen is one of several young players that stepped up for Washington in the first half of the season. Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via AP The transcontinental stretch of games that closed out the first half of the Washington Mystics’ season could best be described as Odyssean: six contests across 11 days, half of them against the top tier of WNBA opponents, and requiring four flights and nearly 6, air miles to navigate before they finally reached home. Along the way, the league’s youngest team nearly everything short of cyclopses, cannibals and sirens. What to make, then, of head coach Sydney Johnson revealing late Wednesday that the top item on his All-Star break bucket list — apart from family time, a little film work and some couch-side viewing of Saturday night’s WNBA All-Star Game — is to take in the new epic remake of “The Odyssey” with his wife? “I just really want to see that movie,” Johnson shrugged, with something short of Homeric grandeur. Truth is, he doesn’t need to see it. He just lived it. By the time the Mystics had slain the last beast on their own odyssey — taking down the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, -99, at home Wednesday night to complete that grueling, six-game stretch with a 4-2 record — it was the rest of the WNBA that was collectively waking up to a realization: The Mystics are officially a problem. Despite having the second-youngest roster in league history, they arrive at the All-Star break, and on the cusp of the Aug. 2 trade deadline, with a 14-12 record, far above most preseason predictions and good for the eighth and final playoff spot if the season ended today. Even more impressive is the way they closed out the first half: with back-to-back wins at Golden State and at home against Las Vegas — the No. 2 and No. 3 teams in the W, respectively — in a 72-hour stretch, with a cross-country flight in between. “They’re very long. They're athletic. They're well-coached. I’m not surprised they're sitting where they're sitting,” Aces coach Becky Hammon said of the Mystics. “They don't go away. They hang around in games, which always gives you a chance to win. There is a skillset in winning together, and even though this team is young they're proving that they're developing [the ability] to win tough games down the stretch. “Their length and their physicality and athleticism are [elite]. I don't think too many teams in this league can deal with that.” On Wednesday night, the Mystics pummeled Hammon’s Aces inside and out. Washington’s three bigs — 6-foot-3 Kiki Iriafen, 6-foot-5 Shakira Austin and 6-foot-7 Lauren Betts — combined for 50 points and 19 rebounds, more than making up for the 38 and seven they conceded to Aces legend A’ja Wilson. Meantime, guard Sonia Citron poured in 20 points (along with eight assists), with 11 of them coming in the decisive fourth quarter, when Citron, who typically plays off the ball, shifted to point guard and the Mystics stormed back from nine points down in the final four minutes. The victory over the Aces made the Mystics the only team this season with wins over all three of the league’s top teams: Minnesota, Golden State and Las Vegas. Regardless of where they finish in the standings, they have become that team no one would want to in the playoffs. Lauren Betts Mystics AP - ( , AR: 1.50) “We don’t make it a secret: We want to make the playoffs. We want to make a push,” said point guard Georgia Amoore, who scored 10 on Wednesday. “We’re not that team that other teams can relax against, or take a night off against. We’ve proven that.” The next stop for Iriafen, Citron and Austin is Chicago, where Iriafen and Citron — the first WNBA teammates in 27 years to earn All-Star berths in each of their first two seasons — will be on opposite squads for the game itself, while Austin, a notable snub in All-Star selections, will participate in Friday night’s Shooting Stars competition. The Mystics’ sooner-than-expected arrival as a playoff threat and their enviable collection of young talent — the 25-year-old Austin and 26-year-old forward Michaela Onyenwere are the only players on the roster with more than one and a half years of WNBA experience — has both given them the appearance of a nascent juggernaut and also made them an intriguing factor ahead of next month’s trade deadline. Up to now, the Mystics have been pointed decidedly and aggressively in the direction of rebuilding, hoarding draft picks and emphasizing player development. A year ago at the trade deadline, sitting on a 13-15 record, they dealt away veteran guard and three-time All-Star Brittney Sykes, then finished the season on a 3-12 skid. Might Washington take the opposite approach this summer, and perhaps spend some of its remaining draft capital and young talent on a veteran or two — in effect stopping the rebuild and turning this into a go-for-it year? Among the team’s needs: a veteran point guard (the assortment of point guards on their roster have amassed -0.2 win shares this season) and/or a deadly three-point shooter (they rank next-to-last in the league in three-point attempts, makes and shooting percentage). Among the available targets: 35-year-old veteran and seven-time All-Star Skylar Diggins, whom the Chicago Sky may be shopping . But the likelier play for the Mystics would be to stand pat at the deadline, let the season play out and make their next push this offseason via free agency and/or the draft. They already own Chicago’s first-round pick in , which is likely to be high. That means the Mystics could have their choice of a game-changing talent like USC’s JuJu Watkins, Texas’ Madison Booker or Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo. The Mystics have been operating without a general manager since parting ways with Jamila Wideman in April, meaning Johnson and Michael Winger, president of basketball operations for Monumental Basketball, will be making the big calls on the Mystics’ direction and philosophy. On Wednesday, Johnson deflected a question about the team’s trade deadline strategy. “Every player on our roster has gotten better. Every single one of them. And that has allowed us as a team to get better. And we’ll lift our heads up in August and just kind of see where we are,” Johnson said. “What we talked about at the start of the season, in terms of having a young group that was eager to get better, to grow individually and as a team — so far, so good. We’re on track in terms of taking a step forward. But the [ ] journey is only a little more than halfway through.” Once they return from the All-Star break, the Mystics a gauntlet of a schedule in the first half of August, including back-to-backs against both Dallas (currently fourth in the standings) and Las Vegas (currently third). There is also another stretch of six games in 11 days featuring another pair of cross-country flights. Which means before Johnson and the Mystics can look too far down the road, he still has one Odyssey to at the cinema and another on the basketball court.

stories.title: You Have Dining Questions. Tom Sietsema Has Answers.
stories.author: Tom Sietsema
stories.summary: In his NOTUS debut, our award-winning food correspondent fields questions on where to eat on the Mall, D.C.'s best sushi deal, and his go-to restaurants right now.
stories.content: Tom Sietsema is joining NOTUS as its food correspondent. Courtesy of Deb Lindsey Photography When NOTUS reached out recently to ask me what I’d like to do, the first idea that came to mind was to host a regular Q&A with readers. During my 25 years as the food critic for The Washington Post, from which I took a buyout last summer, the most important hour of my work week was 11 a.m. Wednesdays, when I’d answer reader rants, raves and everything in between. Ask Tom was a place where I tried to help people find what they wanted, learn something new, solve a dining dilemma. The online exchange was so popular that it often trumped Trump news. The interactions also gave me an immediate sense of what readers were thinking about, which led to a number of my best-read critic’s notebooks. Besides, even after I left The Post, readers followed me with their questions. Why not create a dedicated forum for responding to them? Welcome, then, to my new advice column, Talk to Tom, where I’ll be addressing your dining questions — every Thursday. Got a gripe or concern? Something you’re curious about? Send me an email at TalkToTom@notus.com . Questions and comments may be edited for length. Why do so many American restaurants force us to eat in the dark? We are frequent travelers to Europe, where you can actually read the menu and see your food without using a flashlight. A dim interior accomplishes several things. For starters, it tends to relax people, which makes eating feel more pleasurable and may encourage lingering (say, to order more drinks, a win for the restaurant). Darkness also has a way of compressing even large rooms, creating cocoons of space, at least mentally. Dim lighting can hide flaws, too, in the decor as well as on diners. Don’t we all look better away from klieg lights? That said, a thoughtful restaurant provides sufficient illumination — and a menu with easy-to-read print — for diners to see what’s in front of them. I've long said, restaurateurs need to audition everything diners will touch or see — utensils, chairs, lights — before buying them. I’ve got family coming to D.C. Is there a restaurant on the Mall you prefer? For proximity to the museums and value, I’m partial to America’s Table Cafe inside the lower level of the National Museum of American History, which fuels between 6, and 8, visitors a week around this time of year. Leading the kitchen: executive chef Mollie Kaufmann , who previously served as the culinary operations manager for World Central Kitchen, and who offers food more personal than the crowd-size suggests. (Quick, what other local cafeteria offers shrimp and grits, flavored as if you were in the South?) A recent lunch also embraced a snappy bratwurst striped with brown mustard and topped with tangy sauerkraut; a salad bar that goes beyond the expected; and appealing side dishes to accompany the generous entrees. Fresh-tasting apple-fennel coleslaw, mustard-punched baked beans, and pickled okra outperformed a plate of slightly dry smoked chicken thighs. Nodding to the season was a fine trifle sweetened with blueberries and peaches. I get hungry just typing that. Lines tend to move fast, by the way, thanks to friendly cashiers. “You’re going to fall asleep, eating all that!” one of them teased two of us as we paid. Snare the right table, and you can enjoy your meal with the Washington Monument as a backdrop — a twofer attraction. Help settle a debate. I say it’s just as easy to open a $30 bottle of wine as a $ bottle. An oenophile in my group thinks otherwise — and says the tip should be higher on the more expensive wine. Much as I enjoy wine, which I tip on like the food it is — 20%, the industry standard — I seldom splurge on anything priced in the triple digits. Regarding dearer bottles, I turned to ace wine consultant and former restaurateur Janet Cam , who thinks an extra 10% or so gratuity should be applied to wines in the $ and up range. In those situations, she says, “expertise [is] expected.” Customers should receive proper stemware, “ideally finely made Riedel, Schott Zwiesel and Glassine,” she gives by way of example. “The thin lip of the glass affects the taste and perception of wine.” Cam says the wine should be presented and tasted before the food arrives, as “food aromas enter the glass, distorting the perception of wine.” Higher-priced wine typically involves the sommelier’s “attention, knowledge, time in sourcing the wine” and storing it properly — conditions the wine authority says “should be considered and compensated” with “cash in the hand of the sommelier.” In short, sourcing, storing and serving minor versus major wines requires different effort. Sushi seems to be on everyone’s mind in the District these days. Unfortunately, I find many non-omakase meals to be exceedingly “spendy,” as you say in Minnesota. Can you recommend a spot that doesn’t cost the fish’s weight in gold? Let me introduce you to the youthful Kiyomi from Masaaki “Uchi” Uchino , who made a splash in Washington when he helmed the top-notch Sushi Nakazawa at the back of the late Trump hotel (now the Waldorf Astoria). Since April, the chef can be found behind a handsome wooden door at L St. NW, in a small dining room set off with woven balloon lights overhead and a counter ringed with 16 seats. “Japanese style,” says Uchino, “with American feel.” Friendly, in other words. The lure: a parade of (seven) nigiri or hand rolls plus miso soup for a bargain $40. The pleasure might begin with pale pink tile fish, garnished with lime zest, on a pillow of warm rice, and continue with raw yellowtail, Spanish mackerel, -colored tuna streaked with veins of fat, and porgy splashed with lemon juice and a touch of sea salt. The last gets hit with a blow torch before Uchino places the morsel on a small slate plate in front of you. IMG_0572.jpg ( , AR: 0.75)My neighbors on a recent weekday murmured in unison as they bit into salmon smoked in hay, a technique that elevates the flavor of the fish without masking it. Even if you go the sushi route, the drill includes a hand roll. (Make mine yellowtail ignited with citrusy yuzu, please.) At present, the venue is walk-in only for lunch. Omakase, served on Friday night for $ a person, is by reservation for two seatings and includes grilled and fried dishes while featuring mostly fish from Japan, says Uchino. Kiyomi, the chef’s sister’s name, translates to “pure beauty” — an apt way to describe a deal of a meal in the city. Now that you no longer have an expense account, have your restaurant habits changed? For sure — but not necessarily for budgetary reasons. After decades of eating out, sometimes as many as 10 meals a week for work, I’m rekindling my love for cooking at home. (Meatloaf, roast chicken, composed salads, BLTs and eggs for dinner are my current jam.) While I remain curious about the restaurant scene, locally and beyond, I’m also free to eat wherever I want, not where I feel obliged to visit. There are a handful of places I return to frequently, both because they’re easy to get to (close to home) and their menus are to my taste: Bombay Club and Casa Teresa downtown, Perry’s , Reveler’s Hour and Rye Bunny in Adams Morgan, Donsak Thai Restaurant in Woodley Park, and Buck’s Fishing & Camping near the senior Politics and Prose are where you might find me most often. Finally, I’m probably drinking less than when I was out every night, too; a cocktail followed by a glass of wine. No more bottles of grape juice unless I’m with a group. My liver thanks me. Two food lovers are heading to Iceland for several days. What shouldn’t we miss? You’ll want to book in advance for the top draws, which include Dill, the first Icelandic restaurant to get a nod from Michelin; Ox , which offers the feel of a speakeasy; Moss at the Blue Lagoon, whose seasonal tasting menu focuses on New Nordic flavors and whose view embraces lava fields; and, for something different and more relaxed, Sumac Grill + Drinks . The last is a lively brasserie with a charcoal grill and twists on Middle Eastern accents. Suddenly, I’m hungry for Reykjavik again. I have a hankering for Burmese food. Point me in the right direction. Arlington — specifically Padaek , the largest of the area Thai and Laotian restaurants owned by chef Seng Luangrath . Her partner in the kitchen is Nyi Nyi Myint , a native of Yangon (formerly Rangoon) who recently several flavors from his homeland to the menu. “There aren’t a lot of Burmese restaurants” in the area, Myint says of the decision to broaden the script. Spring for the fermented tea leaf salad — a crunchy-tangy toss that includes shredded cabbage, tomatoes, nuts, lime juice and chiles — and the fish soup mohinga that’s considered Burma’s national dish. Once you start spooning into the steaming, turmeric-tinted mohinga — thick with thin rice noodles, a whole egg, shredded blue catfish, and crisp Lao squash fritters — it’s hard to stop. Fresh ginger, garlic and fish sauce weigh in with their charms, too. Myint says he has more Burmese dishes to add after vacation. September can’t come fast enough for some of his fans.

stories.title: Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp
stories.author: Martenzie Johnson
stories.summary: Washington opens camp next week, and these players have plenty to prove ahead of a new season.
stories.content: Rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams will aim to cement himself as a top pass-catching option during training camp. (Nick Wass/AP Photo) Let’s get this out of the way: You’re not here to read about Jayden Daniels or Terry McLaurin or Laremy Tunsil or Sonny Styles. We all know they’re vital to the Commanders’ success this season. But there’s about 70 other guys reporting to Ashburn for training camp next week, and they could very well dictate whether Washington makes a deep playoff run like it did in or goes 5-12 like last season. Before the pads come out next week, here are five (fine, technically six) key players to watch in the home stretch of the offseason. Nick Allegretti, center The Commanders are set to return 80% of the starters on their offensive line: tackles Tunsil and Josh Conerly and guards Chris Paul and Samuel Cosmi. The only change will be at center, where Allegretti is expected to replace Tyler Biadasz, who was released back in March. Allegretti has spent most of his eight-year NFL career at guard, including five seasons with the Chiefs. But he’s played center since childhood and was a top center prospect coming out of high school, according to 247Sports. He spent time at both center and guard over four seasons at Illinois. While the offensive line has continuity on its side, it wasn’t exactly the best unit in the NFL last season: ESPN placed the group in the bottom half of the league in its run- and pass-block rankings. Allegretti started last season at guard while Cosmi recovered from injury, but he was removed from the starting unit after just two games. Allegretti has said he’s sat in on center-quarterback meetings since signing in , and he put that experience into practice by starting the last two games of the season at center. There’s reason to believe the Commanders feel optimistic about Allegretti. They signed him to a multi-year contract extension in March after letting Biadasz go, waited until the sixth round of April’s draft to take a center (Michigan State’s Matt Gulbin) and didn’t add any veteran competition in free agency. Trey Amos, defensive back They say the best ability is availability. Another popular idiom: You have to see it to believe it. Both of those apply to Amos. The second-year cornerback didn’t participate in organized team activities (OTAs) or minicamp in June after fracturing his fibula during a Week 10 loss to the Lions. Amos proved last season he’s one of, if not the best one-on-one defender in Washington. He allowed just one touchdown in coverage last season, and his six pass deflections ranked third on the team despite the fact that he appeared in just nine and a half games. He played particularly well against the Packers in Week 2. The Commanders need Amos’ speed and physicality. Last season’s pass defense was more accommodating than an AirBnB host, allowing the second-most pass plays of 40 yards or more. It’s not clear how Washington feels about Amos’ recovery, but it’s apparent the team is focused on the secondary: Earlier this month, they signed veteran Rasul Douglas to a one-year contract. Douglas started 13 games for the Dolphins last season and was one of the better lockdown defenders in football last season with 13 pass deflections and a 54% completion percentage allowed in coverage. For what it’s worth, Amos said on a Twitch stream last week that he’s healthy and ready for training camp, according to the Full Command Youtube channel . Croskey-Merritt Commanders AP - ( , AR: 1.50) Bill Croskey-Merritt, running back On paper, Croskey-Merritt had as good of a season as could be expected of a seventh-round draft pick who played one game in his final season of college ball. He finished with a team-high rushing yards and eight touchdowns. But look closer and you can see areas Croskey-Merritt will need to improve. He lacked the pass-catching skills and explosive runs that make an offense dangerous: Of players with or more rushing yards last season, he ranked last in receptions (9) and receiving yards (68) and tied for last in rushes of 20 yards or more (3). Croskey-Merritt also tied for the third-most fumbles (3) by a running back. If the second-year back, who has visibly bulked up this offseason, wants to be more of a bell cow than a member of a committee, he’ll have to prove it in these coming weeks. And that’s not me talking, that is his head coach: After minicamp, coach Dan Quinn said he wanted to see improvement from Croskey-Merritt in pass-catching and explosiveness, and foresees him splitting reps with the other backs, including free agent signee Rachaad White ( receptions, 1, receiving yards and 11 receiving touchdowns in four seasons with Tampa Bay). “I do like the competition in the group,” Quinn said. “I think we'll for sure be more than just one [running back].” Leo Chenal, linebacker Seeing as most Americans choose the Super Bowl as the one NFL game they watch each season, Chenal’s name should sound familiar. In the Chiefs’ championship wins in and , he totaled 12 tackles, two tackles for loss, a forced fumble and one quarterback hit. The linebacker, who signed a three-year deal with the Commanders this offseason, stuffed All-Pro 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey at the line of scrimmage on a third-and-2 in the fourth quarter of Super Bowl LVIII. That nose for the football is desperately needed in Washington. The Commanders missed the second-most tackles ( ) in the NFL last season, according to Pro Football Reference. Chenal’s 5.2% missed-tackle rate is the lowest among linebackers since , per Next Gen Stats . Chenal will be battling for first-string camp reps with first-round draft pick Styles and returning starter Frankie Luvu, but his ability to pursue, cover tight ends in coverage and fight through offensive linemen should go a long way towards improving a defensive unit that has struggled the past three seasons. Antonio Williams and Treylon Burks, wide receivers To paraphrase the immortal words of Rick Pitino: “ Brandon Aiyuk ain’t walking through that door.” For all the chatter about the Commanders needing another receiver ahead of training camp, it seems pretty clear they’re rolling with what they currently have. Which means someone has to line up opposite McLaurin, and it would appear Williams, a third-round pick, and Burks, a first-rounder in Tennessee, have the upper hand. During 7-on-7 and 11-on-11 drills at OTAs and minicamp, Williams and Burks got a lot of time working with quarterbacks Daniels and Marcus Mariota. Williams was primarily used out of the slot at Clemson last season, and his production didn’t exactly scream modern NFL starter (55 receptions, yards, 11.0 yards per reception). But he is versatile and slippery, often used in jet sweeps and screens that take advantage of his speed. Much like most of the rest of the receiving corps, Williams is not a deep threat, but he can feast on defenses in intermediate routes. Injuries have derailed Burks’ career, limiting him to just 35 games played in the last four years. But he’s shown big-play ability , albeit in spurts. If Williams can find gaps in coverage and Burks can stay healthy, there’s a good chance one of them will earn a starting spot by the end of camp.

stories.title: Smithsonian Showdown
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: Anthea Hartig, director of the Smithsonian Institute's National Museum of American History, is sworn in to the House Oversight and Government Reform Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past," in Rayburn building on Tuesday, July 21, . Tom Williams/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: The Smithsonian under scrutiny, Carter Barron’s (temporary) return and a fresh look at the Commanders’ stadium plans. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Republican lawmakers grilled the director of the Smithsonian’s U.S. history museum yesterday over concerns the institution is too “woke.” The two-hour hearing was the latest installment in President Donald Trump ’s “ ongoing review ” of the Smithsonian and his continued effort to remake Washington and its cultural institutions. Representatives took aim at several exhibits, including ones on slavery, the American entertainment industry and girls going through puberty, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports . “History is incredibly challenging and … if we tell it in its richness, we absolutely, I think, have objects that can make people uncomfortable,” director Anthea Hartig fired back. There are signs of life in Rock Creek Park, despite the cultural climate. Carter Barron Amphitheater, the park’s 76-year-old outdoor venue that has been shuttered and in disrepair for a , will host a three-night concert series in August featuring jazz, gospel and go-go. But this isn’t a permanent reopening. Carter Barron still needs significant work, and a local effort to upgrade the iconic site is ongoing. FROM THE DISTRICT Trump’s plans to renovate the golf links at East Potomac Park could affect the park’s other public spaces, worrying everyone from cyclists to fishers, NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad reports . Metro wants automated doors on Red Line platforms to be installed as part of a $ million modernization project, ABC7 reports . D.C. firefighters will get higher wages after their union reached a new collective bargaining agreement with the District yesterday, following nearly two years of contentious negotiations. They’ll receive a 3.5% increase next fiscal year and retroactive 2% and 3.5% increases for the and fiscal years, too. “Like everybody else, we're all struggling with higher utility bills, elevated grocery prices, you name it,” the union’s president, David Hoagland, told NOTUS. “It's a much-needed increase at a time when affordability is [at] the top of everybody's mind.” FROM VIRGINIA A new Virginia law extending the grace period for paying rent to 14 days is just one of the tenant protection policies being rolled out by the state, the Virginia Mercury reports . FROM MARYLAND Marylanders are fighting back against data centers and getting results, WAMU reports . Montgomery and Prince George’s counties have paused the development of new data centers, and one state senator told WAMU they may propose a statewide moratorium this summer. PLAN YOUR WEEKEND For the Swiftie: Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf, Friday. For the Potterhead: Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park, Saturday. For the history buff: District Vibes at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, ongoing. For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here . SPORTS Commanders stadium updated rendering ( , AR: 1.90) Check out this fresh rendering of the new Commanders stadium. Buried in a recent presentation to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts is one of the first comprehensive views of what the new stadium will look like for most fans approaching from the west, including what’s being called Festival Plaza and the residential and retail development that will frame one side of it. There’s lots more to dig through here . Congratulate AJ Dybantsa on a new position. More young athletes are opting for LinkedIn as their social media of choice, The Banner reports , using the buttoned-up, business-centric platform as a way to connect with fans without sharing too much. The Wizards rookie has gotten in on the trend, posting last month that he was starting a new full-time role as “Professional Basketball Player.” What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Rockies, 3:10 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Aces, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. One last thing: that three-bedroom house with a pool we showed you yesterday is located in Virginia, and 36% of you guessed that right. The most common guess was Maryland.

stories.title: From Cycling to Fishing, Concerns About East Potomac’s Future Go Beyond Golf
stories.author: Shamira Muhammad
stories.summary: President Donald Trump’s plan to renovate the island park’s golf course has created an uncertain future for the area’s other public spaces.
stories.content: Will Edwards and his family are regulars at East Potomac Park. (Shamira Muhammad/NOTUS) Will Edwards, born and raised in southwest D.C., has been coming to East Potomac Park his entire life. On a warm Monday evening, he and his family set up camp near Hains Point, the island park’s southern tip. They had a portable table, some chairs and some toys for Edwards’ son. A dinner of chicken and biscuits was spread out in front of them. Fishing rods hung on the fence. “This has been a landmark for years,” Edwards said. “Years.” Before he was married, Edwards said he used to come down here looking to meet women at social events. His wife, Carla, has different but also fond memories: as a child, she used to crawl on The Awakening, a large sculpture that was once located at Hains Point but has since moved to Maryland. The lines from Edwards’ rods were being gently tugged by the water as he discussed the many types of fish he hoped to catch. “Catfish, maybe a cod. Alligator gar,” he said. Not far from the family sat a discarded container of chicken gizzards, popular bait for blue crabs. To Carla, the park creates a sense of community. “Most people see you fishing, they offer their bait,” she said. But the future of these Edwards family trips to East Potomac is uncertain. The park has served as a political football in the months since President Donald Trump announced his intention to renovate the golf links at its center — an extensive project that would likely impact the entire island. Much of the discussion in the months since has been centered on golf and golfers, but the park has a long history of recreation beyond the links. East Potomac also features tennis courts, a playground and abundant green space. Hains Point is a popular destination for picnics and weekend gatherings. In nice weather, the wide road that encircles the park is often filled with runners and bicyclists. Hains Point recreation family ( , AR: 1.50) Early renderings of Trump’s plan seemed to spare Hains Point and other adjoining areas. But recently, Trump has been seen with new blueprints that suggest otherwise, creating a panic regarding the future of the park. On Saturday, the Washington Area Bicyclist Association hosted a rally called “Hains Point Hoopla” to raise awareness about the public amenities that could be at stake. Trump has said he would like construction to begin in September, but his plan is certain to red tape. In the meantime, the park continues to serve its regulars. On Monday night, plane after plane landed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, located directly across the water from the Edwards family. Will said any large-scale changes to the park would be “devastating.” “This is somewhere people need to come, just to relax, despite a day,” he said. “Anybody could have a bad day, but they come here, they sit in the car, you know. Just relax.” Earlier this month, four senators sent a letter to the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service seeking clarification on final plans for the park. The agencies are defendants in an ongoing lawsuit brought by the D.C. Preservation League and local residents, aimed at halting any proposed overhaul. Neither the National Park Service or the Department of the Interior could be reached for comment. This past winter, the Trump administration terminated a 50-year lease with the National Links Trust, the nonprofit tasked with managing the course. The Department of the Interior has since allowed the trust to operate the course until a “historic renovation” begins. Torrence, who declined to give his last name because of privacy concerns, is also a District native who’s been coming to the park most of his life. Although he wasn’t aware of the proposed changes to the golf course, he has sensed more tension in the area. “I've never had anybody ask for a fishing license down here, but now all of a sudden you have to have a fishing license, and they try to give you a citation or a ticket,” he told NOTUS. “This place was very peaceful at one point.” Torrence said he comes to the park to “breathe life” and escape the reality of his densely populated city. “We live in an inner city surrounded by concrete,” he said. “It's not too much wildlife out here, outdoors things you can do. So this is one of the places that a lot of inner city people come to just release.” Many regulars admit that the park needs upgrades. Some bathrooms are out and there is overgrowth on the waterfront. The park is not perfect, but it is where they choose to spend their time. “If anything, give it a facelift,” Torrence said. “Pick up some of these broken-down trees and stuff around there. Invest money into this place.”

stories.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (July 24)
stories.author: Torrie Herrington, Rebecca Ritzel
stories.summary: A Taylor Swift tribute band, Harry Potter Day at Nats Park, and performances across the DMV.
stories.content: Brayden Bambino (Pippin) with Hank von Kolnitz, Calvin L’mont Cooper, and Ben Bogen in Pippin at Signature Theatre. Daniel Rader Thursday ¡Puro Ritmo! The Musical Journey of Salsa at the American History Museum Constitution Ave. NW, D.C., 10:30 a.m., free Located in the Molina Family Latino Gallery. Explore the rhythm, history and energy of salsa music through a guided tour. This is a bilingual multimedia exhibition presented by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino. Summer Culture Hub: Textile Techniques at Montpelier Historic Site and Museum Muirkirk Road, Laurel, MD, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., free. Through Sunday, July 26. Laurel’s Georgian plantation house hosts a weekend of family-friendly, hands-on crafting workshops. Learn about historic textile arts that would have been practiced by both enslaved artisans and wealthy landowners at this event run by the Maryland National-Capital Park and Planning Commission. Girl Scouts block party at Franklin Park I St. NW, D.C., 6:30 p.m., free Enjoy sweet treats and dance the night away to Be'la Dona, an all-women group performing live go-go music. There will also be food vendors, paintings, glitter tattoos, nail art and other interactive activities for all ages. More to explore: Analog Dinner Nights: Mahjong! at Flor Coffee + Books Board Game Speed Dating at Dacha Beer Garden (Shaw) Friday Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf Wharf St. SW, D.C., 7 p.m., free Every Friday night at the Transit Pier, enjoy free live music next to the water. This Friday, The Fearless Eras, a Taylor Swift tribute band, will be playing all the hits. All ages are welcome, as are dogs on leashes, and enjoying food from the Wharf’s many restaurants is encouraged. Pianist Joyce Yang with the Baltimore Symphony at the Music Center at Strathmore Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, MD, 7:30 p.m., $35 to $ (second show Saturday) In early 1800s Italy, rumor had it that violinist Niccolò Paganini sold his soul to the devil in exchange for virtuosic talents. A century later, Russian composer Sergei Rachmaninoff arranged one of Paginini’s signature motifs into his fiendishly difficult “Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini.” Pianist Joyce Yang takes the devil down to Strathmore, with Lidiya Yankovskaya in the conductor’s seat. Candlelight: ’90s Hip-Hop on Strings at National City Christian Church 5 Thomas Circle NW, 6:45 p.m., $63.50 to $ Prefer your Snoop Dogg played by a string quartet? Fever, the national event presenter that curates romantic musical evenings outside of traditional concert halls, has arranged a memory-lane playlist including Lauryn Hill, the Notorious B.I.G. and the Wu Tang Clan, to be performed by the Listeso String Quartet. Rooted in Resistance dinner at the Festival Center Columbia Road NW, D.C., 7 p.m., $50 to $ Enjoy Palestinian food, art and performance at the dinner that kicks off the Rooted in Resistance: Here Eternally festival weekend, organized by the Museum of the Palestinian People. Alongside dinner, guests can experience live music, spoken word, dance, art and a moderated panel, with proceeds supporting the museum. More to explore: Jazz in the Garden at the National Gallery of Art Sculpture Garden D.C’s Best comedy showcase at Hotbed Saturday Poet Life Fest at Gateway DC pavilion Martin Luther King Jr. Ave. SE, D.C., Noon, free Part of a weeklong lineup of events, Poet Life Fest is a family-friendly, daylong experience for attendees to enjoy performances of poetry and music, plus vendors, food trucks and community. Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park South Capitol St. SE, D.C., 4:05 p.m. As the Washington Nationals play the Arizona Diamondbacks, Nationals Park will transform into Hogwarts for Harry Potter Day. There will be a themed photo booth, painters, balloon artists, caricaturists and a potion-making station. “Pippin” at Signature Theatre Campbell Ave., Arlington, VA, 8 p.m. Signature Theatre will stage its final showings of “Pippin,” a coming-of-age musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Schwartz. A traveling troupe of performers takes the audience through the story of Pippin, the restless heir of Charlemagne, on his quest for purpose. More to explore: “The Sound of Music” screening at the National Gallery of Art “CrazySexyCool” matinee at Arena Stage (includes child care) Ringside wrestling at Anthem Row Sunday District Vibes at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library G St. NW, D.C., 1 p.m., free (through Sept. 27) The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library is celebrating America’s 250th birthday with “District Vibes / American Pride: How D.C. Changed American Culture.” The exhibit focuses on the contributions of D.C. to America, from the football hurdle to the modern blood bank. More to explore: District Fringe at the University of District Columbia Piña Colada Festival at Colada Shop

stories.title: Suspicion and Doubt at the National Civics Contest
stories.author: Sam Fortier
stories.summary: America’s finest young scholars competed to mark their country's birthday. It led to a disputed finish in the age of mistrust.
stories.content: Aangad Singh, 15, competes in the Presidential Award competition. Jalani Morgan for NOTUS The morning after the competition, Aangad Singh's family was trying to figure out what went wrong. They were walking through the National Museum of Natural History, going over answers, doing the math. “It doesn’t make sense,” said his mother, Ramandeep. Ramandeep was good at numbers. But she couldn’t make them explain how her 15-year-old son had missed the top three in the Presidential Award competition, the civics contest for high schoolers that President Donald Trump’s party planners had created to celebrate America’s 250th birthday. She had watched the first round, when the field was whittled from 20 to eight, and the second round, when it went from eight to three. There was celebrity host Mario Lopez, an exclusive broadcast deal with CBS and a Kennedy Center stage that mixed game show spectacle with civic pageantry. The only thing missing was a scoreboard. She told herself not to complain. She didn’t want to be that mom, a sore loser whose kid could never fail. On their way out, though, other parents kept stopping them. “Shocked,” said more than one. Later, a boy stopped her and said a group of contestants had kept score themselves. “We thought he won,” the boy said. She approached an official from the Department of Education, which had helped run the contest, and asked for the final scores. “Proprietary,” the official said. In the museum, Ramandeep furrowed her brow. “How did they count the numbers?” she said. “That’s something we need to understand.” “We can only find out when they telecast it,” said her husband, Bhalindar. Ramandeep pursed her lips. The broadcast was three weeks away. -S3410642- - ©Doug Coulter (1).jpg ( , AR: 1.78)It wasn’t like them to feel skeptical. She and Bhalindar were Indian immigrants whose trust in the American system had led to degrees, careers and citizenship. They bought a four-bedroom Colonial in a quiet Connecticut city and sent their kids to public school. They passed their faith in the United States down to Aangad, who won awards for his speeches about the country’s founding ideals. But now they, like so many others, were wondering whether the game was rigged. It was a reluctant half-step into the age of suspicion. The U.S. was just one of many democratic nations riding the same wave of paranoia, with polls showing trust in major institutions at or near all-time lows. In America, the president questioned whether the elections were free and fair as citizens sank deeper into the embrace of their tribes. The world’s leading deepfake expert told The New York Times that he no longer trusted his own eyes, that our whole visual system was on the verge of collapse. And just as the Singhs were walking the halls of the museum, senators and Trump judicial appointees on Capitol Hill were sparring over the results of a presidential election that happened six years ago. Aangad’s parents didn’t want to accuse anyone of fixing the competition. But they felt compelled to ask questions because their son never would. When his mother had dropped him off for his first day of kindergarten, he did not cry, even though she could tell he wanted to. For years the story served as a tidy summation of her son, a rule follower who hid his emotions, an intellectual who didn’t mind having more books than friends. But at some point she had figured out how to tell he was upset: He would take little sips of water over and over again. Shortly after noon, the Singhs left the museum and went to a café. When Aangad opened the door, he ran into the blond girl from Wyoming, Miriam Washut, who he was pretty sure had won the whole thing. She must be headed to the White House for the special tour of the Oval Office, he thought. Her father, wearing a black cowboy hat, stuck out his hand. “You did extremely well,” he said. “Thank you,” Aangad said. P20260610MR- (1) copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.78)Aangad turned to Miriam, whose eyes dropped to the floor. Her voice pitched up. She waved her hands at her sides. “That was insane,” she said. “You clearly knew everything.” Aangad nodded, blank, and Miriam’s family went on their way. Aangad walked over to his parents’ table. “What did she say?” his father asked. “That I should have won,” Aangad said. No one said anything for a long time. Aangad took a small sip of water. * * * Three weeks later, Aangad’s family took positions in the living room. His dad was on one couch, laptop open to a spreadsheet titled “1776_Broadcast_Audit.” His mother was on the edge of the other couch, drumming her right foot like a kick pedal. Aangad was between them, lying on a recliner with his feet up, talking quietly to his little sister. On the side table was a black metal water bottle. He had just filled it. They were at his uncle’s house in suburban Toronto, where they vacationed every year. Ramandeep and her brother had grown up on a farm in India. They didn't go back much; they liked how little their kids knew about homesteading. Now, the siblings were competing to see who could own the biggest house in North America, and her brother, a hardware engineer, was winning. Ramandeep had done everything to help her kids get ahead, too, including giving them names that started with two As in part so they'd always be first in alphabetical lists at school. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM017 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM055 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)“It began online with the Impossible Civics Test,” Mario Lopez said on TV, and everyone in the room stopped talking. CBS didn’t show the round of 20. And it cut the opening speech from Education Secretary Linda McMahon. “There is hope for the next 50 years that the flame of liberty still burns bright in the next generation,” she had said. "The great American story is still being written by you.” They’d hoped the broadcast would include a live scoreboard, so they could see where things went wrong. But the first segment sped by without one. “Why aren’t they showing scores?” his uncle asked. Then the second segment sped by too. “What’s the score?” Aangad said, looking at his dad. “I don’t know,” his dad said. The show was going too fast and the commentary in the living room was too loud for him to keep up. Aangad knew he’d been behind at this point. He’d won the buzzer race only once in eight questions. But the final two segments were far more valuable, and he knew he’d done well. On TV, Mario Lopez introduced the third segment: Each contestant would stand alone at the lectern to answer a multipart question about the U.S. Constitution. Then each of the five judges would grade it. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM086 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad watched the contestants. The boy from Michigan got a full 20 points. The girl from Washington did too. So did the girl from Wyoming. “According to Article 3 of the U.S. Constitution, in which cases do the federal courts have jurisdiction?” the proctor said to Aangad on TV. “List at least four for full credit.” As he answered, little summary boxes popped up on screen. “Maritime jurisdiction.” Green. “Parties of state and citizens of another state.” Red. “What?” Aangad said on the couch, his voice sharp. He got two more green boxes, then another red: “Case with state and foreign nation.” “What?” he said again. He handed his dad his phone. He’d pulled up the Constitution and highlighted a paragraph with the phrases “between a State and Citizens of another State” and “between a State, or the Citizens thereof, and foreign States, Citizens or Subjects.” “Read this, read this, read this, read this right now,” Aangad said. His dad read it. “It’s within the Constitution,” he said. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM038 copy.jpg ( , AR: 2.02)At the end of the segment, a scoreboard flashed onscreen. Michigan was first with 23 points. Aangad was sixth with 16. He took a sip from his water bottle. “They just made this whole thing for show,” his uncle said. “They know who they want to win.” The final challenge was a lightning round. Each contestant had 30 seconds to answer as many questions as possible, and each correct answer was worth two points. Michigan got 10 right. Washington, 10. Wyoming, 10. Then Aangad came to the stage. The first question flashed on the monitor: “Which amendment ended slavery?” Aangad answered. Incorrect. “Thirteenth!” Aangad cried on the couch. “I said Thirteenth!” After that, TV Aangad started flying. All the nights he and his dad had practiced the lightning round were paying off. He processed questions nearly instantly and answered almost without thinking. The screen said +2, +2, +2. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM097 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad got one more wrong. But watching from the couch, he didn’t protest. He saw now the judges had wanted a more technical answer. In the end, the judges marked 12 answers correct. Aangad concluded they must have thought he pronounced thirteenth like fourteenth. “I say that TH irteenth like an ‘F’ sound.” Later, he’d feel validated when he realized the auto-generated subtitles said “thirteenth.” Before Mario Lopez revealed the top three, he walked around the stage and interviewed every contestant. Aangad gave a polished answer about being proud to share his knowledge of the nation’s founding principles. The girl from Washington was brought to tears again. A boy from Arizona said winning would mean everything: “I’ve always wanted to meet the man, the myth, the legend — Donald Trump!” After the finalists were announced, Aangad watched Michigan, Washington and Wyoming take center stage. On TV, he calmly applauded. On the couch, he picked up his water bottle and took a big gulp. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM068 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) * * * Aangad’s family watched the rest of the program in relative quiet. Miriam from Wyoming won, just as Aangad had suspected, and then the finalists took a trip to the White House. They stood by the Resolute Desk, a snapshot of Trump’s education agenda. Miriam was homeschooled. The boy from Michigan attended a private Catholic school. The girl from Washington, who went to public school, had told CNN that she supported Trump and believed the most important thing was “everyone walking away from the competition knowing this is the greatest country of the world.” In the Oval Office, she told the president she wanted to go to Hillsdale College. “Hillsdale?” Aangad’s father said. “Republican college,” Aangad reminded him. They’d been on campus in Michigan last month for the American Legion’s National Oratorical Contest. The school had donated $10 million to the president’s Freedom committee and helped develop its history programs. “I can give you a recommendation,” the president said to the girl. “I think we should get you in.” SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM104 (1) copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.00)The finalists left with two commemorative coins, one of which said “THE FINAL MISSION,” a reference to the education secretary’s promise to “sunset a 46-year-old, $3 trillion failed federal education bureaucracy in Washington, D.C.” Then the broadcast ended. “You could have been there,” Aangad’s father said. Everyone let his words hang in the air. * * * Over a late dinner of curry chicken, two factions began to form. Aangad and his father thought the judges must just be incompetent or mistaken. Aangad’s mother and uncle suspected a conspiracy: Someone had not wanted the brown kid in the turban to represent the youth of America in the Oval Office. His uncle advised them to go directly to the Education Department. “The whole point is to initiate the investigation,” he said. “They may have some kind of intention that these people shouldn’t be there,” his mother said. “You don’t know that,” Aangad replied. “You’re just assuming.” Aangad spooned out more chicken and rice. “I personally think that they just had faulty sources,” he said. Discussion turned to the five judges. They were all teachers from across the country who were past recipients of the prestigious James Madison Memorial Fellowship to study the Constitution. At least three of them must have mistakenly graded the constitutional answers as incorrect, Aangad said, and it seemed likely to him that they hadn’t memorized Article 3 as well as he had. Or maybe his answers didn’t match the phrasing on their rubrics. “That shows ineptness,” he said. After tiramisu, Ramandeep made an impassioned case for justice. She didn’t care about the share of $ , in scholarship money, she said. She wanted recognition for Aangad’s hard work. And if the system really was biased, they had to fight on behalf of every kid who could be hurt by it. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM107 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)“But we don’t know if it’s systemic,” Bhalindar replied. He defended trusting the system, trusting the nation’s founding documents, which he had devoted hours to helping their son study. A few bad judges don’t undermine an entire system. Aangad’s uncle had gone to bed. Aangad was on the couch, eyes closed. If they made a strong case, Bhalindar said, maybe the Education Department would admit its mistake. Ramandeep doubted they’d even get a response. She was equally pessimistic that they could get anywhere by filing a lawsuit. “We will not be able to afford to fight against the system.” On that point, Bhalindar had to agree. The best strategy, Ramandeep said, was media attention. They could present their findings and let the public decide. "That's your power," she said, turning to me. This was uncomfortable. Weeks earlier, as I looked for a way to write about America’s 250th, the Education Department had recommended I reach out to the Singhs. I then followed Aangad through the competition, not knowing if he would even advance. Now, their predicament felt like a window into something bigger: If the government or the courts couldn’t bring them justice, then maybe, they thought, the media could. All I could do was write what happened. But the Fourth Estate was another institution at low ebbs in trust and influence, and Bhalindar knew it. He doubted the government would bow to media pressure. “At least our story is in front of the public,” Ramandeep said. “That’s our closure.” “‘Closure’ is the right word,” Bhalindar said, and just before midnight, all out of words, he reassured his wife that they would figure this out together. She gave him a tired smile and went upstairs. Bhalindar sat on the couch for a while and looked at the dark TV. * * * The only way to know whether the system was fair was to test it. So, back home in Connecticut, Bhalindar used a chatbot to find lawyers with experience in federal education, federal agencies and administrative law. “Dear Counsel,” he wrote to them, “I am seeking a confidential initial consultation regarding a potential dispute.” He attached a packet of evidence that included their calculation of the final scores. Michigan, 43. Wyoming, 42. Washington, 41. Aangad, 40. If either of Aangad’s “incorrect” answers had been scored correctly, his father argued, he would’ve finished in the top three. “I am looking for counsel who can objectively evaluate the facts, advise on preservation of evidence and procedure, and determine whether there is a viable legal or administrative path forward,” Bhalindar wrote. Aangad moved on. He followed the U.S. in the World Cup and enjoyed fireworks on the Fourth of July. He didn’t see Miriam, the girl from Wyoming, tell her local newspaper that she was surprised by who made the top three. He didn’t see the Education Department use Miriam’s homeschooling as a cudgel in the culture war. His dad would email the Department of Education to ask for a review, and then ask again, and hear nothing back. His belief in the system would remain steadfast, though he’d wish someone would acknowledge his requests. The Education Department would tell NOTUS that the competition questions were “developed, judged, and scored independently by the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation.” The foundation would not respond to a detailed list of questions. Meanwhile, Aangad focused on the future. He made videos about public speaking and wrote a speech about Sikhism and looked into the U.S. Senate Youth Program. He geared up for junior year and tried to figure out what to study in college. Law, maybe? Anything but medicine, for sure; blood made him queasy. But first, he would accept an award from the Connecticut American Legion. His winning speech had focused on the dangers of civic ignorance. As long as people have the power to make choices, he said, democracies are a series of infinite crossroads. The Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Federalist Papers — they embody these crossroads. And on the nation's 250th anniversary, Aangad urged his fellow Americans to choose to learn their history before a tyrant defined their rights for them. He stood in a suit at a lectern at the front of a ballroom. The audience was mostly old, white men, but the traditional American Legion caps they wore were shaped like Aangad’s red turban. 20260517_Connecticut_Aangad Singh_JAB3324 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad told the crowd his favorite article in the Constitution was Article 3, Section 3, which in three sentences established a high bar for what could be considered treason against the United States. “It truly is extraordinary how our founders had incredible foresight, and the various methods to which our Constitution attempts to integrate its people into government,” he said. The people applauded. Aangad stepped back and nodded. He hadn’t brought any water with him. He didn’t need it now.

stories.title: Smithsonian Director Defends U.S. History Museum Against Republican Attacks
stories.author: Eric Katz
stories.summary: Lawmakers say the museum should not focus on the negatives of American history.
stories.content: Anthea Hartig, Director of the National Museum of American History, rebutted Republicans' accusations that the Smithsonian Institution is an “ideological” political organization. Jacquelyn Martin/AP “History is incredibly challenging,” the director of the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of American History testified in the House, rebutting the Republican-led effort to reshape what the nation’s government-sponsored museums say about America. For two hours Tuesday, Anthea Hartig a hostile panel of Republican lawmakers who cast the Smithsonian Institution as an “ideological” political organization and aired what they saw as perceived slights against the founding fathers, cultural icons and conservative ideas contained in the museum’s galleries. Hartig pushed back, saying the museum "tries to reflect the richness of our history" without advancing any political agenda. “If we tell it in its richness, we absolutely, I think, have objects that can make people uncomfortable,” Hartig said. She continued, “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic, it’s for me to determine what’s accurate.” Republicans during the hearing largely focused on specific exhibits and merchandise within the museum they found controversial, including a display centered on the U.S. entertainment industry and another on girls going through puberty. They grew increasingly frustrated throughout the hearing after accusing Hartig of deflecting from their most pointed questions. “You have pictures of bondage,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), who chaired Tuesday’s Delivering on Government Efficiency subcommittee hearing, said before a poster board displaying some items and photographs featured in the museum. “You have some overtly sexual things up there. You have transgender folks, I assume that’s what they are.” Rep. Nancy Mace, (R-South Carolina), focused her questions more explicitly. “My staff tells me this little trinket around the penis, this is BDSM in a setting where children are walking through,” she said. “That's disgusting. Like, what kind of message are you trying to send to kids with BDSM imagery?” Hartig said the puberty exhibit was not designed for children and contained a warning about its contents. After the hearing, Burchett told NOTUS that Congress should withhold funds from the Smithsonian but speculated leadership is not “going to do a dadgum thing.” He he would talk to the Smithsonian Board of Regents, composed of Vice President JD Vance, lawmakers from both parties and others, to voice his concerns. Shortly after taking office last year, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at “restoring truth and sanity to American history” that prohibited Smithsonian exhibits that "divide Americans based on race.” In subsequent letters to the institution, the White House requested all descriptions and plans for current and upcoming exhibits to ensure compliance with new policies. While the agency is only partially government funded, Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought noted he could withhold funds if the Smithsonian did not comply with Trump’s order and document production requests. On July 4, the White House issued a report finding the American history museum strayed from its mission and has become a “political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” It accused the museum of demonstrating activism toward “illegal aliens,” transgender individuals and against white Americans. The Trump administration has also directed the National Park Service to remove signage and displays it deemed as promoting diversity, equity and inclusion, though those efforts have been held up in ongoing legal disputes. Hartig, who is set to testify again on Wednesday before the House Administration Committee, rejected the White House’s findings, arguing they contained several inaccuracies. She said she takes the White House’s concerns seriously, but noted the report erroneously suggested that several pieces of U.S. history were not on display, including passages from the Declaration of Independence, a uniform and writing desk belonging to George Washington and celebrations of the country’s 250th anniversary. “We unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum,” Hartig said. “There is always room for improvement, but I also know the beauty and the inspiration and the expertise that lies in our collections, our exhibits and our programming.” David Blight, a history professor at Yale University who also testified at the hearing, similarly castigated the White House for its report. “The recent report by the White House Domestic Policy Council is nothing less than a declaration of political war on the historian's profession, as well as on the freedom and curiosity of anyone who reads,” Blight said. “In other words, President Trump has declared war on free minds and free education.” Republicans, meanwhile, repeatedly criticized the museum for its exhibits on slavery, saying it should focus on efforts to abolish the practice rather than its horrors. Democrats chided Republicans for holding the hearing, saying they were looking to erase key parts of U.S. history. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) called it a “white pride rally disguised as a congressional hearing.” Other Democrats questioned the majority’s intentions. “I think what’s actually happening is not that you don't want ideology in the museum,” said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Virginia). “You want your ideology in the museum.”

stories.title: What $1 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (With a Pool!)
stories.author: Rebecca Ritzel
stories.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
stories.content: Courtesy of Garland Gay It’s summer, D.C. is steamier than a crab pot, and even casual Zillow browsers might be thinking: If only I could step straight out my door and into a pool. For NOTUS’ inaugural D/M/V real estate column, we found listings in the District, Maryland and Virginia that, for a million dollars, will make that dream a backyard reality. One caveat: Getting a pool of your own in the District isn’t easy for a cool million. (Although, for $15 million, this seven-bedroom compound in Georgetown comes with a courtyard pool.) So, we found what we think is the closest thing. Here are three homes we found priced at a million dollars and ideal for anyone prioritizing pool access as they house-hunt. (Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.) D.C. The listing: Sutton Place NW, Unit D The price: $ , Untitled The specifics: A two-bedroom, two-story, three-bathroom townhome with a private courtyard. Built in but recently renovated with fresh paint and white trim throughout. The pool: Shared between just 42 homes, the Sutton Place pool is perfect for splashing, lap-swimming or relaxing. Be sure to budget for $ a month in condo fees. Sell us on it: “Private community pools are a rarity in Northwest, D.C., especially for homes around the $1 million price point,” said Northgate real estate agent Ilse Padron, who also noted the location is “just minutes from Cathedral Commons, Georgetown, downtown D.C. and some of the city's top public and private schools.” Maryland The listing: Putters Ct, Upper Marlboro, Md. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: The former third home for a family of jet-setters, this property functions like a year-round resort, with an outdoor pool to enjoy in the summer. Prefer the après-ski lifestyle? You’ll enjoy the patio jacuzzi, indoor sauna and multiple fireplaces. The walk-out finished basement currently houses a gym, perfect for a pre-swim workout. There’s no HOA fees, but the Marlton Golf Club is just on the other side of the woods for anyone who wants to hit the greens. (Hence the road name, Putter’s Court.) The pool: Surrounded by a wrought-iron fence, and with woods rimming the nearly four-acre lot, the pool feels extra private. There’s a lengthy shelf perfect for splashing toddlers, and on the opposite side, built-in bar stools for adult swim. Sell us on it: “I can’t believe this home is still on the market,” said broker Tina Marie Marshall, adding: “The owners kept it immaculate. We barely had to stage it, this is how they lived.” Virginia The listing: Annandale Road, Falls Church, Va. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: Who needs a large house when you have a pool house? This modest, three-bedroom, brick Cape Cod is all business in the front yard and party in the back. A stone patio connects the main house with a pool house, creating additional year-round space for noisy kids or a quiet work-from-home office, depending on your family’s needs. The pool: Surrounded by willow trees and other lush landscaping, this in-ground pool has a new companion salt-water spa in . Sell us on it: “You're not just buying a house; you're buying an excuse to cancel your vacation plans,” said Compass listing agent Ana Maria Menendez. “You're going to be … wondering why you ever paid resort prices when your own backyard feels better.”

stories.title: Welcome to NOTUS Metro
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: A view of the U.S. Capitol building in Washington DC. (Mark Alfred/NOTUS) Mark Alfred/NOTUS Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A welcome, a scathing audit, free buses (maybe) and the AJ Dybantsa hype train. HELLO! Welcome to NOTUS’ daily newsletter focused on all things D.C. We’re building Washington’s next great newsroom, and over the past two months, we’ve formed a team of local reporters to cover news, sports, food and all the quirks and curiosities that make our region tick. Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman will keep you in the know and set the tone for your day. We’d love to hear from you! Send us an email or ping us on social media — let us know what you’re interested in, what you’d like to see us cover and what we might be missing. THE LATEST Add a scathing audit to the mountain of problems plaguing D.C.’s housing authority, which has also struggled to address poor housing conditions, leadership turnover and a recent cyberattack . Auditors from the D.C. inspector general’s office, who released their findings last week, couldn't verify how much money the agency had, or where it was, to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars, according to NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright. The housing authority also didn’t adequately protect millions of dollars in bank deposits, and there were signs that money designated for certain federal programs may have been used for other purposes, the audit found. The mistakes could have serious implications. The housing authority, which receives a significant amount of its funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, submitted “material misstatements” to the federal government, the report said. The agency did not dispute the findings. It is working to remedy the issues, many of which were repeated from last year, and noted that a transition to new accounting software exacerbated some of them. DEEP DIVE Where are D.C.’s free buses? District leaders, including Mayor Muriel Bowser and council member Charles Allen , have tried for years to make it happen. It’s never stuck. Janeese Lewis George (who’s all but certain to be D.C.’s next mayor) wants to make the Metrobus free for SNAP recipients, who already get a 50% discount. She’s not ruling out eventually making it free for all, her campaign told Zara. Will it happen? It’s not just a District decision, since WMATA is a multistate agency, and JLG would need to find the revenue. WMATA relies on bus fares for 10% of its passenger revenue, but only 1 in 4 riders paid to board this May. In May , it was 3 in 4. Rather than writing that off, WMATA is cracking down. The agency asked bus operators to start quoting the fare again as riders board — something drivers say can lead to violence. Expect a debate next year once a new mayor is sworn in, Allen told NOTUS. FROM THE DISTRICT D.C.’s cyclist community gathered at East Potomac Park over the weekend to protest President Donald Trump’s planned renovations there, NBC4 reports . Protestors also rallied outside an old hospital campus in Southeast D.C., worried it will be redeveloped into an ICE facility, WTOP reports . Three people were arrested after a car crash near D.C.’s World War II Memorial, including two people who stopped to help the driver but were later picked up on drug charges, ABC7 reports . FROM VIRGINIA Vice President JD Vance is reportedly moving into a second home in Middleburg. The affluent Loudoun County town has mixed feelings about its newest resident, The Washington Post finds . FROM MARYLAND Ten people were hospitalized , and a Tesla Cybertruck was cut in half, in a Silver Spring collision Saturday that involved at least 11 vehicles, WTOP reports . D.C. TRIVIA Which president was famous for skinny-dipping in the Potomac River? James Madison John Quincy Adams Teddy Roosevelt Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter. SPORTS The AJ Dybantsa hype is real, with Wizards owner Ted Leonsis going so far as to compare the NBA’s No. 1 overall pick to an all-time great. "What I was impressed with was when we introduce him to people, he makes eye contact, he asks, 'What's his name?' Shakes his hand. He's a very magnanimous personality," Leonsis told ESPN . "It reminded me, I hate to say this, of Alex Ovechkin , where he just lights up the room.” Josiah Gray may have been forgotten by many Nationals fans, but he’s still fighting to get back on the mound. NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty has the exclusive interview. What to Watch Today Nationals at Rockies, 8:40 p.m., MLB.TV Mystics at Valkyries, 10 p.m. Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Jeff Dooley and Nikie Johnson. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com .

stories.title: Will Free Buses Ever Arrive in D.C.?
stories.author: Zara Norman
stories.summary: Janeese Lewis George wants to make the metrobus free for residents on SNAP, but that "doesn’t need to be where we end."
stories.content: The Alexandria Transit Company (DASH) has figured out how to make buses free for all residents. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Janeese Lewis George, who is all but sure to become the D.C.’s next mayor , wants to make the Metrobus free for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. “A bus system that’s free for people on SNAP would mean residents in all eight wards, no matter their economic status or background, would be able to get to jobs, grocery stores, medical appointments, community gatherings, and social events,” her campaign told NOTUS in a statement. If that comes to pass, Lewis George won’t rule out eventually expanding “the universe of people receiving free transit” if and when revenue is available. “I see SNAP recipients as a good place to start but it doesn’t need to be where we end,” her campaign wrote. It’s not the first time the District has floated free bus access for residents, more than 70% of whom already evade the fare, a Metro board member said during a May meeting . Mayor Muriel Bowser once made the Circulator service free, but that didn’t stick . The city already offers kids free rides and gives discounts to government employees and those receiving SNAP . Neighboring cities like Baltimore and Alexandria , Virginia, have figured out how to make buses free for all residents — so, why not D.C.? For starters, Alexandria and Baltimore receive state money to operate their buses, while the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority is a multistate agency without a dedicated revenue stream. When D.C. Council member Charles Allen, chair of the District’s transportation committee, proposed a monthly $ credit on every D.C. resident’s Metro card in to fund city transit, Maryland and Virginia nixed the idea. Allen’s bill passed without the credit, but did implement 24-hour bus service. He told NOTUS that he had hoped the credit could remedy D.C.’s “upside down” transit-benefit system. “The overwhelming majority of people with transit benefits have high-paying jobs,” he said. “The majority of low-wage workers do not have a transit subsidy.” That’s the demographic Lewis George is targeting with her proposal, which her campaign told NOTUS does not yet have a revenue source. Still, Allen called the idea “incredibly achievable” given that SNAP recipients already get a 50% discount. Some transportation advocates argue that free buses should not be the focus of transportation reform. Alex Baca, the D.C. policy director at Greater Greater Washington, said increasing bus frequency and reliability are better targets. “It doesn’t really matter if the bus is free if it doesn’t show up,” she told NOTUS. Though bus fares accounted for 10% of WMATA’s total passenger revenue in the first quarter of fiscal year , the agency says fares are a key part of its ability to deliver services. Fare evasion leads to around $50 million in lost revenue annually, Metro estimates . While Metrobus ridership has largely recovered since the COVID-19 pandemic, fare payment has not. The bus saw 10.4 million boardings in May, but only one in four of those trips were paid for. Compare that with May : 10.9 million boardings, but three in four trips paid for. boost revenue, WMATA introduced a policy in May requiring bus drivers to quote the fare as riders board. Operators aren’t happy . “Chasing down fare evaders isn't going to solve the systemic budget shortfalls that WMATA or other systems in the country ,” said Ben Lynn, a spokesperson for the local union representing more than 15, regional transit workers. Quoting the fare can lead to disputes, which sometimes end in violence, Lynn said. D.C. recorded assaults on bus operators this past fiscal year and the year prior, according to data a WMATA spokesperson shared with NOTUS. Al Clements, an operator who lives in southeast D.C. but drives Alexandria’s DASH bus, almost quit his job after one such confrontation. It was , and he’d just quoted a rider the fare. “He talked to me real crazy, he called me all kinds,” Clements said. “We was going down the road, and he just kept verbally abusing me. Sitting right there in that first seat.” Since DASH went fare-free in , Clements said he doesn’t have to worry about riders getting embarrassed or agitated and confronting him. “It went from ‘F you,’ and ‘you an A-hole’ to ‘I appreciate you,’ ‘thank you,’” Clements said. “It makes the job a lot more tolerable.” _C0A4629 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)DASH ridership has increased from 3.77 million boardings in to 5.67 million last year. Assaults on bus operators have fallen “dramatically” in that time, said Raymond Mui, DASH’s chief infrastructure and development officer. There were two incidents recorded last year, as compared to nine in . “We made public transit as easy to use and as carefree to use as a public sidewalk, or as an elevator, or as a park, or as a library,” Mui told NOTUS. But going fare-free didn’t come at the expense of frequency or reliability, Mui said. The city has been able to get people on and off the bus much faster, meaning the bus travels faster, too. “We were able to speed our buses up, increase our services and get more bang for the buck for the community,” Mui said. Alexandria is a fraction of D.C.’s size and serves a fraction of its population, but leaders in the District think there’s a way to eventually roll out free access citywide. The route to that reality will begin if and when Lewis George is sworn in and makes her push to bring free transit to SNAP recipients. “It’s absolutely a goal that she and I share,” Allen said. “It’s something I want to do. It’s something we’ve been working on different ways to get at.”

stories.title: Josiah Gray Still Wants to Help the Nats. Maybe Even This Year.
stories.author: Jesse Dougherty
stories.summary: Once the of the Nationals’ rebuild, the 28-year-old pitcher is nearing a comeback after two years of injury rehab.
stories.content: Nationals pitcher Josiah Gray hasn't played in a major league game since April of . (AP Photo/John McDonnell) John McDonnell/AP For a while there, all Nationals fans had to get excited about were debuts. Or, to parrot the social media hype machine, all they had to get excited about were DEBUTS. There was Keibert Ruiz and CJ Abrams, MacKenzie Gore and Cade Cavalli, Jackson Rutledge and Brady House, James Wood and Dylan Crews, DJ Herz and Robert Hassell III, Daylen Lile and Jake Irvin. For the darkest days, there was Blake Rutherford. For the waiver nerds, Alex Call. For the sickest of sickos, Jake Alu. But before all of them was Josiah Gray, who debuted for the Nats on Aug. 2, — when, maybe more than ever, fans needed a sign that things might eventually be OK again (heavy emphasis on might). Three days earlier, he had arrived in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner trade, which had capped a deadline fire sale that saw eight veterans go out and 12 unproven players come in. Gray was, in turn, the roster’s first public of the rebuild. And because of that, he would answer so many questions about patience, about sticking with a broken club, about what it would take for an odd collection of dreamers and has-beens to eventually play respectable baseball. Sign up for our Metro Newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region. And he pitched, of course, at one point so well that he was an All Star in . And then he basically disappeared. “Man, where to even begin …” Gray said to me over the phone last week. He picked up the call from South Florida, where he’s spent the better part of the last two years and three months, stretching and throwing and eating quiet breakfasts at the Nationals’ team facility, marooned. Because for that entire time, he’s been trying to get back from injury, first with a long recovery from Tommy John surgery, now after a devastating setback at the end of spring training. He last pitched in the majors on April 4, , when some of the fielders behind him were Joey Gallo, Jesse Winker, Trey Lipscomb and Ildemaro Vargas. But after throwing off a bullpen mound in West Palm Beach on July 10 , Gray, 28, feels closer to a return than he has in a good while. “When it’s been this long, it can be hard not to feel like you’re forgotten about,” Gray said. “But that’s one of the things that you just try to not let build up in your head.
