Safe & Affordable D.C. has raised and spent more than $1.5 million – largely from unions – to run ads and mailers attacking McDuffie; the local chapter of the Sierra Club has $ , of its own. On McDuffie’s side, People for a United D.C., another independent expenditure group, has raised and spent more than $ , against Lewis George, while Opportunity D.C., a pro-business committee, has also raised $ , . For context, Lewis George and McDuffie, both of whom are participating in the city’s public financing program for candidates, have each pulled in more than $3 million for their own campaigns. In that program, candidates cannot accept more than $ from any individual, and donations coming from D.C. residents are matched 5-to-1 with public funds. When a NOTUS reporter asked McDuffie whether he could pledge to D.C. voters that his campaign has not coordinated with the outside groups supporting his campaign – the very charge Lewis George has – he responded: “Unequivocally. Yes. I could tell voters that. And there's been no allegations of such, either.”

stories.title: This Lawyer Spent Years Fighting His $100 D.C. Speeding Ticket
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle
stories.summary: Matt Ricciardi got the citation tossed out by the D.C. Court of Appeals. His victory could benefit other drivers.
stories.content: Matt Ricciardi’s successful argument against his ticket revolved around a flaw in the margin of error. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS When Matt Ricciardi was caught on camera speeding along a stretch of D.C. Route , he could simply have paid the $ ticket and gone on with his life. Instead, the D.C.-based attorney chose a far lengthier route: He appealed, and appealed again, and appealed once more after that. The decision paid off. In May, the D.C. Court of Appeals — the city’s highest court — tossed out his speeding ticket on a novel technicality, ending a three-year legal odyssey. But the ruling also opened the door for potentially thousands of other drivers to contest tickets handed out by the city’s many speed cameras. “The case wasn’t about the $ citation,” Ricciardi said. “I pursued it because I believed that the District was wrongly citing tens of thousands of area drivers at a higher speed than it could prove.” Ricciardi’s case taps into a daily challenge for many area motorists: navigating the District’s extensive network of traffic cameras, more than of them , which catch drivers speeding, running red lights, blocking bus-only lanes or illegally passing stopped school buses. Proponents argue that the cameras are a key tool in improving roadway safety for pedestrians and cyclists, while critics — including House Republicans, who have tried to ban the city’s use of the cameras — say they’re a money grab. From October to September — the last fiscal year for which full data is available — the city’s traffic cameras led to more than 3.3 million tickets, and took in more than $ million in fines. When Ricciardi first got the speeding ticket in the mail in April , he saw he was cited for driving 61 miles per hour with a speed limit of 50. The city’s speed cameras — of which there are more than — traditionally flag a driver that is 11 miles over the posted limit. Fines start at $ and increase according to designated ranges — $ for 16-20 and so on. Ricciardi’s successful argument against his ticket revolved around the flaws in that formula. His fight was aided by his knowledge of the law and a background in computer programming. “I recognized instantly that the speed measurements can’t be perfectly accurate. There has to be some margin of error,” he said. “That prompted me to look at the [camera’s] deployment log, which had the margin of error, and to look at what the District’s burden of proof was. It was the technical recognition that there was a margin of error problem that kicked it off.” Ricciardi found that D.C.’s speed cameras have a margin of error of plus or minus 1 mph and that the city needs “clear and convincing evidence” that a driver was speeding to issue a ticket. Ricciardi didn’t contest that he may have been driving above the posted speed limit of 50. But he argued that the camera’s margin of error meant that the city couldn’t actually prove he was going 61 miles an hour as claimed. He could just as well have been driving 60. traffic_camera_edits/_C0A2314 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) His argument didn’t convince an appeal officer at the D.C. Department of Motor Vehicles, nor did it later sway the Traffic Adjudication Appeals Board. It did, however, win over a judge in D.C. Superior Court, at least temporarily — that decision was reversed when the city appealed it. And so he found himself arguing his case to the Court of Appeals in late November , 31 months after he received the ticket. On May 7, the high court took his side. “The District did not present clear and convincing evidence that Ricciardi was traveling 61 mph or above because its evidence showed only that he was traveling between 60 and 62 mph, making it just as likely that he was traveling beneath the 61 mph threshold as above it,” wrote Associate Judge Joshua Deahl, dismissing the ticket and $ fine. Ricciardi’s win is noteworthy, but so too is the simple fact that he got as far as the Court of Appeals. When the court heard a similar case in , it noted that such challenges to tickets from D.C.’s traffic cameras are “vanishingly rare.” Data from the DMV bears that out — only 15% of D.C. traffic camera tickets are regularly appealed, largely because the grounds for appeal can be limited and, Ricciardi said, the process can be opaque. “There’s probably people lost in the process,” he said. “I had an advantage being an attorney doing litigation, but an average driver might be intimidated. It’s not a user-friendly process.” In a statement, the D.C. Department of Transportation — which runs the traffic cameras — said the ruling in Ricciardi’s case was largely the case of regulations that haven’t kept pace with the technology. According to an official, the cameras actually have a much smaller margin of error than they did when they were first rolled out almost two decades ago. “[Traffic camera] enforcement continues to be an effective tool for reducing dangerous driving and improving compliance with posted speed limits,” the official said. “DDOT is reviewing regulatory and administrative changes to accurately reflect the current state of operations and standards.” Ward 6 Council member Charles Allen, who chairs the Council’s transportation committee, said that despite their unpopularity, the cameras are important for keeping the city safe. traffic_camera_edits/_C0A2280 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) “Nobody likes to get a ticket,” Allen said. “The overwhelming majority of people when they get one they change their behavior and drive safer. And that’s what it’s gotta be about. We’ve got to be able to have the tools to do enforcement for these repeated dangerous drivers who don’t seem to give a damn.” Ricciardi said he wasn’t trying to make a broader case about the merits of traffic cameras, but rather hoped to ensure tickets and fines are assessed fairly. “It was never my motivation to get out of the ticket and I don’t want the case to encourage people to drive recklessly, and I don’t think the decision encourages that,” he said. “The court didn’t say speed cameras are invalid, they said if you’re at the bottom of the [speed] range the District needs to charge the lower one.” On a practical level, that means that a driver caught going 16 mph over the speed limit and fined $ could now argue that margin of error would have put them at 15 over, qualifying them for a $ fine instead. Or, like Ricciardi, a driver fined $ for going 11 mph over the limit could argue that they shouldn’t be fined at all. Data shows that might be a large group: In , there were 1.9 million tickets issued to drivers going between 11 and 15 mph over the speed limit. In the wake of the ruling, other lawyers have taken notice. “I’m a little jealous of Mr. Ricciardi for thinking of the argument,” said Randy Chen, an attorney with class-action firm Migliaccio & Rathod in D.C., which has started investigating and seeking potential clients for a case linked to problems with the city’s traffic cameras. “I’m actually all for traffic enforcement. I hate it when people blow through stop signs or speed,” Chen said. “There’s nuance here. You can be in support of traffic enforcement and also hold the government to fairness principles.” Ricciardi said his $ fine has been reimbursed by D.C., but he is waiting on $ in court fees. In the meantime, there have even been some plaudits. “A [man] I don’t know sent me an e-mail thanking me,” Ricciardi said. “He got his own D.C. speed camera ticket dismissed based on my case.”

stories.title: Trump Threatens D.C. Takeover if Janeese Lewis George Becomes Mayor
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Trump cannot legally revoke self-governance from the city; only Congress can do so.
stories.content: Trump said, "We won't put up with it," when asked his feelings on Lewis George potentially winning her June 16 primary. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo President Donald Trump said Thursday he might “take back” D.C. depending on who wins the mayoral race in the city, stating he would be opposed to Janeese Lewis George winning next week’s Democratic primary. In the Oval Office, a reporter compared Lewis George, a democratic socialist, to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and asked Trump how he would feel if she wins. “Well, I wouldn't like it,” Trump said in response. “And maybe we'd take back Washington and run it on the federal basis. We won't put up with it.” In response, Lewis George said D.C. is not going to be able to get Immigration and Custom Enforcement off the streets by “fearing the president.” “We are not going to protect our rights or Home Rule by obeying in advance,” Lewis George said in a statement. “Threatening Home Rule because you do not like how residents vote is an attack on democracy itself. The people of DC elect the mayor of DC. And they want someone who will stand up to Donald Trump.” Lewis George, a front-runner in the race, will Kenyan McDuffie, Rini Sampath, Gary Goodweather, Ernest E. Johnson, Hope Solomon and Vincent Orange in the June 16 primary. "The stakes of this election couldn’t be higher, but DC decides who will be the next mayor, not Donald Trump," McDuffie said in a statement. "As Mayor, I’ll fight tooth and nail to protect Home Rule and defend against MAGA federal overreach, keep our city safe and revive our economy that Trump’s policies have decimated." Trump cannot legally revoke self-governance from the city; only Congress can do so. Lewis George has promised to be aggressive against Trump if she wins, specifically against the command of the local police force and deployment of National Guard troops and ICE into the city, though she has also said she would try to “find agreement” where possible.

stories.title: Sen. Jim Justice and Babydog's Unlikely War Room: An Outback Steakhouse in a Strip Mall
stories.author: Emily Kennard
stories.summary: “Much like JFK wrote part of his inaugural address in a booth at Martins Tavern, Senator Justice has worked on statements / strategy in the booth of the Outback,” a staffer texted NOTUS.
stories.content: Sen. Jim Justice’s favorite place to eat steak in the DMV isn’t one of the many swanky restaurants scattered across Washington. It’s not The Occidental, The Capital Grille or Butterworth’s on Pennsylvania Ave. near his Capitol Hill office. Nor is it Le Diplomate in Logan Circle, or Joe’s Seafood near the White House. It’s an unassuming Outback Steakhouse tucked in a strip mall in the suburbs of Arlington, Virginia, where he and his constant canine companion, Babydog, a very plump English bulldog, have a regular table.

stories.title: Federal Judge Holds DHS in Contempt Over Immigration Agents’ Text Records
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: DHS must pay $ a day until it turns over data from agents’ personal cellphones used in Operation At Large in Los Angeles last year.
stories.content: Federal agents in Los Angeles used personal cellphones during Operation At Large last year, and messages sent on them are now part of a court case. Wally Skalij/AP A federal judge in California held the Department of Homeland Security in contempt for not complying with an order to search and turn over communications in federal agents’ cellphones about immigration operations in Los Angeles, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday. U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong wrote in her order, filed July 28, that the court had provided the federal government “plenty of time” to find messages kept on agents’ personal phones relating to 15 immigration enforcement actions under Operation At Large last year. The American Civil Liberties Union, Public Counsel and other immigration advocacy groups requested the material as part of an effort to halt federal immigration agents from using an individual’s perceived race to conduct stops. “Given that Plaintiffs have shown by clear and convincing evidence that the Defendants violated a specific and definite order of the court, the burden shifted to Defendants to demonstrate why they were unable to comply,” Frimpong wrote in her contempt order. “They have failed to do so.” Frimpong ordered DHS to pay $ every day until it complies with the order to turn over imaging of the phone messages. DHS must also reimburse the lawsuits’ plaintiffs — five Latino workers and other advocacy organizations — for the “time and costs spent by their attorneys in getting the government to comply” with the order. Body camera footage obtained through court-ordered discovery has revealed federal immigration agents calling Latinos racial slurs during Operation At Large. Text message screenshots filed as exhibits contained conversations of agents exchanging locations of where Latino workers gather, as well as worried talks about possible violations of a temporary restraining order that prohibited indiscriminate arrests. In December, DHS told the court that agents do not use texting functions on their mobile phones for professional duties, the court order says. Five individuals later testified that month that they, in fact, did use their personal phones for work. DHS argued again in April that agents’ personal phones were outside its possession, custody and control. A magistrate judge rebutted DHS’ arguments in July and stated that the forensic imaging order remained in effect. DHS submitted its first payment for violating the court on Tuesday in the amount of $3, , according to court documents.

stories.title: Armed Man Arrested at Trump’s LA Golf Course Ahead of the President’s Visit
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Deputies found a loaded pistol with a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition on the man, the sheriff’s office said.
stories.content: The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said Monday there’s “no credible threat” to President Trump’s visit to his golf course in Rancho Palos Verdes after an armed man was arrested Sunday. John Antczak/AP A heavily armed man was arrested at President Donald Trump’s golf course in Los Angeles days before his Tuesday fundraiser there, authorities said. Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department deputies detained Jeanine John Taele, 38, on Sunday after he was seen taking photos and “appearing to monitor security-planning activities” at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, the sheriff’s office said. Taele was arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed firearm and possessing prohibited ammunition after the deputies found a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition tucked into his pants, along with a loaded pistol and additional ammunition in his car, according to a statement from the sheriff’s office. Deputies later searched his residence and found an illegally modified AR-style rifle, body armor, more high-capacity magazines and notebooks consisting of “concerning statements.” The deputies also discovered that Taele was under investigation for robbery by the El Segundo Police Department, the sheriff’s office said. Trump was aboard Air Force One on his way to speak at a Republican National Committee fundraiser at the golf course when authorities first announced the arrest Tuesday afternoon. The FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force and the Secret Service are investigating, but authorities have determined there is “no credible threat,” the sheriff’s office said. The Secret Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

stories.title: States Warn Supreme Court That Trump’s Mail-In Voting Order Would Create Chaos
stories.author: Adora Brown
stories.summary: The Supreme Court will soon decide whether the Trump administration can move forward with the president’s changes ahead of the midterms.
stories.content: States told the Supreme Court there would be a limited window to correct errors, which could disenfranchise the voters that rely on mail-in voting, such as older Americans and people with disabilities. Matt Slocum/AP A group of states told the Supreme Court on Monday there would be “extraordinary consequences” if the Trump administration is allowed to move forward with an overhaul of mail-in voting rules so close to the midterm election. The filing responded to a Trump administration request that the justices allow federal agencies to implement two parts of an executive order that directed the U.S. Postal Service to create mail ballot rules and the Department of Homeland Security to compile a national database of eligible voters. A lower court order has blocked those parts of the order in nearly half of all states and the District of Columbia. Those states told the Supreme Court there would be a limited window to correct errors, which could disenfranchise the voters that rely on mail-in voting, such as older Americans and people with disabilities. Other voters would be confused about getting their ballots or whether the USPS would deliver them. “State and local elections administrators would be forced to divert time and resources away from critical election-preparation tasks,” the states said. Attorneys for the administration have argued that an injunction against the policies is “premature” because the agencies have not yet implemented the executive order. The states argued that it would “not be sensible” to force states to wait to sue to stop the policies they call “plainly unlawful.” “It would be extremely difficult — if not impossible — to obtain a definitive judicial resolution with enough time remaining for States to redesign and reorder their ballot mail, train elections officials, and adequately educate the public before the November midterms,” the filing states. The ongoing court battle stems from a March executive order that would require the Social Security Administration and DHS to create a list of eligible voters for the Postal Service to send ballots to. The Trump administration is seeking to lift an injunction in a Massachusetts lawsuit, which was brought by 23 states and D.C. In another case brought by Democrats in D.C, an appeals court determined that the legal challenge was premature . The decision upheld a prior D.C. ruling from District Judge Carl Nichols, a Trump appointee, who also said the policies need to be implemented before they can be blocked. Democrats argued in Monday’s response to the Supreme Court that although the courts consider their arguments to be “unripe,” the administration has clear plans and dates to implement these changes as soon as possible under the looming deadline of Nov. 3. And the USPS is already moving forward with rulemaking. The Federal Register shows that the agency submitted a rule with changes that comply with the president’s executive order, on the contingency that it succeeds in the courts. “The proposal to amend the [Domestic Mail Manual] is the subject of active litigation, including two injunctions that are currently being appealed. The Postal Service will not publish a final rule unless and until the government obtains relief from all relevant injunctions,” the rule says. With the midterms now 92 days away, President Donald Trump continues to push last-ditch efforts to oversee elections and message to voters that noncitizen voting is rampant, despite reports that it occurs rarely . Several issues would need to be reconciled if the Supreme Court allows the administration to change mail-in voting rules, including how the USPS would screen eligible voters under such a tight deadline. The USPS is already hearing complaints from election officials about delays for mail-in ballots.

stories.title: Trump Says Jeanine Pirro ‘Choked’ in Dropping Reflecting Pool Prosecution
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia was seen at the White House after Trump criticized her decision to dismiss the case.
stories.content: U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro “made a mistake,” the president said, in dropping criminal charges in the Reflecting Pool vandalism case. Tom Williams/AP President Donald Trump railed against U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro on Monday, days after her office dropped charges against a man accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and admitted in court the issues were due to “flawed installation by the contractor,” not vandals. “Jeanine Pirro made a mistake,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday. “There was vandalism.” The Justice Department moved to dismiss the criminal case on Friday against David Hearn of Maryland, a former Olympian who was indicted by a grand jury on charges of purposefully destroying part of the new coating applied to the pool during a Trump-directed renovation. The president is weighing firing Pirro after he was “blindsided” by her decision to dismiss Hearn’s case, CNN reported. Pirro was spotted entering the White House’s West Wing on Monday afternoon. Trump earlier Monday reiterated his assertion that the administration has recordings of vandals cutting the Reflecting Pool with box knives. “Now I'm not saying I was % thrilled with the contractor, but the contractor was rushing,” Trump said. “We wanted to get it open for July 4, and we got it done. But in addition, there was vandalism.” The president said Pirro visited the Reflecting Pool after the Fourth of July celebration when the water was filled with debris from the record-breaking fireworks display. Trump said Pirro “choked” after a judge questioned the government’s evidence and the handling of the prosecution. Trump called the judge "vicious” but blamed Pirro for dropping the proceedings against Hearn. “She folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things,” Trump said. “It's a disgrace.” Pirro’s filing to dismiss the case cast blame on the Interior Department, saying new information provided to her office undermined the evidence — supplied by Interior and U.S. Park Police — that the damage was “entirely caused by vandals” rather than botched construction. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum backed Trump’s assertion that vandals damaged the Reflecting Pool and touted his commitment to seeing through cases against any alleged vandals. “We won't back down to deranged people who want to destroy, , or degrade our monuments,” Burgum wrote Saturday on X. Trump and Pirro spoke on the phone on Saturday about the court filing, and one unnamed source told CNN the conversation “wasn’t pretty.” Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, was one of at least seven people arrested at the Reflecting Pool over allegations of destruction of property and vandalism, according to the White House. Hearn was arrested June 19 and indicted by a grand jury July 2, and pleaded not guilty. Hearn’s legal team told MS NOW that he is weighing “all remedies,” including potential legal action, now that his case has been dismissed.

stories.title: Trump, Burgum Blast Pirro For Dropping Reflecting Pool Damage Case
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: The president and interior secretary criticized the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia’s office for dropping a vandalism charge against a former Olympian.
stories.content: Pirro’s office cast blame on the DOI and other agencies in the court filing, saying the department had erroneously presented a grand jury with evidence of vandalism despite recently unveiled documents that proved otherwise. Alex Brandon/AP President Donald Trump and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum still say vandals damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a day after federal prosecutors said government contractors — and the DOI — were to blame. Trump criticized U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro’s motion to dismiss the case after the agency assessed that a “flawed installation by the contractor” caused damage to the famed water feature. The filing contradicted the president and other White House officials’ weekslong allegations of vandalism. “I don’t know what she was thinking?” Trump said of Pirro, one of his staunch allies, on Truth Social Saturday. “There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!” Trump attached an image of a sizable imprint of the numbers “ ,” a sequence interpreted by the White House as a threat against the president, left on the National Mall’s grass. Authorities have said they were investigating the matter. Burgum also decried Pirro’s decision not to prosecute David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, and others accused of vandalism. Pirro’s office cast blame on the DOI and other agencies in the court filing, saying the department had erroneously presented a grand jury with evidence of vandalism despite recently unveiled documents that proved otherwise. Burgum maintained on Saturday that his department provided the U.S. attorney’s office with “expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool.” Some of the vandalism was also caught on camera, Burgum said. “We won't back down to deranged people who want to destroy, , or degrade our monuments,” Burgum wrote in an X post. Trump had ordered changes to the Reflecting Pool ahead of the Fourth of July holiday. Algae blooms appeared shortly after the nearly $15 million work was completed and blue material surfaced at the pool, likely from the coating Trump wanted to be painted “American flag blue.” Hearn’s legal team said on Friday after his charges were dropped that the Justice Department should never have brought the case forward to begin with. They demanded a public apology.

stories.title: Trump Administration Admits Contractors to Blame for Reflecting Pool Damage
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.summary: The Justice Department moved to dismiss all charges against former Olympian David Hearn, who stood accused of vandalizing the water feature.
stories.content: The government initially alleged that an undisclosed portion of the pool's fresh caulk was cut “with a sharp knife or razor” just days after the renovations were completed earlier this month. Rahmat Gul/AP The Justice Department moved to drop a criminal case against a former Olympian who stood accused of purposefully destroying part of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool floor. The damage resulted from “flawed installation by the contractor,” the administration admitted in a Friday afternoon court filing — not vandalism, as President Donald Trump and top White House officials have insisted for weeks. David Hearn, a three-time Olympic canoeist, was one of at least seven people to be arrested at the Reflecting Pool for alleged destruction of property and vandalism, according to the White House. He was arrested June 19 and pleaded not guilty to the vandalism charge after being indicted by a grand jury on July 2. The government initially alleged the pool sustained “destruction of delaminating surface material” and that an undisclosed portion of its fresh caulk was cut “with a sharp knife or razor” just days after the renovations were completed. But on Friday, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia held another agency responsible for the errors throughout the 20-page filing: The Department of the Interior and U.S. Park Police had presented the grand jury with evidence that vandals had damaged the pool, government lawyers wrote, but the DOI later provided new documents proving otherwise. “It was not until after these documents were produced that USAO-DC first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism as initially represented by DOI,” the attorney’s office wrote, partially blaming a “rush to complete the project” ahead of the country’s America celebrations. “It was not until USAO-DC repeatedly reached out to DOI dozens and dozens of times that DOI slowly started trickling information to USAO-DC,” the filing reads. “Had DOI been forthcoming with the information clearly in its possession, the government would not have sought a grand jury indictment.” The filings also note a National Park Service engineer had alerted officials about a “peeled area” that measured less than a square foot and could be attributed to “overspray” from the contractor who completed the project. This description did not match Trump’s characterizations of the damage, which stretched from feet to feet to feet long, depending on when the president was discussing the issue. David Hearn reflecting pool AP - ( , AR: 1.50)Hearn told NBC News in June that he stopped by the Reflecting Pool after a bike ride on the day of his arrest “to satisfy my curiosity as a citizen of what was happening with all the algae and the peeling blue coating.” He said he only touched the paint, but did not pull at it or otherwise damage the surface of the pool. “The Trump administration's case against Davey Hearn should have never been brought,” his legal team told NOTUS in a statement after the DOJ moved to drop the case. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong. The government’s approach was ready, fire, aim. The administration owes Mr. Hearn an apology.” Hearn was scheduled to next appear in court on Aug. 5. Trump had also said chemicals were “illegally placed in the water,” which has turned green in parts because of what experts say is an algae bloom. Three ducks were found in the vicinity, but toxicology reports have yet to determine a cause.

stories.title: Judge Appears Skeptical of Trump Administration’s Arguments About Anthropic Posing Security Threat
stories.author: Hamed Ahmadi
stories.summary: Judge Rita F. Lin said at Thursday’s hearing that the record “in some ways, has gotten worse for the government.”
stories.content: Anthropic sued after the Pentagon designated it a national security supply chain risk and the administration moved to cut it off from federal work. Li Hongbo/VCG via AP A federal judge said Thursday that the Trump administration’s case against Anthropic had “gotten worse,” sharply questioning whether officials labeled the AI company a national security threat because it had publicly criticized the government. “I don’t see additional evidence from the government really justifying what it did,” U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin said at the start of a hearing in the lawsuit the company brought against the administration. “If anything, it seems like the record, in some ways, has gotten worse for the government.” Anthropic sued after the Pentagon designated it a national security supply chain risk and the administration moved to cut it off from federal work. The company says officials retaliated after it resisted efforts to remove restrictions on using its Claude models for domestic surveillance of Americans and lethal autonomous warfare. The lawsuit seeks to overturn the designation and prevent the administration from excluding the company from federal contracting. Lin made the comments during a 2.5-hour hearing Thursday in California, where she was considering motions from each side to decide the lawsuit in their favor at this early stage in the case. Lin said she saw no evidence Anthropic could alter its AI models after delivery, flip a kill switch or seed them beforehand with a hidden control mechanism. She also said she saw no specific reason to suspect the company would do any of those things. Instead, Lin said, the record appeared to show that Anthropic’s public criticism of the Defense Department caused the administration to lose trust in the company. “I find that position, if that’s really what the government’s position is, to be really troubling,” Lin said. “It seems at odds to me with the First Amendment, with Section ,” the statute the administration relied on to designate the company a national security supply chain risk. She later described the government’s apparent position as “quite extreme.” Lin also questioned whether President Donald Trump had evidence that Anthropic posed a security threat when he first publicly targeted the company on Feb. 27. “For me, looking at the record doesn’t look like as of February 27th, there’s any information in the record about what Anthropic could or couldn’t do, or whether it posed a threat,” Lin said. The risk analysis cited by the government was dated March 2, after Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued their directives against Anthropic. The company has argued that a memo prepared later could not justify actions officials had already taken. Lin questioned whether the government had shown any specific reason to believe Anthropic would place hidden restrictions in future models. “What are the specific articulable facts that suggest Anthropic might sabotage its software in this way?” she asked. Justice Department lawyer James Harlow pointed to several things, including Anthropic’s refusal to permit all lawful uses, an executive’s questions about Claude’s use during an overseas military operation and concerns about the company’s handling of sensitive information. Anthropic’s attorneys said none of those showed an intent to interfere with military operations. The company also noted that it had offered contract language promising not to do so. Anthropic lawyer Michael Mongan argued that the government had shifted from its previously stated concerns about interference with deployed models to the possibility of hidden restrictions inserted before delivery. That “shifting of rationales” was “powerful evidence of pretext” and weakened the government’s defense against Anthropic’s First Amendment and Administrative Procedure Act claims, he said. Lin previously issued a preliminary injunction blocking parts of the administration’s actions. The Pentagon continues to wind down its use of Anthropic products and expects to finish by Sept. 30, Harlow told the court. Several pilot programs at other agencies are scheduled to expire Aug. 30. Mongan said most agencies had continued working with Anthropic, two had paused negotiations for new contracts, and others were negotiating new deals. He said the company was not aware of any agency canceling a contract after the injunction. The Justice Department declined to say in open court whether any agencies had increased their use of Claude for national security work since the injunction. Lin said that conduct could shed light on the government’s original intent and that she may order the parties to provide more information. Anthropic and the Justice Department have each asked Lin to resolve the case through summary judgment, arguing that there are no material factual disputes that require a trial. Lin did not rule at Thursday’s hearing. She took the competing motions under submission and said she would issue a written order.

stories.title: Texas Immigrant Is First to Face Terrorist Deportation Court
stories.author: Jose Pagliery
stories.summary: The case against a woman admitted to the United States as a lawful permanent resident in is the first in the 30-year existence of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.
stories.content: Documents show that the legal proceeding relies largely on evidence the government has deemed classified. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) The Justice Department awakened a terrorist deportation court this month to remove the mother of an Afghan teenager who was convicted of plotting an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in , according to newly released filings. A public hearing Thursday morning will be the first for the “ Alien Terrorist Removal Court ,” an untested tribunal also handling its first case in its 30-year existence. The Justice Department said Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Fort Worth, Texas, was arrested earlier this week. She is accused of helping plot a planned attack that was to be carried out by her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, who was 17 at the time of his arrest in , and her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, 28, a DOJ news release said. Nazira Zada’s case, detailed in some documents posted on the court’s website late Wednesday, provides the first glimpse into a legal venue where prosecutors can rely on secret evidence — and an accused person does not have the otherwise fundamental right to challenge that it was illegally obtained. Those documents show that the legal proceeding relies largely on evidence the government has deemed classified, meaning that prosecutors are not willing to make public the materials it’s using to support its accusation. An unclassified FBI summary of the evidence says Nazira Zada “worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology” and helped the attackers while keeping it all from her husband. A separate declaration by a high ranking Immigration and Customs Enforcement official says that the woman’s husband was employed from until at Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan, a main hub for the United States military during the 20-year war in the country. That declaration also said Nazira Zada was admitted to the United States as a lawful permanent resident in , as a derivative on her husband’s immigrant visa application. The case is being overseen by U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen of Minnesota, who is currently serving as the Alien Terrorist Removal Court’s chief judge. The government’s attempt to move forward on the case earlier this month was slowed down, because Ericksen “had questions about the application and the evidence submitted to support it,” she wrote . That supplement is also classified, and only the cover page was posted publicly. The initial status hearing is set to begin at 11 a.m. Thursday at the federal courthouse in Washington, D.C. DOJ had initially planned to arrest the woman, fly her to the nation’s capital, and present her in court “all within the same day,” according to a court filing . However, a department news release said “Zada was arrested earlier this week.” That release called Nazira Zada “the matriarch of an alien Afghan family,” and said court documents in the criminal case say that the family, to raise funds for the attack, “started selling off their property, including furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and the family’s two vehicles.” Government officials say the woman speaks Dari, understands little English and will need an interpreter in court. “This is a historic step asking this court for the first time to remove an individual from the United States who supported a plot by ISIS-sympathizing family members to commit an act of terrorism in America,” FBI Director Kash Patel said in a prepared statement. “No one should be allowed to come into our country and then betray it. The FBI and our Justice Department partners will not hesitate to use all available resources to protect the American people.” The ATRC is a deportation proceeding that is civil, not criminal, in nature. It’s yet unclear what evidence the government has to accuse Nazira Zada of assisting her son and son-in-law. Her son, who terrorism charges, was sentenced to 15 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to receiving a firearm and ammunition to commit a terrorist attack. Tawhedi, who is also accused of terrorism, underwent a psychological evaluation and was subsequently committed “for an additional period of evaluation and treatment” as per a judge’s order.

stories.title: Immigration Agents Bristled at ‘Stunt’ Operation Outside Newsom Rally, Texts Show
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: “Hopefully I can get replaced soon,” one agent groused after the incident.
stories.content: Armed federal agents appeared outside a museum in Los Angeles’ Little Tokyo neighborhood on Aug. 14, , where Newsom was hosting a press conference for a redistricting proposition. (AP Photo/Marcio Jose Sanchez) Federal immigration agents privately bristled at their participation in a controversial operation outside of a press conference held by California Gov. Gavin Newsom in August , text message screenshots filed in federal court this week revealed. Two agents discussed the event — as well as their anxiety over the possibility of violating court orders — in messages that were among the exhibits submitted Monday by the American Civil Liberties Union in a California federal court. The exhibits also contained numerous incidents of federal immigration agents using crude and racist language toward Latinos. Federal personnel from Border Patrol, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies conducted widespread raids in Los Angeles last summer under Operation At Large, part of the Trump administration’s aggressive mass-deportation push. The texts between the unidentified federal agents — one of whom was recognized in court documents as a Homeland Security Investigations special agent, referred to as Agent G.A. in the filings — offer a candid look into how agents privately viewed their roles in Operation At Large. The agent conversed with their colleague, or Agent W, in redacted records. The incident in question occurred when Gregory Bovino, a polarizing former Border Patrol commander who was placed in charge of the Los Angeles operation, appeared with armed federal agents outside a museum in Los Angeles’ Little Tokyo neighborhood on Aug. 14, , where Newsom was hosting a press conference for a redistricting proposition. The agents detained several people and lingered at the scene, sparking a flurry of media coverage. At the time, DHS contended that the operation was about “enforcing the law.” Screenshot -07-28 at 7.46.08 PM.png ( , AR: 1.54)Newsom said in a social media post Wednesday that the released texts prove that the operation was targeted. The governor’s office referred to the posts when asked for comment. “This is crazy. I never thought I would actually see anything like this. We got pulled off the HD and car wash to run this stunt,” Agent G.A. wrote that day, referencing sites such as Home Depot where agents would often appear to arrest day laborers and other workers. The agent claimed they were told to “stand down” while at the press conference. “We’re told to assist with targeted enforcement,” Agent G.A. wrote. “That is not target enforcement. That was just a political agenda. Hopefully I can get replaced soon.” Agent G.A. wrote to Agent W again on Aug. 15, “I had no interest in going out with BP to Little Tokyo lol.” They said agents just “stood around to get media attention” after marching from a federal building in downtown LA to Newsom’s press conference and arresting a few people. “Would you have went?” Agent G.A. asked. “If I knew what they were doing probably not,” Agent W responded. W brought up Bovino, saying they had heard he was a “good dude and really good at his job” but at times did “things like this that are a little out of pocket.” “I think BP is mostly just excited because they don’t usually get to do this so they’re kind of loving the media attention maybe,” Agent W wrote. Agent G.A. said in a subsequent deposition interview that he wanted to be removed from Operation At Large because of the controversial operation outside Newsom’s press conference, as well as internal pressure to carry out what he worried were possible violations of a temporary restraining order. “It seemed to be pushing into public spaces, you know, more and more frequently,” Agent G.A. told a lawyer during the deposition, which was also included in the ACLU’s court filings. “It seemed to be escalating to less and less targeted.” Agent G.A. and Agent W’s conversation in the exhibit spans from Aug. 11, , to Aug. 15, . At the time, a federal district court had issued a temporary restraining order that stopped federal agencies from conducting indiscriminate immigration stops. The Supreme Court later paused that ruling on Sept. 8, . The federal agents questioned among themselves whether they could be held liable for continuing the indiscriminate stops, despite the restraining order. Agent G.A. said they were no longer assigned to Home Depot raids after complaining to management that the raids could violate the court order. Agent W said they were “pretty sure” the raids violated the order, and said they had signed up for professional liability insurance. “Still they shouldn’t ask us to do anything that violates a court order,” Agent G.A. said. “I think they only know one way to operate,” Agent W replied. “See bodies, chase bodies.”

stories.title: James Comey Accuses DOJ of Lying and ‘Vindictive’ Prosecution in Seashell Case
stories.author: Derek Hawkins
stories.summary: The former FBI director’s lawyers seek to suppress evidence and dismiss the indictment over an “86 47” social media post.
stories.content: The indictment “is not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts,” James Comey’s lawyers wrote in one of the motions. (AP Photo/Charles Krupa) Attorneys for former FBI director James Comey accused Justice Department officials of misleading judges, omitting key facts and making false statements in their case charging him with threatening to kill President Donald Trump via a social media post. In three court filings late Tuesday, Comey’s lawyers also argued the Justice Department had improperly singled out Comey for prosecution because Trump was upset that Comey had publicly criticized him. The motions – hundreds of pages in all – attacked a central theory in the government’s case and sought to suppress some evidence, allow Comey’s attorneys to review grand jury transcripts and dismiss the indictment as a vindictive and selective prosecution. The indictment “is not based on a good faith application of the law to the facts,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in one of the motions. “Instead, it effectuates a yearslong campaign by the President to use the criminal process to punish Mr. Comey for his protected speech and because of the President’s deep-seated animosity.” The filings are the second this week from Comey’s legal team and represent a sweeping attempt to cut short a case that Trump’s critics say is emblematic of the president’s retribution agenda. In a separate motion on Monday, Comey asked the judge overseeing the case to throw out the charges, arguing his post did not constitute a true threat. A White House spokesperson referred questions about the case to the Justice Department, which doesn’t typically discuss pending cases. A Justice Department spokesperson didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Comey’s lawyers zeroed in on the extensive efforts federal investigators made over nearly a year to turn up evidence that Comey intended to threaten Trump’s life when he uploaded a photo to Instagram of seashells spelling “86 47.” Echoing claims from Trump’s allies that the slogan was a call to violence, prosecutors alleged that “86” had roots in organized crime as jargon for “kill” and that Comey would have known this from his time investigating and prosecuting mobsters. They say the “47” represents Trump as the 47th president. But Comey’s lawyers said investigators found no such connection, despite spending months combing through case files and organized-crime trial transcripts and interviewing experts to substantiate the theory. “Those efforts, which preceded the government’s applications for the warrants, failed to find any evidence proving that Mr. Comey learned that ‘86’ means ‘kill’ in the organized crime context — because it does not,” the lawyers wrote. The FBI case agent who applied for the warrants, which sought records from Apple ID and Gmail accounts associated with Comey and his wife, Patrice Comey, made no mention of investigators’ failed searches, despite having personally ordered it, according to the filings. The omission, Comey’s lawyers said, “is all the more egregious because all of those investigations supported Mr. Comey’s assertion that he did not recall ever hearing ‘86’ used to mean ‘kill’ during his prosecutorial days.” Comey’s filings include a blistering sworn statement from John Gleeson, a former federal prosecutor and judge in Brooklyn who tried crime boss John Gotti. He said he’d never heard a mafia member use the term “86,” nor had it come up in reference to killing in his thousands of hours of conversations with mafia witnesses. “The claim that ‘86’ is mafia jargon for ‘kill’ is preposterous,” Gleeson wrote. “In my expert opinion, there is literally no support for the central allegation on which the case rests.” Comey’s lawyers also said the Justice Department had “distorted” statements from an unidentified associate of the Comeys who spoke with Secret Service and FBI agents. The affidavits claimed that the person “immediately” thought “86” could have been a call to violence, when in fact the person told investigators that they initially viewed the term as benign restaurant lingo, according to the lawyers. The person had no insight into Comey’s mental state, having not spoken to him in two years, and had been exposed to a false claim that “86” had been used to indicate violence in cases Comey had prosecuted, according to the filings. And the person had told investigators that they hoped Comey “goes to jail” and described their views about Comey as “speculation,” his lawyers said. “These inconvenient facts — all disproving the government’s central theory, and all known to the agent who sought the warrants — appeared nowhere in the affidavits seeking to obtain the private digital records of Mr. Comey and his wife,” his lawyers wrote. The lawyers also targeted what they said was a false implication in one of the warrants that one of Comey’s lawyers had obstructed the investigation. The lawyer, a former federal prosecutor, had sent a screenshot of the seashell photo to a Secret Service agent who informally requested it, according to the filing. The FBI’s search warrant affidavit suggested that the lawyer had tried to conceal evidence in doing so, even though the agent had never asked for the original file. Comey’s lawyers are seeking what’s known as a Franks hearing, in which a judge determines whether investigators lied or left out important facts to secure a search warrant. In a separate motion, his lawyers asked the court to force the government to turn over grand jury transcripts and audio recordings. They said the government’s alleged omissions and false statements raised “a significant risk that irregularities in the grand jury process influenced the grand jury to return an indictment.” Comey’s lawyers also argued that the case should be thrown out because the Justice Department’s prosecution was “vindictive,” “selective,” and designed to retaliate against Comey for publicly criticizing the president. Vindictive prosecution is a legal doctrine in which a prosecutor improperly charges a person in retaliation for exercising legal rights such as free speech. Selective prosecution occurs when a prosecutor targets a person with charges that haven’t been brought against people who did the same thing in similar situations. Both practices are unconstitutional and represent serious prosecutorial misconduct, but they are difficult to prove in court. Federal judges have recognized broad discretion in how prosecutors bring cases, and defendants who raise vindictive or selective prosecution claims rarely prevail. This is Comey’s second indictment by Trump’s Justice Department. Under heavy pressure from Trump, prosecutors in Virginia charged Comey last fall with lying to Congress. That case stemmed from his congressional testimony about alleged leaks to journalists related to FBI investigations of Trump and Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaigns. Comey had argued vindictive and selective prosecution in that case, but a judge dismissed the case on the grounds that the lead prosecutor, White House appointee Lindsey Halligan, had no authority to bring the charges. Frustrated by the failed indictment and the pace of other prosecutions of high-profile figures, Trump in April fired then-attorney general Pam Bondi and allowed her deputy, Todd Blanche, to assume the role on an acting basis. Under Blanche, who served as Trump’s criminal lawyer between presidencies, the Justice Department indicted Comey again in North Carolina, this time on counts of threats against the president and making threats across state lines. Several weeks after the new indictment was filed, Trump nominated Blanche to be attorney general. When Comey posted the “86 47” image last year, many of Trump’s allies claimed it was a call for the president’s murder. Comey denied he had any violent intent, saying the message was political, and quickly deleted the post. Secret Service agents interviewed him in Washington shortly after. Comey’s lawyers said in their filing Monday that “86 47” has become a well known and widely used political slogan expressing opposition to Trump with no significant violent connotations. The government’s claim of a “true threat,” they wrote, “is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense.”

stories.title: ACLU Seeks Government Payouts for Immigration Agent Misconduct
stories.author: Jackie Llanos
stories.summary: “I'm an ordinary woman, and I want to stand up,” one of the ACLU clients said.
stories.content: The ACLU said it seeks to hold federal immigration agents accountable via the Federal Torts Claim Act. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon) American Civil Liberties Union affiliates across the country said they filed 30 claims this week seeking damages for the wrongdoing of federal agents involved in immigration enforcement. The litigation effort announced Wednesday includes 54 claims filed since February in 17 states and Washington, D.C. The claims include allegations of abuses in immigration detention, attacks against people exercising First Amendment rights, racial profiling and unlawful arrests of U.S. citizens and immigrants. The ACLU said it seeks to hold federal immigration agents accountable via the Federal Torts Claim Act, a statute that allows people to get compensation for federal employees’ misconduct. But attorneys multiple hurdles and yearslong battles before the possibility of a settlement or bench trial. “We are filing these coordinated claims for the clients to have a path for accountability, to be able to show and demonstrate the harms that they have endured, and to have redress for that,” Yasmin Cader, an ACLU deputy executive director, said. “But it is also really important that we expose the abuse, and that we elevate the human toll of the Trump's administration's brutal enforcement practices.” Willy Wender Aceituno and Norma Bowe are two of the clients ACLU affiliates are representing. Immigration agents twice stopped and detained Aceituno, a U.S. citizen, on Nov. 15 in Charlotte, North Carolina, according to a notice of the claims sent to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection. The agents shattered his car window, which resulted in cuts, and took him in an SUV for 15 minutes, releasing him after confirming his citizenship. His detention caused physical, emotional, and psychological harm, the notice says. Bowe, a 68-year-old professor of public health at Kean University and registered nurse, brought forward a claim this week that says ICE officers outside of the Delaney Hall detention center threw her to the ground on May 25. The nurse, who operates an RV clinic outside the New Jersey detention center, argues that at the time she was trying to help a woman protesting whose shirt had ripped. Bowe says she still has doctors’ appointments related to the injuries from hitting the pavement. Acetituno is seeking $1.2 million in damages and Bowe is seeking $ , . “I'm an ordinary woman, and I want to stand up,” Bowe told NOTUS. “I want people to know my story, and I'm hoping that it will help other folks also stand up with their story.” A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson, asked how many claims ICE and CBP have received since January , said agents will continue to arrest the “worst of the worst” immigrants who are illegally present in the U.S., no matter how many lawsuits are filed. “FTCA claims remain under review. Agitators who obstruct or assault federal law enforcement officers will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” the spokesperson said in an email. To bring forward an FTCA claim, the person who suffered the injury has to do so within two years and wait six months for the agency employing the federal worker to respond, according to a congressional research report . If the agency denies the claim or doesn’t respond, the claimant can move forward with a federal lawsuit. Before Congress enacted the FTCA, the only way to obtain compensation for federal employees’ wrongful actions was to petition lawmakers to pass a bill. “That was a horrible system,” said Paul Figley, a law professor who was the deputy director of the Justice Department’s FTCA division for 15 years. Figley said immigration-enforcement-related claims are difficult and that the factual details of each case, rather than the policies of the Trump administration, would matter to reach a successful outcome for the ACLU. And he warned these cases could become too political and attempt to curb the administration’s policy-making decisions, which wasn’t Congress’ intention with the statute. “The FTCA isn't there to provide a remedy for everybody that's been hurt,” Figley said. “It's there to provide a remedy for run-of-the-mill, everyday kinds of things that don't affect how the government's operating.” Cases arising from President Donald Trump’s second term might not be solved until the next administration. For example, a federal court approved a $ , total settlement in March for four undocumented mothers whom Border Patrol agents expelled to Mexico days after giving birth in , according to court documents. The National Immigration Litigation Alliance and the law office of Bardis Vakili represented the mothers in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. NILA was also part of the legal team that obtained a $1.4 million settlement for a group of mothers and their children separated under the first Trump administration’s “zero tolerance” policy. Their lawsuit was filed in and the court approved the settlement in . Fathers and their children got $1.9 million in a similar lawsuit. “If the government injures an individual, that individual should be compensated for that injury, if it was an unlawful injury,” Mary Kenney, NILA’s deputy director, said. “And our client population can use the money.”

stories.title: 'Systemic Breakdown'
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Jenny Gathright, Zara Norman
stories.content: A Metropolitan Police Department D.C. vehicle is parked along Pennsylvania Avenue in front of the Four Seasons Hotel in the Georgetown neighborhood on August 12, in Washington, D.C. Samuel Corum/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: a D.C. police probe, an unsigned budget and the return of Max Scherzer. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST D.C.’s police department is facing more scrutiny about its crime data. According to an investigation by the D.C. inspector general’s office that was released Tuesday, the department has experienced a “prolonged, systemic breakdown” in its crime reporting and lacks adequate controls to ensure its data is reliable. NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright reports that the investigation adds to a growing list of probes examining crime classification at the police department, an issue that has put city law enforcement in the public spotlight and the Trump administration’s crosshairs. While past investigations accused department brass of pressuring subordinates to underreport crime, the inspector general’s report tackles more systemic problems in the department that could lead to inaccurate data. Classifying and reporting crime is one of the central responsibilities of any police department. Crime data informs staffing decisions, helps residents understand what is happening in their neighborhoods and aids the public in holding the government accountable. While the IG’s investigation did not examine whether the city’s crime statistics are accurate, it did find that the department lacks a system for ensuring reporting errors are routinely corrected. One example: An independent unit responsible for reviewing police reports and crime classifications was shut down in , and the department only recently launched an effort to revive it. Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll took a cooperative tone in response to the findings, agreeing to all of the report’s major recommendations and vowing “strict accountability” going forward. DEEP DIVE Muriel Bowser is backing away from the city’s budget. In what’s mostly a symbolic move, the mayor said Tuesday that she won’t be signing the budget bill for the coming year. In a letter to D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson, Bowser said she was displeased with some of the spending decisions made by lawmakers, accusing them of choosing to “kick the can down the road” on fiscal challenges to come. She specifically warned of an $ million “fiscal cliff” the city could next year, when it’s likely to have a new democratic socialist mayor and more progressive council. Bowser’s decision caps years of growing tension between her and the council over spending. The conflict goes both ways: Lawmakers say that for all the talk of fiscal rectitude, Bowser herself has been more than willing to engage in the same budget gimmicks she’s now criticizing. Still, lawmakers say they are aware that next year’s budget deliberations will probably be even harder than they were this year. This fall, the council is expected to consider a variety of revenue-raising proposals to address a growing gap between what the city spends and what it takes in. At the same time, Republicans in the House are threatening to prohibit D.C. from considering any tax increases at all . FROM THE DISTRICT A key witness testified that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool’s lining was already seriously damaged by the time former Olympian David Hearn touched it, NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández reports . Luxury home sales and prices in Washington ticked up this past quarter, Axios DC reports . But the broader homebuying market is softening: Redfin found that last month, sellers outnumbered buyers by 26% in D.C. FROM VIRGINIA Loudoun County, home to the world’s densest cluster of data centers , is the latest region to suggest hitting pause on new development while weighing how to regulate the industry, Virginia Business reports . A $22.5 billion renovation of Dulles Airport, expected to be unveiled by President Donald Trump this week, will scrap the airport’s famous mobile lounge transportation system, CBS News reports . Plans include a major terminal expansion and a new underground aerotrain system. PLAN YOUR WEEKEND For the anime fan: Otakon at the Washington Convention Center, Friday. For the mover and groover: The Funset at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company, Friday. For aspiring dancers: Maryland Youth Ballet’s “Sleeping Beauty" at Wolf Trap, Sunday. For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here . SPORTS Nationals fans took a brief trip to the past on Monday as Max Scherzer — now sporting a Blue Jays uniform — made what could be his final start in Washington. As NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty writes , the 42-year-old pitcher provided a reminder of what it means to care deeply about each game. Are you ready for some football? The Commanders officially open training camp today. Fans will be allowed to attend 11 practices over the next month, including a joint session with the Dolphins on Aug. 12. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals vs. Blue Jays, 1:05 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) NWSL: Spirit at Utah Royals, 9 p.m. ( NWSL+ ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Samuel Corum/AP. One last thing: that $1.2 million house we showed you yesterday is located in Maryland, and 56% of you guessed that right.

stories.title: Federal Immigration Agents Called Latinos Racial Slurs While Conducting Stops, Video Shows
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: Body camera footage and texts showed federal immigration agents using racist and crude language when discussing immigrants, according to court filings submitted Monday.
stories.content: A screenshot from ICE body camera footage that was among many videos, texts and other transcripts submitted Monday by the American Civil Liberties Union in federal court. ACLU As federal immigration agents swarmed Los Angeles last summer under orders from the Trump administration, some used crude language and racial slurs as they moved to detain immigrants. “Yeah, just plug us in wherever you see some tonks,” said one officer, using a derogatory term for the sound a flashlight makes when it hits someone’s head. “We’ll jump out.” The remarks were recorded in body camera footage that was among the multitude of videos, texts and other transcripts submitted Monday by the American Civil Liberties Union in federal court after a monthslong, court-ordered discovery. Monday’s motion — filed by the ACLU, Public Counsel and other advocacy organizations — requested a preliminary injunction to stop federal immigration agents from using an individual’s “apparent status as low-income or working-class and Latino” to conduct detentive stops. “This filing should shock the conscience,” Mayra Joachin, deputy director of immigrants’ rights at the ACLU of Southern California, said in a statement. “Evidence gathered from the government has confirmed what our communities have known all along: immigration officers are flagrantly violating the law by detaining people without justification and often primarily because of the color of their skin.” ACLU Body Cam Footage.mp4 Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Border Patrol and other federal agents carried out sweeping raids in Los Angeles last year as part of the White House’s aggressive mass-deportation push. The federal immigration agents would often target sites where day laborers would congregate and indiscriminately carry out arrests. The activities sparked tense protests, leading to President Donald Trump unlawfully deploying the National Guard. “Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement Tuesday to NOTUS when asked for comment. The videos, which did not clearly distinguish from which federal agencies the agents came, included body camera footage from June to September . Agents were not identified in the videos or court filings. The Los Angeles Times and CalMatters were first to report the court filings. In one video recorded Aug. 6, Border Patrol agents are seen in the back of a cargo van. One agent points to a backpack and asks, “Who’s backpack is that? Tonk’s backpack?” Another video recorded on June 12 showed an agent lament, “One tonk fucking got away, dude.” The agent repeats the phrase again later before touching the body camera, asking, “How do you turn off the camera?” Footage from June 19 showed two federal agents discussing an operation they just completed. “There was a guy, I'm pretty sure he's wet,” one agent said, using a racial slur for immigrants. “He was just sitting in that minivan." Federal agents were also recorded mocking a vulgar chant from anti-ICE protesters. Another video recorded on Sept. 23 contains a conversation between two officers that appears to be about a woman that was tracking their whereabouts. “She's a white lady, too,” one officer is heard saying in the footage. “They like being oppressed for other races,” his colleague replies. “I don't know why.” In a series of text messages exchanged on July 2 one federal agent asks if they could “pull facial rec off of profile pies of people who are self admitting in tik tok comments to being illegal.” The agent sent a photo which was redacted in the court document, adding, “This bitch good enough to facial rec?” A colleague replied that the photo did not result in any matches. “Some of these people are stupid,” the first agent replied. “Why would you post on social media that you're wet.” In a separate text exchange on July 4, an agent wrote, “tonks everywhere selling food for the 4th festivities in long beach right now.” Armando Gudino, executive director of the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, a plaintiff in the lawsuit along with five Latino workers and other organizations, said the exhibits “reinforce the urgent need for accountability and an immediate end to these unconstitutional and illegal practices against our communities.” A federal district court issued a temporary restraining order on July 11, , that barred indiscriminate immigration stops. The Supreme Court put that ruling on hold in August , allowing the federal government to continue the practice while litigation continued. A hearing for Monday’s motion is scheduled for Sept. 24.

stories.title: Federal Workers Have No Recourse for Sexual Harassment at Work, Lawsuit Says
stories.author: Eric Katz
stories.summary: The Trump administration’s anti-discrimination agency has stopped hearing class-action discrimination cases from federal workers.
stories.content: A certified class-action case of Bureau of Prisons employees is currently before EEOC alleging widespread sexual harassment against women that management failed to address. Carolyn Kaster/AP Federal employees facing sexual harassment and other forms of discrimination are currently blocked from collectively seeking relief before the federal government’s anti-discrimination agency, some workers alleged in a lawsuit filed Tuesday. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has paused adjudication of class-action discrimination cases brought by federal workers against their employing agencies, according to the complaint filed in the U.S. District Court in Washington, which accused the agency of flouting its fundamental responsibilities. Deanee Chelette is a Bureau of Prisons employee who works as a correctional officer at the Federal Correctional Institution in Pollock, Louisiana, and a plaintiff in the lawsuit. She is a member of a certified class-action case currently before EEOC alleging widespread sexual harassment against women that management failed to address. According to that case, male inmates routinely exposed themselves, masturbated and made rape threats in front of female employees. Management is aware of the situation and has not taken meaningful steps to improve it, the complainants have alleged. In December, an EEOC administrative judge issued a notice that all processing in the case was suspended and any deadlines and appearances were canceled. “This notification applies to all class cases in the federal sector, including those alleging disparate impact,” the judge said. Plaintiffs, represented by the American Federation of Government Employees, asked the court to deem the pause unlawful and compel EEOC to resume processing of class complaints. “While the class case remains suspended, women employed at FCC Pollock continue to suffer daily sexual harassment that materially and adversely affects their working conditions, without a forum in which to obtain relief,” they said. AFGE attested that it has hundreds of cases before EEOC, though thousands more are caught up in the pause. Claimants in the Pollock case estimated that women are in the class after eight submitted declarations and the bureau acknowledged that at least 50 women had filed incident reports. “The EEOC’s decision to suspend federal-sector class complaints undermines the fundamental right of employees to seek justice,” said Taryn Wilgus Null, an attorney at Democracy Defenders Fund, one of the law firms that filed the case on AFGE’s behalf. “By failing to process these cases, the commission is abandoning workers and disregarding its mandate to uphold the rule of law. The complaint alleged that EEOC is violating the Administrative Procedure Act for taking actions that are “arbitrary and capricious.” Specifically, the agency failed to follow its own regulations, implementing a blanket policy without explanation and unreasonably delaying action that it is required by law to take, the complaint alleged. EEOC did not respond to a request for comment. The agency has not stated any reason for the pause nor suggested when it would end, according to the plaintiffs. While the pause remains in effect, the plaintiffs, claimants cannot complete discovery, obtain a hearing or decision or secure injunctive relief. The Civil Rights Act prohibits discrimination in federal employment and requires the EEOC to take “necessary and appropriate” steps to enforce that ban. The commission has, through regulation, created a comprehensive procedure for processing and adjudicating both individual and class complaints of such discrimination. The plaintiffs suggested that the delays would hurt their cases as “witnesses become unavailable, memories and documents become more difficult to locate.” “Justice delayed is justice denied, and the EEOC’s refusal to act on these class-action complaints is causing direct harm and personal injury to our members,” said AFGE President Everett Kelley. In its Project blueprint , the Heritage Foundation suggested that EEOC should no longer hear complaints from federal employees and that those responsibilities should instead be transferred to the Merit Systems Protection Board. In an unprecedented move, Trump fired the commission’s Democratic members, Charlotte Burrows and Jocelyn Samuels, a week after taking office. The agency last week moved to cease its collection of workplace demographic data, a shift that critics said would undermine the enforcement of anti-discrimination laws.

stories.title: DHS Stats Chief Rips Trump’s ‘War on Immigrants’ in Blistering Resignation Letter
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The former executive director of the Office of Homeland Security Statistics said he is “thrilled to end [his] relationship with the current administration.”
stories.content: The Trump administration launched expanded immigration enforcement efforts at the beginning of the president’s second term, but critics on both sides of the aisle have requested better data on the impact of those efforts. Anthony Behar/Sipa USA via AP A top official at the Department of Homeland Security announced his resignation over the weekend in a blistering letter that lashed out at President Donald Trump and excoriated what he described as the administration’s “war on immigrants.” Marc Rosenblum, the former executive director of the Office of Homeland Security Statistics, wrote in a public LinkedIn post on Saturday that he was “sad, and thrilled, to say that yesterday was my last day working at DHS.” Rosenblum joined the Office of Immigration Statistics in , and said he watched the team grow from a “scrappy team of 11” to a staff of 45 prior to Trump’s second term. In the more than 10 years Rosenblum served at the agency, he said, his team expanded its data processing and reporting efforts. “But it will come as no surprise that I’m thrilled to end my relationship with the current administration,” Rosenblum wrote. “Between the war on immigrants, the war on feds, and the war on facts (not to mention the crazy war in Iran and the brazen corruption), I just need a change.” A representative for DHS told NOTUS that while the department does not comment on personnel decisions, "people are always welcome to their opinion — that doesn't make it right or factual.” The White House declined to comment. The Trump administration launched expanded immigration enforcement efforts at the beginning of the president’s second term, but critics on both sides of the aisle have requested better data on the impact of those efforts. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not release data on either detentions or deportations from April 9 until July 24, , missing multiple semimonthly “Detention Management” reports that typically include arrests, detentions and deportations, according to The Marshall Project . Rosenblum did not address the data-sharing lapses explicitly in his resignation letter — though he described a “challenging and often hostile work environment” that he and others allegedly experienced at DHS. Multiple organizations have taken legal action against the Trump administration, seeking data on immigration enforcement and detention practices. The Oversight Project, a conservative-leaning advocacy group, filed a lawsuit this month against DHS to release the updated data. American Oversight, a nonpartisan watchdog group, filed a lawsuit against the department in June seeking records relating to deaths in immigration custody.

stories.title: Reflecting Pool Witness: Lining Was Damaged Before Olympian Touched It
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: Defense attorneys also called into question the legal procedures that resulted in the indictment of David Hearn.
stories.content: The allegations come after the Trump administration spent more than $14 million on a renovation of the reflecting pool, including work intended to address its longstanding leaks. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP A key witness in the criminal case against a former Olympian accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool testified that the landmark had sustained significant damage prior to the alleged incident, according to a court filing submitted this week. “The testimony failed to establish that he caused any damage at all,” the attorneys wrote in a Monday filing, arguing that the charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, 67, should be dropped. Hearn’s attorneys argued that the government’s own witness could not establish that Hearn caused any compensable damage, a critical issue because the felony charge requires at least $1, in loss. Hearn pleaded not guilty to the charge last month. According to the filing, the National Park Service witness told the grand jury that the pool was already leaking more than 1 million gallons of water per week. The witness also testified that repairs were necessary to address those preexisting conditions, according to Hearn’s lawyers. Prosecutors estimated the repairs would cost between $6, and $15, , but Hearn’s attorneys argued the figure reflected the size of the affected area rather than damage specifically caused by Hearn.
