The allegations come after the Trump administration spent more than $14 million on a renovation of the reflecting pool, including work intended to address its longstanding leaks. The project, which Trump has promoted as part of his effort to restore and improve the National Mall ahead of the nation’s 250th anniversary, has numerous problems with the new lining and a subsequent, headline-grabbing algae bloom. At least five people have been arrested and five others have been cited for vandalism related to the reflecting pool. Hearn’s attorneys are now questioning whether the grand jury was given sufficient evidence and properly instructed on how to determine the amount of damage attributable to Hearn. They are also asking a judge to release the grand jury’s legal instructions and the complete transcript of its proceedings. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region .

stories.title: Inspection Finds ‘Systemic Breakdown’ in D.C Police’s Crime Reporting
stories.author: Jenny Gathright
stories.summary: A new report from the city’s inspector general found that the department’s policies around crime data are outdated or incomplete.
stories.content: Interim police chief Jeffery Carroll said he agreed with all of the report's core findings and hoped to ensure accountability. Mark Schiefelbein/AP Crime reporting oversight at D.C.’s police department experienced a “prolonged, systemic breakdown” over the past as the department operated with outdated policies and failed to properly review its crime reports for accuracy, the city’s inspector general found in an investigation released Tuesday. The inspector general’s report adds to a growing number of probes into crime statistics and reporting at the department, including an internal investigation that resulted in the proposed firing of 13 top police officials and investigations by the Department of Justice and Congress that heaped scrutiny on D.C. police leadership. In addition to roiling the department for the past year, the inquiries have placed the city in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, which has been eager to flex its authority over the nation’s capital. Last year, when President Donald Trump took the unprecedented step of seizing temporary control of the city police department despite a precipitous drop in violence, he justified the move by alleging that police officials had manipulated crime statistics to make the city appear safer than it actually was. Now, the inspector general’s report — and the response from interim D.C. Police Chief Jeffery Carroll, who said he agreed with all of its findings and was already taking steps to reform the department’s crime-reporting practices — chart one path forward for the department as it continues to wrestle with the fallout from the controversy. Police officers and close observers of crime generally do not doubt that the city has grown significantly safer after a generational spike in violent crime in . Homicides — perhaps the most challenging crime to conceal — have dropped every year since, according to D.C. police data. The OIG audit did not examine whether the department has been reporting crime statistics accurately. Instead, investigators looked into whether the department had adequate quality-control systems for crime data and reporting. They found several significant shortcomings. A spokesperson for D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser, who requested the inspector general's investigation, declined to comment on the findings. NBC4 Washington was first to report on a draft of the report. The police department shut down an independent unit that reviewed crime reports for accuracy in , and its records system also failed to flag reports with classification errors or incomplete narratives, leaving them uncorrected, the report said. In the absence of an independent review unit, ensuring the accuracy of crime reports fell on district commanders and their teams, who are stretched for time, and identifying mistakes “depended largely on individual initiative rather than structured oversight,” investigators wrote. The police department’s policies are also outdated and incomplete, according to the report, which said that officers are subject to a “patchwork of overlapping and sometimes conflicting policies” on how to report crime. About a third of the department’s general orders, the rules that govern officer behavior, are more than 20 years old. Some of the policies about crime reporting reference the independent review unit that no longer exists, for example, or refer to a computer system that the department no longer uses. And, significantly, no single document describes how crime should be classified and reported from start to finish, according to the audit. Investigators also found that cultural issues have hampered the department: In interviews, officers described an environment where they felt hesitant to express concerns about crime reporting because they feared retaliation and had no way to submit anonymous complaints. The report noted that concerns about crime statistics are not unique to the District. “Research has consistently found that when the same personnel responsible for crime reporting are also the ones whose performance is measured by that crime data, there is an inherent incentive to influence the numbers,” it said. The department has already taken some steps over the past several months to address the concerns brought up by the audit, the report said, including launching mandatory training on crime classification for officers and starting to reestablish an independent unit to review police reports for quality and accuracy. Carroll, in a letter responding to the audit, said he agreed with all of its core findings and said his goal was to ensure “strict accountability across the department.” As Carroll seeks to tackle the systemic problems identified by the inspector general, lengthy discipline proceedings will continue for the top officials accused of improperly changing or manipulating crime reports. Those discipline recommendations came out of a -page internal affairs investigation that painted a picture of a department where officials struggled with immense pressure to reduce crime in their districts — pressure that led some of them to violate department policy, investigators allege. Several police officials stand accused of pressuring officers to classify violent assaults, robberies and thefts as lesser offenses, according to a copy of the investigation, which concluded in the spring and has been reviewed by NOTUS. Others are accused of improperly editing police reports, either at the direction of a higher-up or of their own accord. The department has not released the investigation, in keeping with its policy of not revealing those disciplinary records to the public. The internal probe, along with previous investigations conducted by the Justice Department and Republicans in Congress, also criticized the leadership of former D.C. Police Chief Pamela Smith, who resigned in December. Though she said she did not resign because of the inquiries into crime statistics, Smith’s departure came after a draft report from the Justice Department and a published report from Republicans on the House Oversight Committee both excoriated her leadership, accusing her of creating a climate of fear that incentivized commanders to artificially suppress reports of serious crimes. The D.C. police internal affairs investigation featured interviews with officials who said Smith would frequently berate top command staff. It concluded that her treatment of those under her command had a “drastic and negative effect” on the department, but did not find that Smith had personally ordered anyone to misclassify a crime. Smith has repeatedly denied claims that she manipulated statistics. Bowser defended the police chief, too; she requested the inspector general’s probe after the release of the DOJ and House Oversight probes, saying she hoped the city office would provide a less biased perspective.

stories.title: Judge Allows Trump to Refile His $15 Billion New York Times Defamation Suit
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: An amended complaint must be filed by Aug. 27.
stories.content: Evan Vucci/AP A federal judge in Florida is allowing President Donald Trump to amend and refile his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against The New York Times after the publication moved to toss the case on First Amendment grounds. The amended complaint must be filed by Aug. 27, United States District Judge Steven D. Merryday ruled Monday. Merryday, who was appointed by former President George H. W. Bush, postponed a ruling on the Times’ motion to dismiss the case. Trump’s legal team sued the Times in September , claiming that three articles and a book written by Times’ journalists contained “repugnant distortions and fabrications about President Trump.” The complaint argued that the book and articles, which were published ahead of the election, sought to maliciously harm Trump’s “worldwide reputation for success.” Trump and Trump-backed organizations have continually sued — and lost — defamation cases against news publications. In April, a federal judge tossed Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal after it reported that a sexually suggestive letter with the president’s signature had been gifted to disgraced financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And in July, a separate federal judge in Florida dismissed a $3.8 billion defamation lawsuit brought by Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, against The Washington Post over an article about a mysterious financial entity’s connection to the Trump-owned social media platform. The Times, which has been repeatedly sued by Trump, argued that Merryday should either dismiss the case or have it transferred to the Southern District of New York. After Merryday denied the newspaper’s motion to move the case, Trump celebrated on Truth Social. Lawyers for both parties delivered oral arguments for more than two hours on July 22. Merryday’s ruling on Monday did not indicate what parts of Trump’s original complaint could be amended. Trump’s legal team had proactively requested for Merryday to grant them an amended complaint that would “cure any … deficiencies” and show evidence of how “the Challenged Statements are not substantially true, along with additional facts and innuendo by Defendants to show why the Challenged Statements are defamatory, and additional evidence of actual malice for each Defendant.” The Times will have 21 days to file a response after the amended complaint is submitted, Merryday said.

stories.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow New Mail-In Voting Rules
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: President Trump wants to lift a lower court ruling that blocked parts of his new regulations on mail-in voting.
stories.content: Attorneys for the administration argued that an injunction against the policies is “premature.” (Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images) The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to allow federal agencies to move forward with new mail-in voting policies. The application seeks to lift a lower court ruling that blocked, in nearly half of all states and the District of Columbia, two parts of an executive order from March that directed the U.S. Postal Service to create mail ballot rules and the Department of Homeland Security to compile a national database of eligible voters. Attorneys for the administration argued that an injunction against the policies is “premature” because the agencies have not yet implemented the executive order, which gave them “substantial discretion” to do so. “Accordingly, much remains uncertain as to what a final USPS rule might include or what the contents or uses of any DHS lists might be,” the filing says. And, with fewer than days until the midterm elections, the administration said it does not have time to let the lower court process play out first. “Even if the agencies’ implementation plans end up being entirely lawful, there is not enough time to obtain ordinary appellate relief from the injunction in order to carry them out before the November election, especially given that any such plans will need to be implemented well before November given the timing of election procedures concerning voter-roll verification and mail voting,” the filing says. Efforts to implement any DHS rule or USPS rule would need to begin as soon as early- to mid-August to be in place for the election, the filing argued, “particularly given that absentee and mail-in voting begin (in some States) several weeks prior to Election Day.” The order would require USPS to regulate the redesign of mail-in ballots and envelopes. A state must also notify USPS if “it intends to allow for mail-in or absentee ballots to be transmitted by the USPS,” 90 days before the election, and any mail-in ballots submitted must be checked through a preapproved list of eligible voters. Under the order, DHS and the Social Security Administration would develop the approved list of voters and transmit them to states to develop their “State Citizenship List.” The president has said the new policies will help safeguard elections from noncitizen voting — though noncitizen registration is rare , according to experts. The Trump administration’s emergency filing comes after a federal appeals court decision Saturday upheld a ruling that temporarily halted the new regulations in states that filed a lawsuit, which argued that Congress has the constitutional authority to regulate elections rather than the president. The Supreme Court asked to hear from the states who brought the lawsuit by Aug. 3.

stories.title: James Comey Filed a Motion to 86 his ‘86 47’ Criminal Charges
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: Attorneys for President Donald Trump’s longtime foe say the seashell-based social media post lacked “a true threat.”
stories.content: Former FBI Director James Comey's lawyers argue in part the indictment “targets protected speech at the heart of the First Amendment.” (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) Former FBI Director James Comey asked a judge to dismiss a federal indictment against him Monday, arguing that posting a photo last year of seashells spelling out “86 47” did not constitute a “true threat” against President Donald Trump. In a court filing , Comey’s attorneys argue that “86 47” is a well-known political slogan that expresses opposition to Trump, and was commonly displayed at protests ahead of Comey’s post, with thousands of items featuring the slogan sold on the internet that are available to this day. “But the government now singles out Mr. Comey to prosecute one of the President’s most prominent critics for publishing another person’s statement of political opposition,” the filing states. “To justify this prosecution, the indictment alleges that Mr. Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat’ on the President’s life,” the filing states. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.” “Most dictionaries do not even list the meaning—’to kill’—that the government now proposes,” the filing says. Comey’s lawyers also argue the indictment “targets protected speech at the heart of the First Amendment.” And forcing Comey to stand trial would itself be a punishment of free speech that would “invite future prosecutions by the Executive Branch against perceived political enemies for their opposition to the President,” they wrote. A federal grand jury indicted Comey in April with making threats to harm Trump. The Justice Department claimed that Comey knowingly and willfully made a “threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm upon the President of the United States.” Comey was also charged with disregarding a “substantial risk that his communication would be viewed as threatening violence.” If Comey’s motion prevails, it will be the second case against the former FBI director that has been dismissed. A federal judge threw out a separate case against Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James in November after concluding that a Trump ally, interim US Attorney Lindsey Halligan, was illegally appointed to the role without Senate confirmation. The Justice Department appealed Halligan’s dismissal in the case. Former President Barack Obama appointed Comey to lead the FBI in , but Trump dismissed him from the post in . In a two-and-a-half page memo , then-Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein cited Comey’s “handling of the conclusion of the investigation of Secretary [Hillary] Clinton’s emails.” Comey ultimately did not recommend any charges for Clinton. While Comey was FBI director, he also handled an investigation into the Trump campaign’s ties to Russia, which the president later cited as a factor in his decision to fire Comey. Special Counsel Robert Mueller took over the investigation into Russian interference in the election, and ultimately found that Trump did not commit obstruction of justice by firing Comey. Trump has frequently referred to his longtime foe as “James ‘Dirty Cop’ Comey,” in the years since his firing and throughout the subsequent court battles.

stories.title: New Rule Could Send Hundreds of Thousands Seeking Asylum to Immigration Courts
stories.author: Jackie Llanos
stories.summary: The Trump administration said the change was meant to decrease the backlog of applications.
stories.content: The rule change would allow U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to send certain applications to immigration judges without interviewing the migrants seeking asylum. (AP Photo/Gregory Bull, File) The Trump administration plans to funnel potentially hundreds of thousands of asylum cases to immigration courts that are denying relief to nearly all applicants. A Department of Homeland Security rule change announced Monday could more quickly shift asylum applications from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to immigration judges. The change in how the federal government handles certain asylum petitions is meant to reduce the 1.4 million-case backlog at USCIS, according to the interim final rule going into effect Tuesday. “For far too long the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection,” USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said in a news release. “America’s asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole.” USCIS asylum officers handle applications for immigrants who are not in the deportation process, while immigration judges, who are Justice Department employees, oversee cases of those actively facing removal. However, the rule change would allow USCIS to send certain applications to immigration judges without interviewing the migrants seeking asylum. That includes applications where the migrant is barred from applying for asylum because of a one-year filing deadline or is not eligible on the merits of the claim, according to the rule. Vanessa Dojaquez-Torres, director for US policy and advocacy for HIAS, said the international Jewish humanitarian organization worries the change would lead to more deportations with less due process. She called the number of the cases that could be moved under the rule “quite astounding.” “This rule helps design a potential process where asylum seekers never once get to speak to any government official about their claim,” Dojaquez-Torres said. “One of our biggest concerns is that this is creating a streamline for asylum applicants to be returned back to countries where they'll be harmed.” More than , cases a year could get transferred from USCIS to the immigration courts under the change, DHS estimates. Overall, 31% of the cases in the USCIS backlog could be affected, according to the Federal Register notice. Asylum denials from immigration judges have soared during the second Trump administration. Immigration judges denied 62% of cases in January , but they denied 94% of cases in June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. The speedy closure of cases has decreased the backlog within the court system, which is down to fewer than 3.2 million cases from a peak of 3.7 million in , according to TRAC. Immigrants seeking asylum have a better success rate if USCIS handles their application, according to agency data. In the fiscal year , the agency denied 61% of petitions that it issued decisions for. In the first quarter of this year, the denials reached 78%. Last week a federal judge in Massachusetts temporarily blocked USCIS from rejecting asylum applications and starting the deportation process for immigrants who fail to pay the $ annual fee enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Three days after that decision, the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a decision that asylum applications should be considered abandoned if the immigrant doesn’t pay the annual fee.

stories.title: Trump’s Border Czar Says Vetting and Training for ICE Agents Is ‘Under Review’
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The ICE agent who allegedly shot and killed a man in Maine should have had “an almost impossible time” passing vetting, Tom Homan said.
stories.content: Border czar Tom Homan says an ICE agent who shot and killed an immigrant in Maine should not have gotten through the agency’s vetting if his past history was known. Mark Schiefelbein/AP White House border czar Tom Homan said the vetting and training processes for Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents are “under review” after revelations that the agent who allegedly shot and killed an immigrant in Maine had been accused of domestic violence. Homan said law enforcement agencies routinely review their training operations and ICE would evaluate “some additional training” as well as find out what may have gone wrong in vetting the ICE agent in Maine. “Did we have that information? Did we not have that information?” Homan said Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union. “If that was factual, he would have an almost impossible time to pass vetting.” ICE has not officially identified the agent who shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13 — though The Associated Press and Boston Globe have reported that he is 37-year-old David Brouillette, who had previously served in the Army. Brouillette’s family members and ex-wives have accused him of violent behavior and said he has a long history of psychiatric issues, several news outlets reported. If the accusations against Brouillette are true, Homan told CNN, he never should have cleared the vetting process. “If this person had that type of history, it would have been a vetting issue, and it should have been brought to the attention of those who make those decisions,” Homan said. The shooting in Maine happened less than a week after another fatal shooting in Houston where an ICE agent killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a 52-year-old Mexican national. Homan told CNN he did not “know specifically” the status of the officers involved in the shootings in Maine and Texas, but per ICE policy “they're usually put on administrative leave pending the investigation.” Durán Guerrero and Salgado Araujo were both shot during vehicle stops. After the shootings, ICE temporarily paused most vehicle stops to review the enforcement tactic, but within a day, President Donald Trump directed the agency to resume traffic enforcement actions. Homan said “changes have been made” to vehicle-stop procedures after acting ICE Director David Venturella gave officers new guidance on body-worn cameras. The Department of Homeland Security recently signed contracts for over $30 million to purchase the cameras. Venturella has also training for officers, according to Homan. “David Venturella sent an instruction out that he wants at least one body camera on those vehicle stops, so we have everything on video,” Homan told CNN.

stories.title: Democrats Hope Transparency Helps Weather GOP Criticism Over Voter Controversy
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: Democratic lawmakers are attempting to ward off attacks from Trump and Republicans casting the incident as evidence of rampant election fraud.
stories.content: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and other lawmakers are leaning hard into transparency — especially as the party has little ground available to lose in the midst of the White House's push to tighten elections laws and claim more control from the states. Seth Wenig/AP Republicans wasted no time in going after Democrats when news broke that 6, noncitizens were erroneously registered to vote in New Jersey, casting the incident as evidence of rampant election fraud. But Democrats, led by New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, are leaning hard into transparency on the issue — especially as the party has little ground available to lose in the midst of President Donald Trump’s aggressive push to tighten elections laws and claim more control from the states. “It is the right thing to do — to be clear with the public about anything you find and to build trust in a system that generally works really well,” said Ben Olinsky, a senior fellow at the Democratic think tank Center for American Progress. “That is also the right strategy for dealing with someone who has repeatedly and habitually lied about elections in the form of Donald Trump.” The erroneous registrations were caused by a software error, Sherrill said Tuesday — an explanation that IDEMIA, the France-based company in charge of transmitting information through New Jersey’s motor vehicle system, has denied . Former Democratic Gov. Phil Murphy also denies having any knowledge of the incident after Sherill said the mistakes occurred under her predecessor. But during that news conference, Sherrill momentarily pivoted to the president: “Donald Trump has zero credibility on the issue of election integrity.” “The difference between my administration and this White House is stark,” the governor said on Tuesday. “We don't deflect, deny or exploit problems for our own gain. We find them, and we fix them, because that's what a good, accountable government should do.” Sherrill’s rebuke appeared to be an attempt to deter Trump and Republicans from using the incident as evidence for widely debunked assertions of mass voter fraud as the party pushes Congress to pass the SAVE America Act , the president’s signature “election integrity” bill. Trump had already jumped on the issue, exaggerating at a Wednesday rally that “thousands and thousands” of votes had been illegally cast in the state after the software glitch. A preliminary review found that fewer than people out of the 6, accidentally registered went on to illegally vote, Sherrill said. The White House claimed credit for the situation going public at all: Press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Sherrill’s initial announcement was prompted by a letter from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, but the governor previously said she learned about the incident and launched an investigation days before she was contacted by DHS. Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R-New Jersey) and 18 other House Republicans sent a letter to Sherrill on Friday, stating that conservatives’ concerns about election integrity over the past few years had “too often” been dismissed as “exaggerated or unfounded.” The letter said the incident showed that “these vulnerabilities are real.” “The fact that this happened — with or without software playing a role — can neither be ignored by Congress nor dismissed as a simple, garden-variety computer glitch,” Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) posted on X . “We need the SAVE America Act to stop this from happening.” The rhetorical tug-of-war demonstrates how an anomaly can be equipped to bolster baseless claims, Democratic lawmakers say. The way to combat attacks on election integrity, lawmakers and experts said, is to swiftly inform the public and take responsibility. “That's the kind of transparency we need,” Sen. Andy Kim (D-New Jersey) told NOTUS. “We need to make sure it’s fixed, and someone needs to be held accountable for the fact that this wasn’t all squared away as soon as possible.” Multiple lawmakers said the issue hasn’t swayed their confidence in New Jersey’s — or the country’s — ability to conduct accurate elections. Election officials being honest about “isolated problems” strengthens trust in the broader election system because it “demonstrates that safeguards are working,” said Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia), vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “There are those who will choose to weaponize this issue in an attempt to undermine confidence in our elections — we cannot allow that,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) said in a statement. Any concern about voting integrity from Trump and right-wing Republicans is a pretext for further federal overreach in states running their own elections, California Sen. Alex Padilla, the top Democrat on the Rules and Administration Committee, said in a statement. Noncitizen voting is a rare occurrence, and no evidence has been uncovered that shows it changed the outcome of an election, said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research. Becker said “no one credible” is denying that noncitizen voting has never happened. Election law experts, he said, are quantifying the incidents and contextualizing them “in relationship to the voter lists and the actual votes cast.” Becker said the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote, would not have changed the situation in New Jersey because that information was accurately collected. The individuals marked that they were not citizens but were to voter rolls anyway. “It’s voters in the state of New Jersey after a glitch. If you don’t have the glitch, that number is much smaller. This is a tiny blip,” Becker said Thursday. “They’re trying to use a nuclear bomb to kill an ant.”

stories.title: A Heritage Employee Was Caught With Drugs Trying to Get Into the Senate, Police Say
stories.author: Daniella Diaz
stories.summary: Matthew Christopher Wingate was stopped and searched for having a pistol magazine in his briefcase, according to a court affidavit.
stories.content: Capitol Police officers detained Matthew Christopher Wingate after a routine screening at the entry of the Russell Senate Office Building. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite, File) A Heritage Foundation employee faces a drug-possession charge after a security screening at a Senate office building turned what tested presumptively positive as cocaine and fentanyl, according to court records. Capitol Police officers detained Matthew Christopher Wingate on July 14 after he entered the Russell Senate Office Building and placed his bag on the X-ray belt as part of routine screening, according to an affidavit filed in Washington, D.C., superior court. Wingate is the government-relations director for defense and foreign policy at the Heritage Foundation, and previously worked as a national security adviser for Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) and a military legislative assistant for Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), according to Legistorm . An officer observed an image consistent with a pistol magazine inside the brown briefcase, and a secondary screening found a magazine with 10 rounds of 9 mm ammunition, the affidavit states. Officers placed him under arrest, the affidavit states. That was apparently because of the magazine. Firearms and ammunition are generally prohibited from being carried into Senate office buildings. Officers ran a check through the Metropolitan Police Department's Gun Registry Unit, which confirmed Wingate held a valid license to carry a firearm in D.C., the affidavit states. A crime-scene officer discovered a plastic sandwich bag in the exterior pocket of the briefcase containing four capsules and three blue-pressed tablets, the affidavit states. Field testing of the blue pills, which were imprinted with the letter “A” on one side and “7 6” on the other side, returned a presumptive positive result for cocaine and fentanyl, the affidavit states. Under questioning, Wingate said he forgot the magazine was in the briefcase and “explained that the drugs were his and were prescribed to him from a medical professional,” the affidavit states. Wingate did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The Heritage Foundation and Wingate’s lawyer did not respond to requests for comment. Wingate was released from custody on the misdemeanor charge and has an Aug. 27 court date, according to court records.

stories.title: DOJ Agrees to Withdraw Subpoenas Issued to New York Times Reporters
stories.author: Jose Pagliery
stories.summary: Government admits “mistakes” in probe of sources for articles about Air Force One security concerns.
stories.content: Lawyers sought to quash subpoenas that targeted New York Times journalists. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura) NEW YORK — The Justice Department agreed Thursday to withdraw an attempt to force New York Times reporters to reveal to a grand jury their sources for a story on national security concerns about the Qatari-gifted airplane to replace Air Force One. After rapid-fire questions from an upset judge and a mention of potential sanctions against prosecutors for the Justice Department, the government admitted to making several “mistakes” when launching an investigation that targeted journalists with subpoenas. During an hourlong court hearing, U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian grilled one of the highest-ranking prosecutors at the Southern District of New York over the DOJ’s ongoing attempt to identify the sources behind Times articles that revealed that security concerns prevented President Donald Trump from using his new airplane on a return trip from Turkey earlier this month. Prosecutors told the judge that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche personally signed off on subpoenas that sought to force Times reporters Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Eric Schmitt, Tyler Pager and Adam Goldman to reveal the identities of the government officials who spoke to them. Lawyers for the Times sought to quash those subpoenas. Sean Buckley, a longtime SDNY prosecutor who is currently listed as the chief counsel to the U.S. attorney in that office, remained defensive as he stood to answer a barrage of questions from the judge. Buckley said he oversaw the investigation and knew about the established restrictions limiting the government’s ability to pressure journalists to give up their sources, but that “those additional steps were not yet identified” by prosecutors before they pursued subpoenas. “No one was looking to pull a fast one on the courts or anyone else,” he told the judge. Subramanian asked a series of questions about the way the government sent FBI agents to reporters homes on July 10 to serve subpoenas compelling them to testify before a grand jury — and later tried to order communication service providers to fork over records of the reporter’s phone exchanges. The backdrop to his questions is decades of government attempts to spy on journalists that resulted in First Amendment legal protections — in the form of official DOJ internal policies and case law — that demand prior authorization from DOJ brass and an investigation involving immediate risk to human lives. The DOJ is also limited in its ability to force companies to keep silent about government attempts to acquire records of their customers’ private communications if the target is a reporter engaged in their constitutionally protected right to free speech. Subramanian repeatedly asked Buckley if the government would be willing to simply withdraw the subpoenas. For the first hour, the prosecutor wouldn’t budge. Subramanian quickly brought up how prosecutors, in court filings earlier this week, said they at first had not alerted lawyers for the journalists about subpoenas to third parties for phone numbers. The revelation came in a letter on Monday in which prosecutors cited “additional case law that the government identified after the issuance of the subpoenas.” “Doesn’t that mean you failed the Gonzalez test?” the judge asked, referring to the appellate case that created that requirement. “Those additional steps were not yet identified,” Buckley responded. “Why doesn’t that mean that the motion to quash is granted?” the judge replied, shaking his head. Subramanian remained focused on what he described as the government’s failure to properly investigate a matter before threatening journalists with jail time if they didn’t reveal their sources. The judge stressed that prosecutors were bound by a responsibility to investigate the matter before resorting to a drastic measure that would implicate “the profound First Amendment and free press issues.” “Doesn’t that turn the law and regulation on its head?” the judge asked. “Subpoenas are the last step, not the first step.” Subramanian : “It’s a matter of just basic compliance to the law.” Buckley contended there was an exception to those restrictions that allows the nation’s attorney general to approve intrusive subpoenas, but that only drew further rebuke from the judge after he read the statute. “How is this an exception of the basic rule that’s literally two provisions above it?” Subramanian said. He referred to the provision that says “the government should have made all reasonable attempts to obtain the information, communications records, or business records from alternative sources.” The DOJ was placed yet again on the defensive when the judge demanded that prosecutors explain why they had also sought the communication records of two Times reporters’ spouses and another reporter’s mother. “That was an error which we own,” Buckley said. “It was a consequence of us trying to move quickly.” Subramanian then demanded to hear from Kevin Sullivan, a prosecutor who normally works on high-profile terrorism cases but was on this investigation’s team. The judge commanded Sullivan to get up from the gallery, where he was sitting with the crowd, and position himself at the prosecution team’s table. Subramanian then questioned why Sullivan signed off on a subpoena on July 14 that stated the investigation was not public — days after the Times had already published a story about it. “Your Honor, the wording was imprecise,” Sullivan said. And when Sullivan tried to privately converse with his fellow prosecutors, the judge interrupted him with a “hold on!” Subramanian then asked Sullivan why his subpoena application to another judge made no mention that the supposedly non-public investigation was in fact a highly publicized and controversial national story involving the Times. “Judge, it was an oversight on the government’s part,” Sullivan said, while throwing up both hands with a shrug. Subramanian raised the possibility of personally holding the prosecutors accountable for misconduct, noting that, in a civil case, he would now be considering sanctions. He then turned back to Buckley. “Are you still on this investigation?” he asked. “Yes, Your Honor.” “So, are you going to do this again?” the judge said. “Absolutely not, Your Honor,” Buckley said. Subramanian later pressed Buckley on how the senior prosecutor could make so many missteps while claiming to have already been familiar with the rules. Buckley then said he doesn’t “review every piece of paper” under his command. Prosecutors called for a five-minute break, during which Buckley walked out of the courtroom. He was seen placing four phone calls and quickly typing messages on his phone as he paced along a window that Lower Manhattan. When someone called him, Buckley ducked into a conference room. Once he was back in the courtroom, Buckley said the government was now prepared to “unilaterally withdraw” the subpoenas — but that the investigation would continue and that reporters might be subpoenaed again in the future. “Moving forward, we’re not going to have the kinds of errors that have plagued this case so far?” the judge asked. “No, your Honor,” Buckley said. Subramanian then made Buckley “pledge” that he would follow the law and regulations, referring to the exchange as a necessary “soliloquy.” David O’Neil, a Washington lawyer representing the newspaper, noted that “the record here is replete with bad faith.” Buckley leaned into the microphone. “We dispute any allegation of bad faith, and we’ll leave it at that.”

stories.title: Minnesota Man Sentenced to Life in Prison for Killing Democratic Lawmaker Melissa Hortman
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: Vance Boelter was sentenced to two consecutive life terms after pleading guilty to a politically motivated attack that killed two and wounded two others.
stories.content: At Thursday’s hearing, relatives of the victims spoke about the attack’s enduring consequences, while federal prosecutors characterized Boelter’s actions as politically motivated violence aimed at elected officials. Alex Kormann / Minnesota Star Tribune / AP Vance Boelter, a Minnesota man who shot and killed former state House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband in a politically motivated attack, was sentenced to life in prison on Thursday. The 59-year-old man pleaded guilty in June to six federal charges, including the killings of Hortman and her husband, Mark, and the shootings of state Sen. John Hoffman and his wife, Yvette Hoffman, who were wounded but survived. His sentencing came more than a year after he stalked the Democratic lawmakers’ homes while pretending to be a law enforcement officer. The judge from the bench said the sentence was “well-deserved.” At Thursday’s hearing, relatives of the victims spoke about the attack’s enduring consequences, while federal prosecutors characterized Boelter’s actions as politically motivated violence aimed at elected officials. Boelter offered an apology in court before being sentenced to two consecutive life terms and an additional 40 years behind bars under the terms of his plea agreement. The federal sentence does not resolve all the charges against Boelter. He continues to a separate state prosecution in Minnesota, where he is charged with two counts of first-degree premeditated murder, four counts of attempted first-degree murder, impersonating a police officer and animal cruelty. The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office has indicated it intends to move forward with that case. Federal prosecutors announced in June they will not seek the death penalty following Boelter’s plea that month. "Bringing justice to the families and loved ones of victims of violence is the number one priority of the Department of Justice," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement last month. "Prosecutors worked hard on this case to make sure he was held accountable to the fullest extent possible."

stories.title: States Sue to Stop Trump Administration Effort to Control Elections
stories.author: Anna Kramer
stories.summary: The Trump administration has threatened to withhold federal emergency disaster preparation funding from states that don’t comply with new election rules.
stories.content: The Department of Homeland Security has threatened to withhold funding from any state that doesn’t adopt strict new election procedures. (AP Photo/Ross D. Franklin) Twenty-five states and Washington, D.C., are suing the Trump administration for trying to use federal emergency grant funding to control state election rules. The Department of Homeland Security has threatened to withhold 20% of Federal Emergency Management Agency homeland security funding from any state that doesn’t adopt strict new election procedures preferred by President Donald Trump. Those rules from DHS include using hand-marked paper ballots instead of machines, the implementation of the SAVE database to search for registered voters who could be noncitizens, and handing the federal government information about state voter rolls. “The conditions DHS is trying to impose would require states to make sweeping changes to the way we conduct elections, including rewriting state election laws and privacy laws,” Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul said in a news conference with the attorneys generals for Rhode Island, California and New Jersey, the four states leading the lawsuit. The lawsuit , filed in federal court in Rhode Island, asks a judge to block implementation of the conditions, arguing in part that DHS overstepped Congress’ role and violated the regulatory process. State coalitions have already twice sued the Trump administration over its attempts to withhold FEMA disaster funding from states that do not cooperate with new Trump administration immigration policies. In both cases, courts granted summary judgment to the states and forced the release of funds. “I am disappointed, but not necessarily surprised, that our coalition is filing its third lawsuit today to protect this funding,” Raoul said. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. States, not the federal government, have central authority over their election rules. Imposing requirements on the distribution of federal disaster preparation funding is the latest strategy from the Trump administration to try to get around that limitation. Many states rely heavily on FEMA’s Homeland Security Grant Program to invest in law enforcement and plan for and protect against terrorist threats. The SAVE database was originally created by DHS to check the citizenship status of people applying for government benefit programs. But since , Republicans in Congress have been trying to pass versions of the SAVE Act, the most recent iteration of which would force states to use the database to cut people from their voter rolls. The version of the bill is currently stalled in the Senate. Election experts have repeatedly warned that implementing the SAVE database for voter roll checks could lead to accidentally disenfranchising people who are eligible to vote. With the legislation stalled in Congress, DHS is instead trying to use grant funding to force states to implement SAVE. “We’re back in court to ensure that these funds are distributed as Congress intended, not conditioned on an unlawful political agenda,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said in the news conference. “Public safety should never become a bargaining chip.”

stories.title: White House Says It Won’t Intervene in Tate Brothers’ Extradition Process
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: Vice President JD Vance still follows both “manosphere” influencers on X, despite new allegations of rape and human trafficking.
stories.content: The Tate brothers were arrested in Florida last week following an extradition request from the United Kingdom. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, Pool) White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday that the Trump administration would not intervene in the extradition process of the controversial “manosphere” influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate. The Tate brothers, who were first formally indicted in Romania on charges of human trafficking and organized crime in , were arrested by U.S. Marshals in Florida last week following an extradition request from the United Kingdom in connection with new criminal charges of rape and sex trafficking in the country. Though both siblings deny any wrongdoing, at the beginning of the month the British government brought additional charges against the two, including seven more counts of rape and child pornography against Andrew, and two more counts of rape against Tristan; both counts of sexual assault and sex trafficking. Self-proclaimed “misogynist” Andrew Tate is a prominent voice in the manosphere — a loose-knit group of male internet personalities — and popular in some MAGA circles. Some of his supporters include Donald Trump Jr., who has publicly defended Tate , and Richard Grenell , a longtime Trump ally who serves as a special presidential envoy. But when asked whether the president or any of his top officials would step in to assist the pair, Leavitt answered emphatically. “No. We've already answered that question,” Leavitt said. As of Thursday, Vice President JD Vance still follows both brothers on X. The Trump administration reportedly raised concerns with Romanian officials in over the travel restrictions placed on the brothers while a separate criminal case remained ongoing. President Donald Trump denied any personal involvement in the matter.

stories.title: Private Prison Employee Accused of Shooting of Anti-ICE Protester in Colorado
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: Brandon Booth fired a shot between two protestors, hitting one, after they were involved in a verbal altercation, according to local police.
stories.content: Vehicles are parked outside the entrance to the GEO Group's immigrant detention facility in Aurora, Colorado. (AP Photo/David Zalubowski) An individual working for a private prison contractor has been charged in connection with a shooting that injured a protester outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Colorado, prosecutors announced Wednesday. District Attorney Brian Mason charged Brandon Booth, who is currently on administrative leave from detention center operator GEO Group, with assault and attempted assault. Booth allegedly discharged his personally owned weapon on July 16 near protesters outside an ICE facility in Aurora, Colorado, according to an arrest affidavit obtained by local media including news station Denver7 . Aurora police said Booth fired a round between two demonstrators and hit one, Emma Landis, in the foot. Booth left the scene in his vehicle but was apprehended by police, who said in the affidavit that Booth realized the incident had been caught on cameras and that he had “done some dumb shit.” Booth said was attempting to scare the protestors, who were blocking employees from entering, according to CBS News . He told police that as Landis and the other demonstrator walked by, they said, "We got your license plate, we're gonna run you down, we're gonna have people at your kids' school." Booth said his anger grew to "a 15 out of 10," after hearing the comment. Several days after receiving medical treatment for her injuries, Landis returned to the ongoing protest outside of the ICE facility, Colorado Public Radio reported. “I will continue to advocate for this stuff,” she said in an interview with More Perfect Union . “I got shot for it. I care.” The incident in Aurora follows a pair of fatal shootings in Texas and Maine by federal immigration agents. In both shootings, the individuals were killed in their vehicles. Booth is facing two felonies, with the assault charge carrying a sentence of 10 to 32 years in prison under Colorado law. GEO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NOTUS, but a spokesperson told NBC News on Friday that Booth had been placed on unpaid administrative leave. Booth’s next court date is scheduled for Aug. 13.

stories.title: A Decades-Old Terrorist Deportation Court Is Being Used for the First Time
stories.author: Jose Pagliery
stories.summary: Judges on the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, created in , have never heard a case — until now.
stories.content: The Justice Department filed its first application to a little-known and untested venue for the government to deal with terrorism suspects in the U.S. The Justice Department’s decision last week to activate a terrorist deportation court for the first time in its 30-year existence has surprised the judges who once sat on this dormant tribunal — and long wondered what hearings would even look like. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court is a little-known and untested venue for the government to deal with terrorism suspects in the U.S. with something other than regular criminal charges. For suspects abroad, the U.S. has used spies, drones and commandos to hunt down those accused of terrorism — to either kill them or drag them back to charges in the U.S. Why deport a terrorist? It’s a question that still confounds Alfred Wolin, 93, a retired federal judge who served on the ATRC for eight years and is the only jurist still alive of the five who were initially assigned to the special court in . “I don’t really know what the assignment was going to be in its totality,” he told NOTUS from his home in New Jersey. “And I'm not even sure to whom we would report.” Wolin never met with his fellow ATRC judges. Plans to convene and discuss how the court would operate were scrapped. And he distinctly remembers being told by a high-ranking court official that the special tribunal never got any cases because “the FBI blocked any cases being sent to us.” “I have no idea why,” Wolin said. “As far as I was concerned, it died.” Last week, the DOJ revived it, filing its first application to the court — a process shrouded in mystery that doesn’t even include the name of the person it seeks to deport or why. Prosecutors with its National Security Division presented the case directly to Judge Joan Ericksen, a U.S. District judge in Minnesota who also serves as the ATRC’s chief judge. The only public part of the July 15 application is a cover page that makes reference to the classified nature of the case, first reported by Court Watch. Prosecutors presented their arguments to Ericksen behind closed doors on July 16, and she responded with a follow-up order demanding more information. “The court had questions about the nexus that the government alleges between the actions of the respondent and the specific sections and subsections it invokes with respect to those actions,” she wrote. The judge gave prosecutors until this Wednesday to include additional “factual or legal analysis to satisfy its statutory obligations” in its application, but the court website didn’t show any additional public filings on Thursday morning. Congress created the court with ’s Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act , a Republican-led pushback on the Clinton administration that limited death row appeals and made it easier to deport immigrants convicted of crimes. Then-Rep. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) called it a “better-than-nothing anti-terrorism bill” that he would “sadly and reluctantly” support. President Bill Clinton signed it into law. Then-Sen. Bob Smith, a New Hampshire Republican, tucked the provision for a new, secret deportation court into the bill. Smith said it would be modeled after the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act court, which considers security agency requests for surveillance warrants against foreigners inside the United States. Warning of a growing threat of terrorism, Smith envisioned a legal process that would allow prosecutors to withhold classified evidence from an immigrant accused of terrorism. He also noted the bill was passed “in memory of the one-year anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombings,” despite the FBI calling it “the deadliest act of homegrown terrorism in U.S. history.” The bombing was planned and perpetrated by Timothy McVeigh, a U.S. Army veteran who joined the Ku Klux Klan and counted the racist book “The Turner Diaries” among his favorite literature. “Far too often, deporting dangerous terrorists is complicated and difficult for our law enforcement officials. The bill we passed tonight would alleviate some of the problems with this process," Smith said in a press release at the time. Smith is now a member of the Trump’s administration’s Homeland Security Advisory Council . He did not respond to a request for comment. During congressional debate over the bill, then-Sen. Joe Biden criticized what he called “a secret hearing, using secret evidence.” He envisioned a defendant saying, “Hey, tell me who said I was a terrorist. How do you know that?” only to have the government respond, “Oh, no, we can’t tell you. We know you did it, and we can’t tell you how we know.” Part of the new law was immediately used in the summer of to crack down on immigrants, with the Supreme Court ordering the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to reconsider its postponement of an Egyptian man’s deportation over selling $ worth of hashish. But the Clinton DOJ refused to file a terrorist deportation case in the special court, prompting then-Sen. Orrin Hatch to write to Vice President Al Gore later that year to complain that not “a single terrorist alien [has] been deported pursuant to the terrorist alien removal provisions.” The letter cited the Centennial Olympic Park bombing in Atlanta that summer, which investigators later found was carried out not by an immigrant but by U.S. citizen Eric Rudolph , an anti-abortion zealot. Wolin, the retired judge, recalled how he got put on the new tribunal. It all started at the Greenbrier resort in West Virginia, where federal judges had gathered to mingle. Chief Justice William Rehnquist needed a tennis partner and asked Wolin to play with him against U.S. Judge H. Lee Sarokin of the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals and a second appellate judge in Pennsylvania. “Rehnquist was not what I would call an accomplished tennis player,” Wolin remembered with a chuckle. “I think he was relying on me.” A week or so after the game, the chief justice leaned on him again. A Supreme Court administrative assistant called Wolin, then a trial judge in New Jersey, to inform him that the chief justice wanted to appoint him to something called the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. “It sounded like something I would be interested in doing, but we never received a case,” said Wolin, who still keeps a letter signed by Rehnquist in a plaque hanging on a wall in his basement. Liam O’Grady, another retired federal judge who served on the special court from to , said he never held any meetings with fellow judges on this assignment either. He said the current case’s true nature is anyone’s guess. O’Grady acknowledged that it would make little sense for the U.S. government not to imprison a person deemed a true danger to the American public — unless, that is, some spy agency has concluded that convicting the person would require exposing sensitive information or espionage tactics in open court. However, the U.S. justice system already has an established process for handling this kind of volatile evidence: the Classified Information Procedures Act of , which allows defense lawyers with security clearances to build their cases while keeping their clients largely in the dark. This process has been used in cases against government employees accused of selling military secrets, foreign secret agents and even President Donald Trump when he was charged with retaining classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. So why go this route for the first time in 30 years? O’Grady reasoned the DOJ might head to the Alien Terrorist Removal Court if the evidence is so sensitive that the government isn’t even willing to share it with a vetted defense lawyer — or expose vague summaries of it in open court. The ATRC permits the government to present evidence directly to a judge without the typical due process that allows a defendant to understand the nature of the charges against them. According to a legal paper written by Jonathan H. Yu, then an adviser to DOJ immigration lawyers, lawful permanent residents accused in this special court get an extra layer of protection via a panel of vetted attorneys who may review the evidence in the judge’s chambers to “challenge the veracity of that classified information.” A legal paper written by a Duke University law student noted that the court’s procedure “does not implicate the Sixth Amendment right to confront one’s accuser because ATRC proceedings are immigration rather than criminal proceedings” and the accused are non-citizens. A provision in the law says the accused person doesn’t even have the right to challenge evidence that was illegally obtained. American law professors David Cole and Stephen Vladeck decried these exceptions to widely accepted civil rights in an essay included in a legal compendium, “Reasoning Rights: Comparative Judicial Engagement.” “The right to confront the evidence used to deprive a person of his liberty is essential to fundamental (and indeed, constitutional) notions of fairness,” Cole and Vladeck wrote. They noted that Canada’s supreme court in rejected that government’s attempt to deport several men accused of Islamist extremism while relying on a secretive court and hidden evidence. (One of the men is an imam named Adil Charkaoui who would give a speech in calling for Allah to “kill the enemies of the people of Gaza,” which led to an investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but no criminal charges.) The Canadian supreme court decision led the country to adopt a system in which defendants are still kept in the dark but third-party “cleared counsel” can see secret evidence and make legal challenges on their behalf. That experience could serve as a warning as the United States begins to employ its secret deportation court for the first time. O’Grady, who was a federal district judge in Virginia, suspects that the DOJ never filed a terrorist deportation case until now because “it's out of sight, out of mind, and it's never been used because no one knew how to use it.” But he said he recognizes concerns over the Trump administration’s attempt to expand the definition of “terrorism” with two executive orders that aim to designate anti-fascists as a “domestic terrorist organization” and direct law enforcement to combat those who hold views considered to display “anti-Americanism,” “anti-capitalism” and “extremism on migration, race, and gender.” “It's not an idle thought. This administration has looked for many different ways to aggressively respond to what it believes are big immigration problems, and they believe they have a mandate from the public to be aggressive,” O’Grady said. “So, are they curious as to whether this is another tool they can use? That may be part of the inspiration, but again, who knows. We're going to have to see what shakes out.”

stories.title: Software Vendor Denies Responsibility for New Jersey Voter-Registration Error
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: IDEMIA, a French company that operates globally, said New Jersey was ultimately responsible for validating and adjudicating voter registrations.
stories.content: IDEMIA refuted the allegations in a statement to NOTUS, saying the 6, files submitted to the MVC and Division of Elections contained accurate information “according to the design specifications as set out by the state.” Matt Rourke/AP Photo The biometrics and cryptography company that New Jersey officials said was responsible for erroneously adding thousands of noncitizens to voter rolls denied any mishandling — stating that the responsibility of voter registration lies with the state. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced Tuesday that a serious software error caused by IDEMIA, a French company that operates globally, led to roughly 6, non-citizens being accidentally registered to vote between June and June . Fewer than went on to illegally cast ballots, Sherill said, and a preliminary review found that the votes did not sway any elections. The debacle comes in the middle of intensified debates about election integrity aggravated by President Donald Trump’s widely-debunked assertions that the election was rigged against him. Trump mentioned the incident during a Wednesday speech in Georgia, falsely stating that “thousands and thousands of votes” were illegally cast. IDEMIA said in a statement it had worked with the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) for more than 40 years, supporting the system that allows eligible residents to indicate they want to register to vote when they apply for or renew a license or state ID. “IDEMIA's role is to transmit information through the motor vehicle system,” the statement said, adding that voter registration data is transmitted to the state Division of Elections, which “ultimately” holds responsibility for verification. “Information submitted by IDEMIA must still be validated and adjudicated by the Division of Elections.” On Wednesday, a Sherrill spokesperson said IDEMIA’s system error could be attributed to the records of people who answered “No” to the citizenship question erroneously being transmitted to the Division of Elections. IDEMIA refuted the allegations in a statement to NOTUS, saying the 6, files submitted to the MVC and Division of Elections contained accurate information “according to the design specifications as set out by the state.” The 6, individuals had checked “Yes” to wanting to register to vote and “No” to being a citizen, IDEMIA said. The files were always available to MVC officials and did not indicate at any point that the individuals were citizens, IDEMIA said. In June , the Division of Elections had alerted the MVC to 6, files that were missing a party affiliation, IDEMIA said, but the company did not have confirmation that those individuals were ever registered to vote. “IDEMIA does not control or manage voter enrollment, our role is simply to collect self-reported citizenship and interest data,” the statement said. “This leads to more questions — if the Division of Elections had missing information which is required to register in the State of New Jersey, did the Division of Elections approve these individuals be to the Voter Rolls.” Those who were erroneously registered to vote are being notified by mail and are being removed from the voter rolls, Sherill said on Tuesday. She heavily criticized IDEMIA for releasing software with “such a glaring error,” the MVC for taking more than a year to patch the issue and former Gov. Phil Murphy’s administration for not being transparent about the incident at the time. Sherrill acknowledged on Tuesday that Trump would likely use the incident to back up his claims of widespread vulnerabilities in the country’s election security system, despite little evidence to support the claim. She said Trump “has zero credibility on the issue of election integrity.” Noncitizen voting is extremely rare, election officials say, and there is no evidence that it has happened on a scale that could change the results of an election. The incident has sparked further scrutiny. On Wednesday, Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-New Jersey) demanded a government-wide audit into IDEMIA’s federal contracts, saying the company handles “an excessive amount of the federal security apparatus.” “This incident raises serious concerns about the reliability of IDEMIA’s software, the company’s quality control practices, and the federal government’s reliance on a single contractor to manage highly sensitive identity and biometric systems,” Gottheimer wrote in a letter to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and U.S. General Services Administration Administrator Edward C. Forst.

stories.title: Judge Sets Maduro Criminal Trial for June 2027
stories.author: Jose Pagliery
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein noted that he would have to spend significant time privately reviewing sensitive evidence behind closed doors.
stories.content: The court hearing was the ousted Venezuelan president’s first public appearance in months. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig) NEW YORK — Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro’s criminal trial in New York City will start in June , a judge ruled during a Wednesday hearing, a timeline that reflects the mountain of classified evidence in a case that involves spy agencies, the U.S. military and law enforcement. The court hearing was the ousted Venezuelan president’s first public appearance in months, as his case slowly advances. It was brief, with little discussion about the pending issues in the case. Maduro appeared healthy and composed when he entered the courtroom at noon, sporting thick-framed glasses and a tan, short-sleeved prison uniform. He scanned the crowd in the tightly packed gallery before nodding and saying “good morning” in a firm tone. He made a tight smile beneath his signature mustache as he made his way toward his lawyers, then sat and put on black headphones to hear a translation of the proceedings. Maduro, who remained in power after contested national elections, was captured in a U.S. military operation in Caracas in January and brought to the United States, an action he described as “kidnapping.” The DOJ charged him with multiple offenses including conspiracy to commit narco-terrorism and conspiracy to import cocaine, alleging that the South American dictator had morphed into a corrupt public official and drug kingpin. The U.S. approach echoed the American military-led capture of Panamanian military dictator Manuel Noriega, who was convicted of drug charges and spent decades in U.S., French and Panamanian prisons before his death. Maduro, 63, and his wife, who was also seized, potential life sentences if convicted on charges he flooded the United States with cocaine. A major hang-up early on pertained to the Trump administration’s initial refusal to allow Maduro to tap Venezuelan public funds to pay for his defense lawyers, but the government has since relented. Defense lawyer Barry Pollack alluded to making future arguments about Maduro being protected by sovereign immunity and limitations in the U.S. government’s jurisdiction. U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein noted that he would have to spend significant time privately reviewing sensitive evidence behind closed doors as part of the Classified Information Procedures Act of and asked repeatedly whether the next year would be enough time for him to decide what documents and information can be used by prosecutors in open court. “This is a realistic schedule,” Pollack said. A defense lawyer for the ousted president’s wife, Cilia Adela Flores de Maduro, who was also in the room, concurred. Lawyers must lay out their legal arguments in time for the next court hearing, set for Nov. 17, and the judge scheduled a final conference on May 25, a week before the trial is expected to start. Hellerstein, 93, struggled to walk to the bench and speak during the hearing. He could oversee what could be a weeks-long trial. Prosecutors and defense lawyers made no mention in court of how long the trial could go. Hellerstein appears to be sensitive to the optics of having a foreign leader justice in American courts; at one point he asked an agent with the U.S. Marshals Service, who had tapped Maduro’s shoulder, to back away when Maduro began to whisper to his lawyer. “Let them speak. Let them speak,” Hellerstein said in a hoarse voice. When the hearing was over, Maduro stood and adjusted a second pair of reading glasses in his left chest pocket. He shook hands with defense lawyers and left the courtroom.

stories.title: The Trump Administration Moves to Stop Collecting Workplace Demographic Data
stories.author: Natalie Alms
stories.summary: Democrats say the race, sex and ethnicity data is central to enforcing antidiscrimination laws.
stories.content: President Donald Trump made the unprecedented move of firing two of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's three Democratic commissioners. AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana The Trump administration has moved to stop requiring companies to report demographic data, undoing a 60-year-old precedent that Democrats and civil rights experts say could make it harder to enforce antidiscrimination laws. Republicans on the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, which is charged with enforcing civil rights laws against workplace discrimination, voted on Tuesday to end the agency’s decades-long practice of collecting race, sex and ethnicity workforce data. The commission’s Republicans argue that these reporting requirements may actually lead to discrimination because they “may encourage employers to discriminate against employees who are not considered ‘minorities,’” the proposed rule reads. The agency’s lone Democratic commissioner, Kalpana Kotagal, said that ending the collection of race and sex data would “kneecap the agency’s ability to investigate discrimination and protect workers.” “These efforts should be seen for what they are: an attempt to weaken equal employment opportunity, and to undermine progress for women and historically marginalized communities,” Kotagal said in a statement. The move to halt data collection is the latest change in an ongoing transformation of the workplace civil rights agency, which Congress created under the Civil Rights Act of . The bipartisan commission is typically composed of five presidentially-appointed members who serve five-year terms. No more than three members can be from the same party. But early in his administration, President Donald Trump made the unprecedented move of firing two of the panel’s three Democratic commissioners, leaving only Kotagal and Republican Andrea Lucas, currently the EEOC’s chair, on the commission. Another Republican commissioner, Brittany Bull Panuccio, has since been appointed and confirmed by the Senate, giving the Republicans the majority at the EEOC, which is at its lowest staffing levels in over 45 years after about a quarter of its workforce since Trump took office. Under Lucas, the EEOC has prioritized “remedying DEI-related race and sex discrimination.” Late last year, she posted a viral video on X asking, “Are you a white male who has experienced discrimination at work based on your race or sex?” and telling viewers that they may be able to file a claim. In addition to claiming that the demographics data collection may promote discrimination, the EEOC is also arguing that there are also constitutional concerns that the reporting requirements may violate equal protection guarantees and that ending the reporting requirements will result in cost savings. Kotagal, in her statement, said that the constitutional claim is “untethered from reality” and that the EEOC may now have to resort to subpoenas and requests for information to get the data from employers, processes that could wind up in expensive court battles. Democrats have also questioned the administration’s reverse-discrimination concerns. Chai Feldblum, who was a Democratic EEOC commissioner for over eight years beginning in , told NOTUS that it is an “absolutely false assumption” that employers that discover a discrepancy such as a lack of Black people in management will “necessarily violate the law” by deciding, “My next three hires will be Black people.” “That is illegal,” said Feldblum. But “there are many legal ways to remedy a disparity.” The data collected by the EEOC is instrumental to the agency’s enforcement capacity, said Kotagal, pointing to a $5.5 million settlement with trucking company Central Transport over allegations that the company intentionally refused to hire qualified female truck drivers as an example. Analyzing the company’s data showed statistically significant disparities in the hiring of male drivers, which helped the EEOC find cause that there had been discrimination, Kotagal said. Demographic data helps the EEOC put discrimination allegations into context and guide investigations, said Karla Gilbride, who previously served as EEOC general counsel after being appointed by former President Joe Biden. “Losing this data will take an important tool out of the EEOC's law enforcement toolbox and slow down the investigative process, as the EEOC will have to request the same type of information from employers after a charge is received instead of already having it at the investigation's outset,” Gilbride told NOTUS in a statement. The decision to halt reporting requirements, if finalized, would also affect what information employers can access to see how their workforce compares to industry norms. Currently, the EEOC publishes aggregate level summaries of the data it's moving to ax. Even with the EEOC changing its priorities, employers could still be subject to legal challenges if they have discrimination problems, said Feldblum, noting that “the law does not change because chair Lucas wants it to change.” The EEOC is one of many parts of the government that is moving to dismantle demographic data collection. LGBTQ+ data has especially been targeted, and data scientists fear that race and ethnicity data is becoming another target for the Trump administration, as NOTUS has previously reported . The EEOC is collecting public comments on the proposed rule to roll back reporting requirements for 30 days and is holding a public hearing on the plan on Aug. 11.

stories.title: Judge Rules Trump Must Turn Over Financial Info as Part of His Lawsuit Against the BBC
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: It’s still unclear whether the president’s legal team will appeal the decision.
stories.content: Trump claims that the documentary, which aired days before the presidential election, was deceptively edited and implies he incited the Jan. 6, , attack on the U.S. Capitol. Mark Schiefelbein/AP A federal judge ruled on Tuesday that President Donald Trump must turn over his financial information to substantiate claims made in a $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC. U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett of Florida determined that to justify Trump attorneys’ complaint that the president endured “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” due to a BBC documentary titled “Trump: A Second Chance?,” the president must provide a detailed account of his financial information. Trump’s attorneys put financial and reputational consequences at the core of the original lawsuit . The attorneys have since moved to narrow the case to reputational damages alone. But the federal judge on Tuesday rejected the claims. “All of President Trump's brand, properties and businesses are impugned or said to have been impugned. Reputational, economic damages, all of that is now at issue in this case,” the federal judge argued, according to Politico. It’s still unclear whether Trump’s attorneys plan to appeal the ruling. The president claims that the documentary, which aired days before the presidential election, was deceptively edited and implies the president incited the Jan. 6, , attack on the U.S. Capitol. Even though the BBC apologized to Trump for “the manner in which the video clip was edited,” the British news organization insisted its documentary did not defame the president. During his second term, Trump has sued multiple news outlets for billions of dollars, including The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times . He’s also received more than $30 million in settlements with ABC News and CBS News.

stories.title: DHS Plans to Spend Over $30 Million on Body Cameras
stories.author: Jackie Llanos
stories.summary: Each arrest team will have one agent with a body camera, DHS said.
stories.content: Homeland Security Sec. Markwayne Mullin arrives for a closed-door conference with fellow Republicans as Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., tries to advance a spending package for the Iran war and President Donald Trump's push for strict new voter ID requirements, at the Capitol in Washington, Tuesday, July 21, . (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) The Department of Homeland Security plans to spend more than $30 million for body-worn cameras after the fatal shooting of two immigrants in the past two weeks renewed scrutiny of the Trump administration’s aggressive enforcement approach. DHS ordered body cameras from Axon Enterprise in two separate awards Friday, one for $17.8 million and another totaling $13.1 million .
