Merkley, who is the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that oversees funding for the Interior Department, asked Burgum to respond to the letter by Aug. 7 with a full accounting of how NPS has spent the $ million provided in the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” for semiquincentennial events and activities. “It is unacceptable to ask the American people to bail out Freedom . Congress already appropriated $ million—without bipartisan input—with the administration promising that private donors would help finance the rest. If the administration designated Freedom as the responsible entity for these events, Freedom —not taxpayers—should be paying the remaining costs,” Merkley wrote. He said that Interior Department staff also held a closed-door briefing with senators that failed to elicit answers to his questions about where, exactly, the additional money would go. “Our understanding from the administration was that taxpayer funds would contribute $ million and private donations would contribute the balance of the funding,” Merkley wrote. “Given that understanding, what has gone wrong that has led to this additional request for taxpayer funds?” The Interior Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NOTUS, but told The Washington Post on Wednesday that the extra funding was needed to help address security needs, citing recent threats at the White House correspondents’ dinner and the UFC event held on the White House lawn. “Given the elevated security threats against high-profile events in Washington, D.C. … an elevated security posture was needed to ensure the safety of the public at these events. This funding would help address the expenditures associated with the elevated security posture,” a spokesperson for the department said.

stories.title: Trump Administration Announces Another Data Center on Federal Land
stories.author: Mara Hoplamazian
stories.summary: The Energy Department is partnering with developers and utilities to build an artificial intelligence “innovation campus” in Kentucky.
stories.content: The Trump administration is attempting to help private companies build data centers on federal land, including public lands. (AP Photo/Rod Lamkey) The Trump administration is accelerating its push to build data centers on federally controlled land — allowing developers and utility companies to sidestep permitting battles and community backlash. The Energy Department announced Wednesday it is partnering with NextEra Energy, Brookfield and three utilities to build an “artificial intelligence and high-performance computing innovation campus” on portions of DOE’s Paducah Site in western Kentucky, which was built in the 1950s to enrich uranium. The plans include 2 gigawatts of new natural gas-fired power generation and more than 2½ gigawatts of battery storage. That’s more power than the data center is expected to need, which would allow the generators to deliver power to nearby homes and businesses, according to DOE. Building data centers on federal sites has been a main goal of the Trump administration’s push to accelerate the pace of AI development. Last year, DOE offered up sites in Idaho, South Carolina, Tennessee and Kentucky for data center developers. Another project on federal land, a combination of gas generators and a 10-gigawatt data center, was announced in southern Ohio this year. Federal officials are leasing land to SB Energy for that project, which DOE is branding as the world’s largest AI data center. Energy officials say data centers can be constructed more quickly on federal sites, using fast-tracked permitting processes. Building a data center on an existing DOE site comes with other advantages, too. Many of them are already set up with costly transmission infrastructure, previously used for Cold War-era nuclear enrichment facilities, to support national laboratories or for other energy-intensive programs. Developers will also probably fewer environmental hurdles, because many of these sites — especially those still undergoing nuclear cleanup — are already experiencing environmental degradation. Those sites allow data center developers to avoid the major stumbling blocks that many other recent projects have : fierce local opposition and zoning and permitting issues. The administration is attempting to help private companies build data centers on public lands as well, but facing bigger roadblocks. Developers must obtain a right-of-way on public lands, a process that involves additional evaluations and obligations to prevent environmental harm. The more complicated process means more chances for outside groups to stop the efforts: A plan to build a center on federal lands in Nevada is currently facing legal pushback from national environmental groups and local residents. Michigan Democratic Rep. Rashida Tlaib has introduced a bill to ban AI data centers on all lands owned or managed by the federal government, citing the concerns of pollution and increased energy costs. Rep. Andy Barr (R-Kentucky) called the new project in his state “historic” and said he personally advocated for the development. “Together with our private sector partners, this investment will create jobs, strengthen our energy security, and deliver lasting economic growth for Paducah and the Commonwealth for decades to come,” he said. The development will involve more than $ billion in private investment, federal officials said, and create 8, construction jobs and permanent jobs.

stories.title: The Secret Service Is Spending $90M to Supersize its Force
stories.author: Derek Hawkins, Eric Katz
stories.summary: The agency is looking for 80, applicants. One contract to hit half of that goal is already breaking records.
stories.content: Secret Service leaders are racing to staff up for a security calendar that includes the presidential campaign, party conventions and the Olympic Games in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) The Secret Service awarded a $90 million contract to an untested firm this month for a nationwide advertising campaign aimed at recruiting thousands of personnel ahead of a grueling protective schedule in . The contract appears to be the largest the Secret Service has ever awarded to an outside company for recruitment, according to former officials and government records. And it sheds light on a hiring surge the Secret Service launched late last year to ease pressure on a workforce that has been understaffed for years. The Secret Service wants the company to deliver more than 41, applicants in the next year, about half of the Secret Service’s overall goal of drawing about 80, applicants in that period, contracting documents say. “That’s a massive campaign for them. It’s unprecedented,” said a former senior homeland security official familiar with Secret Service operations, who requested anonymity to discuss the contract. Secret Service leaders have said they want to hire 4, new employees by to reduce burnout from an unforgiving operational tempo and make up for an attrition of experienced agents, which current and former officials say has worsened in recent months. Secret Service spokesperson Anthony Guglielmi said in a statement that the agency’s recruitment campaign is designed to “rightsize and properly staff the agency to meet the demands of a significantly heightened mission.” “Through the federal procurement process, the agency selected a strategic marketing partner to support recruitment goals,” he said. The Secret Service received $1.2 billion in a sweeping reconciliation package last year, including for recruiting, retention incentives and recruitment bonuses. Still, as of May, the agency had gained fewer than employees since President Donald Trump took office, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management. Secret Service leaders are racing to staff up for a security calendar that includes the presidential campaign, party conventions and the Olympic Games in Los Angeles. If the agency meets its hiring goals, it would expand by about 20%, topping 10, employees for the first time in its history. The $90 million award went to a small contractor, Avvy LLC, based in Fairfax, Virginia, which has never previously won a federal contract. Avvy is on the hook for producing advertisements on television, radio and streaming services, including during prime time. Streaming videos should generate 84 million impressions in the first year, while streaming audio ads should result in million, contract documents state. The contract calls for non-skippable video ads and streaming audio ads running in Washington, D.C., and 10 states, including Texas, Florida and Georgia. The ads are supposed to target people ages 20 to 39 who are involved in law enforcement, the military, or are veterans, according to contracting documents. Guglielmi said the contractor will support Secret Service staff in recruiting and event logistics, but the Secret Service “remains responsible for evaluating applicants and making all hiring decisions.” He that in-person events had accelerated the hiring process, but “no qualification, suitability, security or training standards have been reduced or eliminated.” The scope of the contract highlights how the Secret Service is casting a wide net for its candidates, only a small fraction of whom make it through the agency’s arduous hiring process. Some former homeland security officials cautioned that such a large batch of applicants could create bottlenecks in hiring, training and onboarding. Secret Service agents train for months alongside other federal law enforcement recruits at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Georgia, before spending several more months training in eastern Maryland and then joining field offices around the country. That will require a delicate accommodation at FLETC, which is still moving through new hires to support Trump’s surge of immigration personnel. FLETC paused training for most non-Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel for several months last year as part of that push. “None of the demands they’ve placed on FLETC for surge training have been realistic,” a current FLETC trainer, who requested anonymity over fear of reprisal, said of the administration’s efforts. One former Secret Service official who handled personnel matters questioned whether the agency has enough workers to vet prospective agents and send them into the field in time to make a significant difference in the workload. “The bottom-line question is still: The company delivers 41, applicants, then what?” said the former official, who requested anonymity to discuss the situation. “You still can’t get them on the street. Maybe you put them in a holding pattern and work from there.” The former official that while the Secret Service, like other law enforcement agencies, had struggled to hire, “That doesn’t mean $90 million just to get applicants is a smart idea.” Many applicants don’t make it through the process to begin with. Background checks and a notoriously exacting polygraph exam screen many candidates out. Recently, questions about drug usage and financial issues have disqualified some young recruits, according to people familiar with the process. Officials say the physical fitness exam has also been a growing barrier for many candidates. The Secret Service offers recruitment bonuses of $40, or more, but it faces competition from other law enforcement agencies offering similar incentives and roughly equal pay for less demanding work. “They’ve got a lot of forces conspiring against them,” the former senior homeland security official said. The Secret Service has seen some positive signs on the hiring front. In roughly the first five months of , the agency received more than 22, job applications, the Department of Homeland Security said at the time. That marked a more than % increase over the same period in , officials said. Despite that success, the number of new hires dropped off slightly in following a spike in onboarding in President Joe Biden’s last year in office, according to OPM data. Guglielmi said the agency is on track to exceed hiring goals in fiscal , with more than 1, new special agents and more than Secret Service Police officers expected to be hired by the end of September. The contract was awarded to Avvy on an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity basis, meaning its final terms are flexible based on what the Secret Service demands and what the contractor can deliver. Federal regulation states a preference for awarding such contracts to multiple vendors, though in this case the Secret Service chose just one. Avvy is a “joint venture” of two other firms — Arillic and the larger DCG, both based in Virginia. They have formed a partnership under the Small Business Administration’s Mentor-Protege program, which enables larger companies to win contracts set aside for small businesses in exchange for providing support to the smaller firm. Arillic has won a few federal contracts, according to government records, with the largest being a $3.5 million award to the Health and Human Services Department. DCG has won hundreds of contracts collectively worth hundreds of millions of dollars. Some of DCG’s contracts have involved communications and advertising for the Department of Veterans Affairs and the U.S. Army’s public affairs office. Arillic CEO Arthur Tamayo said a combination of both teams would provide the work. In a brief phone call, he said he appreciated NOTUS’ interest in the contract, noting there was “a lot of crazy stuff coming out” in the government contracting space lately including “people turning the Reflecting Pool green.” Tamayo, who is also listed as the point of contact for Avvy, did not answer detailed questions about the Secret Service contract. DCG did not respond to a request for comment. While Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection have set significantly larger hiring targets in Trump’s current term, the Secret Service contract appears to be the largest award the department has provided to one company for recruiting or hiring since he came back into office. In Trump's first term, CBP signed a $ million contract with Accenture to help it bring on 7, border personnel and solicited offers for a similar contract at ICE. DHS canceled the CBP contract after Accenture only successfully helped the agency hire 15 employees and aborted the ICE contract before it got off the ground. Jeff Neal, a long-time career federal human resources official who most recently led DHS’s personnel shop, said it was not unusual for agencies to seek outside help when looking to surge hiring. But he said he didn’t think the applicant goals were realistic. “The thing I question,” he , “is a company that doesn’t have experience. But that appears to not be out of the ordinary for this administration.”

stories.title: The FDA Is Officially Codifying DOGE-Era Changes
stories.author: Margaret Manto
stories.summary: The agency will stop specializing its field inspectors starting in October.
stories.content: The Food and Drug Administration shed thousands of staff during DOGE-era cuts. Aaron M. Sprecher/AP The Food and Drug Administration will officially consolidate administrative staff across the agency’s nine centers and stop specializing its field inspectors starting in October. The Trump administration approved the agency’s reorganization proposal, according to an internal agency announcement reviewed by NOTUS. In the announcement, Melanie Keller, the FDA’s deputy commissioner for operations and chief operating officer, said the reorganization proposal known as “Simple Reform” will go into effect on Oct. 1. Under the revised structure, individual centers like the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research will no longer conduct their own administrative affairs like human resources, finance and information technology services. Instead, the agency will operate under a “shared service” model in which the FDA Office of Operations controls those functions across the agency. The agency will also stop assigning its specialized field inspectors, who oversee the safety of medical products and clinical trials, to specific subject areas. Instead, they’ll operate as generalists and conduct inspections and investigations across multiple industries. “Shared Services seeks to maximize efficiency and consistency,” the internal FDA website detailing the plan states. Some former agency staff criticized the changes as not understanding how specialized different aspects of the agency are. One former acting commissioner, Janet Woodcock, called the changes a “mindless approach” and a “really, really bad idea” when the proposal was first announced in , according to the regulatory news publication Pink Sheet. The reorganization will not drastically change the roles and responsibilities of the agency’s nine centers. Nor will it result in any current FDA employees losing their jobs, according to the internal agency web page. The changes formalize shifts to the agency’s operations and administrative structure that were put in place by the Trump administration over the past 18 months. Like other agencies across the Health Department , many of the FDA’s administrative staff were let go in the reductions-in-force led by DOGE in . The agency let go a total of 3, employees in the DOGE cuts and is now hiring about 2, new employees. The FDA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the reorganization. Steven Grossman, a regulatory consultant who writes the blog FDA Matters, said that while he wasn’t familiar with the specific changes proposed, he was concerned that they could oversimplify an agency that’s complicated for a reason. “Centralization is not always good and efficient,” Grossman said, adding that it “often leaves functions understaffed. It often misses the contours of how work is actually done.” Some experts also pointed out that the changes will generalize the duties of inspectors who oversee medical products and clinical research. The agency moved in to place inspectors within specific programs of expertise, rather than requiring them to work across multiple programs. The approved plan would reverse that change . “Proper assessment requires FDA investigators with matching skills and knowledge, and it’s absurd to expect ‘generalists’ to develop those traits,” Steven Silverman, a former director of the FDA Office of Compliance, Center for Devices and Radiological Health, wrote in a blog post when the proposal was announced. “How and why would a generalist build these strengths while going from a drug inspection one week to a biologics site the next with a device inspection the week after?”

stories.title: RFK Jr.’s Big Promise to Ban Pharmaceutical Ads Is in the Slow Lane
stories.author: Paige Winfield Cunningham
stories.summary: Meanwhile, drugmakers are spending more on TV ads this year than last year.
stories.content: Top spenders of pharmaceutical advertising over the past year were makers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and drugs to treat psoriasis and Crohn’s disease. David J. Phillip/AP Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has the power to stop pharmaceutical companies from advertising directly to consumers. He could do it almost instantaneously by revising the ’90s-era guidance giving drugmakers the opening to run 30-second TV ads on their products. However, the Department of Health and Human Services is taking a different approach — one that indicates the matter is not as high on the Trump administration’s priority list as Kennedy told his supporters. The Food and Drug Administration has posted its intent to require drugmakers to disclose all risk and safety information within ads instead of directing consumers to an external source — a way to effectively end television and radio drug ads by rendering them untenably long, experts say. The push is through the traditional regulatory process. A senior administration official told NOTUS that the rule is “on the priority list” but there is no firm timeline to get it enacted. “I don’t take it seriously at all,” Lars Noah, a law professor at the University of Florida who focuses on pharmaceutical regulation, said of Kennedy’s pledge to ban drug commercials. Two days before the general election, Kennedy promised to halt the prescription drug ads millions of Americans see on their screens every day. “Let’s get President Trump back in the White House and me to DC so we can ban pharmaceutical advertising,” he wrote on X. Last September, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum ordering HHS to go after pharmaceutical advertising. Forcing drug companies to report all the side effects in their advertisements “might create an advertisement that’s four minutes long,” Kennedy said at the time. The FDA also sent letters to dozens of pharmaceutical companies ordering them to either halt or revise ads the agency considers misleading. But even as Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” report last year decried drug advertising, it stopped short of calling for a ban. And Kennedy himself has spent far more time talking about his efforts to prevent chronic disease with healthy eating and exercise in speeches around the country. Nearly a year later, the drug industry’s ad spending continues to climb. When Americans tune into cable and network news and sports games, they are increasingly likely to see ads for medications. Since Trump’s September memorandum, drugmakers have spent $5.2 billion on TV ads, according to an analysis provided to NOTUS by iSpot, a TV measurement company. That’s 8% more than the same period the year prior. Top spenders over the past year were makers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and drugs to treat psoriasis and Crohn’s disease. In February alone — the month of the Super Bowl — Novo Nordisk spent $33 million on an ad for the weight-loss drug Wegovy. The industry fiercely opposes stricter rules on drug ads. Pharmaceutical commercials can bring in revenue five times the cost of making the ad, industry analysts say. Drugmakers, who court doctors to prescribe their medications, use commercials as a way to drive demand directly among patients. “Clearly there is value to the companies that are buying these expensive ads, otherwise they wouldn’t do it,” Noah said. The American Medical Association and other critics of pharmaceutical advertising say ads can mislead consumers by emphasizing the benefits of treatments while downplaying negative side effects. The consumer advocacy group Public Citizen wrote Thursday to acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, urging the agency to ban direct-to-consumer advertising. “The advertisements appeal to patients’ emotions, distract them, and distort their perceptions of a drug’s benefits and risks,” the letter said. Kennedy, who believes too many Americans take medications instead of fixing their underlying health, says ads convince people they need medicines they don’t. Such ads are confusing patients and “distorting the doctor-patient relationship” by causing people to think they need medications they don’t, the FDA notice says. Drugmakers contend that existing regulations are sufficient. “Direct-to-consumer advertising helps patients make informed prescription medicine decisions with their health care providers,” said Andrew Powaleny, deputy vice president of public affairs at PhRMA, the pharmaceutical industry association. PhRMA has been lobbying against Trump’s memorandum and on a bipartisan bill from Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) that would create civil penalties for online influencers saying false or misleading things about prescription drugs, according to lobbying disclosure filings. “If this administration is serious about wanting to address DTC advertisements, I welcome ways to work together to get it done,” Durbin said in a statement provided to NOTUS. The United States is one of just two countries that allows direct-to-consumer drug advertising. Ad spending spiked after , when the FDA issued guidance allowing companies to summarize a medication’s risks briefly enough to fit into a 30-second TV spot. Kennedy could easily rescind that guidance, experts said, although it would almost certainly be challenged in court by drugmakers. A federal judge blocked an effort during the first Trump administration to require ads to mention the drug’s price. “I think it is unlikely that we will see drug advertising be totally banned under the current legal framework,” said Aaron Kesselheim, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. Before entering office, however, that appeared to be a legal fight Kennedy was eager to get into.

stories.title: The White House Is Back in the Pandemic Preparedness Game. Barely.
stories.author: Margaret Manto
stories.summary: “You can’t run an Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy as an army of one,” a former White House official said.
stories.content: The White House's pandemic preparedness office has been empty since mid- . Alex Brandon/AP Since dismantling the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy, or OPPR, the Trump administration has been tested by a record-breaking measles outbreak, a cruise-ship hantavirus outbreak, an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and a lettuce-dwelling parasite that sickened thousands. The White House recently staffed the office, which at its peak in had 15 employees, with just one health official, along with a second biosecurity specialist at the National Security Council. Former government health officials say that is far from where the office needs to be to effectively combat dangerous pathogens. “That is a start, but it is not nearly enough,” said a former White House official familiar with the health security functions of the National Security Council and OPPR, who requested anonymity to speak freely about their former employer. “You can’t run an Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy as an army of one,” they continued. OPPR was created to coordinate cross-agency responses to major public health risks. But that office has been empty since mid- , after all of the staffers from the Biden administration left and the health official appointed by the Trump administration to lead it, Gerald Parker, resigned. Since then, the Trump administration has been dogged by criticism from public health experts for having a slow or inadequate response to major outbreaks. In early July, the administration appointed Sara Brenner, a former Food and Drug Administration official, to lead OPPR, Bloomberg reported , effectively reforming the office. Another health official, Rachel Idowu, was reappointed to the National Security Council to serve as its director of bioresponse. Former health officials say the appointments could indicate that the White House is seeking to be more involved in outbreak response. “Sometimes it’s hard for the agencies to coordinate alone, and somebody needs to break the tie and say who’s in charge,” one former government official said. A White House spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the the National Security Council, Homeland Security Council and Domestic Policy Council are “together handling pandemic preparedness functions to fully account for the global and domestic needs in close partnership with the agencies.” “Dr. Sara Brenner is on detail from HHS to lead the Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response in order to assist with the White House’s response to the multiple ongoing outbreaks,” the spokesperson wrote. Two former health officials told NOTUS that Idowu and Brenner were experienced and well positioned to strengthen the administration’s pandemic policy and response. Idowu in particular, they said, indicated that the administration wants to strengthen its response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Congo, which has exploded in case counts and is on track to be the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Idowu, a career epidemiologist with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, was heavily involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak. “Truly the right person to have in that office. She can do the work of two or three,” one health official said of Idowu. Even so, former officials said that wasn’t enough. “There is a tremendous amount of work to be done,” Bryon Cohen, a former adviser to OPPR, said in an email. He that Idowu and Brenner are two “very experienced, capable people” to lead pandemic preparedness activities. “Those two individuals only have so much time in the day, and they deserve a full staff to help them carry out their mission,” Cohen said. “What they’ll have to do is be very selective in terms of what they prioritize,” the first former health official said. Under the previous administration, a large part of the office’s job was putting together a playbook on how to respond to outbreaks. That playbook was transferred to the National Security Council last year when OPPR was closing up shop — though it’s not clear if the Trump administration has made use of it since. “I do think they have pulled it out. I don’t know how they’re following it, necessarily,” the second former official said. They expected Idowu and Brenner to take advantage of it. Several former officials pointed out that during the Biden administration, OPPR also played an important role in getting biothreat policy out the door. Trump signed an executive order in putting a moratorium on so-called “gain-of-function” research, or infectious disease research that has the potential to create a pathogen that is more harmful to humans. That executive order set deadlines of 90, and days for the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy to release modified guidelines for researchers. Those new guidelines have yet to be released. “We’re now a year later, and those policies still have not been finished. And that’s because the people who work these issues at NSC and OSTP keep turning over,” a former government official said. “The government can't do interagency long-term preparedness policy when they don't have the people to coordinate that.” The former official said they felt like Brenner’s appointment to OPPR signified a desire to have someone the administration could trust in the role. Brenner has publicly aligned herself with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., though she has not spoken publicly about her views on gain-of-function research. In a statement, the White House spokesperson said the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are “prioritizing innovation and gold-standard science to ensure pandemic preparedness while also correcting course to prevent dangerous gain of function research and apply lessons learned from the damaging Biden approach of prolonged lockdowns and vaccine mandates.” With limited staffing, all five former health officials who spoke to NOTUS said the U.S. is at risk of being underprepared for future infectious disease threats. One used the World Cup to explain the danger. “We are a team on the field with half of our players having been given red cards, and we're going up against the Argentinas, Spains and Brazils of the world,” they said. “Viruses and other infectious diseases and threats don't stop playing.”

stories.title: FDA Advisers With Ties to the Peptide Industry Recommend Unapproved Peptides
stories.author: Paige Winfield Cunningham
stories.summary: Pro-peptide appointees by the health secretary are at odds with FDA scientists who say peptides need more study.
stories.content: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is a fan of the injections touted by online wellness influencers for a range of health benefits. Jose Luis Magana/AP A panel of advisers partially appointed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is recommending the government expand access to six peptides not approved by the Food and Drug Administration. If the FDA accepts the Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee’s recommendations — which is at odds with recommendations by its own scientists — select pharmacies could start using these typically gray-market substances in the specialized medications they create for customers, something that is currently illegal. An FDA spokesperson said Friday that the agency “appreciates” the panel’s recommendations and will propose a rule the public can comment on, but didn’t provide a timeline. The FDA doesn’t have to accept the panel’s recommendations but it usually does. Peptides, which are typically injected, are chains of amino acids that serve as the building blocks of protein. Some peptides, including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, have been heavily studied and approved by the FDA for years. The peptides the panel recommended are currently marketed for ulcerative colitis, migraines, pain, wound healing, anti-aging, memory and stroke recovery. Kennedy, who is a fan of the injections touted by online wellness influencers for a range of health benefits, appointed eight of the panel’s 19 members, all of whom voted to expand access to peptides. Six of those members run clinics that sell peptides. The meeting over Thursday and Friday attracted unusual attention as the latest illustration of tension between the ballooning wellness industry — which largely views Kennedy as an ally — and government scientists and mainstream medical experts who tend to be more wary of products not approved by the FDA. “The committee weighed the evidence, followed the science and stood up for medical freedom,” said Lee Rosebush, chair of the American Academy of Peptide Medicine. The panel did vote 7-6 against recommending one peptide, emideltide, which is believed to promote sleep. An FDA official said the agency was recommending against the peptide due to “a lack of data to support safety in these substances when used in humans.” FDA officials also recommended against approving the other peptides, stressing they haven’t been studied enough. That concern was echoed by panel members who voted against recommending the peptides. One member, Todd Durham, cited “low-quality evidence around efficacy and the fact there are approved medical therapies for all the proposed uses.” But Kennedy appointees who sell peptides stressed anecdotal evidence that they’re beneficial. “There’s been a mismatch in real-world data versus evidence,” said Gabriel Alizaidy, who works for a telehealth company that sells growth-hormone peptides. A broad array of other peptides without FDA approval are booming in the United States, promoted by social media influencers touting a broad range of health benefits including speeding healing, improving skin or boosting athletic performance. Kennedy told podcaster Joe Rogan in February that he was “very anxious” to make peptides more accessible to people from ethical suppliers. “I’ve used peptides myself and used them to really good effect on a couple of injuries,” Kennedy said. Access to the six peptides would dramatically expand if the FDA approves them for use by compounding pharmacies, which create customized medications on-site by mixing raw ingredients to fit a specific patient’s health needs. People often buy unapproved peptides from vendors who label them “for research use only” or websites that source from China, creating safety concerns peptide advocates say could be alleviated by adding them to the list of substances U.S. compounding pharmacies can use. The American Medical Association has said unapproved peptides should undergo regulatory review by the FDA and third-party testing “to demonstrate their safety and efficacy before marketing or clinical use."

stories.title: U.S. Firefighting Resources Are Already Maxed Out — And It’s Only July
stories.author: Anna Kramer
stories.summary: National wildfire response coordinators are triaging across fires raging primarily in Oregon, Colorado and Washington.
stories.content: Limited snowpack and extreme drought conditions in the West have primed the landscape for an early, aggressive start to the fire season. AP Photo/Ethan Swope Ethan Swope/AP The United States does not currently have enough resources to fight every wildfire with a full force. The country is using nearly all of its wildfire fighting resources far earlier in the season than usual, according to data from the National Interagency Fire Center. On July 18, the country reached “Preparedness Level 5” status, the highest possible level on a scale that measures how much wildfires are taxing resources. National wildfire response coordinators are currently deciding how resources are deployed across fires raging primarily in Oregon, Colorado and Washington. If another especially big fire starts while resources remain strapped, federal coordinators will have to decide which ongoing and smaller fires will need to be handled with fewer resources. Since , the United States has only reached a 5 out of 5 on the preparedness level scale by July 18th two other times — and . Usually, if the country reaches PL5 at all, it happens sometime in August. Under PL5, national coordinators are forced to make decisions about which fires most deserve hotshot crews, engines, aircraft and other specialized equipment and teams. “Not every fire that's ongoing is going to get everything that they need to be able to fight the fire and contain the fire,” said one Forest Service official who was granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. “There's a lot of hard decisions that are going to be made as far as allocating resources.” The fire season has been growing longer in recent years in the United States, stretching from May to November. This year, there are two main reasons for the resource constraints. Perhaps most critically, limited snowpack and extreme drought conditions in the West have primed the landscape for an early, aggressive start to the fire season. Second, wildland firefighters have been warning for years that the United States has not properly invested in the firefighters and equipment needed to adequately combat fires during increasingly bad seasons. The Trump administration exacerbated staffing issues when it made cuts to support staff across the federal government, a second firefighting Forest Service official told NOTUS. “It's both. It truly is. It is declining capacity combined with a continuation of the trend in fire behavior that we're seeing,” this person said. “As we get into August, certainly September, especially with the activity that we're seeing now, we’ll have to pay attention to just the fatigue that's going to be in the system, and the health of the people that are out,” said the first Forest Service official. The U.S. Wildland Fire Service did not respond to a request for comment. “Reaching PL5 earlier than usual increases pressure on national resources, but the incident response system is built for these conditions and is operating as intended," a spokesperson for the U.S. Forest Service told NOTUS. "We use longstanding interagency processes to prioritize the highest-risk incidents and move resources around the country efficiently to where they are needed most.” New Zealand and Australia are currently sending firefighting resources to the United States to help in the most needed areas, a partnership frequently invoked during PL5 status. The Air Force and the Wyoming and California National Guards have also been called upon to help, sending aircraft and personnel to southern Oregon and northern California. While Canada and the U.S. often share resources, the same two officials within the Forest Service told NOTUS that is unlikely at the moment because Canada is battling its own severe fires. Even the extra assistance doesn’t completely alleviate firefighters’ needs. “When it gets to PL5, I know it’s going to be tough. I know it’s going to be tougher getting fighters to my fire,” said Bobbie Scopa, a retired wildland firefighter who used to manage fire response in Oregon. “You just know that you’re going to have to make tough decisions.” Oregon has already seen more acres burn this year than the total for the entirety of last year’s fire season. Thousands of lightning strikes from powerful thunderstorms have been starting dozens of fires across the state. More than 1, firefighting personnel spent the last week battling an especially large fire still threatening the 4, -person town of Sisters, Oregon. Even so, fire experts said that they are more concerned about what could be coming down the pike in the next month or two. California has so far escaped the massive, out-of-control fires that usually characterize an especially bad year. Scopa worries about what happens if that changes. “All you need is a couple of days with high winds and some sunny skies and that uncontained fire line does have the potential to get up and run,” she said.

stories.title: National Guard Signs $292M Housing Contract for Troops in Washington, D.C.
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: The deal would provide 2, “apartment-style lodging units” for service members deployed in the city.
stories.content: Nearly 5, troops from across more than 20 states have been deployed in D.C., and the National Guard will maintain its presence in the city through the rest of Trump’s term. Jacquelyn Martin/AP The National Guard Bureau will spend $ million to house thousands of troop members deployed in Washington, D.C., in partnership with the city government and the U.S. General Services Administration. The guards — first deployed last summer after President Donald Trump declared a crime emergency in the District — have been staying in hotels across the region. Officials say the contract allows for a “long-term housing solution” for the deployed personnel and the deal, facilitated through the online rental platform Placemakr, will secure 2, “apartment-style lodging units” for the service members. “This contract delivers stable, secure housing for our Soldiers and Airmen while achieving significant cost savings for the government,” Monica Williams, executive director of acquisitions and head of contracting activity for the National Guard Bureau, said in a statement. The contract is set to cover the housing fees for troops through June , according to the military news site Task and Purpose. It’s unclear how long the National Guard Bureau will rent the apartments. These housing moves mark the latest step in what has evolved from a temporary deployment into a long-term mission in the nation's capital. Nearly 5, troops from across more than 20 states have been deployed in D.C., and the National Guard will maintain its presence in the city through the rest of Trump’s term. The administration’s continued use of deployments would cost $95 million per month, the Congressional Budget Office estimated in January — months before the government mobilized 1, additional members to D.C. in May.

stories.title: Democrats Are Staffing Up to Unwind Trump’s Changes to the State Department
stories.author: Eric Katz
stories.summary: A no-bid contract to a conservative fundraiser is raising questions about State’s recruiting.
stories.content: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) is currently interviewing staff to investigate the cuts at State and the U.S. Agency for International Development. (Ida Marie Odgaard/AP) Andrew Crapuchettes says his employment-matching company is the “anti-woke jobs board.” He thinks employers should avoid any applicants using they/them pronouns and “screen for values alignment” rather than just skill. More Christians should be in government, he says. His firm, RedBalloon, won a no-bid $1 million contract to help the State Department recruit candidates earlier this year. The State Department shed more than 20% of its staff last year as part of the Trump administration’s push to slash the federal workforce. But the agency cited an "unusual and compelling urgency” to bring on new employees in awarding the contract to RedBalloon without any competition. The company had never before won a federal contract. Its subsidiary, Military Hire, a company that helps members of the military transition into civilian jobs, will carry out the work. Crapuchettes’ comments on “CrossPolitic,” a podcast with the slogan “Christ over politics,” were first reported by Mother Jones . The no-bid nature of the contract has not been previously reported. On the podcast, Crapuchettes said RedBalloon was contracted as “the official recruiting arm for their foreign service officers.” He suggested he was taking the department in a new direction and encouraged the podcast listeners to apply for State jobs. “A lot of the recruiting was focused on DEI. It was trying to get in the guy with a PhD in Black dance, rather than people who can do the best job,” Crapuchettes said. “I would love to see a lot of Christians applying, taking the test, doing the hard work, becoming a foreign service officer.” In blog posts on RedBalloon’s website, Crapuchettes said applicants using nonbinary pronouns are “more likely to have unsettled emotional issues, and perhaps bring a contentiousness in demanding everyone conform to their version of reality.” Federal contracts like RedBalloon’s are now the subject of Democrats’ new oversight initiative — one that can really only operate at full force if they win back the House majority in November. Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, is currently interviewing staff to investigate the cuts at State and the U.S. Agency for International Development, the process for deciding which offices to dismantle and the ways to assist impacted staff. “We're going to up our counsel staff so that we're ready, because I can't let folks get away with this,” Meeks said in an interview with NOTUS. “We're not going to just sit back and let that happen and, when we get in charge, let that go away.” House Democrats told NOTUS they are already taking steps to investigate, and potentially unwind, the approach State is now taking with Crapuchettes’ help. “The State Department should recruit from all segments of society and hire people based on their ability to do the job rather than their religious beliefs or personal political views,” Meeks said. “But the Trump administration instead is intent on corrupting and politicizing the State Department and not hiring based on merit, as the law requires, but instead favoring extreme ideologues. At a press conference last week, Democratic lawmakers and former employees blasted the cuts and vowed to help terminated employees, some day, get their jobs back. “It's an effort to try to replace merit-based employees with political hacks,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) said of the department’s gutting. Meeks vowed to put laid-off State employees “back where you belong,” saying he would bring the subject up at every committee hearing going forward. He derided Republican leadership for allowing President Donald Trump to slash and revamp the department without additional oversight or congressional input. The State Department laid off 1, employees last year, including foreign service officers, and has shed more than 3, employees in total under Trump. Meeks said he’s been readying his staff to be back in the majority. Last week he cosponsored the Foreign Service Test-Free Reentry Act, which would ease the process by which laid-off foreign service officers could reenter government. The department has already onboarded multiple foreign service classes since the layoffs last summer. “We're going to exercise our oversight responsibilities, and we're going to start preparing right now,” Meeks said. Meeks' preparations mirror those underway by Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. NOTUS previously reported that the committee’s top Democrat, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, is taking steps to submit subpoenas and otherwise launch investigations into the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files, conflicts of interest within the Trump family, rollbacks at the Health and Human Services Department and potentially nefarious contract awards at the Department of Homeland Security. RedBalloon’s contract could similar scrutiny. Crapuchettes operates a political action committee in Idaho — where RedBalloon is based — which says its mission is to “counter the far Left’s unrelenting assault on the very fabric of American values.” Its priorities include securing the U.S. border that "is being overrun," curbing abortion rights and preventing the influence of "liberal teachers unions" in schools. Donald Trump Jr. has endorsed the company and encouraged employers to use its services. A State Department official said the contract would help recruit veterans and that the department is “committed to recruiting the strongest possible pool of applicants to represent the United States.” The official did not respond to questions regarding why the contract was not bid out, nor how RedBalloon got on the department’s radar. “The department’s recruitment strategy has been restructured to a centralized approach which focuses on the needs of the department and the workforce,” the official said. “The recruiting process is aligned to attract individuals who can defend U.S. interests among the evolving issues of the world through leadership, negotiation, and by embodying American values.” The State Department last year scrapped its Diplomats in Residence program, which sent senior foreign service officers around the country to engage with local communities about careers in diplomacy. It also a “fidelity” section to the performance-evaluation process, requiring managers to assess employees' commitment to “completely aligning oneself and one’s team to the most current [U.S. government] goals.” Crapuchettes, when reached for comment, said his "schedule is crazy right now” and referred NOTUS to a spokesperson, who stressed that Military Hire’s team would conduct the work. The State Department awarded the contract to Red Balloon, however, which first registered as a federal contractor in June . The government originally asked potential contractors to find qualified applicants to take the foreign service exam, as well as diplomatic security special-agent recruits. It also, despite Crapuchettes’ plea for Christian applicants, requires all activities related to the contract to “be conducted in full compliance with merit-based hiring principles.” Scott Amey, general counsel for the Project on Government Oversight, said a more traditional contracting process may have led the State Department to receive "better services for cheaper." “I know their name is RedBalloon, but this raises a lot of red flags as far as why they were selected and how they were selected,” Amey said. “Why couldn't this be planned and why couldn’t they hold a competition, and what are they doing to ensure they got fair and reasonable prices? When you buy quickly, a lot of times that leads to wasteful spending.”

stories.title: Senate Democrats Ask Watchdog to Probe Trump Gutting Offshore Wind
stories.author: Mara Hoplamazian
stories.summary: Sen. Martin Heinrich asked the Government Accountability Office to review the Interior Department’s offshore wind leasing and permitting practices.
stories.content: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Martin Heinrich asked the Government Accountability Office to look into the Interior Department’s leasing and permitting practices for offshore wind. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Senate Democrats are ramping up efforts to investigate the Trump administration’s push to shut down offshore wind development. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico), asked the Government Accountability Office to look into the Interior Department’s leasing and permitting practices for offshore wind. “The Trump Administration has shown a strong willingness to go to any lengths to kill wind projects, including stretching the bounds of the law,” Heinrich, the top Democrat on the Senate’s Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, wrote to GAO. “It is imperative that Congress and the American people understand how DOI’s actions have crippled the development of wind energy in the country.” The Government Accountability Office can decline requests from members of Congress, but requests from ranking members like Heinrich are prioritized. Heinrich’s request comes after a group of senators launched an investigation into buyout agreements totaling almost $2.6 billion that halted offshore wind projects planned for waters off of Maine, New York and California. The senators asked the companies that received those buyouts — TotalEnergies, Ocean Winds, Duke Energy and Invenergy — to respond to questions about their communications with the Trump administration by Aug, 6. President Donald Trump has taken a sweeping approach to halting the offshore wind industry, temporarily withdrawing leases in U.S. waters, pausing projects, canceling funding , requiring heightened review by the Interior Department, and paying developers to cancel planned projects. Federal judges have deemed several of those actions unlawful, including the halting of new leases and a requirement for the interior secretary to sign off on all wind and solar projects on federal lands and water. The administration’s efforts to shut down clean-energy projects has become a sticking point in bipartisan discussions of permitting reform, which Heinrich is leading for Democrats along with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island). Streamlining the permitting process for energy projects and other infrastructure is a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, but longstanding partisan gridlock has made an agreement elusive.

stories.title: Three Airports Opt Into Trump Administration’s New Private Airport Security Model
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The TSA workers’ union say the TSA Gold+ program “jeopardizes the safety of the flying public.”
stories.content: Twenty airports across the country have used the SPP to fill gaps in their workforces during previous shutdowns, including earlier this year, when TSA agents worked without pay for 76 days during the partial government shutdown. Yuki Iwamura/AP Airports in Tampa, Des Moines and Charleston will be the first to opt into TSA Gold+, the Trump administration’s new initiative that allows private contractors to manage the screening and security processes. Under the new program , the Transportation Security Administration is still in charge of oversight, but some industry leaders are calling the decision a “step backwards” for aviation security. The American Federation of Government Employees, which represents TSA agents, denounced the expansion of these public-private partnerships. “Make no mistake – this is a major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the Sept. 11th terrorist attacks in and the deadly bombing of Pan Am Flight over Scotland in ,” Everett Kelley, the national president of AFGE, said in a press release . TSA announced the new program in May in an email sent to employees, and the agency recently began accepting applications from private contractors, due at the end of the month. The agency bypassed congressional approval by relying on existing statutory authorities found in the Screening Partnership Program launched by TSA in . The White House $52 million to the fiscal year budget proposal to help advance the push for privatization in security and screening at airports — which includes a mandatory expansion of the SPP that could affect up to of the nation’s commercial airports, according to the AFGE. “Changes of this magnitude should not be made behind closed doors without the input of Congress, the flying public, the local airport authorities, and TSA employees themselves,” Kelley said. Tampa International Airport cited increased efficiency and the need to supplement their workforce during government shutdowns as reasons for opting into the program. “The change to privatization not only reduces disruption risks caused by lapses in federal appropriations or government shutdowns but also allows greater flexibility in exploring new screening checkpoint infrastructure and technology to enhance the customer experience,” an airport spokesperson said. Twenty airports across the country have used the SPP to fill gaps in their workforces during previous shutdowns, including earlier this year, when TSA agents worked without pay for 76 days during the partial government shutdown. Des Moines International Airport praised the program’s potential to provide “leap forward in technology” at security checkpoints, but the airport also acknowledged the concerns current transportation security officers may have about adopting TSA Gold+. "TSA officers have done an outstanding job serving Central Iowa, and we recognize there is uncertainty whenever a new program is discussed," Brian Mulcahy, CEO of the Des Moines Airport Authority, said in a press release. “TSA Gold+ presents a new way for airports to deliver exceptional service to every traveler, while advancing security, efficiency, and the overall airport experience,” TSA said in a statement. “Throughout the transition of these airports, we remain committed to operational stability and supporting our employees.” The Homeland Security Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Des Moines International Airport is set to adopt TSA Gold+ in January , with Charleston International Airport following in February and Tampa International Airport in May, according to correspondence shared with NOTUS by the AFGE. The labor union argued that the potential expansion into airports across the country not only impacts TSA employees but also the overall safety of the aviation system. “The administration’s actions should concern all Americans, and AFGE will continue to speak out against any proposal that threatens our members’ jobs and jeopardizes the safety of the flying public,” Kelley said.

stories.title: Trump Expands His Ratepayer Pledge With Republican Governors, Utilities
stories.author: Mara Hoplamazian
stories.summary: The White House’s non-binding pledge encourages data centers to bring, build or buy their own power generation.
stories.content: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry signed President Donald Trump's Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Alex Brandon/AP Photo President Donald Trump announced Thursday an expansion of a pledge to protect ratepayers from increasing energy costs as power-hungry AI infrastructure springs up across the country. Fifty-five utilities including Avangrid, Dominion, Entergy, NextEra and PG&E joined the pledge, along with energy cooperatives, 28 data center developers and 23 governors — all Republicans. Seven AI companies had already signed on in March. Democratic governors Wes Moore of Maryland and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, who were involved in a previous White House agreement, were not part of the pledge. Spokespeople for Shapiro and Moore said they were not invited to sign on to the pledge. Companies that sign on to the pledge agree to build, bring or buy their own power supply, paying for the full cost of that energy and for the grid upgrades required to serve data centers. They also agree to pay for the power and grid upgrades whether they actually use the electricity or not. The pledge, which is non-binding, also pushes companies to invest in local jobs and to contribute to grid resilience, making their backup generation systems available to prevent shortages and blackouts. “It’s hard to believe, but you need double the electricity that we have right now, maybe even more than that, to really fulfill what you want to do,” Trump said at an EPA event announcing the expanded pledge. “We’re leading China by a lot, and using our old grid would not have worked.” Republican Govs. Brian Kemp of Georgia, Jeff Landry of Louisiana, Brad Little of Idaho, and Jim Pillen of Nebraska spoke at the event, addressing recent pushback against local data center development across the country and highlighting the benefits to their residents. Landry described an agreement between Richland Parish, Louisiana, and Meta that generated enough revenue to give teachers in that community five-figure bonuses . “This is a moment where we get to protect our people, empower our communities and unleash unprecedented economic opportunity,” he said. The Trump administration has aggressively pushed building data centers as part of its commitment to building the artificial intelligence industry in the United States. But several top officials have acknowledged the political backlash to rising utility rates stemming from their development. This week at a summit for AI stakeholders both inside and outside the government, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the “noise” around data centers is “not going to slow the progress of artificial intelligence.” Americans overwhelmingly oppose data centers being built in their communities. The implementation and enforcement of ratepayer protections is overwhelmingly the responsibility of states. Jeff Dennis, executive director of the Electricity Customer Alliance, said the addition of utilities and governors to the pledge could push protections forward. “I think it makes a meaningful difference in terms of the ability of the pledge to drive forward progress at the institutions that have the authority to actually give teeth to it,” he said. Implementing and enforcing ratepayer protections would require state public utilities commissions, which regulate the rates utility companies charge customers, to step in. Some states have already started to create large load tariffs — special contracts with big customers that can dictate which costs they pay, and whether they’ll pay for the cost of the power and upgrades to the grid built for their needs, even if they don’t use it all. But the major tenet of the pledge — the push for data centers to bring their own power to the table — has been harder to work out, Dennis said. “It's notable that utilities have joined the ratepayer pledge in this regard because utilities take a few different positions on whether their customers can actually participate in the market directly in that way to procure their own power,” he said. “We'll be interested to see how utilities that have signed this pledge go about implementing that specific piece.”

stories.title: Staffing Cuts Are Threatening NASA’s Plan to Land on the Moon
stories.author: Eric Katz
stories.summary: The space agency “may not be able to staff all planned work” going forward, auditor finds.
stories.content: NASA shed 4, of its permanent staff last year. AP Photo/John Raoux Workforce cuts are putting NASA’s plans to send astronauts to the moon and, eventually, Mars, at risk, according to a new audit from the government’s top watchdog. NASA shed 4, of its permanent staff last year, an overhaul officials said is now impacting 70% of its major projects. The agency has felt the cuts throughout its headquarters and in each of its centers across the country, the Government Accountability Office found in a report released on Thursday. The Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland was the hardest hit, shedding more than one-third of its workforce through a hiring freeze and various separation incentives, followed by the Langley Research Center in Virginia and the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The Jet Propulsion Laboratory, operated by the California Institute of Technology, also laid off 10% of its workforce. “The civil servant departures have left NASA’s workforce out of balance with NASA’s programmatic needs,” GAO said. Staff working on 25 of NASA’s 36 major projects told the watchdog they were suffering ill effects from the workforce cuts. The Space Launch System, the vehicle for launching the Artemis missions, lost 20% of its civilian workforce. The program is still analyzing the impacts of those losses but considers staffing issues as a possible risk to future Artemis missions. Artemis II sent four crew members around the moon earlier this year. Artemis III is set to serve as another test run next year before Artemis IV’s planned landing on the moon in . The Orion program, which provides the spacecraft used by the Artemis missions, shed 10% of its civil servants and has struggled to backfill “key positions.” Projects related to Artemis reported technical and programmatic risks that “were likely to delay their schedules” going forward, GAO said. Layoffs at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory hit both leadership and “hands-on hardware” development staff in the Near Earth Object Surveyor project, a planned infrared space telescope that will detect asteroids and comets that threaten Earth. A program designed to study Venus’ atmosphere lost so many program managers and engineers that it canceled various risk-reduction activities last year, but it has since sought to restore staffing. Most of NASA’s major projects still made it through without significant schedule delays or cost overruns, GAO found, though more challenges may be on the horizon. “Moving forward, some centers may be challenged to meet the workforce needs of the mission directorates because of the reduced civil servant workforce,” GAO said. “Some centers, particularly those that encountered large workforce losses, may not be able to adequately staff all planned work.” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, a billionaire businessman and pilot who previously led several SpaceX missions, has put NASA on a different trajectory since taking office in December. He announced earlier this year that the agency would resume hiring after an extended freeze and address skill gaps. The agency recently launched NASA Force with the Office of Personnel Management to recruit technical employees to key roles in two-year stints, which could be converted to permanent roles. OPM Director Scott Kupor recently told NOTUS that NASA would look to fill many roles that had been outsourced to contractors with government staff. In response to its report, Isaacman told GAO that NASA encountered “many challenges” in , including the “departure of over 4, civil servants.” “I commend the NASA workforce advancing the major programs and projects included in this year’s assessment — people who were able to adjust and respond in creative ways to continue their missions,” Isaacman said. The administrator’s push to restaff the space agency could run into further resistance if the Trump administration has its way: The president’s fiscal budget proposed slashing NASA’s budget by 23%. President Donald Trump similarly suggested a $6 billion, or 24%, funding cut, the elimination of 19 projects and a 32% workforce reduction in fiscal , though Congress largely ignored those proposals and kept the agency flat funded.

stories.title: Hegseth Picks New DOD University Partners After Dumping Ivy League Schools
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: UNC-Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech are the first universities selected after the Pentagon cut ties with several elite schools.
stories.content: Under his leadership, Hegseth said the department had realigned its academic partnerships to better reflect the administration’s goals. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP The Defense Department this week announced the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and Virginia Tech as the newest hosts of a reworked educational program for service members, a decision that came after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth cut ties with several Ivy League institutions. The two universities were the first to be selected by the department and will soon offer the Senior Service College Fellowship, a 10-month professional program for senior military officers. “We are deeply honored to participate,” UNC-Chapel Hill Chancellor Lee H. Roberts said in a statement. “The program fits well within the context of our mission of service, and we take tremendous pride in our deep, longstanding relationship with the United States military.” Earlier this year, Hegseth announced the Defense Department had canceled the fellowship program at several Ivy League schools, including Columbia University, Harvard University and Yale University — institutions that had historically offered the program for military members. Under his leadership, Hegseth said the department had realigned its academic partnerships to better reflect the administration’s goals. In a social media post in February, the secretary argued the elite schools had become the grounds for “woke indoctrination” and that the universities fomented “anti-American resentment and military disdain.” The Pentagon has canceled at least 93 fellowship programs and cut ties with 13 higher education institutions. Hegseth's decision to end fellowships that sent senior military officers to select U.S. universities has sparked confusion within the armed services and concerns that officers will lose access to some of the nation's top academic institutions, NOTUS previously reported. More universities are expected to join the new cohort in the coming weeks. In a memo, the department suggested several conservative-leaning schools, such as Hillsdale College, Liberty University and the University of Florida, as likely partners.

stories.title: Labor Pains
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
stories.content: One of D.C.’s largest hospitals will shutter one of its two postpartum wards on Sunday. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Medicaid changes hit a D.C. hospital, the House advances a bill restricting home rule and Tom Sietsema answers your dining questions. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST One of D.C.’s largest hospitals will shutter one of its two postpartum wards on Sunday. It’s the first health provider in the District to reduce service citing, at least in part, recent changes to Medicaid. “Similar to hospitals nationwide, we are facing increasing financial pressures, including significant changes in Medicaid that affect all our services,” a spokesperson for MedStar Washington Hospital Center told NOTUS, adding that D.C.’s birth rate is also steadily declining. President Donald Trump’s “one big beautiful bill,” passed last summer, cut more than $ billion from Medicaid and changed its eligibility requirements. D.C. officials estimated 95, residents were at risk of losing coverage, and the District has seen a 9% reduction in enrollment in the past year. “We do have a lot of patients on Medicaid,” one nurse in MedStar’s postpartum unit, Mel Rode, told NOTUS, adding: “We deliver 1 in 3 babies in the District and so, by closing a whole third of the postpartum beds, you are putting so many babies and so many delivering parents and mothers at risk.” The hospital saw a 17% decline in newborn admissions this past year , but Rode said that both of its postpartum units have been over capacity multiple times this summer. Council member Christina Henderson, who chairs the health committee, wasn't surprised to hear Medicaid could be a factor in the closing. But Janeese Lewis George , D.C.’s likely next mayor, cast doubt on how culpable it could be for the decision. “Most Medicaid cuts have not yet gone into effect ,” Lewis George told NOTUS in a statement. “MedStar's decision to close its postpartum delivery unit at Washington Hospital Center is a policy decision — one that must be reversed because of the critical role these units play in maternal health outcomes.” Henderson said the hospital has no immediate plans to repurpose the unit and could reopen beds if patient numbers recuperate. FROM THE DISTRICT No new taxes, D.C. That’s the message a House committee sent Wednesday when it advanced a bill that would broadly restrict the city’s ability to increase taxes or fees. Martin writes that Republicans say the measure is intended to help the city become more economically competitive, while city officials counter that it would “straightjacket” them. While D.C. officials loudly criticized Republican House members over the vote, another unexpected target emerged: DoorDash. The food-delivery platform supports the bill, largely over its opposition to a 20-cent delivery fee the D.C. Council recently approved . Some advocacy groups are calling on residents to boycott DoorDash, and social media has shown several people doing just that . A high-profile lawsuit against D.C. over its ban on firearm magazines that can hold more than 10 bullets is on hold — for now. The plaintiff in the case and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb have agreed to pause litigation pending a pair of cases the U.S. Supreme Court is expected to hear this year on the constitutionality of state laws banning AR-15 assault rifles, which D.C. similarly prohibits. Agriculture Department workers say mandatory relocations from Washington to regional offices are mass layoffs in disguise, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence, Eric Katz and Natalie Alms report . The Trump administration and D.C. Council finally have something they can agree on: razing the 11-acre Forrestal Building in Southwest D.C., City Cast DC reports . TALK TO TOM Tom Sietsema is here to answer your burning questions about the D.C. dining scene. Sietsema, a James Beard Award winner, is NOTUS’ food correspondent. Previously, he was The Washington Post’s food critic for 25 years. Got a question for Tom? Submit them here . Each Thursday, we’ll turn this section over to him to give you some answers. Question: I’ve got family coming to D.C. Is there a restaurant on the Mall you prefer? For proximity to the museums and value, I’m partial to America’s Table Cafe inside the lower level of the National Museum of American History, which fuels between 6, and 8, visitors a week around this time of year. Leading the kitchen: executive chef Mollie Kaufmann, who previously served as the culinary operations manager for World Central Kitchen, and who offers food more personal than the crowd size suggests. (Quick, what other local cafeteria offers shrimp and grits, flavored as if you were in the South?) A recent lunch also featured a snappy bratwurst striped with brown mustard and topped with tangy sauerkraut; a salad bar that goes beyond the expected; and appealing side dishes to accompany the generous entrees. Fresh-tasting apple-fennel coleslaw, mustard-punched baked beans and pickled okra outperformed a plate of slightly dry smoked chicken thighs. Nodding to the season was a fine trifle sweetened with blueberries and peaches. I get hungry just typing that. In the full Q&A : Where to find the best sushi in D.C., why American restaurants are always so dark, how to tip on expensive wine, and more. SPORTS The Commanders open training camp next week, meaning football season is suddenly around the corner. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson takes a look at five players with a lot on the line in Ashburn, including a young pass-catcher and a newly arrived Super Bowl champ. The Nationals have started calling some pitches from the dugout, The Athletic reports , with Washington becoming the latest team to break a baseball norm in search of an analytical advantage. Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com .

stories.title: States Are Struggling to Replace the Election Cybersecurity Infrastructure Trump Dismantled
stories.author: Samuel Larreal
stories.summary: Election officials from across the country say the administration has pared back support.
stories.content: Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/AP Top state election officials are warning the federal government is not doing enough to help states prepare for the possibility of cyberattacks ahead of the midterm elections. President Donald Trump has had an unflinching focus on election integrity issues, which he has pushed Congress to address through legislation that would tighten voter-identification requirements. In the meantime, several state officials told NOTUS that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which supports state and local election offices in their efforts to bolster security against hackers, has stopped providing regular intelligence briefings as well as cut technical assistance and financial support for election administration to their states. “The federal government knows that there are nation-state actors desperately trying to come after us and cause chaos in our elections, yet, they are reducing resources,” Steve Hobbs, Washington’s Democratic secretary of state, told NOTUS. “We're doing everything we can to try to protect ourselves with far less resources than we did before.” Republican state election officials confirmed that the cuts have also changed their states' cybersecurity operations. “If you go back to , we had 30 different federal threat briefings. This year we received none,” Brad Raffensperger, Georgia’s Republican secretary of state, told NOTUS. “We benefited from that regular coordination with CISA. It was just another set of eyes with extended reach over the horizon and that many times our state agencies just don't have that available to them.” “We know that there's a lot of threats currently between the Ukraine war and Russia not being pleased with our response there,” Raffensperger said. “The ongoing situation with Iranians, and then obviously AI has opened the door to a host of bad actors.” The administration has aggressively reduced election-security personnel within CISA since Trump returned to office. Earlier this year, Congress cut hundreds of millions of dollars from CISA’s budget. The White House has proposed even deeper cuts to the agency’s budget. The results of that are playing out as states prepare for the midterms. Three state election officials told NOTUS that CISA has stopped providing election-focused cybersecurity support and does not have the same capacity to operate as a central hub for state officials to communicate with federal agencies and to other states during cyberattacks. Attempted cybersecurity attacks happen frequently, including during the election. “The federal government has abandoned a large share of its previous commitment to helping states administer secure elections,” Steve Simon, Minnesota’s secretary of state, said. “There are a host of services that they previously provided under multiple administrations — including the first Trump administration — that are no longer available to us.” Abigail Jackson, a White House spokesperson, did not respond to questions about the decrease in federal cybersecurity support for elections. Instead, her statement focused on the Trump administration’s efforts to clamp down on noncitizen voting. “President Trump is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections, and that includes totally accurate and up-to-date voter rolls free of errors and unlawfully registered non-citizen voters,” she wrote. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement that under President Joe Biden, CISA had a “ballooning budget” that concealed “censorship, branding, and electioneering.” “Under Secretary Mullin, CISA is focused squarely on executing its statutory mission,” this spokesperson wrote. “We are committed to delivering timely, actionable cyber threat intelligence, supporting federal, state, and local partners, and defending against both nation-state and criminal cyber threats.” Many states have been forced to create and fund their own resources to replace federal services.
