stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: “The World Cup is not for sale,” the European association said after news that Jared Kushner’s brother may be eyeing a stake in the tournament.
stories.content: Union of European Football Associations and its president, Aleksander Ceferin, left, voted to boycott international competitions hosted by FIFA after its leader, Gianni Infantino, right, proposed selling private shares in the organization. Fernando Calistro/AP The governing body of European soccer voted to boycott international competitions hosted by FIFA after its president, Gianni Infantino, announced plans to allow private investors to buy stakes in the World Cup. FIFA said it would open up the tournament to private investment on Wednesday, after Infantino reportedly ran the plans by officials in President Donald Trump’s administration. Joshua Kushner — the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — has been considered a potential key investor in the proposal, and other figures within Trump’s orbit have been involved, sources told The Times of London , which first reported on the plans. “The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product,” the Union of European Football Associations wrote in a statement . “No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale.” The coalition said its 55 nations “stand as one” and voted “unanimously and unequivocally to reject FIFA’s proposal.” “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football and always will,” The Football Association, the governing body of association football in England wrote on X , backing UEFA’s decision. FIFA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. UEFA said none of its teams will participate in any future matches unless they have assurances that Infantino will block FIFA competitions from future private ownership. The World Cup is scheduled to take place across stadiums in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. FIFA hopes to raise up to $4.2 billion in private-sector capital for a new organization that would oversee key business aspects of major soccer tournaments like the World Cup. Infantino’s proposal would open up a new subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise, in which select third-party companies could invest in competitions. FIFA, which overwhelmingly controls the global soccer network, has approached Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital and is partnering with J.P. Morgan. Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee blasted reports of discussions between FIFA and Trump’s administration on Tuesday, when the news broke about Infantino’s plans to sell shares. “Infantino is trying to bribe every member country in FIFA with a $40 million payoff to sign off on his scheme to turn the World Cup into a get-rich-quick extraction industry for oligarchs and billionaires,” the Judiciary Democrats’ account said on X . “It’s time for everyone who loves soccer to oppose this sinister.” Trump and Infantino have enjoyed a close relationship, with the FIFA president making frequent visits to the White House and Mar-a-Lago. Trump presented the World Cup Trophy on July 19 in New Jersey, a few months after Infantino awarded him the newly created “FIFA Peace Prize” in December. Infantino set a Sept. 19 deadline for the federations to approve the plans. The controversial FIFA initiative would give each of them access to $40 million in funding, ESPN reported. Other multinational soccer governing bodies are still reviewing Infantino’s plans. The Confederation of African Football is set to hold a meeting of its executive committee next week to evaluate FIFA’s proposal.

stories.title: Palestinian Authorities Petition SCOTUS to Stave Off Massive Legal Judgment
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: They argue the massive $ million penalty will destabilize critical government services in the West Bank.
stories.content: Mariam Zuhaib/AP Palestinian authorities filed an application with the Supreme Court on Thursday in a last-ditch attempt to block a more than $ million judgment against the groups, which they say would result in the loss of critical services, cause untold human suffering and destabilize the war-torn region even further. On March 30, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit reinstated a $ .5 million judgment against the Palestine Liberation Organization and Palestinian Authority in an Anti-Terrorism Act case brought by U.S. victims and survivors of terrorist attacks in Israel. The Palestine Liberation Organization is the internationally recognized representative body for the Palestinian people, and the Palestinian Authority was created by the PLO in the 1990s to manage civil and security affairs in parts of the West Bank. The United States does not officially recognize either as a terror organization today. However, in Congress passed the Anti-Terrorism Act, labeling the PLO as a “terrorist organization and a threat to the interests of the US.” The PLO does have a history of armed conflict against Israel, and while the Palestinian Authority was created to be a governing body committed to a diplomatic framework, elements within it have engaged in localized violence. The Oct. 7, , attacks, led by Hamas, triggered a war in Gaza that has severely destabilized the West Bank, resulting in a surge of military raids, Israeli settler violence, economic distress and heightened political friction for the Palestinian Authority. Now, the PLO and the Palestinian Authority are arguing the multimillion-dollar judgment against them will only make the situation in the area worse, saying that civic life is hanging “by a thread” in the West Bank. “Immediate enforcement of the $ .5 million judgment may cut that thread, depriving millions of people of government services they depend on, and which provide security and stability for Israel, Palestine, and the region alike,.” the briefing reads. “The security, sanitation, and school services provided by Petitioners in the West Bank are hanging by a thread.” The judgment against both groups was initially rendered after a jury verdict in , but it was subsequently vacated in on the ground that U.S. courts lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendants. In response, Congress enacted new legislation, dubbed the “Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act,” designed to enable jurisdiction in similar cases. Following the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Fuld v. Palestine Liberation Organization , which confirmed that the congressional act is compatible with the Fifth Amendment, the case returned to the Second Circuit, which agreed to recall its earlier mandate, effectively undoing its ruling. The application submitted by the PLO and the Palestinian Authority to halt the lower court’s order is up to the discretion of the Supreme Court itself, which has a history of accepting fewer than 1% of appeals in similar cases, according to Justice Department data .

stories.title: Iran-Focused U.S.-Israel Meeting Sidelines Allies’ Other Disagreements
stories.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed
stories.summary: Despite growing fears over Israel’s policies in Lebanon and the Palestinian territories, Trump and Netanyahu put a positive spin on their brief meeting.
stories.content: President Donald Trump called his Tuesday meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, "very good." Evan Vucci/AP President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu put a positive spin on their Tuesday meeting, which Trump called “ very good ” and Netanyahu deemed “excellent.” But the summit did little to resolve central issues in the U.S.-Israel relationship — suggesting disagreements between the allies and unprecedented skepticism of Tel Aviv among the American public are likely to continue. On its surface, the summit addressed the Iran war, which Trump launched in partnership with Netanyahu and neither has been able to resolve, despite its rising toll for Americans, regional security and the global economy. Netanyahu said the countries share the goal of preventing Iranian development of nuclear weapons (an objective Iran denies having) and Trump on Wednesday issued a fresh threat toward Tehran after an Iranian missile attack on U.S. forces in Jordan. Trump has suggested Netanyahu should be more deferential toward the U.S., and before the Israeli leader arrived in Washington, his government finally approved a step forward for Trump’s plan for the Gaza Strip, allowing foreign troops to enter a small part of the territory. The development regarding Gaza encapsulated the general mood: little headway in areas where stated U.S. and Israeli preferences diverge . Israel slashed the number of forces permitted and maintains it must continue controlling nearly 70% of the Palestinian territory, though Trump has spoken of Israeli withdrawal. Tuesday’s meeting “was a meeting Trump preferred not to have, but was ultimately pressured into,” Eran Etzion, a long-time Israeli diplomat and former deputy head of the country’s national security council, told NOTUS. Netanyahu was visiting town for the first time since the Iran war began, for the funeral of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. Etzion argued the White House summit seemed designed to avoid tough conversations about simmering tensions. “It was orchestrated to minimize both media exposure and one-on-one time. The number of attendees was bloated, which probably means sensitive issues were off the table,” said Etzion, who is now seeking a seat in Israel’s parliament as a member of the Democrats party, a rival to Netanyahu. A spokesperson for the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Meanwhile, Israeli policies that have fueled a backlash among Americans and complicated Trump administration gambits, like attempted diplomacy with Iran and a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia, are intensifying. U.S. sentiment toward Israel has cratered over the country’s devastating American-backed offensive in Gaza since . An Economist/YouGov poll conducted July 27-29 shows 43% of Americans (including 22% of Trump voters) now say the policy constitutes a genocide. Nearly 1, Palestinians have been killed since a Trump-enforced ceasefire in October, according to Palestinian authorities, and millions more still Israeli attacks. And relief groups say Israel continues to sharply restrict the flow of humanitarian aid. In Gaza, 67% of residents are at a crisis level or worse of food insecurity, the United Nations-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification monitor said this month, and chickenpox has begun rapidly spreading in overcrowded camps of displaced Palestinians. Rebuilding the strip — part of the mission of Trump’s Board of Peace — would require over $71 billion, more than seven times the cost of reconstruction following past Israeli campaigns, Oxfam, the Palestine Economic Policy Research Institute and the Palestine Trade Center said in a July 22 report . Meanwhile, concerns from human rights groups and U.S. lawmakers are ongoing about people from Gaza who Israel has detained and is accused of torturing, like Hussam Abu Safiya, a former head of a hospital who has been held since December . Diana Buttu, an analyst and former peace negotiator who is monitoring Abu Safiya’s case, told NOTUS there have been no updates despite growing international calls for his release this summer following suggestions he may be on the brink of death. Broadly, for detained Palestinians, “nobody is held to account” within Israel’s system, Buttu said. (Israel denies mistreating Palestinian detainees.) In the West Bank, the other Palestinian territory occupied by Israel under international law, increased violence by Israeli settlers close to Netanyahu’s far-right political partners and government moves targeting Palestinian families have spurred fears of a major conflagration. Ahead of Netanyahu’s U.S. visit, several hundred former senior officials in Israel's national security forces signed a letter asking Trump to pressure Netanyahu to limit “Jewish terror.” Among those targeted by orders disrupting Palestinian life is, Buttu said, a family of 14 in a village called Umm al-Khair who can no longer access their own bathroom because it has been deemed a “closed military zone.” Together, the trajectory is a far cry from Trump’s talk of delivering Israeli-Palestinian peace and progress for the Middle East. For the president, that has broader ramifications. He has tied his marquee effort to sell American nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia to Saudi recognition of Israel. But Saudi officials and those close to them continue to reiterate that is impossible without concrete action toward establishing Palestinian statehood. Beyond Israel-Palestine, a conflict and humanitarian crisis are ongoing in Lebanon — and Iran has said developments in that country are crucial to any U.S.-Iranian diplomacy. Israeli forces control much of the country’s south, enforcing what Buttu, who recently visited the Israeli side of the border, called “Gazafication” by demolishing homes and communities. Israel says its campaign is necessary to deter the Iran-backed Lebanese militia Hezbollah. The U.S. is promoting the idea that Lebanon’s government and military will disarm Hezbollah. Continued Israeli occupation undermines their authority to do so, analysts say — and Trump has declined to deploy American pressure over Netanyahu for a withdrawal. With a settlement over Lebanon stalled and signs of fresh escalations, there’s no end in sight for the Iran war. In turn, there’s little chance of addressing the frustration with Netanyahu and with Trump for launching that conflict that has grown nationally, including among conservatives who are seeking a U.S.-Israel reset.

stories.title: Trump Promises Iran Would ‘Get a Beating’ After Attack on U.S. Forces
stories.author: Ben T.N. Mause
stories.summary: The president delivered profanity-laced threats after a ballistic missile attack was intercepted in Jordan overnight.
stories.content: President Donald Trump said that the U.S. would be “hitting them hard. They’re going to get a beating.” Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo President Donald Trump plans to retaliate against Iran after a ballistic missile attack on U.S. forces in the region was intercepted, telling Fox News on Wednesday that the U.S. will “beat the fucking shit out of them.” The attack occurred overnight in Jordan , according to Iranian state media. Trump said that the U.S. would be “hitting them hard. They’re going to get a beating.” The White House declined to comment further, and the Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The attack and pledge to respond came after Trump met on Tuesday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to discuss the ongoing war against Iran. Though Netanyahu helped convince Trump to go to war with Iran in February and has sought continued aggression from U.S. forces, his relationship with the president had been under strain as it dragged on, increasing political pressure on Trump. In a Truth Social post on Tuesday, Trump called his sitdown with Netanyahu “a very good meeting.” Iran said on Wednesday that the intercepted attack targeted an American military base in Jordan, after U.S.-Saudi joint forces struck Iranian-allied forces in Iraq. Jordan’s military said it intercepted five missiles. The U.S.-Saudi forces struck Iran-backed “logistics and weapons sites,” according to U.S. Central Command, hitting the Popular Mobilization Forces. The PMF said at least 20 people were killed in the attack. Although Trump has sought an exit from the war for some time, the overnight action marked an escalation with Saudi Arabia’s entry into the fighting. The U.S. conducted airstrikes against Iran last week but had seemingly paused the attacks after military leaders reportedly warned against escalating further. There are growing concerns over the military’s depleted stockpile of advanced air defense missiles. Experts have estimated the remaining number of Patriot interceptors in the U.S. arsenal to be around , with only THAAD ballistic missile interceptors remaining, according to a report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. But the president said last week in Georgia that Iran wasn’t ready for a peace deal. “They want to make a deal, but I say they’re not ready to make a deal,” Trump said. “They’re not ready. They’ll be ready very soon.”

stories.title: Senate Advances Russia Sanctions Bill
stories.author: Joe Gould, Hamed Ahmadi
stories.summary: The legislation cleared a procedural hurdle hours after the funeral of Lindsey Graham, who championed the package.
stories.content: “We are thankful that this bill is very important,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after meeting with senators. “Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important. It's not only about how to stop financing this war. But it's also a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people. So I'm very thankful.” Bill Clark/AP The Senate on Tuesday advanced sweeping new sanctions targeting Russia, moving long-stalled legislation that supporters say would squeeze one of the Kremlin’s most important sources of wartime revenue. The Senate voted 86-12, clearing the way for legislation named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican whose death this month spurred supporters to try to get it done . The legislation would authorize the president to impose tariffs of up to % on the largest purchasers of Russian energy, while also targeting Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and other supporters of Moscow’s war effort and vessels in Russia’s so-called shadow fleet. The legislation split Democrats, with 11 voting “no” amid concerns about the bill expanding President Donald Trump’s authority to impose tariffs on foreign countries. Negotiators in recent weeks had narrowed the measure from an earlier proposal that called for tariffs as high as % to broaden support. The administration would retain discretion over the precise tariff rate and could waive individual sanctions or tariffs after certifying to Congress that doing so was in the national interest. Supporters hailed the procedural vote, taken after Graham’s funeral and a Washington visit from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, as a long-awaited bipartisan rebuke of Russian President Vladimir Putin. “With this vote, we are going to show Putin he can't bully Ukraine,” said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. “America stands behind Ukraine. We are going to back Ukraine, and they're going to win and beat Putin.” After Zelenskyy met with Trump at the White House to discuss Patriot missile coproduction and diplomatic efforts, he met privately with senators in the evening as the chamber prepared to vote . He then watched the vote from the Senate gallery. “We are thankful that this bill is very important,” Zelenskyy said after meeting with senators. “Sanctions pressure on Russia is very important. It's not only about how to stop financing this war. But it's also a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people. So I'm very thankful.” The visit also underscored Graham’s role as one of Ukraine’s staunchest advocates in Congress. Zelenskyy said he opened his Oval Office meeting by offering condolences over Graham’s death, calling him “a true friend of Ukraine.” Zelenskyy returned to Washington for Graham’s funeral less than three weeks after Graham traveled to Kyiv to discuss the sanctions package with him. Days later, Graham announced the bill had Trump’s support after months of delay. If the Senate ultimately passes the legislation before its August recess, it would hand Trump one of the most aggressive sanctions tools Congress has considered since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in , while cementing one of Graham’s final legislative achievements. “There are a number of stars aligned,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the bill’s lead Democratic sponsor, told NOTUS. “Ukraine's turning the tide, Trump's support, Zelensky visiting, and very definitely Lindsey Graham's passionate advocacy for it — and obviously for me they're all important, and they've enabled us to come closer to the finish line than ever before.” But several Democrats expressed concerns ahead of the vote about Trump’s tariff authority. “The sanctions on [Russia’s] energy sector is something, definitely, I support,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia) , who voted “no.” “But this bill in its current form gives the president a wide margin in the continuing advancement of this tariff regime, and I don't know that we have much evidence that he's going to use it to do what we need him to do.” The version of the bill that advanced Tuesday included several new provisions. It would extend existing sanctions authority over Iran's energy and weapons sectors through . Trump insisted that Iran be included in the legislation, but Blumenthal credited his new co-sponsor, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina), with the provision. The Iran provision also has relevance for Zelenskyy. The Ukrainian president has repeatedly urged allies to treat Moscow and Tehran as linked military partners, citing Iran’s supply of attack drones that Russia has used against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. The bill also includes a five-year sunset for the new Russia sanctions authorities. The additions appeared intended to help address concerns from some Democrats that the bill’s tariff authorities were too sweeping, though supporters argued those fears were overstated. The bill would also limit when the administration could lift the Russia sanctions. The president generally could not terminate them unless Moscow signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine’s government and ended its military campaign and efforts to subvert Kyiv. If the president determines those conditions have been met and moves to lift the sanctions, it would trigger a congressional review period during which lawmakers could attempt to block it through a joint resolution of disapproval. “This is not a new idea,” said Senate Foreign Relations Chair Jim Risch (R-Idaho). “The president has finally signaled that he's ready to go. We did negotiate some additional provisions.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune said ahead of the vote that he hoped a strong showing would put pressure on holdouts in each party to agree to fast-track a vote to pass the bill before the recess. Tuesday’s vote would not guarantee final passage. Without a time agreement, the Senate would still have to complete additional procedural steps and resolve any demands for amendment votes. The legislation would also have to pass the House, where lawmakers have already raised separate concerns over the tariff authority it would offer to Trump.

stories.title: Democrats Decry FIFA Head Infantino’s Plans to Sell Stakes in World Cup
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee have called for Infantino to appear in Congress over his relationship with President Trump.
stories.content: FIFA president Gianni Infantino and President Donald Trump have maintained a close relationship over the years: The FIFA president has made visits to the White House and Mar-a-Lago, and awarded Trump a newly created “FIFA Peace Prize” in December. Trump also presented the World Cup Trophy on July 19 in New Jersey. Bradley Collyer/AP House Judiciary Democrats blasted reports of alleged discussions between President Donald Trump’s administration and FIFA President Gianni Infantino over newly reported plans to sell stakes in the World Cup. FIFA is seeking to raise up to $4.2 billion in private-sector capital for a new organization that would oversee commercial rights and operational delivery — consolidating all of the money-making branches. Joshua Kushner — the brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — has been considered a potential key investor in the proposal, and other figures within Trump’s orbit have been involved, sources told The Times of London , which reported first on the plans. But Democratic committee members, who this week called on Infantino to appear for an interview regarding an investigation into alleged corruption between FIFA and Trump, said the new program constitutes “more corporate tarnishing of the beautiful game.” “FIFA, Donald Trump’s favorite corrupt racketeering enterprise in world sports, is now going directly into business with the Trump family!” the Judiciary Democrats’ account wrote in a post on X . “Apparently the fake Peace Prize and giant lease with Trump Tower weren’t enough — now Infantino performs a kickback hat trick by pursuing a multibillion-dollar deal with Jared Kushner’s brother to sell ownership stakes in the World Cup to private investors.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Infantino and Trump have maintained a close relationship over the years: The FIFA president has made visits to the White House and Mar-a-Lago, and awarded Trump a newly created “FIFA Peace Prize” in December. Trump also presented the World Cup Trophy on July 19 in New Jersey. The pair sparked controversy during this summer’s World Cup, when U.S. player Folarin Balogun had his one-match ban overturned after Trump made a call to Infantino to review consequences stemming from the player’s red card. The president also reportedly wants to tap Infantino to be the next secretary-general of the United Nations — a decision that would buck an informal tradition of geographically rotating the position, which could next go to someone from Latin America or the Caribbean. Infantino is from Switzerland and is of Italian descent. Infantino’s proposal would open up a new subsidiary in which select third-party companies could invest. FIFA, which overwhelmingly controls the global soccer network, has approached Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital and is partnering with J.P. Morgan. Infantino celebrated the plan, saying the funding development “lifts the whole game” by concentrating the commercial side of operations in one place. But some multinational soccer groups are concerned about the increased push for private investors to fund the sport. The Union of European Football Associations, or UEFA, held an emergency meeting Tuesday and released a statement criticizing Infantino’s plans. “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross. UEFA takes it extremely seriously,” UEFA wrote in a statement calling on all “leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments” to join their opposition to the move. UEFA nations plan to discuss a World Cup boycott in opposition to FIFA’s proposal, according to Sky News . The organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment on any future deliberations.

stories.title: ‘Truly Hawkish’
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: An Armed Forces Body Bearer Team moves the casket of Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., upon arrival for a Congressional tribute in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol, Tuesday, July 28, , in Washington. Mark Schiefelbein/Pool AP via AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 28, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Donald Trump met with two foreign leaders today: Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu . Zelenskyy and Trump discussed diplomacy and the recent U.S. pledge to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot air defense systems. Zelenskyy will meet with senators this evening ahead of the chamber’s procedural vote on Russia sanctions. He’s hoping to persuade as many Democrats as possible to sign on to the measure despite a provision expanding Trump’s tariff authority on countries that purchase Russian energy products. Trump’s meeting with Netanyahu — the pair’s first since the Iran war began — was closed to the press. The Israeli prime minister later called their 90-minute conversation “one of the best” they’ve had. Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral service took place at the National Cathedral this afternoon after a Hill ceremony earlier this morning. At the rotunda, JD Vance , John Thune and Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina) spoke about the late senator, and Sen. Darline Graham broke down while approaching her brother’s casket. Much of the Senate attended, including John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) in a rarely worn suit. Trump described Graham as “truly hawkish — he never saw a war that he didn’t like” in his 14-minute eulogy at the cathedral. THE HILL Gov. Andy Beshear called on Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) to provide proof of his capacity to serve — or resign. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) says there is “no ‘deal’” concerning acting Attorney General Todd Blanche ’s nomination: “They know what they have to do.” Cornyn suggested to reporters that Thursday’s committee vote may be postponed if Republicans lack the votes, noting the DOJ has been “radio silent” about the fund. THE ADMINISTRATION Senators will vote on Jay Clayton ’s nomination to be the next director of national intelligence this evening. Acting director Bill Pulte — whose own nomination prompted swift Senate backlash — announced a final sweep of agency firings just hours before his successor’s confirmation vote. Scoop: The FDA will officially consolidate administrative staff across the agency’s nine centers and stop specializing its field inspectors starting this fall. The U.S. delegation to the United Nations walked out of a Security Council meeting this week during a French speech that criticized American human rights stances, including characterizing them as authoritarian. FIFA President Gianni Infantino is planning to sell private World Cup stakes, The Times reports , with sources saying figures close to Trump have been consulted about the plan — including Joshua Kushner , the brother of Trump’s son-in-law. THE COURTS Trump can refile his $15 billion New York Times defamation lawsuit, a federal judge ruled today. The Reflecting Pool had already sustained significant damage before a former Olympian was accused of damaging it, defense attorneys say in a new court filing. JIMMY TIMMY POWER HOUR THANK YOU FOR READING Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: Pentagon Plans to Rename South Carolina Base After Lindsey Graham
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Graham served 33 years in the Air Force after he graduated from the University of South Carolina School of Law in .
stories.content: Tom Williams/AP The Pentagon is taking steps to rename a South Carolina military base after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, according to an internal Air Force memo obtained by NOTUS. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink wrote a letter July 27 that ordered staff to begin work with Air Mobility Command and Joint Base Charleston leadership to begin converting the name to Joint Base Lindsey Graham. “Senator Graham’s lifelong devotion to the military was shaped by his own military service and his public service in both the United States Senate and the United States House of Representatives,” Meink wrote in the letter. “His steadfast advocacy was instrumental in modernizing our military infrastructure and enhancing aviation security, ensuring that Joint Base Charleston remains as one of America’s premier military installations.” The memo was first reported by South Carolina newspaper The Post and Courier and amplified by the White House on social media. Graham served 33 years in the Air Force after he graduated from the University of South Carolina School of Law in . He served six years in active duty before transferring to the South Carolina Air National Guard in . Graham was first elected to the South Carolina House of Representatives in and was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in . He became a U.S. senator in , where he served until his death earlier this month. While in office, Graham served in both Iraq and Afghanistan. Retired Army Gen. David Petraeus, who oversaw U.S. military operations in the region in the late 2000s, commended Graham for his service. “I am not aware of any other current Member of Congress who, while in office, spent remotely as much time deployed in Iraq and Afghanistan. Those of us who were privileged to serve with Colonel Graham remain grateful to him for the contributions he made to our nation while in uniform,” Petraeus said in a Graham campaign press release . The same day the internal memo was revealed, hundreds gathered at Washington National Cathedral to honor Graham and his public service. The senator’s death was announced by his office on July 12. He had died the previous day of an “Aortic Dissection due to Arteriosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease,” according to preliminary findings by the D.C. Medical Examiner’s office.

stories.title: U.S. Delegation Storms Out of UN Meeting Over Criticism From France
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: The two longtime allies are embroiled in a feud over human rights policy.
stories.content: “This disingenuous grandstanding is tiresome, but we have tolerated it out of a sense of comradery and mutual respect,” said U.S. Ambassador Dan Negrea. John Minchillo/AP The United States delegation to the United Nations walked out of a security council meeting this week during a speech by France that sharply criticized U.S. human rights stances, including comparing U.S. foreign policy to that of authoritarian nations. A representative for the United States addressed the strained relations between the two longtime allies following the walkout, saying that it would continue to protest France’s actions as long as it sought to second-guess President Donald Trump’s foreign policy priorities. “This disingenuous grandstanding is tiresome, but we have tolerated it out of a sense of comradery and mutual respect,” said U.S. Ambassador Dan Negrea, who serves as an alternate representative to the U.N.’s General Assembly, adding that the delegation would continue to walk out until France abandons its “condescending and disrespectful rhetoric.” The meeting, which addressed Russia’s war against Ukraine, came mere days after the U.N.’s General Assembly opened a rift between the U.S. and allied nations over a vote to confirm Volker Türk for a second four-year term as the chief human rights officer for the organization. Türk has been an outspoken critic of Israel’s war on Gaza and publicly criticized the U.S. government for its handling of its war with Iran. The U.S. previously accused Türk of leading the organization’s human rights mission “to its deathbed.” Türk was confirmed by member nations. Quickly after the vote, the U.S. denounced Volker’s confirmation as “another example of the UN’s inherent corruption and incompetence.” At least 10 countries voted against Volker’s nomination alongside the U.S., including Israel, North Korea, and Russia. Before the walkout, the U.S. and France’s delegations shared heated exchanges online. “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore. Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it,” France’s mission to the UN posted on X . “France voted for someone who has been lecturing, free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors,” U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz responded . Under the Trump administration the U.S., which had historically been the U.N.’s largest financial contributor , has cut funding by more than $8 billion to U.N. specialized agencies and peacekeeping missions.

stories.title: Bibi’s Senate Fan Club
stories.author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Ronen Zvulun/Pool Reuters via AP Today’s notice: Netanyahu’s Senate defenders. Democrats furrow their brows at the DNC. Republicans grumble about Mike Lee. Unblocking FISA. Two names to watch as AI policy grows. One last Michigan Senate primary debate. A conversation with Genevieve McDonald. And: Another campaign gets ripped off. THE LATEST Senate Republicans are sticking with Benjamin Netanyahu even as public polling shows most Americans have little to no confidence in the Israeli prime minister to “do the right thing regarding world affairs.” Netanyahu will meet with many Republican senators, and Donald Trump , during his visit to Washington. Today, he’ll attend the memorial service for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Bibi’s strongest allies in the GOP. It’s ironically a time of a relatively large split between Trump and Netanyahu, with the former theoretically trying to bring the Iran war to an end and the latter saying the only real end is regime change. Again, polling shows the American public never really bought into the war Bibi and Trump launched to begin with. We tried to find out if there’s been a shift on Netanyahu’s leadership among Republicans as the war drags on. It was not readily apparent. “I think we should listen to Bibi Netanyahu on the issue of Iran,” Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) told us. There’s no apparent YOLO Caucus on this issue. “I think we ought to help Israel all they need,” said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas). “They’re a good, important ally.” Senate Democrats are sticking with Ken Martin: This weekend’s string of embarrassingly bad coverage of the goings-on at the Democratic National Committee was greeted with furrowed brows of concern among the Senate caucus last night, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic reports . No Democrats we talked to called for Martin to step aside. It’s “up to the DNC to decide how they want to handle,” said Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada). Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) said Martin inherited a bad situation, but did draw one line. “You should not throw things at staff,” he said, referring to reports that Martin threw a phone toward (but did not hit) an aide. Open tabs: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow New Mail-In Voting Rules (NOTUS); McConnell says he is unable to return to US Senate yet (Reuters); Judge dismisses challenge to Trump’s Religious Liberty Commission (The Hill); Democratic Hill offices employ more interns (Legistorm) From the Hill “A total nonstarter” is how one senior Republican Senate aide responded to Trump’s suggestion that the chamber should cancel August recess to stay in D.C. and vote on the SAVE America Act (which they cannot pass, because there are not enough Republican senators willing to end the filibuster). NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports that the already grouchy conference is extra salty over the suggestion they stick around next month. Trump’s Senate SAVE Man, Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), has said he’ll object to the usual unanimous consent to start recess, potentially forcing Republicans to take a tough vote in favor of working from home Aug. 8 to Sept. 13. “The worst threat to a GOP majority: Mike Lee’s continued SAVE Act antics,” a second senior Senate GOP aide told NOTUS. Changes with Clayton: The Senate is scheduled to vote on whether to confirm Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence today. If confirmed, some Democrats say that could be enough for them to support the reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports . “The hurdle is for the current, acting DNI to get that out of the way, and I think there’s a path to try to expedite this,” Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) said. Riding the AI policy wave: Fluency in the thorny political questions around artificial intelligence is an increasingly valuable currency in Washington, NOTUS’ Samuel Larreal reports . Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California), the Republican conference policy chair, landed the leadership gig earlier this year in part due to his AI literacy, according to Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma), who held the job before Obernolte and endorsed him to take over. And Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts) has raised her profile as a result of her work with Obernolte on AI safety. (A source says Trahan is planning to run for vice chair of the Democratic caucus next year.) From the campaign trail Haley Stevens’ fight night: The establishment pick for the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan came prepared for the final televised debate of the contest last night, NOTUS’ Alex Roarty reports from Southfield. Fresh off a wave of endorsements from respected Democratic officials in the state, Stevens took her chance to show voters she has more to offer than viral clips might indicate. She was feisty against the corporate- and AIPAC-stooge accusations coming at her from progressive opponent Abdul El-Sayed . “I am beholden to the people of Michigan,” she said. It was by no means a lopsided loss for El-Sayed, Alex tells us. He continually attacked Stevens over the special interests funding her campaign and appeared to gain momentum as the debate went on. In keeping with the general theme of the race, Stevens won the half that aired on TV and El-Sayed did better in the half that aired only online. Genevieve McDonald speaks out: The former political director of Graham Platner ’s Senate campaign, who resigned last October and warned the campaign could end basically exactly like it did, is not buying the recent high-profile apology tour by top Platner strategist Morris Katz . “I don’t believe him,” McDonald told Alex . “I mean, consultants shouldn’t have main character energy. We have lost the plot when consultants are doing PR tours for themselves, for their own redemption, and that is what this felt like.” NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Local news: What $1.2 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia Real Estate , by Torrie Herrington Sports desk: Commanders’ David Blough Has Been Preparing for This Moment His Whole Life , by Martenzie Johnson NEW ON NOTUS Rogers robbed: Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers ’ joint fundraising committee lost about $16, after a vendor’s email was hacked and the committee unknowingly paid a deceptive invoice, NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno reports . Campaign spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet told Taylor that the campaign wasn’t able to get the money back. Though the sum is paltry compared to the $1.5 million Rogers’ campaign has raised this election cycle, it’s the latest example of financial crimes targeting political campaigns — and the costs could go up if the criminals get bolder. NOT US ‘Climate hushing’ has swept the Democratic Party. New polling suggests it’s a mistake. By Kate Yoder for Grist Congress Budgeted Billions for Big Transit Projects. Trump Isn’t Spending It. By Emily Badger and Alicia Parlapiano for The New York Times A desert town may run out of water. Others could the same fate. By Hannah Knowles for The Washington Post How Bots Took Over Our Lives , by T.M. Brown for The New Yorker Thank you for reading! stories.title: Trump Ramps Up Threats Against Iran Despite Pause in Strikes
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The president posted a series of AI-generated images on Truth Social, including one calling himself “Guardian of the World.”
stories.content: President Donald Trump departs his golf club in Virginia on Sunday after posting multiple times to Truth Social about Iran. Jacquelyn Martin/AP While the United States paused strikes against Iran this weekend, President Donald Trump let loose on social media with artificial intelligence-created images depicting explosions in Iran or on ships labeled with that country’s name. The U.S. halted airstrikes Friday after 13 consecutive days of attacks as news reports raised alarms about depleted stockpiles of American missiles and Trump suggested a possible diplomatic solution. Trump said negotiations with Iran were ongoing , telling reporters in the White House on Friday that he thought the country’s leaders were “‌being ⁠by far the most serious that we've seen them” but that they might not be ready to make a deal. “It's giving diplomacy some space,” U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz told CBS’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday. “It's giving diplomacy a little bit of time.” Trump, who visited his Sterling, Virginia, golf course on Sunday, posted a series of AI-generated images to Truth Social about the conflict. One image depicts Trump standing behind a B-2 Spirit, one of the aircraft that has been used in the strikes, labeled “U.S.A.,” with explosions over land labeled “Iran.” The text on top of the image reads, “Guardian of the World.” A different image depicts Trump at the helm of a naval ship flanked by military members; Trump is wearing a red hat with the letters FAFO — which stand for “fuck around and find out.” Another image appears to depict Trump onboard an Iranian oil tanker while holding the American flag, with armed service members standing behind him and men with turbans jumping off the ship. “It’s Our Oil Tanker Now!” the image’s caption reads. Speculation over depleted weapons stockpiles has continued to grow since, according to The Wall Street Journal reporting, Trump called senior Pentagon officials and the top military contractors to the White House in June amid munitions supply concerns Stockpiles of Tomahawk, THAAD and Patriot missiles, all of which have been used in the war with Iran, could take three to five years to replace, according to a report published in May by the Center for Strategic and International Studies . Trump has said the U.S. is “locked and loaded” for more strikes on Iran, while Waltz downplayed concerns over depleted munitions inventory. “The U.S. military, and I’ve verified this every which way, has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be,” Waltz said Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.” “And I have to just tell you, the people that are leaking this nonsense deserve to be in jail.” Waltz blamed any depleted inventories on President Joe Biden’s handling of the war in Ukraine and the ongoing fight with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels — though he acknowledged that the Trump administration is actively exploring cheaper munitions options. Defense contractor Lockheed Martin announced plans last week to build a new version of the Patriot missile for half of the current $3.7 million cost.

stories.title: Trump Is Veering Toward Abandoning International Law
stories.author: Akbar Shahid Ahmed
stories.summary: The “best” hope for de-escalation with Iran is that the president is “super distracted beautifying the District,” a source told NOTUS.
stories.content: Emrah Gurel/AP President Donald Trump wants to make a dramatic show of force against Iran — potentially one that implicates U.S. soldiers in war crimes under international law. And he has consistently been unwilling to back down during internal conversations, sources familiar with administration discussions said. Combined with the Trump administration’s ongoing push to delegitimize the International Criminal Court, one of the global institutions meant to uphold standards for warfare, observers fear the U.S. is rapidly moving to abandon norms meant to shield human rights. “It’s not the first time the U.S. has gone on a rampage to try and kill the court,” said Rebecca Hamilton, a former International Criminal Court lawyer, who noted that U.S. officials also tried to limit the body’s reach during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. “When they’re attacking the court like this, it raises the question of, Why are you so scared of this court?” The U.S. has launched renewed strikes against Iran for 13 days in a row, and Trump threatened on Wednesday to destroy an Iranian bridge or power plant each time Iran strikes a ship attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz. Such an attack could have severe consequences for many civilians, who under international law countries are supposed to shield from military campaigns. “The threat itself may violate [international law], and if U.S. forces actually carried through on the threat then yes, that would likely violate” the law, said Brian Finucane, a former State Department lawyer. He noted that rules around war bar indiscriminate attacks — those without clear military objectives — as well as threats against civilian objects or those intended to terrorize civilians. Trump is showing signs of moving forward. Two sources familiar with administration thinking told NOTUS they expect a significant U.S. blitz against Iran in the coming days, motivated by Trump’s desire to look as though he is dominating Tehran. Neither source was authorized to speak on the record. The “best” hope for de-escalation “is Trump is super distracted beautifying the District,” one source said, nodding to the president’s fixation on design choices around Washington. The likeliest outcome, they said: “pointless escalation.” But the second source said many Cabinet members and military leaders have failed to be frank with Trump about the risks of launching his war on Iran in partnership with Israel, where officials have urged an assertive approach over diplomacy. Both sources expressed frustration with Brad Cooper, U.S. Central Command’s current chief, with one saying he could be the driving force behind but likely futile American attacks. U.S. Central Command did not respond to a NOTUS request for comment. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, wrote in an email: “The United States signed [a memorandum of understanding] with Iran and they broke it, shot at commercial ships, and killed American soldiers. President Trump is not going to stand by and allow this terrorist behavior to occur. Iran is paying in massive bombs, night after night, and they will continue to pay until they come to the table in, what President Trump deems, a meaningful way.” Experts on Iran say U.S. military pressure has a low chance of securing the outcome Trump seeks: normal traffic through the strait for vital oil and gas shipments. Despite the U.S. signing an agreement with Iran in June that references Hormuz — among other disagreements between the two countries — and providing escorts and naval coordination for ships, energy flows remain low, with Iran arguing the U.S. is not respecting its claims to the strait. And now, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen has warned it will close another major shipping route on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, which could further damage the global economy. Trump has also threatened the Houthis in response. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has launched a campaign against the International Criminal Court, saying this month the body poses “an intolerable threat to U.S. sovereignty” and alleging it seeks to target Americans. “There are certainly grounds for being very concerned” about the legal implications of Trump’s discussion of targeting Iranian infrastructure, said Hamilton, who is now a professor at American University. The International Criminal Court, established by the Rome Statute in , considers serious crimes and violations of international law that are not being fairly examined by domestic courts, serving as a court of last resort. U.S. officials were heavily involved in crafting the Rome Statute, but the country has never joined the court, despite previously supporting its investigations into figures including Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump has reportedly spoken of aligning with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to undermine the body. Trump has also defended Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who judges at the International Criminal Court say should stand trial for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity over Israel’s U.S.-backed military offensive in Gaza. (Netanyahu has denied any criminality.) The court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant, as well as a leader of the Palestinian militant group Hamas, in . New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this month he would like to uphold the warrant and arrest Netanyahu if he visits the city for a United Nations summit in September, but lacks the legal ability to do so. Trump has retorted that Netanyahu will not be arrested if he comes to the U.S. The U.S. and Iran aren’t members of the International Criminal Court, which limits its ability to probe either nation’s actions in this war. (Palestine is a member, which allowed the court to investigate Netanyahu and Gallant for actions on its territory.) But nations — most of the world’s countries — are members. With Rubio calling the court a threat to American sovereignty, Hamilton argued the U.S. should respect other states’ sovereign choices. On Friday, member states attempted to address a controversy that has plagued the court for more than a year by voting to remove its prosecutor, Karim Khan, over accusations of misconduct. Khan suggested he was targeted for his work on Gaza. For now, the warrants for Netanyahu and Gallant remain valid, though some worry a new prosecutor will downplay them, weakening the court’s work and the idea that some norms for behavior must be upheld. Amid concerns about eroding international law, Mark Kersten, a professor at the University of Fraser Valley in Canada, said other nations could defend the court by increasing actions to uphold its warrants or allotting it more resources. “The real story here is just how sensitive the United States is to the probability of being named in any kind of investigation” as its wars expand, he said.

stories.title: Trump Threatens the EU With Tariffs Over Fines on Tech Companies
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: The president accused the European Union of “illegal and highly discriminatory” practices against U.S. companies.
stories.content: Rod Lamkey, Jr./AP President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. will launch an investigation into the European Union and potentially impose tariffs, claiming the bloc unfairly imposed billions of dollars in fines on the U.S.’s biggest tech companies. “This illegal and highly discriminatory practice started at these high levels during the first year of the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration, but it’s not going to continue during the Trump Administration. The United States of America is not a ‘PIGGYBANK’ for Europe, nor will we allow it to be!” Trump wrote on Truth Social Friday, listing Apple, Meta, Amazon and Google as companies that have been excessively fined. Trump said his administration will "immediately" launch an investigation under Section of the Trade Act of . The law allows for the imposition of tariffs if the investigation ends up providing evidence of unfair trade practices. “The European Union will pay a very big price for this illegal and highly unethical conduct, which I have consistently warned them about,” Trump wrote in the post. “The penalties will be entirely reversed and, we anticipate, a substantial TARIFF to be placed on them at the earliest possible moment.” The EU announced Thursday that it was fining Google the equivalent of $1 billion for what it said were breaches of antitrust rules through Google Play and its search engine. The Trump administration condemned the fine later Thursday. “The EU’s various fines of Google alone add up to over 2 percent of the EU’s budget—a larger 'contribution' to the budget than many EU member states. Add in the recent announcement of the largest ever state-backed loan to Airbus, and it becomes clear that the EU continues to target the most competitive U.S. companies,” Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said in a statement . Trump a large setback to his tariff policy earlier this year when the Supreme Court decided in a 6-3 ruling to strike down the president’s sweeping tariffs on U.S. trade partners. However, he’s found new ways to implement tariffs, including through Section of the Trade Act. On Thursday, the U.S. imposed tariffs on 60 economies “for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.”

stories.title: The Pentagon Faces Questions After Casualties Disappeared From Public Tracker
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: The number of service members listed as casualties of the Iran war dropped from 18 soldiers on Wednesday to 14 overnight.
stories.content: The unexplained revisions raise questions about the agency’s official public accounting of the war’s death toll. Manuel Balce Ceneta/AP The Department of Defense removed four deceased U.S. service members from its public casualty tracker for the Iran conflict overnight, lowering the number of publicly listed fatalities. The removal, first reported by The New York Times , lowered the Pentagon’s reported count of U.S. service members killed in the Iran conflict from 18 on Wednesday to 14 on Thursday. The Defense Department attributed the removal to “temporary data disruptions on the Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) website” on DAY, though the 14 casualties figure remains on the site. But sources told the Times that the Trump administration decided to remove the last four casualties “because their deaths occurred after President Trump declared a ceasefire in the war in April.” The Defense Casualty Analysis System, a public Pentagon database intended to provide an official accounting of military casualties, is used by journalists, researchers and the public to track the human toll of U.S. conflicts. The unexplained revisions raise questions about the agency’s official public accounting of the war’s death toll. Asked about the removal, the White House referred NOTUS to the Department of Defense, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Online though, senior administration officials have denied the soldiers were purposely removed. “This is one of the worst instances of the Fake News media manufacturing lies out of thin air for absolutely no reason at all but to cause distress among the American people,” Sean Parnell, who serves as chief Pentagon spokesperson and assistant to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, posted on X. The four service members removed from the list were killed during the latest round of hostilities in the region, including 25-year-old 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan of Hawaii, 28-year-old Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad of New York, and 19-year-old Pvt. Isabella Gonzales of Texas, who were killed in an Iranian ballistic missile attack in Jordan last week. Thirty-year-old Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton of North Carolina , who died while conducting a controlled demolition of an Iranian one-way attack drone in Iraq, was also removed from the list. The tracker has also lowered the number of wounded soldiers in combat from to . Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, who serves on the Armed Services Committee, and other Democratic senators sent a letter to Hegseth and other Pentagon officials on Thursday questioning the inconsistencies between the agency’s reported numbers and other official statements. They requested detailed answers by the end of the month, including an exact casualty breakdown and an explanation of the discrepancies. “Erasing their sacrifices is a disgraceful attempt by this fragile President to minimize the costs of his illegal war,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois), a member of the Armed Services Committee, posted on Friday.

stories.title: Dinner, Take 2
stories.author: Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Weijia Jiang, president of the White House Correspondents' Association, speaks at the annual dinner after a gunman shot a security agent near the ballroom of the Washington Hilton on Saturday, April 25, . Jason Dick/AP Today’s notice: White House reporters defend their big dinner. Maine Democrats hope for some stability. The speaker has had it. Russia sanctions stall. And: Democrats readying to take on the “anti-woke jobs board.” THE LATEST To redo or not to redo? It’s Washington’s most glamorous — and most controversial — night. Again. Donald Trump , most of his Cabinet and White House journalists are making a second attempt at the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner after a shooting halted April’s event. This time, the dinner will be held at the Waldorf Astoria, formerly Trump International, even as the president derides reporters, sues news organizations and his White House keeps a list of “ media offenders .” (The Justice Department dropped subpoenas against New York Times journalists yesterday, so they have that going for them.) The perennial, and now more pertinent, question remains: Should journalists continue to host Nerd Prom? And what does it mean in the second age of Trump, when his administration is working harder than ever to find leakers and target reporters who break well-sourced stories? Some journalists and eight press organizations say the dinner should go . NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause and Manuela Silva surveyed White House reporters this week on whether there’s credibility to the argument that having the dinner is the same as honoring Trump. Many said canceling the event would be giving in. “Some of the journalists he subpoenaed and has gone after verbally are going to be on stage with him receiving awards. I think that image, and celebrating a free press, will say more than boycotting the event would,” a White House reporter told us. The contrary take: The dinners “into the narrative that D.C. journalists are elitist and out of touch with everyday Americans. ‘Look at them eating lobster, dressed in designer gowns and rubbing elbows with the very people they cover,’” another White House reporter said. That said, they , don’t disinvite Trump — use the opportunity to call out his treatment of the media. Open tabs: Number of U.S. troop deaths suddenly appears lower on Pentagon website (NYT); U.S. intelligence agency quietly cut about jobs since June 1 (WaPo); Trump administration drops demands for list of Jewish employees at UPenn (Politico); Mortgage rates hit highest levels in nearly a year (WSJ); Oil surges to $ per barrel after Red Sea attacks (NBC); Key Republican senator says he will support Trump’s pick for C.D.C director (NYT) From the campaign trail Southern swing: Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a potential Democratic presidential candidate, is headed south this weekend, campaigning for Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Murphy’s team shared exclusively with NOTUS’ Igor Bobic. His message? Democrats need to become a “big tent” party. Hat trick: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is on a 3x losing streak with high-profile losses that are causing House Democrats to question the campaign arm’s primary strategy. Democrats want the DCCC to improve how it communicates with members and takes feedback, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports . The Maine question: Democrats think they’ve stopped the bleeding in Maine’s Senate race with Troy Jackson as their heir apparent. “I think it’s going to be hotly contested, but I think it’s very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico). Jackson, the former state Senate president, has no federal political experience and only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent, Sen. Susan Collins . But as his nomination becomes formal on Saturday, Democrats tell NOTUS’ Alex Roarty, Igor Bobic and Christa Dutton they think Jackson might be in a better position than Graham Platner was even before the sexual assault allegations. From the Hill Mike Johnson’s doom loop: After months of dealing with rebellions from members of his own party, the normally even-keeled speaker of the House had finally had enough and snapped, “I’m sick of this shit,” at Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida). It was just one of a slew of daily crises Johnson has dealt with this year as members of his own conference threaten to derail their party’s agenda, NOTUS’ Reese Gorman reports . And rank-and-file Republicans are increasingly upset that a few of their colleagues hold so much power. Some are thinking of ways to actually hold the rebels to account. “The Republican conference is a diverse gathering of people, some of whom are really effective at getting things done and others who are more interested in knocking things down,” Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-South Dakota) told Reese. Still stalled: The long-championed (and long-stalled) bill by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham to enact more sanctions on Russia was poised to finally pass, boosted by the politician’s unexpected death. Instead, the measure is at risk of stalling out — again, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic and Joe Gould report. “We’re going to screw around here and lose this bill if we don’t go vote,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told our reporters. “We just pissed away two weeks. Now we got a week and a half left, and I don’t know if a vote is scheduled.” From the White House Thune v. Leavitt: Senate Majority Leader John Thune and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt exchanged not-so-friendly fire yesterday over the SAVE America Act, the voter-ID bill Trump considers his top priority, NOTUS’ Al Weaver writes . Leavitt told reporters at a briefing that the president’s “patience was running out.” In turn, Thune shot back that “she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?” THE BIG ONE The opposite of woke: A firm called RedBalloon, which claims to be the “anti-woke jobs board,” received a $1 million no-bid contract to help the State Department recruit candidates after the department laid off 20% of its workforce last year, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports . “A lot of the recruiting was focused on DEI. It was trying to get in the guy with a PhD in Black dance, rather than people who can do the best job,” Andrew Crapuchettes , the firm’s owner, said in a podcast interview recently. “I would love to see a lot of Christians applying, taking the test, doing the hard work, becoming a foreign service officer.” Democrats, who say they want to help employees booted under a reduction in force get their jobs back, are planning to investigate if they retake power in Congress. “We’re going to up our counsel staff so that we’re ready, because I can’t let folks get away with this,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) told Eric. NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Sports desk: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA , by Dave Sheinin NEW ON NOTUS McConnell’s absence impact: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) has not voted since being hospitalized June 14, and his absence has complicated the math on some key Republican priorities, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Al Weaver report . One example: The Senate Appropriations Committees is made up of 15 Republicans and 14 Democrats. Without McConnell, the committee cannot move any legislation forward that does not have bipartisan support. More: House Republicans Focus on Democrats’ Plans, Not Their Own Wins , by Kadia Goba Trump Expands His Ratepayer Pledge With Republican Governors, Utilities , by Mara Hoplamazian Three Airports Opt Into Trump Administration’s New Private Airport Security Model , by Jenna Monnin Trump Sidesteps SCOTUS With New Tariffs , by Violet Jira NOT US Marco Rubio Takes Aim at Globalists and the Left , by Ishaan Tharoor for The New Yorker How Trump Is Getting Richer in Office , by Andrea Fuller, Daniel Wood and Ben Protess for The New York Times Metro tried to make bus service better. Somehow, ridership and speeds are both down. By Rachel Weiner for The 51st Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. Jason Dick/AP Today’s notice: White House reporters defend their big dinner. Maine Democrats hope for some stability. The speaker has had it. Russia sanctions stall. And: Democrats readying to take on the “anti-woke jobs board.” THE LATEST To redo or not to redo? It’s Washington’s most glamorous — and most controversial — night. Again. Donald Trump , most of his Cabinet and White House journalists are making a second attempt at the annual White House Correspondents’ Association dinner after a shooting halted April’s event. This time, the dinner will be held at the Waldorf Astoria, formerly Trump International, even as the president derides reporters, sues news organizations and his White House keeps a list of “ media offenders .” (The Justice Department dropped subpoenas against New York Times journalists yesterday, so they have that going for them.) The perennial, and now more pertinent, question remains: Should journalists continue to host Nerd Prom? And what does it mean in the second age of Trump, when his administration is working harder than ever to find leakers and target reporters who break well-sourced stories? Some journalists and eight press organizations say the dinner should go . NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause and Manuela Silva surveyed White House reporters this week on whether there’s credibility to the argument that having the dinner is the same as honoring Trump. Many said canceling the event would be giving in. “Some of the journalists he subpoenaed and has gone after verbally are going to be on stage with him receiving awards. I think that image, and celebrating a free press, will say more than boycotting the event would,” a White House reporter told us. The contrary take: The dinners “into the narrative that D.C. journalists are elitist and out of touch with everyday Americans. ‘Look at them eating lobster, dressed in designer gowns and rubbing elbows with the very people they cover,’” another White House reporter said. That said, they , don’t disinvite Trump — use the opportunity to call out his treatment of the media. Open tabs: Number of U.S. troop deaths suddenly appears lower on Pentagon website (NYT); U.S. intelligence agency quietly cut about jobs since June 1 (WaPo); Trump administration drops demands for list of Jewish employees at UPenn (Politico); Mortgage rates hit highest levels in nearly a year (WSJ); Oil surges to $ per barrel after Red Sea attacks (NBC); Key Republican senator says he will support Trump’s pick for C.D.C director (NYT) From the campaign trail Southern swing: Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a potential Democratic presidential candidate, is headed south this weekend, campaigning for Senate candidate Annie Andrews in South Carolina and Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Murphy’s team shared exclusively with NOTUS’ Igor Bobic. His message? Democrats need to become a “big tent” party. Hat trick: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is on a 3x losing streak with high-profile losses that are causing House Democrats to question the campaign arm’s primary strategy. Democrats want the DCCC to improve how it communicates with members and takes feedback, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports . The Maine question: Democrats think they’ve stopped the bleeding in Maine’s Senate race with Troy Jackson as their heir apparent. “I think it’s going to be hotly contested, but I think it’s very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico). Jackson, the former state Senate president, has no federal political experience and only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent, Sen. Susan Collins . But as his nomination becomes formal on Saturday, Democrats tell NOTUS’ Alex Roarty, Igor Bobic and Christa Dutton they think Jackson might be in a better position than Graham Platner was even before the sexual assault allegations. From the Hill Mike Johnson’s doom loop: After months of dealing with rebellions from members of his own party, the normally even-keeled speaker of the House had finally had enough and snapped, “I’m sick of this shit,” at Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida). It was just one of a slew of daily crises Johnson has dealt with this year as members of his own conference threaten to derail their party’s agenda, NOTUS’ Reese Gorman reports . And rank-and-file Republicans are increasingly upset that a few of their colleagues hold so much power. Some are thinking of ways to actually hold the rebels to account. “The Republican conference is a diverse gathering of people, some of whom are really effective at getting things done and others who are more interested in knocking things down,” Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-South Dakota) told Reese. Still stalled: The long-championed (and long-stalled) bill by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham to enact more sanctions on Russia was poised to finally pass, boosted by the politician’s unexpected death. Instead, the measure is at risk of stalling out — again, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic and Joe Gould report. “We’re going to screw around here and lose this bill if we don’t go vote,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told our reporters. “We just pissed away two weeks. Now we got a week and a half left, and I don’t know if a vote is scheduled.” From the White House Thune v. Leavitt: Senate Majority Leader John Thune and White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt exchanged not-so-friendly fire yesterday over the SAVE America Act, the voter-ID bill Trump considers his top priority, NOTUS’ Al Weaver writes . Leavitt told reporters at a briefing that the president’s “patience was running out.” In turn, Thune shot back that “she or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?” THE BIG ONE The opposite of woke: A firm called RedBalloon, which claims to be the “anti-woke jobs board,” received a $1 million no-bid contract to help the State Department recruit candidates after the department laid off 20% of its workforce last year, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports . “A lot of the recruiting was focused on DEI. It was trying to get in the guy with a PhD in Black dance, rather than people who can do the best job,” Andrew Crapuchettes , the firm’s owner, said in a podcast interview recently. “I would love to see a lot of Christians applying, taking the test, doing the hard work, becoming a foreign service officer.” Democrats, who say they want to help employees booted under a reduction in force get their jobs back, are planning to investigate if they retake power in Congress. “We’re going to up our counsel staff so that we’re ready, because I can’t let folks get away with this,” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-New York) told Eric. NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Sports desk: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA , by Dave Sheinin NEW ON NOTUS McConnell’s absence impact: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) has not voted since being hospitalized June 14, and his absence has complicated the math on some key Republican priorities, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Al Weaver report . One example: The Senate Appropriations Committees is made up of 15 Republicans and 14 Democrats. Without McConnell, the committee cannot move any legislation forward that does not have bipartisan support. More: House Republicans Focus on Democrats’ Plans, Not Their Own Wins , by Kadia Goba Trump Expands His Ratepayer Pledge With Republican Governors, Utilities , by Mara Hoplamazian Three Airports Opt Into Trump Administration’s New Private Airport Security Model , by Jenna Monnin Trump Sidesteps SCOTUS With New Tariffs , by Violet Jira NOT US Marco Rubio Takes Aim at Globalists and the Left , by Ishaan Tharoor for The New Yorker How Trump Is Getting Richer in Office , by Andrea Fuller, Daniel Wood and Ben Protess for The New York Times Metro tried to make bus service better. Somehow, ridership and speeds are both down. By Rachel Weiner for The 51st Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend.
