The Arizona Democrat was at a dinner at the time and, after some discussion, decided to stay out, three of the sources told NOTUS. Following dinner, Gallego walked to a nightclub, a source said.

stories.title: Republicans Want Answers on Iran School Strike — But Not Hearings
stories.author: Hamed Ahmadi
stories.summary: The White House and many Senate Republicans said they’re waiting to see what the Department of Defense says about the schoolchildren killed in Iran.
stories.content: Many Senate Republicans say they want answers on whether the U.S. struck a girls’ school in Iran, killing about people, most of them children. But the lawmakers seem satisfied with waiting for the Trump administration to produce those answers rather than publicly pressing them. “Oversight is good,” Sen. James Lankford said. “But again, we’re in the middle of a military operation now. The questions are reasonable questions. The timing and the standing up and doing a public hearing while our troops are in the field, saying, ‘You guys are shooting at schoolgirls,’ when they’re actually defending our families — I think it’s just the wrong way to do that.” Some Republicans took it even further. Sen. Lindsey Graham, a top cheerleader for the war, said he does not support public hearings on civilian casualties or an independent investigation into the strike on the girls’ school.

stories.title: Senate Democrats Are Split Over Supplemental Funding for the War in Iran
stories.author: Avani Kalra
stories.summary: Most say they would need to see a clear statement of the Trump administration’s objectives in the region before authorizing additional financing.
stories.content: Though Senate Democrats continue to publicly oppose the Trump administration’s war in Iran, some say they won’t rule out voting for a supplemental funding request from the Pentagon to support the operation. First, though, they want more confidence that the administration has a clear goal. “We have to have a plan,” Sen. Gary Peters told NOTUS on Tuesday. “I’m still not convinced that the administration has a plan to execute the rest of the war and have an exit strategy.”

stories.title: Senators Look to Closed-Door Briefing for Answers on Venezuela’s Future
stories.author: Hamed Ahmadi
stories.summary: “What our objectives are, what our policy is — I’m not clear on any of that,” Republican Sen. Josh Hawley told NOTUS.
stories.content: Senators are heading into a classified briefing Wednesday morning that’s likely to outline how U.S. forces captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. But many are more interested in something else: what the administration plans to do now. “What our objectives are, what our policy is — I’m not clear on any of that,” Republican Sen. Josh Hawley told NOTUS Tuesday. Some senators said they were skeptical they’d get many answers on the path ahead from the briefing, which will feature Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Pam Bondi, Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.

stories.title: Congress to Be Briefed on Potential U.S. Military Operations Inside Venezuela, Graham Says
stories.author: Amelia Benavides-Colón
stories.summary: “President Trump told me yesterday that he plans to brief members of Congress when he gets back from Asia,” Sen. Lindsey Graham said.
stories.content: Sen. Lindsey Graham said President Donald Trump is preparing to brief Congress on planned military operations inside Venezuela and Colombia once he returns from his trip to Asia this week. “I think President Trump’s made a decision that (Nicolás) Maduro, the leader of Venezuela, is an indicted drug, drug trafficker, that it’s time for him to go, that Venezuela and Colombia have been safe havens for narco-terrorists for too long,” Graham said Sunday on “Face the Nation.” “President Trump told me yesterday that he plans to brief members of Congress when he gets back from Asia about future potential military operations against Venezuela and Colombia.” Sign Up for NOTUS’ Free Daily Newsletter

stories.title: Senate Republicans Side With Trump and Acknowledge Starvation in Gaza
stories.author: Em Luetkemeyer, Helen Huiskes
stories.summary: Even though Republicans blamed Hamas for the problem, it’s a bit of daylight between them and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
stories.content: After President Donald Trump said on Monday that children are starving in Gaza, Republican senators started to show some daylight between themselves and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, siding with Trump and acknowledging the starvation. It’s only a slight departure from the Senate GOP’s overwhelming support for Israel. And senators tried to couch their recognition of the problem by blaming Hamas. But it’s one of the first splits Republicans have shown between them and Netanyahu, after Trump seemed incredulous that there was no hunger problem in Gaza. Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Israel’s closest allies in Congress, blamed Hamas for “it being the way it is,” but acknowledged there was a problem.

stories.title: ‘This Is a War’: AI Impostor of Marco Rubio Has Senators on High Alert
stories.author: Em Luetkemeyer
stories.summary: Some senators are advocating for more regulation after an AI impostor of the secretary of state contacted several government officials.
stories.content: Spoof phone calls and messages to lawmakers in which artificial intelligence programs imitate high-ranking officials are increasingly common on Capitol Hill. The latest report that an AI impostor of Secretary of State Marco Rubio contacted several government officials has put senators on guard, and some are advocating for more AI constraints in light of the incident. “I talk to him frequently, multiple times a day, sometimes,” Sen. James Risch said of Rubio. “And I always say, ‘Is this really you, Marco?’”

stories.title: Democrats Demand Information About What the FAA Is Doing to Overhaul Flight Safety
stories.author: Torrence Banks
stories.summary: The hearing with top leaders from the Federal Aviation Administration comes in the wake of staff cuts and high-profile flight safety incidents, including the deadly crash outside of DCA.
stories.content: The Federal Aviation Administration is facing scrutiny over flight safety and its recent cuts to staffing, and Democratic senators at a hearing on Wednesday with top agency officials expressed frustration over how little information they’re getting. In the backdrop of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation’s hearing were recent high-profile incidents, including the crash outside of Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in January that killed dozens of people. Also repeatedly mentioned were the recent outages in Newark that left air traffic controllers unable to navigate planes, leading to questions about whether it’s safe to fly to that location. Sen. Maria Cantwell, the ranking member of the committee, asked Franklin McIntosh, the FAA deputy chief operating officer, why the FAA’s oversight procedures have been failing, given the number of near misses before and after the fatal crash at DCA.

stories.title: The House Is Opening an Investigation Into Military Use of Airspace Around DCA
stories.author: Torrence Banks
stories.summary: The lawmakers are seeking answers following the crash between a passenger flight and military helicopter that left dozens earlier this year.
stories.content: Members of the House Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs announced Thursday that they opened an investigation into the military’s use of airspace near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The investigation follows the January crash between an American Airlines passenger jet and a military Black Hawk helicopter that killed more than 60 people as it approached for a landing. It’s also happening as there is increased nervousness about flight safety, including from lawmakers. The Republican chair of the subcommittee, Rep. William Timmons, and the Democratic ranking member, Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, wrote a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for a “member-level” briefing on the crash by April 1.

stories.title: Trump's Pick to Be Ambassador to Canada Acknowledges Canada Is a Country
stories.author: Nuha Dolby
stories.summary: President Donald Trump’s positions toward Canada quickly became the subject of heated questions from Democratic senators. The nominees to be ambassadors for posts in Mexico, Canada and Japan were all part of the hearing.
stories.content: A Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearing for ambassador nominees quickly turned to President Donald Trump’s past statements on making Canada the “51st state” and the imposed tariffs on some of the U.S.'s largest trade partners. Thursday’s hearing featured former Rep. Pete Hoekstra, the Trump administration’s pick to be ambassador to Canada, as well as former ambassador to El Salvador Ronald Johnson and former ambassador to Portugal George Glass, who are up for the positions in Mexico and Japan respectively. They’re up for usually quiet roles at a time when the Trump administration has taken aggressive stances toward its neighbors to the north and south. Sen. Chris Coons asked Hoekstra explicitly if he would “agree that Canada is a sovereign state and should not be even jokingly referred to as the 51st state?”

stories.title: Senators Want to Know if DOGE's FAA Layoffs Will Make the Skies Less Safe
stories.author: Em Luetkemeyer, Torrence Banks
stories.summary: The Trump administration has argued that the FAA layoffs will not affect safety or recruiting. But some senators remain concerned about what effects it could have on the industry.
stories.content: Everyone wants answers on whether it’s safe to fly — including senators. The public is on edge over recent high-profile accidents, including the crash between a helicopter and a passenger flight near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The cause of the deadly crash is still unknown, but lawmakers say it’s made clear that this is an area where safety needs to tighten up. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma, which has one of the largest Federal Aviation Administration field facilities in the country, told NOTUS the FAA still needs more air traffic controllers because “as was highlighted three weeks ago in the crash, it’s incredibly important that people are there.”

stories.title: Trump Proposed a U.S. Takeover Of Gaza. Senators Aren't So Sure.
stories.author: Samuel Larreal, Em Luetkemeyer, Emily Kennard
stories.summary: The president said he wants to “own” the Gaza Strip. Senators didn’t endorse the idea — but they also didn’t reject it outright.
stories.content: President Donald Trump’s proposal to take over the Gaza Strip prompted scoffs and disgust from Democrats on Tuesday — and some consideration from Republicans. “There’s probably a couple of kinks in that slinky, but I’ll have to look at [Trump’s] statement,” Sen. Thom Tillis told reporters after the president floated the idea of the U.S. occupying Gaza. Republicans in the Senate didn’t exactly endorse the idea. But they were reluctant to break with Trump — even on a suggestion that could displace about 2 million people, mire the U.S. in war and enrage international allies.

stories.title: Senators Begin to Ask: Should Military Helicopters Even Be Training Around DCA?
stories.author: Ben T.N. Mause
stories.summary: The investigation into Wednesday’s crash is only just beginning, but some senators are questioning why military exercises would happen so close to such a busy airport.
stories.content: While most senators mourning Wednesday’s midair collision between an Army helicopter and a commercial airliner preached patience as an investigation into the accident began, some couldn’t help but wonder: Should military helicopters be flying there in the first place? “We need to get to the bottom of what happened,” Sen. Josh Hawley said. “And we need a thorough report. But one question I have is, why are we doing military training exercises right next to one of the busiest airports in America?” “I don’t know if that makes the most sense to me,” Hawley . “But that’s the kinda thing we need to figure out.”

stories.title: Elise Stefanik Is Already Answering for Trump’s Skepticism of the U.N.
stories.author: Helen Huiskes
stories.summary: Trump’s pick for U.N. ambassador was quick to stand by the blitz of executive orders the president signed immediately after taking office.
stories.content: Democrats on the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations seemed broadly supportive of Rep. Elise Stefanik, President Donald Trump’s nominee for United Nations ambassador. But questions about her future boss’ executive actions and the administration’s commitments around the globe took up most of the time during her confirmation hearing Tuesday. While Republicans and Democrats alike praised Stefanik’s record in the House and qualifications for the role, some of the tensest exchanges came over the actions Trump took in his first 24 hours to withdraw the U.S. from international institutions, including the World Health Organization and the Paris climate agreement. In another executive order yesterday, Trump initiated a 90-day pause in foreign assistance for a review of all foreign development assistance. Stefanik was quick to stand by the orders.

stories.title: House Intel Democrats Aren’t Worried About the Drones but Want More Transparency
stories.author: Emily Kennard
stories.summary: The House Intelligence Committee met with FBI and Pentagon officials in a classified briefing on Tuesday addressing the drones that have drawn widespread attention from the public.
stories.content: Democratic lawmakers who attended a classified House Intelligence Committee briefing on Tuesday said there’s no evidence of foreign adversaries or “little green men” controlling the drones that have drawn widespread attention. But some of them said they still won’t be satisfied until more information is shared with the public. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi told reporters after the briefing: “Show us the data. Show us how it’s manned aircraft.”

stories.title: Senate Republicans Know Exactly What They Want From Biden on Venezuela. Democrats, Not So Much.
stories.author: Oriana González
stories.summary: Senate Democrats are following the White House’s lead in cautiously watching what’s unfolding in Venezuela. Republicans are already blaming the president for a “total fiasco.”
stories.content: Senate Republicans and Democrats are taking opposing tacts in how they’re approaching Venezuela, two days after a disputed election where President Nicolás Maduro declared himself the victor: Democrats, following the White House, are proceeding cautiously; Republicans, condemning the White House, are demanding immediate action. The administration should “stand up for democracy, stand up against the obvious and indisputable election fraud,” Sen. Ted Cruz told NOTUS, pointing to previous Venezuelan elections held under Maduro’s government that are widely considered to be fraudulent. “The president of the United States should clearly and unequivocally call out Maduro as an illegitimate leader, as a dictator that’s subverting democracy. The president should recognize the opposition leader as the duly elected leader of Venezuela.” Sen. Marco Rubio blamed the Biden administration for the results, arguing the deals Biden officials reached with the Maduro regime — which resulted in the U.S. temporarily lifting economic sanctions and extraditing regime allies in exchange for free and fair elections — instead encouraged Maduro to commit electoral fraud.

stories.title: Looking to Wisconsin
stories.author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Francesca Hong at a Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary debate. Nam Y. Huh/AP Today’s notice: Learning lessons from Michigan to use in Wisconsin. New polls in Maine and Iowa. Comer plans to wrap up Epstein investigations while Democrats plot more. And: Inside the weird politics of data centers. THE LATEST Democrats get ready to do it again. Another progressive candidate, this time in Wisconsin, is running circles around the party establishment and scaring leaders about a key race in a key state. DSA member and state lawmaker Francesca Hong seems set to walk away with the nomination in next week’s gubernatorial primary. But now, for some odd, out-of-the-blue, strange reason, there are some questions about the polls. “It’ll probably be closer than people think based on the results in Michigan,” a Democratic strategist told NOTUS’ Christa Dutton . Campaign officials for Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley , the candidate the establishment wants to win the primary, popped a memo yesterday saying they, too, think the polls are wrong. Once again, the Democratic establishment has assembled to back one of several candidates running in a primary: Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers has been campaigning hard with Crowley, whom he urged to get back in after he dropped out earlier in the cycle. Is that really the lesson Michigan taught? NOTUS’ Manuela Silva spoke to Democratic senators about what they took away from Michigan’s Senate primary when it comes to deciding whom to endorse. Sometimes it’s easy, said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who offered the example of a candidate like Roy Cooper in North Carolina. “There are other places where the fight is pretty even, and in those situations, I would prefer that leadership just let it play out,” Murphy told Manuela. Some places are getting a little messy. Take Montana, for example, as NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández explores, where the establishment is backing an independent over the Democratic nominee. Some senators noted that the tools the establishment throws at races — i.e. the millions spent attacking Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in her Senate bid — are clearly not working anymore. “Voters are just tuning that bullshit out,” retiring Sen. Tina Smith (D-Minnesota) said of the cash flowing against Flanagan. What about any lessons for the left next week? One of that side of the party’s kingmakers seemed to suggest people should not pay too much attention to Wisconsin. “To be honest with you, I met Francesca a couple of years ago,” Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) told reporters. “I haven’t talked to her since. It’s not the race that we’re involved in.” “We’re very much involved in Peggy Flanagan’s race in Minnesota,” he . “I hope that Peggy Flanagan wins.” Open tabs: Max Miller resists pressure to drop reelection bid (AP); Darline Graham Takes Over Lindsey Graham’s Leadership PAC (NOTUS); After Michigan Loss, AIPAC Weighs a Second Effort to Defeat El-Sayed (NYT); Inside the GOP hemp wars (Axios) From the campaign trail First on NOTUS: Two new PAC-funded battleground polls. Polling as a, well, concept took a hit in Michigan on Tuesday night, but that doesn’t mean political strategists aren’t still spending a ton of money on surveys to inform their spending plans and other campaign maneuvers. In that spirit, we offer an exclusive look at two polls from groups with pockets deep enough to buy the expensive ones. Maine: Democrats weathered the primary storm? New numbers from Senate Majority PAC (the spending arm of Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer ) shows freshly minted Democratic nominee Troy Jackson with a slight lead over Sen. Susan Collins , the longtime Republican incumbent. NOTUS’ Christa Dutton got the SMP memo , which found Jackson up 49% to 45% over Collins, with 6% undecided. The memo also details why Collins may be more vulnerable this year than the last time she ran, in . Iowa: Democrats see momentum in the 2nd Congressional District. House Majority PAC (the spending arm of House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries ) is trying to win the seat being vacated by Rep. Ashley Hinson after she became the Republican nominee for Senate. Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris in the district by 10 percentage points . A new HMP poll found Democratic nominee Lindsay James with 46% to Republican Joe Mitchell ’s 45%. The survey gave credence to the idea that Trump is a drag on Republican candidates even in Republican places — Trump’s favorability rating is underwater in the poll, 44% fave/53% unfave. From the Hill The state of House Oversight’s Epstein investigation will be largely determined by the voters in November, NOTUS’ Stephen Neukam reports . The committee’s chair, Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky), says it’s time to wrap things up, produce a report and ask the DOJ to consider criminal prosecutions. Democrats on the committee, led by Rep. Robert Garcia of California, say there’s much more to do and want to keep the investigation going if they get the majority. “There’s no question that the investigation will continue into the next couple of years,” Garcia told NOTUS. From the White House Trump in Las Vegas: “The polls say we do better against the communists. So he won, and so I think I’m happy.” Trump also in Las Vegas: "When I watch Abdul, he’s full of shit." More from NOTUS’ Ben T.N. Mause . NOTUS PERSPECTIVES After Abdul El-Sayed’s primary win, Republicans’ rhetoric got real ugly, real fast. Leading the charge was Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who yesterday held a hearing titled “Hidden in Plain Sight: Confronting the Muslim Brotherhood Network in America.” None of Cruz’s colleagues showed up — but Dana Milbank was there . NOTUS METRO Local news: Talk to Tom: Restaurant Recs for D.C., Maryland ... and Germany! By Tom Sietsema Sports desk: Commanders to Sign Stefon Diggs, Shoring Up a Shaky Receivers Room , by Martenzie Johnson NEW ON NOTUS Data center politics continue being just so weird. The ongoing division among Democrats over data center construction — moratorium-ers vs. regulation-ers, basically — is getting more complicated, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports . Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) today will propose a new excise tax and the elimination of tax breaks for data center construction. His plan is not to stop the construction of new centers but rather to ensure there’s some public benefit from them, if only just in tax revenue. That’s part of a growing list of policy ideas Democrats are kicking around to address the electorate’s AI skepticism. Things are weird in MAGA politics, too. In a deep dive, NOTUS’ Mara Hoplamazian reports that the first year of Trump’s effort to accelerate data center infrastructure by clearing away regulatory and permitting hurdles — a promise kept to the tech titans who supported his candidacy — has not actually boosted data center construction. But it has helped spread the data center backlash to red places, often over the same issues his administration is trying to ease oversight around: water quality, air quality and the speed at which centers are built. More: Republicans Roll the Dice on Their Farm Bill , by Tyler Spence Congress’ Watchdog Is Still Struggling to Get Answers on DOGE , by Natalie Alms Max Miller’s Corporate Backers Go Silent on Embattled Congressman , by Dave Levinthal NOT US Mullin’s immigration balancing act grows more precarious , by Myah Ward and Eric Bazail-Eimil for Politico C.I.A. Sets Up Secret Cuba Task Force as Trump Pressures Havana , by Adam Entous for The New York Times Our Fauci Diaries, Ourselves , by Molly Fischer for The New Yorker Thank you for reading! And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr, Brett Bachman and Andrew Burton. Photo by Nam Y. Huh/AP.

stories.title: Wisconsin Democrats Doubt a Progressive’s Prospects After Michigan Results
stories.author: Christa Dutton
stories.summary: Two gubernatorial candidates’ camps are drawing opposite conclusions after Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow victory on Tuesday
stories.content: Stakes for Wisconsin Democrats are high in the state, which Trump won by less than a percentage point in . Nam Y. Huh/AP Photo In Wisconsin, a progressive gubernatorial candidate is polling far ahead of the other candidates before the battleground state’s Democratic primary next week. That was the story in Michigan, too: Polls showed Abdul El-Sayed handily beating Rep. Haley Stevens ahead of Tuesday’s Senate primary — but he had barely edged out a victory by the time the race was called the next morning. Now, some Democrats wonder if the same will come to pass in Wisconsin, where polling has shown state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist , leading her opponents by double-digit margins for weeks. Among the most doubtful is Hong’s leading opponent, David Crowley, who previously suspended his race in July because he wasn’t gaining traction before reentering 10 days later. Tuesday’s disconnect between polls and election day realities in Michigan brings Milwaukee County’s executive to one of the most optimistic points of his campaign so far. His team sent out an internal memo on Wednesday telling supporters his race is similarly closer than polls indicate. “Results in Michigan Tuesday night showed polling that failed to appropriately capture and reflect the primary electorate and well overstated the position of the race frontrunner,” the memo, first reported by WISN , says. “Democrats are in the driver’s seat in Wisconsin to choose David Crowley and have the best fighting chance against Tom Tiffany in November.” If next week’s voter base resembles those of and , the primary “does not have a prohibitive front runner,” the memo continues. While El-Sayed’s win shows how a socialist candidate like Hong can similarly ascend, Michigan’s uneven polling shows how challenging it is to pull off accurate primary surveys, said Barry Burden, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Madison — especially in Wisconsin and Michigan, where voters of any party can opt to participate. “There are questions about where Hong stands,” Burden said. “There’s an opportunity for Crowley, and the Michigan results might be an indicator for him that it’s still a possibility.” Wisconsin and Michigan are two of the country’s most consequential battleground states. Crowley’s camp argues Stevens’ better-than-expected performance proves more moderate candidates can still make good showings despite a recent progressive surge within the party. “We don’t have to talk in theoreticals anymore about how this might work,” said a Democratic strategist who backs Crowley, given anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “Yeah, Haley didn't win, but she lost by one point. But this isn't us just trying to explain what our theory of the case is. … There is more money coming through the door today. There is more enthusiasm.” Hong’s campaign, meanwhile, considers El-Sayed’s victory a harbinger of success in Wisconsin for the party’s left-most flank, which saw several candidates win Democratic primaries in New York City and Denver ’s heavily blue districts. Michigan showed that working-class people are “ready for something different,” Hong said in a statement to NOTUS, adding that her campaign has “never taken the size of any projected margin for granted.” “Polls are snapshots, and Michigan was another reminder that campaigns are won by organizing and turning out voters,” Hong said. Stakes for Wisconsin Democrats are high in the state, which Trump won by less than a percentage point in . The governor’s mansion, currently occupied by Democrat Tony Evers, has alternated between Republican and Democratic administrations since the 1970s. And the left’s gubernatorial candidate pool has and flowed significantly this summer — even prompting a lawsuit from the state party over the ability to recast ballots that was eventually dismissed. Lt. Gov Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in her campaign finance filings. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes ended his campaign last week shortly before the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported it was looking into allegations of sexual impropriety. Crowley himself had dropped out of the race briefly before reentering with Evers’ endorsement. Whoever advances from the Aug. 11 primary will a tough race against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany. State Navigate, a polling firm that mostly focuses on state legislative races, concentrated on including more rural, low-income and Republican voters after seeing Michigan surveys miss those groups, executive director Chaz Nuttycombe said of a new survey coming out this week. A poll the organization conducted in late July showed Hong up by 29 points. “It’ll probably be closer than people think based on the results in Michigan last night,” said another Democratic strategist in Wisconsin, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the race. “I think people thought that it was going to be a little more lopsided than it ended up being, and that’s probably what’s going to happen here in Wisconsin.”

stories.title: Are Montana Democrats Abandoning Their Own Candidate?
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: Democratic leaders are backing an independent Senate candidate in Montana. The Democrat is livid.
stories.content: Robert Yoon/AP Democrats are facing an unusual obstacle in their push to create as many paths to a Senate majority as possible this fall: a Democratic nominee who refuses to quit. Democrat Alani Bankhead is set to Republican Kurt Alme in Montana’s Senate election — the kind of race that would be a reach for Democrats in a normal year but could be on the table in a favorable political environment this year. The problem is Democrats are rallying behind independent candidate Seth Bodnar, who they think actually makes that long shot a possibility. But with both candidates running, beating Alme is nearly impossible. “[Republicans] know that if it’s head-to-head between Bodnar and Alme, Bodnar wins the damn race,” former Montana Sen. Jon Tester, who has endorsed Bodnar, told NOTUS. Bankhead is livid with national party leadership, who she thinks is leaving her out to dry. In an interview with NOTUS, she accused Democratic leaders, nationally and in the state, of “using all their power and money to try to make Montanans accept the person that they pick.” Bankhead alleges Tester has collaborated with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to circumvent the democratic process by backing a preferred candidate, an allegation Tester denies. On top of that, it’s not even clear what would happen if Bankhead were to withdraw before next week’s Aug. 10 deadline. There’s a legal dispute, which lawyers briefed the state Democratic Party on, over whether the party would have to name a replacement for the party line should Bankhead quit. Bankhead has said repeatedly she is not considering exiting the race, “short of God” telling her to drop out. “Montana law says no matter what — [even] if I die — the state party still has to replace me on the ballot,” Bankhead told NOTUS. “No, I’m not dropping out.” In June, shortly after the Democratic primary, 17 state legislators wrote a letter to Bankhead and Bodnar, urging one of them to drop out. “Every week that passes makes it more difficult to unify supporters, consolidate resources, and mount the strongest possible campaign for November,” the legislators wrote. The lawmakers stopped short of supporting either candidate’s campaign. “Based on the information currently available to us, Seth appears to have an advantage,” they wrote. “At the same time, we recognize that [Bankhead] has only recently secured the Democratic nomination.” The state had at least one Democratic senator for a until . But it’s not currently at the top of national Democrats’ priority list as they try to take the Senate majority in November. “I’m just not tuned in on Montana,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS. “I’ve been doing Michigan and Minnesota and Georgia and North Carolina.” Several of her colleagues involved in other Senate races echoed that sentiment, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont). But Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate majority, and some seats currently held by Democrats — including in Michigan — are in reach for Republicans, putting pressure on the party to devise multiple paths to victory. Bankhead, a retired Air Force lieutenant colonel and counterintelligence agent who won the state's Democratic primary with over 48, votes in June, faces myriad challenges. Bankhead’s campaign had only raised just under $60, by the end of June compared to the more than $3.2 million Bodnar has raised since launching his campaign . Bankhead accuses the DSCC of “starving” her campaign of money — and she is facing mounting pressure from former Democratic leaders in the state to drop out. A Tavern Research poll conducted in mid-June, showed an Alme-Bodnar tie in a hypothetical head-to-head, while Alme led Bankhead 56-44 in a hypothetical two-way race. Some polls show Bodnar leading Alme if Bankhead were to drop out. There has been a run of Democratic Senate nominees withdrawing to clear the path for a two-way race with an independent candidate. Democratic nominees have dropped their campaigns in Nebraska, South Dakota and Idaho, giving a boost to independent candidates in each Republican-leaning state. Bodnar, the former president of the University of Montana and a West Point-trained former Green Beret, entered the race as an independent in late March. He has secured the endorsement of major Democratic-aligned groups, including Montana Conservation Voters and VoteVets — the largest progressive veterans’ organization in the U.S. The group previously supported Bankhead . Bodnar also has been endorsed by Tester and former Democratic Sen. Max Baucus, among other leaders. Bodnar’s campaign did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. Bankhead described herself as being up against the entrenched party establishment. “Old guard political leaders want to stay in power and control, and they're trying to use the last bit of power that they have to wield their influence to maintain the status quo,” she told NOTUS. Schumer’s office did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. The DSCC referred NOTUS to the organization’s comments to Semafor , where DSCC executive director Devan Barber said “The DSCC partners with viable campaigns who have a path to victory, which Ms. Bankhead does not.” Montana’s Senate seat is open because Republican Sen. Steve Daines abruptly withdrew in March and endorsed Alme, who had filed to run the same day. Concerns over splitting the Democratic vote have local leaders convinced that keeping Bankhead on the ballot will hand Republicans an easy win in the state. Bodnar, Tester said in the interview, is “the kind of person who’s willing to sit down and listen, and make a decision based on facts, not on conspiracy theories. And for that reason, he’s head and shoulders above the people who he’s running against.” Tester also says Bodnar’s candidacy is viable not because he is an independent, but because “he is somebody that understands politics,” working families, high costs, agriculture and the “shit that this president with support of the Congress have done.” While most Senate Democrats NOTUS spoke to repeatedly said they had not been paying close attention to the Montana race, some said they were relying on Tester to know the best path to contention in the state. “I have a lot of respect for Tester, and so I kind of defer to him in terms of just what can be done,” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey told NOTUS.

stories.title: Trump's Economy Speech Veers Into an Extended Riff on Communism
stories.author: Ben T.N. Mause
stories.summary: The president dedicated several minutes of his Las Vegas speech to denouncing Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin’s Francesca Hong.
stories.content: President Donald Trump speaks at an event at the Red Rock Casino Resort and Spa in Las Vegas, Wednesday, Aug. 5, . Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo President Donald Trump came to Las Vegas on Wednesday to rally voters on the economy and tax relief. But, after a pivotal week for left-leaning candidates in Michigan and Wisconsin, he couldn’t help but turn to communism. “You lose your home, you lose your apartment, and that’s where the communists will take us,” Trump said. “You got to nip it in the bud.” The president’s broadsides at the Red Rocks Casino came during a nearly 75-minute rally, evoking repeated cheers from the audience. Trump diverged from his economic remarks multiple times, including minutes-long segments calling out this week’s main characters: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who edged out moderate Rep. Haley Stevens by a narrow margin, and Wisconsin gubernatorial hopeful Francesca Hong, who went viral over old posts describing a hatred of Thanksgiving (and Christmas, and Halloween). El-Sayed’s primary win was the latest example of left-wing challengers succeeding against more moderate, establishment-backed Democrats. It’s a shift that has coincided with a deepening party splinter since Trump entered office — and one Republicans hope to take advantage of during the summer campaign season by amplifying distrust of communism to push more centrist voters away from progressive candidates. El-Sayed’s victory makes that effort easier, Trump said Wednesday. “The polls say we do better against the communists,” the president said. “So he won, and so I think I’m happy.” Trump has been attacking communism for some time, but he gained fresh ammunition this week after more of Hong’s past commentary — including wanting to abolish Thanksgiving and voicing disdain for other holidays — circulated ahead of the state’s Aug. 11 primary. A member of the Wisconsin General Assembly and the Democratic Socialists of America, Hong has also been criticized for past calls to abolish the police, among other left-wing positions. But her Turkey Day opinion — which Hong has since walked back, telling Politico on Wednesday that it’s actually her favorite holiday — was a welcome talking point and easy target for Republicans. Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany’s campaign even reposted comments from Hong’s own press team . Trump blasted her on Wednesday as he called communism “the greatest threat to our country,” including both World Wars, Pearl Harbor and 9/11. “And in Wisconsin, the communists have a woman who said that the holiday of Thanksgiving should be immediately abolished, and the police — the police only exist to, quote, ‘uphold white supremacy,’” Trump said, calling Hong a “lunatic.” “We can’t let them get into office.” Republicans have a lower opinion of socialism than Democrats, who are the only partisan group to view the ideology more positively than capitalism, a Gallup poll found. Those dynamics have been present in Michigan and Wisconsin’s primaries this month: Multiple polls show Hong with a dominant lead in the primary race, and surveys conducted prior to the Thanksgiving comments’ resurfacing showed her virtually tied with Tiffany for the general election. And El-Sayed will Republican Mike Rogers, who posted a video calling his opponent a “radical leftist” on Wednesday. “But everyone, every time this has happened ... you go through squalor. And add the word again: filth, crime, death, destruction, embarrassment,” Trump said. “When I watch Abdul — he’s full of shit.”

stories.title: Darline Graham Takes Over Lindsey Graham’s Leadership PAC
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The newly inaugurated senator is now listed as a “leadership PAC sponsor” for her late brother’s well-funded political committee.
stories.content: In an unusual move, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) is inheriting the leadership PAC of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Sen. Darline Graham just inherited an unconventional asset from her deceased brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham: his federal leadership PAC. Federal records reviewed by NOTUS now list Darline Graham as Fund for America’s Future’s sponsor. Filings from earlier this year listed Lindsey Graham as the PAC’s sponsor. Such a sibling-to-sibling transfer of a senator’s political action committee is decidedly uncommon. “There's little official guidance from the FEC specifically addressing the transfer of a leadership PAC after the death of its sponsoring lawmaker,” Michael Beckel, the director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a nonpartisan political reform organization, told NOTUS. “In practice, most leadership PACs associated with deceased or retired lawmakers are eventually wound down or terminated rather than transferred to another politician.” After Lindsey Graham died last month at the age of 71, the treasurer of the leadership PAC — long-time Republican operative Cabell Hobbs — could have moved to wind down the committee and dispose of any remaining funds by donating to certain political committees and charitable organizations or refunding donors, according to FEC rules. Hobbs declined to comment on the matter when reached by phone Wednesday. Darline Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the sponsorship transfer. Although Darline Graham inheriting both her late brother’s Senate seat and leadership fund is unique, it is “not surprising” because “the stars aligned in this case,” Beckel said. South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s term, and she decided to seek a full term after President Donald Trump told her to run. Graham Trump ( , AR: 1.50)During the election cycle, Fund for America’s Future has raised more than $ , through a variety of donations and cash transfers, FEC records indicate. It ended June with about $70, cash on hand after having spent much of what it’s recently raised. It is incredibly common for lawmakers to have leadership PACs; 96% of the 119th Congress — out of members — have leadership committees, per Issue One. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) is the only senator who does not have this type of PAC. The committees allow lawmakers to donate to other campaigns, which builds their political network. “Money in the leadership PAC helps you buy friends and allies, so being able to raise money and dole that out to other politicians is a way for her to be helpful to the team,” Beckel said. But Fund for America’s Future isn’t the only PAC that’s thrown its support behind Darline Graham. The Security is Strength super PAC, which has been affiliated with several committees supporting Lindsey Graham, has pledged millions to bolster his sister’s campaign. The committee announced a $ , digital ad buy for Darline Graham on Wednesday, with TV spots attacking one of her opponents, Rep. Russell Fry (R-South Carolina). Republicans in South Carolina will have the chance to vote for a new nominee in a special election on Aug. 11, because Lindsey Graham had already won the nomination for his party in June. Darline Graham is set to Rep. Ralph Norman, former Rep. and Gov. Mark Sanford, businessman Mark Lynch and Fry in the special election. Whoever advances will be running against Democratic opponent pediatrician Annie Andrews in the general election in November.

stories.title: Say My Name, Say My Name
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: Abdul El-Sayed departs following a news conference at the Spirit of Detroit shortly after winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Wednesday, Aug. 5, , in Detroit. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for August 5, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Michigan finally has its Democratic Senate nominee in Abdul El-Sayed , whose razor-thin race was called this morning after weeks of touting expectations for a blowout victory. His previous opponents, Rep. Haley Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow , have lined up behind him. What do his potential colleagues think? A quick search among Michigan Dems shows only Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet and Sen. Elissa Slotkin ’s personal X accounts have congratulated El-Sayed by name today. Rep. Hillary Scholten ’s personal account issued a congratulatory statement that did not name the Senate nominee. Retiring Michigan Sen. Gary Peters — who says he’ll back El-Sayed — bashed reporting that showed the candidate up by double digits based on internal polling. He told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic it was a “technique as old politics itself. We saw polls that were questionable right from the start for me.” The NSRC put up its first attack ad today, calling him “Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed — the most radical Senate candidate in America.” “That’s the only play they got,” El-Sayed told voters this morning. “My name is not raising your gas prices. My name is not taking us to war.” THE HILL The allegations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio) prompted different statements from the House’s two women’s caucuses. Democrats called for his resignation, while Republican Women’s Caucus Chair Kat Cammack said she respected the Ethics Committee’s need to follow due process. Cammack, who is working to tackle workplace sexual misconduct on the Hill, called the situation “painful” for everyone involved: “My heart especially breaks for the little girl caught in the middle.” The Senate confirmed CDC director nominee Erica Schwartz , the agency’s first permanent director in nearly a year. THE ADMINISTRATION Donald Trump’s helicopter taking off triggered an air-traffic safety incident at DCA yesterday when Marine One potentially got closer than the acceptable range between aircraft. A California judge held the Homeland Security Department in contempt for allegedly slow-rolling an order to produce data from last year’s controversial Los Angeles immigration raids. Trump sought to shield his business finances from the BBC in a defamation lawsuit in an emergency stay motion today. THE STATES Amir Hassan , the Trump-endorsed candidate in MI-8, trailed Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points after yesterday’s primary — even though Smith had already dropped out of the race. Smith accepted his nomination in a statement today. Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid in MI-13 to state Rep. Donavan McKinney , and conceded the race today. New Mexico’s attorney general is suing Todd Blanche and the DOJ for allegedly blocking access to unredacted Epstein files, as “one of the few jurisdictions that still may have an opportunity to hold Epstein’s associates accountable.” STRANGER THAN FICTION Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: Rep. Shri Thanedar Loses Reelection Bid to DSA-Backed Challenger
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: He narrowly lost his primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney.
stories.content: Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar lost his reelection bid to a progressive challenger after two terms representing Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, the Associated Press projected Wednesday. Thanedar, who admitted to NOTUS this week that he struggled to garner support from his congressional colleagues, was down by 4 percentage points to state Rep. Donavan McKinney with nearly all of the votes counted. Thanedar conceded in a statement Wednesday, adding his name to the slate of incumbent Democrats who lost their primary to candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America and other progressive groups. “It was a tough election cycle and, in the end, the voters of the 13th District chose him to represent them moving forward,” Thanedar said of McKinney, a lifelong resident of Detroit. Several members of the Congressional Black Caucus also backed McKinney to represent the 13th District, an area with a large population of Black residents. McKinney campaigned on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending military aid to Israel — a topic that loomed over Democratic primaries in Michigan. McKinney previously told NOTUS he saw constituents’ economic struggles as inseparable from the federal government funding Israel’s attacks on Palestinians and working alongside Tel Aviv on a “war for no reason with Iran [that costs] $1 billion per day.” “People around the country are just tired of status-quo politicians,” McKinney told NOTUS. The DSA endorsed McKinney in July, saying he would “fight for strong union jobs, environmental justice and for universal childcare.” Thanedar, a retired entrepreneur and scientist, largely self-funded his reelection campaign. He had picked up endorsements from House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Reps. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) and Cleo Fields (D-Louisiana). When previously asked by NOTUS if he wished he had more congressional support, Thanedar said, “No, no, I have plenty.” “It’s not like a high school,” Thanedar said. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.”

stories.title: Waiting for Michigan
stories.author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: An attendee wears a pin reading "STOP DATA CENTERS" during a primary election night event for Abdul El-Sayed. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Today’s notice: Hope you wanted the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan to go on longer. Max Miller says he has friends in high places. Latest on Todd Blanche’s nomination. Redistricting’s next steps. Private health info leaked with Fauci’s journal. And: Bond market warning signs. THE LATEST The dreaded third option: When the polls closed in Michigan last night, the idea was that Democrats would get clarity on the questions that have plagued them throughout the primary season. A big win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would mean the left could fight off big outside money and wave off pesky worries about electability. A clear win by Rep. Haley Stevens, the establishment pick, would signal that battleground Democrats weren’t ready to take the same ideological risks as safely blue places — and let party leadership breathe a little. El-Sayed remains ahead of Stevens, but the margin is too narrow for there to be a clear winner early this morning. That means the argument about the party’s future goes on. It was a proverbial Groundhog Day for this Democratic primary cycle, and the little guy saw his shadow — forecasting at least six more weeks of Democratic Party angst. Bring on the Wisconsin primary! One thing we definitely learned last night: time to really stop listening to the polls, right? There were a lot of them in this Senate primary and in most cases they were, uh, not accurate . Open tabs: Chuck Edwards Ends His Reelection Following Harassment Allegations (NOTUS); Iran reports positive signs in Hormuz talks with Oman (Al Jazeera); Armed Man Arrested at Trump’s LA Golf Course Ahead of the President’s Visit (NOTUS); Former GOP Sen. Jeff Flake backs Jon Ossoff (AJC); Arizona’s Democratic Governor Set to Pick a Republican Running Mate (NYT) From the Hill Rep. Max Miller says he has allies: The embattled Ohio Republican vowed to stay in his reelection race, called for a House Ethics investigation of his conduct and asserted powerful people still have his back, NOTUS’ Adora Brown writes . “Speaker Mike Johnson, everyone else, they’re standing behind me,” Miller told CNN. “No one has told me to get off the ballot.” Johnson hasn’t publicly joined calls for Miller to step down and didn’t respond to a request for comment. Todd Blanche drama gets one more act: Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said yesterday that she’ll vote against Blanche, Trump’s nominee to be attorney general. That means Blanche must win over at least one of the two remaining Republican holdouts in the Senate to be confirmed, NOTUS’ Al Weaver reports . The senators to watch: Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Bill Cassidy (R-Lousiana). From the redistricting wars Redistricting rekindled: Maryland statehouse Democrats passed a constitutional amendment yesterday that would make it easier to redraw congressional lines ahead of the election, NOTUS’ Manuela Silva reports . And miles away in Missouri, the state’s top elections official blocked a petition challenging a Republican-passed map aimed at eliminating Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver ’s seat. THE BIG ONE Rand Paul’s doxing problem: When the Kentucky senator made public the journal kept by Anthony Fauci last week, Paul also released personal medical information of more than 20 individuals, NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports . What’s included: Names, diagnoses, symptoms and test results of individuals. Two of the people identified by name alongside their medical details were children, Margaret writes. (One of those was the child of Trumpworld players Stephen and Katie Miller, as we first reported .) Some are very public figures like Joe Biden , and others appear to be private individuals whose medical history was posted for the world to see. And those individuals are understandably angry. “If I was a victimizer in the Epstein files, my name would have been redacted,” Leslie Adelman , whose name and medical condition were posted in the document dump, told NOTUS. (Adelman gave permission to use her name in Margaret’s story.) “Instead, I am an innocent and productive member of society, who has donated her time and body to NIH for research that will benefit millions of people — yet MY name and information is blasted to the national news.” NOTUS PERSPECTIVES When Trump called Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz “seriously retarded” last year, it was part of a disturbing pattern. “The use of slurs in general is up,” according to one expert. “But nothing comes near the numbers we’re seeing on the R-word.” Today at NOTUS Perspectives, Sadie Dingfelder explains why this particular insult has become the defining slur of the Trump era. ON NOTUS PODCAST From your favorite podcast app: As the Senate prepares to head home for August recess, some Republicans want to stay behind to pass the SAVE America Act, even if they lack the votes. NOTUS’ Igor Bobic is joined by Avani Kalra and Al Weaver to discuss the inner machinations of the Senate Republican Conference and President Trump’s “dog with a chew toy” focus on the voting act. NEW ON NOTUS Bad signs in the bond market: Last week’s unexpected surge in bond yields — primarily triggered by doubts about the Fed’s commitment to fighting inflation — could hit small- and medium-sized banks hard if the market doesn’t calm, NOTUS’ Jeff Stein reports . The implications for the U.S. economy, not to mention the midterms, are potentially huge. Volatility in the bond markets helped push Trump to back off of his “Liberation Day” tariff scheme, which corrected the situation quickly. But the spike this time was less sudden and has gotten less attention, Jeff writes, and it may also be harder to resolve. More : Mike Lindell Steps Down From MyPillow to Focus on Minnesota Governor Campaign , by Jenna Monnin FEMA Cut Staff Without Planning for Future Work, Watchdog Says , by Natalie Alms Freedom Sponsors Failed to Disclose Donations — A Potential Lobbying Law Violation , by Taylor Giorno NOT US US diesel prices overtake Biden-era average , by Myles McCormick for the Financial Times At least 12 states cyberattacks on their water systems, sources say , by Luke Barr, Jack Date, Katherine Faulders, Josh Margolin and Aaron Katersky for ABC News Ronald Lauder, a Billionaire G.O.P. Backer, Closes His Wallet , by Nicholas Fandos for The New York Times How predatory trade schools drained $ million from the GI Bill and cheated veterans , by Craig Whitlock and Andrew Ba Tran for The Washington Post Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please sign up — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.com . And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Thomas Burr, Brett Bachman and Andrew Burton. Photo by Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP.

stories.title: A House Candidate Who Dropped Out Beats Trump's Pick in Michigan
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: Amir Hassan lost by double-digit percentage points to Thomas J. Smith, who accepted the nomination despite dropping out of the race last month.
stories.content: President Donald Trump listens as Republican congressional candidate Amir Hassan speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground in Michigan. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) A Michigan Republican endorsed by President Donald Trump lost his primary election to a candidate who dropped out of the race but remained on the ballot, the Associated Press projected Wednesday. Amir Hassan, a former federal law enforcement officer from Flint, Michigan, trailed retired engineer Thomas J. Smith by about 17 percentage points. Smith suspended his campaign to represent Michigan’s 8th Congressional District in July. The pair were vying to flip the seat held by Democratic incumbent Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet. Trump-endorsed candidates have won about 97% of their primary elections in , according to a July 10 review by Ballotpedia . Hassan is the only Trump-backed House candidate in Michigan who lost his primary. Trump brought Hassan and other candidates onstage during a rally in Michigan on July 27, where the president made reference to Hassan’s family ties to industry giant General Motors. At the rally, Hassan told attendees that they were putting “this country back on the map because we have a leader who stands up for us.” Hassan acknowledged his apparent defeat in the early hours on Wednesday. “The fight has just begun,” Hassan wrote on X . “Service never stops.” Smith accepted the nomination in a statement early Wednesday to The Detroit News . He said he was “humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet." “I look forward to working with Speaker Johnson and the entire Republican team to expand our House majority and advance President Trump’s America First agenda to lower costs for working families and make America affordable again,” Smith . The Michigan Secretary of State’s office did not immediately reply to a request for comment on whether Smith can proceed with his nomination despite his decision to officially withdraw from the race. After dropping out, Smith had backed another candidate, Al Lemmo, who came in last with about 16.4% of the vote. McDonald Rivet ran unopposed in her Democratic primary election.

stories.title: Michigan Hands the Democratic Establishment Another Brutal Loss
stories.author: Alex Roarty, Elena Schneider
stories.summary: Abdul El-Sayed’s narrow win is a low point for the center-left as Democrats head toward November.
stories.content: Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Democrats will remember as the year their party’s establishment lost its once total control of the primary process. Instead, it was outmaneuvered and overwhelmed by a progressive insurgency whose chosen candidates, backed by a furious liberal base, smashed their way to victories. It’s a low point for the center-left that Democratic leaders can climb out of, party strategists say, but only with a radical readjustment of how they operate. The result of Michigan’s Senate Democratic primary Tuesday — in which outspoken progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens — was arguably the sharpest blow yet. Stevens lost despite having a huge cash advantage, outspending him 11-to-1 in ads, and running a playbook that had worked for moderate candidates for years, including during Hillary Clinton’s and Joe Biden’s presidential campaigns. El-Sayed winning only narrowly, despite his own campaign’s expectations of a blowout victory, just poses more questions of what if anything the party establishment could’ve done differently to head off the rising left. The choice to support Stevens was emblematic of a larger problem with how party leaders anoint candidates, said some Democratic strategists, and a failure to properly understand just how angry their own party’s voters were with the old way of conducting politics. “They value seniority over talent, a fundraising rolodex over ability to make genuine voter connections, institutional comfort over the anger and change that voters are actually demanding,” said Lis Smith, a veteran Democratic strategist who worked for a candidate in the race who dropped out , Mallory McMorrow. “If you put up establishment slop against DSA candidates who may have bad ideas but are exciting and speak to the anger of American voters, Democratic voters are going to choose DSA and far-left candidates, until we get our act together.” Democratic voters, said another party strategist, were “shouting from the rooftops” about their anger. “If we don’t actually respect and respond to this frustration, we’re gonna wind up with heads in a basket,” said the party operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Democratic Party leaders counter that they have mostly gotten their way in primaries this year and more importantly, could be poised for a big midterm election in November in part because of successful candidate recruitment. Democratic Senate candidates from Texas to North Carolina lead in public polling as President Donald Trump’s approval rating sags to all-time lows. Gas prices are still high, and voters say they’re still feeling the cost-of-living pinch. Those environmental factors have put not just the House in play but also the Senate, an unlikely possibility just two years ago. Both the Democratic National Committee and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee quickly rallied around El-Sayed after his win. DSCC chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Democratic Senate leader Sen. Chuck Schumer said in a statement that El-Sayed had “inspired thousands of Michiganders” and that the party is united behind him. But Tuesday’s result in Michigan was only the latest setback for Democrats in Washington this year. In June, Maine Gov. Janet Mills lost her primary race in an embarrassing landslide to political newcomer Graham Platner, despite an endorsement from the DSCC. (Platner later exited the race .) Sen. Michael Bennet of Colorado failed to clinch his gubernatorial race, which revolved around his closeness to Washington leadership . The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has lost three races in California, Arizona and Maine, where it spent money on its preferred candidate. The party has also seen progressive candidates win some House races in which the party establishment split its support among multiple candidates. That happened again on Tuesday night in Michigan, where progressive activist Will Lawrence beat two moderates in a swing district. And a handful of incumbent Democratic House members, from Colorado to New York , have lost their reelection races to Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated candidates, a rarity in a party that traditionally has valued its incumbents. “It’s not the end of the center-left, but they need to do a better job of consolidating earlier rather than letting multiple go in the same lane," said Kevin McKeon, a Democratic strategist who works on Senate and House races. Of course, establishment Democrats still have successes to claim this cycle. Of the 13 candidates on the DCCC’s coveted Red to Blue endorsement list, 10 have won their respective primaries. The DSCC recruited former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown and former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola into their respective Senate races without any incident, instantly putting the trio of states into play. In Iowa, the establishment-backed candidate, state Rep. Josh Turek, also won a contested primary. That’s something DSCC aides are all too happy to point out. “Senate Democrats created a path to win a majority thanks to all-star candidate recruitment, formidable campaigns, and a winning message,” Tommy Garcia, a DSCC spokesperson, said in a statement. “Democratic candidates are out-polling and out-raising their Republican opponents, and in November we will win the majority — which no one thought was possible a year ago.” Democrats are even more bullish on taking the House majority than the Senate, in part because of investments in many key races. “Everyone agrees that the stakes could not be higher for November,” Viet Shelton, a DCCC spokesperson, said in a statement. ”The DCCC is doing everything possible to ensure Democrats win the biggest majority possible and Congress can actually deliver for the American people again. Every poll is proving we are (still) well positioned to do just that.” Center-left Democrats are quick to point to November as the ultimate scorecard for the wings of the party. “It's worth remembering,” said a Democratic consultant granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly, that progressive won primaries in Omaha, Nebraska, and Syracuse, New York, a pair of battleground House districts. But Democrats “went on to win the majority in without winning either of the Omaha or Syracuse seats.” Some Democratic leaders expressed optimism that the party losing some primaries was ultimately good — that it could help expose leaders in Congress to new ideas and energy. “I actually think this is a healthy debate to have,” said Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who has endorsed candidates running against the party establishment this year and previously served as the chair of both the DCCC and DSCC. “I think we need this kind of churning in the Democratic Party.” Even so, party leaders have problems beyond this year’s primaries. Schumer has calls from some candidates and activists to step aside, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has been on the receiving end of frustration from some activists and candidates. Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin has been beset by crises since taking over last year, dogged by controversy over the party’s fundraising tactics and a botched autopsy report. And Michigan isn’t the last crucial test the party will this primary cycle. In Wisconsin, a democratic socialist candidate is favored to win the gubernatorial primary next week, in part because other Democratic candidates failed to consolidate support or gain traction. “Since I've been paying attention to politics, the Democratic Party has never been as weak and unpopular as it is now,” said Ezra Levin, co-founder of Indivisible, a liberal grassroots group. “And I think that’s just an empirical fact.” Levin has been critical of Democratic Party leadership since Trump’s inauguration last year, arguing they haven’t been forceful or creative enough in their opposition to the president. He, like others interviewed for this story, said he thought the base’s frustration with party leadership was more about its failure to defeat Trump in and the perception it has done little to thwart him while in office. Even among Democrats who have represented battleground districts, there’s a concern the party isn’t offering “bigger, bolder policy ideas this year” and the party hasn’t “been inspiring enough,” said former Rep. Susan Wild. “Voters are looking for [an] actual strategy for how we are going to be different, what our plan is,” Wild said, citing “Medicare for All” and subsidized child care as potential policy platforms. “You can’t just talk about an affordability agenda without talking specifics.” During the second Trump administration, Danielle Butterfield, president of Democratic super PAC Priorities USA, voters have identified a “vacuum in Democratic leadership.” “In a world where our party doesn't have any lever of government, our leadership is failing in crazy ways,” Butterfield said. “It has created this circular firing squad of everyone else saying, ‘Maybe someone else will step up.’ And progressive Democrats are the ones who are meeting the moment, and people want that.” Butterfield pointed to the difference she saw in the ads from El-Sayed’s and Stevens’ campaigns. She believed El-Sayed did a better job explaining to voters exactly how he proposed to make their lives better, centered on passing “Medicare for All” and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “As a whole, progressive candidates are meeting that anger more vividly,” she said. “And we're seeing that play out in these primaries.”

stories.title: Missouri Elections Official Blocks Petition Challenging GOP-Friendly Redistricting Map
stories.author: Manuela Silva
stories.summary: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said the petition had the requisite number of signatures but was still “unconstitutional.”
stories.content: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.” David A. Lieb/AP Photo Missouri’s top elections official squashed a challenge to Republicans’ new congressional map that could net them one more U.S. House seat, waiting until the last possible day to block a petition that would have triggered a statewide vote on the gerrymander. Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, on Tuesday rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.” “At issue is not the number of signatures turned into the challenge, the new congressional map, but the fact that the referendum itself is null and void by virtue of the fact that it is unconstitutional,” Hoskins said at a Tuesday press conference. “Therefore, House Bill 1, the Missouri First map, continues to be the law of the land.” Hoskins also said that Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway agreed with his choice. At the press conference, Hoskins said he was “confident in the stance” he's taken, and that the government is “prepared to go to court.” That chance will come soon: People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that led the original petition, confirmed in a statement Tuesday evening that it plans to announce details regarding future litigation tomorrow. The Missouri General Assembly pushed through a new map targeting Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s heavily Democratic district, becoming one of the first states that moved to redistrict after President Donald Trump pushed state lawmakers to redraw their congressional maps to more heavily favor Republicans. Signed into law by Kehoe last September, the map carves Missouri’s largest city, Kansas City, into three congressional districts. Shortly after the assembly pushed the new lines through last fall, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered over , signatures to force a referendum. In Missouri, a petition with enough signatures triggers a veto referendum, or a statewide vote on the law in question. The group filed the signatures in December. Hoskins had until 5 p.m. Tuesday to decide on the legality of the petition — the same day as Missouri’s primary elections. Hoskins was widely expected to not certify the signatures, previously saying that any signatures gathered before the campaign was approved by his office constituted “ a misdemeanor election offense ,” a claim his office later clarified and corrected . “Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, wrote in a statement. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year, and we won’t stop now. There are more than enough signatures, verified by election authorities, to qualify the referendum.”

stories.title: Mike Lindell Steps Down From MyPillow to Focus on Minnesota Governor Campaign
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The CEO is stepping away from his role to focus on his Republican primary after facing a new string of controversies this month.
stories.content: Mike Lindell rose to prominence for supporting President Donald Trump’s attempts to contest the results of the election and has a slate of lawsuits and legal challenges since — including during his current gubernatorial run. Steve Karnowski/AP MyPillow founder and CEO Mike Lindell says he’s stepping away from his post at the company to focus on the Minnesota governor’s race. "After 22 years of leading MyPillow, I know the company is ready for its next chapter and I know Minnesota cannot wait," Lindell wrote in a press release. "This decision is not about walking away. It is about stepping forward to serve.” Lindell rose to prominence for supporting President Donald Trump’s attempts to contest the results of the election and has a slate of lawsuits and legal challenges since — including during his current gubernatorial run. His decision to focus on the upcoming Aug. 11 primary comes as he battles questions about his residency eligibility and a campaign law violation lawsuit. Lindell said the move will allow him to dedicate his “full time, energy, and attention" to the campaign and Minnesotans, while former MyPillow President James Furlong takes over as CEO — a position Lindell has held since he founded the company in . He also reduced his stake in the company to a minority share, but he will remain on MyPillow's board of directors. The Minnesota Republican Party last week asked state officials to clarify the residency rules concerning gubernatorial candidates after reports that Lindell was registered to vote in Texas — the second time in a month the state party has cast doubt upon his candidacy. According to Minnesota’s constitution, gubernatorial candidates must live in the state for at least one year before the election. “The Republican Party does not want Minnesotans who vote for any candidate for Governor to find, after the fact, that their vote was effectively wasted because the candidate did not meet constitutional qualification that could and should have been clarified in advance,” Alex Plechash, the state party chair, wrote in a letter to the Minnesota secretary of state. On Monday, Lindell sent TV station KSTP pay stubs that show he’s paid taxes in Minnesota since at least August . “I don’t know why Alex Plechash, or whatever his last name is, and what he has against me,” Lindell said. “But ever since I got Donald Trump, the president’s endorsement, he has viciously attacked.” The Minnesota secretary of state’s office told the network it does not have the “investigative authority” to review residency claims and deferred to the state Supreme Court. Lindell is currently facing a lawsuit alleging he violated campaign finance rules by distributing promotional pillows at a July 4th parade. He told WCCO the allegations were a “set-up hit job” and he felt “very confident that there was no violations." Lindell's social media accounts have been banned or restricted by several platforms for pushing election fraud claims, including Twitter and YouTube in . He launched multiple social media platforms in response to these restrictions. On Tuesday, Lindell said his Facebook advertising accounts had been restored after calling on Meta to look into his gubernatorial ads apparently being blocked by the platform. Lindell, whom Trump endorsed in July, has also several legal actions related to his false claims that the election had been stolen, including a House committee subpoenaing his phone records in during its Jan. 6 probe. Lindell targeted voting system companies with claims of election fraud, leading to a $1.3 billion lawsuit from Dominion Voting System, now known as Liberty Vote, in . The voting hardware company confidentially settled its defamation suit earlier this month after a former Republican election official purchased the voting company in October. In a separate case last year, a federal appeals court ruled Lindell did not have to pay a $5 million award to a software engineer after he mounted a “Prove Mike Wrong Challenge” over claims China interfered in the election. A recent poll found Lindell leading the Republican field at 35%, followed by Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth at 26% and Kendall Qualls, who earned the state party's endorsement, at 11%. Whichever candidate wins the GOP nomination is likely to Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar, who has steadily outraised her Republican opponents.

stories.title: Democrats in Congress Don't Like Shri Thanedar. He Hopes Voters Disagree.
stories.author: Christa Dutton
stories.summary: The lawmaker faces a democratic socialist challenger in a blue Detroit-area district.
stories.content: “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress," said Rep. Shri Thanedar. Bill Clark/AP How much does it matter if a lawmaker’s colleagues are indifferent about him in Congress? According to Rep. Shri Thanedar, a wealthy lawmaker who represents Michigan’s 13th Congressional District and who has become one of the left’s targets, not much. The popularity contest that matters is among voters rather than his congressional peers. On Tuesday, voters will choose between Thanedar and Donavan McKinney, a young, Black state lawmaker and democratic socialist who grew up poor in Detroit. The House primary has flashes of the different identity crises Democrats are facing this year: How left is too left? Is being an incumbent a net negative when voters are this angry? How important is racial representation? Then there's the one unique twist: Not even Thanedar's colleagues know what to make of him, which he concedes. “It's not like a high school,” Thanedar, acknowledging apathy from his colleagues about his primary challenge , told NOTUS. “I’m not trying to be the most popular member of Congress.” Thanedar, who emigrated from India in and worked as a janitor until he became a pharmaceutical executive, is arguing that he should keep his job in Congress because he understands the struggles his district faces. While some of his colleagues have said that they do not care whether he leaves Congress, he has the backing of party leaders, including Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar. “My constituents know my story,” Thanedar said. “They know my struggles, and I am more like Detroit because Detroit has struggled, but Detroit never gives up.” McKinney, meanwhile, is campaigning on “Medicare for All,” a Green New Deal and ending American military aid to Israel. He’s backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), numerous state lawmakers, local government officials and progressive groups like Sunrise Movement and Justice Democrats. His campaign is hoping to carry the momentum created by progressive victories across the country, including in several New York City House primaries and Colorado’s 1st Congressional District, to a battleground state. “People think this movement is just in New York or just in California or just in certain states,” McKinney said. “This is across the board, and you can win purple states like Michigan. You can win in Middle America. You can win in toss-up country.” One example of how much he’s leaning into the anti-incumbency sentiment is his reluctance to support Jeffries as speaker of the House if Democrats win the chamber. “I don’t have a decision yet. I just want a conversation,” he said. He that while he’d love to see a Black speaker, he wonders if Jeffries can help Democrats keep the majority next cycle. “How long does he want to be speaker if he actually gets elected speaker?” Other primary races in Michigan are also testing how progressives perform in a purple state.
