In a statement released after the Arizona race was called Wednesday, Shah similarly touted his win as a “grassroots victory where Arizona voters made their voices heard,” adding that the “status quo in Washington, D.C., is not working for Arizonans.” The day before, he’d told reporters that if he won the race, “I’m sure we’ll have a phone call, and I will speak to the DCCC and I hope that I can get their endorsement.” “Any Democratic candidate would want to be on the ‘Red to Blue’ list,” a source close to Shah’s campaign told NOTUS. It is unlikely that the DCCC will stop becoming involved in Democratic primaries. Dan Sena, the DCCC’s executive director in the cycle, pointed to the Maine Senate race , where Graham Platner stepped down as the Democratic nominee after being accused of sexual assault — which he denies — as an example of what happens when “you allow things to just happen without heavy input.” “You either get involved in the primaries and you win seven out of 10, or you don't get involved and you come up shy in the majority,” Sena said. “Either way, the Democrats have to ask themselves, wouldn't you rather have the gavels in your hand?"

stories.title: Democrats Lock Back In on Maine
stories.author: Alex Roarty, Igor Bobic, Christa Dutton
stories.summary: Whether they can win is an open question.
stories.content: Troy Jackson’s nomination would cap what has been one of the party’s most tumultuous primary processes in recent memory. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Maine Democrats are on track to select a new Senate candidate later this week. Their likely pick? A former state lawmaker who lost the party’s recent gubernatorial primary, has no federal political experience and has only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent. Most party leaders — including Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, who said she’s “very optimistic that we will win Maine” — say they haven’t felt this good about the race in months. “I think it's going to be hotly contested, but I think it's very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico. On Saturday, Democrats in Maine are expected to pick Troy Jackson as their Senate nominee against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, less than a month after the party’s former nominee, Graham Platner, was accused of sexual assault , the latest in a string of controversies he throughout his campaign. Jackson’s nomination would cap what has been one of the party’s most tumultuous primary processes in recent memory, a series of mishaps that could — and is widely expected to — jeopardize the Democrats’ ability to defeat Collins. That’s especially the case with a candidate like Jackson, who even allies acknowledge is an underwhelming orator with little time to build out a campaign infrastructure. But Democrats in Washington and Maine insist they think he’s still in a better position than Platner, who, despite denying the allegations, carried baggage into the race that party strategists feared would undermine his electability. “Turbulence is never the friend of politics, but I think there’s plenty of time,” Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado told NOTUS. “There's some history, and people have done attack ads, and you know, have in some way vetted him a little more thoroughly than some candidates get.” The sentiment reflects just how anxious many Democrats — especially moderates — had become about Platner’s chances against Collins, so much so that they are relieved to throw in with a candidate few national Democrats know well. More importantly, it indicates that Democrats remain committed to trying to win the Senate race despite everything that has happened there. Democrats likely need to win the race in Maine — the only Senate seat held by a Republican in a state won by Kamala Harris in that is up for grabs this year — to have a chance at flipping majority control of the Senate. Platner’s baggage had made his path to victory “very likely insurmountable,” said Lauren French, spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democrats. “Now we have the opportunity to refocus this conversation where it should be, which is Susan Collins,” she said. National Democrats have pointedly stayed out of the race to replace Platner. Asked if he would support Jackson, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer expressed confidence in defeating Collins, a formidable and well-funded incumbent who is seeking her sixth term in Washington. “We're going to win Maine. Susan Collins is going to lose, and we are going to take back the Senate,” Schumer told NOTUS. “People in Maine don't like Donald Trump, and they don't like that Susan Collins always votes with him.” Jackson told The New York Times this week that he would not support Schumer being the party’s leader in the Senate. He was also wary of receiving support from the minority leader. “I’d have to find out what that entailed,” Jackson told the New York Times. “I mean, if his help comes, absolutely no strings, I would say, you know, possibly. There’d have to be no strings.” Jackson’s team did not comment for this article. Among voters, Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, appears to start the race in a competitive position. He edged out Collins by 3 percentage points in a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire, and, unlike Collins, he is viewed quite favorably by Maine voters. The poll’s margin of error is 2.8 percentage points. But that could change with the onslaught of Republican attacks waiting for him in the general election. Republicans have already begun drawing parallels between Platner and Jackson. They’ve pointed to Jackson’s reported history of growing angry in meetings, and attacked him for views Republicans have cast as extreme, like support for a single-payer health care system. “He's had quite a transformation over the years in his political views, but now seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” Collins told NBC News , referring to Jackson’s conservative positions on social issues, like abortion, more than a ago. Democrats acknowledge that Maine will still be a difficult place for Democrats to win, but President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and rising costs give the party a chance to make a compelling case. “While the Democrats will have a new candidate by the end of this weekend, the fundamental motivation around winning the Senate race hasn't changed at all,” said Emily Cain, a Democratic strategist in Maine. Platner’s departure is a second chance at the seat without the distraction of controversy, some Democrats argue. An open question is whether Jackson can raise the money needed to beat Collins, who had nearly $11 million in the bank at the end of June. He’s raised $1 million in the less than two weeks since he entered the race, Politico reported . “All 49 states of Democratic Party activists and donors — small donors and large donors — are now all eyes on Maine,” said Democratic strategist Mike Trujillo. One Democratic donor who gave the largest contribution they could to Graham Platner told NOTUS they plan to give the maximum donation to the new candidate as well. “Maine is Maine,” the donor said. “My priority is winning in the general in every state where we're competitive, and that definitely includes Maine. No matter who's running, I'm sold.” Still, other Democrats are less than certain about their chances of flipping Maine’s Senate seat after Platner’s collapse and the rushed process for selecting his replacement. “They had to come up with somebody, and they did,” Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono said of Maine Democrats’ likely nomination of Jackson. Asked if he had a better shot than Platner, Hirono burst into laughter. “Let's just say that we have a candidate,” she said.

stories.title: Mark Sanford Jumps Into Crowded Race for Lindsey Graham’s Senate Seat
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Graham’s sister is running. So are Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman.
stories.content: Republican presidential candidate Mark Sanford takes part in a political forum in Nashville, Tennessee. (AP Photo/Mark Humphrey) Mark Sanford, the former congressman and governor of South Carolina, announced Thursday that he will run for the Senate seat held until recently by the late Lindsey Graham. “Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can't sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every days,” Sanford said in a post on X. “I've spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I'm running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.” The post was accompanied by a video of Sanford saying Graham’s death is a reminder of “how short and precious life is.” Graham’s seat is temporarily being filled by his sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve out his term by Gov. Henry McMaster. She also announced this week that she would campaign for a full term, joining a crowded primary field that also includes Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman. The primary is set for Aug. 11. Sanford was South Carolina’s governor from to , and he represented the 1st Congressional District twice, between and and between and .

stories.title: States Are in a ‘Fight to the Death’ for the Democratic Primary Calendar’s Top Spot
stories.author: Elena Schneider
stories.summary: South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan are expected to be early states, according to interviews with DNC members.
stories.content: South Carolina held the first Democratic presidential primary in the cycle. Mike Stewart/AP A last-minute, aggressive lobbying campaign is underway over the phone and through the media, as Democrats from a handful of states jockey to lead off the presidential nominating calendar. South Carolina Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain appeared on Roland Martin’s YouTube show Monday to declare , “we’re first, and we maintain that.” At a private reception Wednesday night, Democratic National Committee members mingled with Nevada Sens. Jacky Rosen and Catherine Cortez Masto, while New Hampshire boosters reached DNC members with one-on-one phone calls. The all-out push will culminate at the DNC’s Rules and Bylaws Committee meeting later this week. The 49-person panel is charged with setting the early-state window, ahead of what’s expected to be a wide-open and unwieldy Democratic presidential primary . Ahead of Friday’s meeting, tensions are already running high. “It’s going to be a bloodbath,” said one of the members, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Most states represented have at least one or two members on the committee, and I think they’re all going to fight to the death for this.” Interviews with nearly a dozen DNC Rules and Bylaws Committee members revealed some certainty about which states will likely be inside the early window — South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Michigan — but not necessarily the order. South Carolina and Nevada appear to be front-runners for the first spot over New Hampshire, according to these interviews. Members aren’t sure if they’ll add a fifth state to the slate, though if they do, New Mexico and Virginia lead that discussion. “I believe South Carolina is in a good position, and our vote count is good. We made the case in May to be first, and we’ve been talking to members ever since then,” said Spain, the South Carolina party chair. “I believe we have the votes, but I think Nevada is the next-highest vote-getter.” Setting the presidential primary calendar is one of the DNC’s most consequential tasks ahead of the presidential primary, and the Rules and Bylaws Committee must contend with its own internal politics over which states to elevate or demote — triggering debates over racial diversity and representation. Members said they hoped to recommend a slate by Friday and send it to a full vote of the DNC at their meeting in Austin, Texas, next month. At least a few members are pushing to delay the decision until after the upcoming midterms, though others insist they must wrap it up as soon as possible. “We need to rip the Band-aid off,” said a second rules committee member. “We’re going to make people mad no matter what, and it’s not going to get any easier after the midterms.” Reordering the slate also made people mad in , when then-President Joe Biden eliminated Iowa as an early state, elevated South Carolina to first and Michigan. The party came under pressure to shake up its calendar after the presidential primaries, when technical difficulties upended the Iowa caucuses and candidates criticized Iowa and New Hampshire for their lack of racial diversity. “There’s real ramifications, long-term ramifications, if we don’t make the right decision on the calendar,” said Jaime Harrison, the former DNC chairman who also served as the South Carolina Democratic Party chair. “Black voters are paying very close attention to this.” Jim Clyburn AP- ( , AR: 1.50)South Carolina’s boosters are making their pitch publicly and privately, sharpened by the Supreme Court’s decision to further gut the Voting Rights Act this spring. They also argue that South Carolina’s relatively cheap media market, compactness and majority-Black primary electorate will be the best proving ground for future presidential candidates. In a letter to DNC members and obtained by NOTUS, Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) warned in May that it would be a “profound mistake for our Party to retreat” from Black voters and Southern states in the nominating process, adding that South Carolina’s role in the nominating process “has been about ensuring that candidates engage deeply with the diverse coalition.” Officials from Nevada are also campaigning aggressively to be first. They, too, leaned into their state’s racial diversity, particularly its Latino population. Over the last year, Nevada’s elected officials have made personal appeals to DNC members and frequently hosted events to promote the state. More than 20 Latino leaders and groups signed on to a letter Wednesday, urging members to elevate Nevada in order to “reverse” the trend of losing Latino voters to Republicans. “Choosing Nevada to go first is a strategic decision, as we work to win back the coalition we need to win back the White House in ‘28,” said Daniele Monroe-Moreno, the Nevada Democratic Party chair. “That coalition of rebuilding has to be a broad coalition, which has to include Black voters, Asian voters.” Some members have suggested that the battle for first may include horse-trading on a fifth addition to the line-up. If Nevada were selected to go first, then members may add Virginia, putting two Southern states in the early window. And if South Carolina were to go first, then they could add New Mexico, another western state with strong Latino representation. But DNC members have raised concerns about Nevada’s mail-in balloting, which could delay the results of the primary. Monroe-Moreno said the Nevada secretary of state’s office is “implementing adjustments and improvements” to its mail-in ballot counting. “It may take a little more counting than another state,” she said. “I want to make sure that everyone's votes are counted.” Without a Democrat in the White House, the 49-person committee is charged with making its own decision on the calendar. DNC Chair Ken Martin has largely remained hands-off, but that could change over the next few days, the committee members said. “I don’t think Ken needs any more headaches than he’s already got,” said one Democratic operative involved in the calendar process and granted anonymity to speak candidly. The chaos of selecting a new calendar comes during a rocky year for the DNC. Martin has questions over his leadership after presiding over an incomplete autopsy of the election and staring down serious fundraising challenges. The Republican National Committee is sitting on $ million in cash, while the DNC holds $16.3 million with $18.5 million in debts, according to the most recent Federal Elections Commission filings. It’s not clear whether states or candidates will follow the DNC’s decision on the primary calendar, given the committee’s weakened position. At least three potential Democratic presidential candidates told NOTUS last month they were considering skipping the DNC’s debate schedule, while Iowa’s backers have already said they are seriously considering hosting a rogue caucus. Last month, the DNC instituted stiffer penalties if a state jumps the line to head off these challenges. For example, if a candidate campaigns in a rogue contest, they’ll sacrifice debate stage access and the state will lose its delegates at the party’s convention. New Hampshire already tested those boundaries in , when it ran its own unsanctioned primary after Biden demoted the state from its first-in-the-nation status. The state is still expected to be in the early window, but several DNC members said “New Hampshire is a very distant third” behind Nevada and South Carolina for first. “They just don’t have the votes,” a third DNC member said. New Hampshire Democratic Party Chair Raymond Buckley defended the state’s position, arguing in a statement that “anyone who suggests New Hampshire isn’t in a strong position is mistaken.” “We’ve been focused on having conversations one-on-one with committee members, and we’re encouraged by how those have been going,” Buckley continued. “New Hampshire serves as a critical testing ground for whether candidates can attract independent voters — an issue that couldn’t be more pressing for the Democratic Party nationally.”

stories.title: Darline Graham? Republicans Don’t Know Her.
stories.author: Igor Bobic, Al Weaver, Oriana González
stories.summary: Graham decided to run for a full Senate term after being appointed to the seat after her brother’s death, but people are still learning what she stands for.
stories.content: Republican senators are still getting to know Sen. Darline Graham, who cast her first votes in the Senate this week after a whirlwind appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. Tom Williams/AP Darline Graham made it official that she wants to run for a full term to represent South Carolina in the Senate. But unlike her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly earlier this month, few people know where she stands on most issues. President Donald Trump and top Senate Republicans quickly endorsed Darline Graham to become South Carolina’s next full-term Republican senator. But few Republican lawmakers personally know Graham, who was appointed to the seat just last week. The low profile could put Graham, a longtime disability advocate who previously served on the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, at a disadvantage, even with Trump’s backing effectively making her the frontrunner in next month’s special election. “These are people with legislative records that they can point to, that are proven to say, ‘Hey, prices are up, we can bring prices down if we do X, Y and Z. Here’s what I’ve done in the past,’” CJ Westfall, chair of the Dorchester County Republican Party, told NOTUS. Darline is “somebody that’s unproven and just has the stamp of approval by the president. I don’t think that’s the end-all, be-all for South Carolina,” Westfall . As a county party chair, he cannot endorse any candidate in the race. Republican senators are still getting to know Graham, who cast her first votes in the Senate this week after a whirlwind appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. Initially, many believed she would serve as a caretaker for the last six months of her brother’s term, with several South Carolina Republicans expressing interest in the job, until a surprise Trump endorsement for a full six-year term upended the race. “She certainly seems competent from the little bit I’ve seen. But competence isn't even a requirement in this job, as I can demonstrate and prove,” Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) joked to NOTUS. “That’s what primaries are for — to discover those things,” he . “It’s a very short time frame to prepare. Others who are in the business of politics may have that edge. On the other hand, her answers will be very instructive.” Graham doesn’t have long to convince South Carolina voters to keep her in Washington. The state will hold a special election on Aug. 11, giving her roughly two weeks to introduce herself to voters after her brother’s funeral plans take place next week. The winner will compete against Democrat Annie Andrews in the November election. Trump’s endorsement of Graham isn’t scaring off rivals from challenging her. Reps. Ralph Norman and Russell Fry have hopped into the race, along with businessman Mark Lynch . Former Gov. Mark Sanford and Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette are expected to throw their hats in the ring. Evette, notably, came up short in her bid for governor last month despite having Trump’s endorsement, underscoring that Graham’s campaign for Senate is no sure thing. “Each candidate has a strength,” Tyson Grinstead, chair of the Richland County GOP and a former campaign adviser to Lindsey Graham, told NOTUS. “Darline’s a newcomer but she has Sen. Graham’s campaign and she's got Sen. Graham's structure in place to help her, and so I think that kind of evens out with some of the other candidates.” “Russell Fry’s definitely got longstanding relationships. Ralph Norman has just come out of the governor’s race,” Grinstead, who cannot endorse a candidate as a county party chair. “And then you’ve got Darline with Sen. Graham’s campaign, which was one of the only statewide campaigns that had a lot of money spent on it.” Fry and Norman are pushing for a debate in Charleston on Aug. 4, the day before early voting starts. While the details are still being worked out, Norman suggested that’s where voters will have the opportunity to “find out” more about Graham, who hasn’t yet indicated whether she will participate. Graham did give a hint about her priorities as senator in a recent interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity indicating she may focus more on domestic rather than foreign policy. “I used to see him on the talk shows,” she said of her brother. “I would watch him, and I’d be like, ‘Lindsey, are you just talking about national security all the time?’ And I understand that’s important. Protecting our borders, national security, absolutely. I said, ‘But talk about also what matters to the average person. The price of groceries, the price of gas, health care, insurance, those kind of things.’ That’s what I’m worried about,’” Graham said. She has moved to quickly align herself with Trump’s key legislative priority, a sweeping bill that would change some voting rules, known as the SAVE America Act. And she has the support of top Senate Republicans who immediately backed her campaign, including Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas, chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee and a staunch defense hawk. Senate Republicans are also hoping that Graham’s support for a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill, which her brother long advocated for, will help get the legislation across the finish line in Congress and to Trump’s desk. “Senator Darline Graham has worked for the people of South Carolina for almost 30 years, and now the U.S. Senate is an extension of that service. God calls on ordinary people to do extraordinary things, and it’s clear she has met the moment,” said Taylor Reidy, a Graham spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement. Touting her work so far, Reidy pointed to her votes to confirm judges and the president’s nominees and , “Sen. Darline Graham was sworn in eight days ago and in that time alone, she has led the introduction of major sanctions legislation, cosponsored the SAVE America Act and a host of pro-life bills. Still, policy groups have yet to decide on Graham’s qualifications. Students for Life America, a prominent anti-abortion group, has yet to decide whether it will endorse Graham in the primary, with a spokesperson telling NOTUS on Tuesday that the group is still evaluating her positions. The late senator was an outspoken anti-abortion ally in Congress, and SFLA backed some of his efforts to restrict abortion. Graham is working quickly to shore up support on the right. On Wednesday, she announced she is co-sponsoring more than a half-dozen anti-abortion rights bills, including the Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act. Despite the questions about her background, Graham does have a number of things working in her favor. Due in large part to her brother and to Trump, she has high name recognition that others running may not enjoy. “It’s huge statewide. It’ll be low turnout so name recognition will be an even bigger factor,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), a member of Republican leadership who has endorsed Graham. One South Carolina Republican strategist who spoke to Graham recently said she wants to chart her own path in the Senate. “True to Graham fashion, she wants to own her own lane. And it’s not Lindsey’s lane,” the strategist told NOTUS. Republicans are expecting Graham to begin campaigning in earnest after her brother’s funeral services on July 28. The late senator died at age 71 from a rupture of his aorta due to a hardening of his arteries, according to a preliminary analysis by the D.C. medical examiner. “I know I’m a hard worker. I learned that from Lindsey,” Graham said in her interview with Hannity. “I feel like I can do it. I feel an inner peace about it. Will it be difficult? Yes. Absolutely.” Capito conceded that Graham could a challenge getting her message out in such a short time frame, but indicated she should be able to gather enough financial support. “I think she will have a challenge getting her own voice out, and I don’t know if that’s a choice she’s going to make,” Capito said. “Is it her own voice, or is it just ‘I’m going to be the voice of my brother’ plus?”

stories.title: Trump Celebrates After Election Deniers Sweep Arizona’s Republican Primaries
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: Some of the Republican nominees would have critical roles in overseeing the election if they were to win in November.
stories.content: Andy Biggs will incumbent Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs in November. Ross D. Franklin/AP President Donald Trump claimed victory after his favored candidates — including deniers of the election results — won their Republican primaries in Arizona on Tuesday. At the forefront of Tuesday’s winners was Rep. Andy Biggs, the former chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, who will be the Republican nominee for governor after besting his colleague, moderate conservative Rep. David Schweikert. Biggs, a Trump ally, voted not to certify results of the election. Biggs will incumbent Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, in November’s general election. “MAGA candidates won everything last night in Arizona, a complete sweep!!!” Trump wrote on Truth Social in all capital letters. “I won Arizona 18 months ago. The Dumocrats are dumbfounded. After decades, Arizona is becoming a Republican state.” If Trump’s preferred candidates prevail in November, they could play key roles in overseeing and certifying the election. And Biggs isn’t the only newly minted nominee who questioned the results in , when Trump lost the state. The second Trump administration has targeted Arizona’s Maricopa County as part of its efforts to investigate long-debunked claims that the election was rigged. The FBI subpoenaed election records from the county in March, which were handed over by state Senate President Warren Petersen. Petersen received the Republican nomination on Tuesday for attorney general. He previously assisted in launching a controversial audit of the election overseen by Cyber Ninjas, a Trump-friendly cybersecurity company. The audit found that former President Joe Biden won the election. State Rep. Alexander Kolodin secured the Republican nomination for secretary of state, the state’s top election official. Kolodin was disciplined in by the State Bar of Arizona for his role in various lawsuits attempting to overturn the election. Trump praised Petersen and Kolodin during a Turning Point USA rally in April, stating that they would help achieve his plans of “building a red wall.” Other Trump-backed candidates who won congressional primaries on Tuesday include Mark Lamb , who has been accused of sexual misconduct, which he has denied. Former NFL kicker Jay Feely and Rep. Juan Ciscomani also won their primaries for the House.

stories.title: Wisconsin Democrats Ask Elections Commission to Allow Voters to Recast Absentee Ballots
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: The bipartisan panel blocked the ability to revote earlier this month after Democrat Missy Hughes exited the governor’s race.
stories.content: Over 80, ballots have already been submitted, but the party argues many of these votes are going to waste due to candidates dropping or reentering the race. Morry Gash/AP Photo Wisconsin’s gubernatorial candidates keep shuffling before next month’s primary. Now, the state Democratic party is requesting Wisconsin’s elections panel allow voters who already cast an absentee ballot to vote again. After thousands of Wisconsinites had already submitted their absentee ballots ahead of the Aug. 11 primary, Democrats’ candidate slate shifted twice within days. Front-runner Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez ended her campaign last Friday. A day later, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley rejoined the race a week after he suspended his campaign, reentering with current Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement. Earlier this month, the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission blocked the ability to revote if a candidate drops out after a different Democrat, Missy Hughes, exited the governor’s race in June. Because of that ruling, Rodriguez voters and people who would have backed Crowley may have lost their chance to vote for a candidate who will actually be in the running through August, the state Democratic party argues. Over 80, ballots have already been submitted, but the party argues many of these votes are going to waste due to candidates dropping or reentering the race. The commission voted 4-2 on July 9 to issue the guidance limiting voters’ ability to “spoil” their ballots and excluded circumstances like someone deciding to vote for another candidate. Wisconsin Democratic Party Chair Devin Remiker said “some voters will not be able to truly participate in our Democratic primary process” if the guidance is not reversed to allow new absentee ballots. “Allowing voters to spoil and recast their ballots was standard practice in Wisconsin prior to attempts by Republicans to file frivolous lawsuits to muddy the waters,” Remiker said in a statement . The state Democratic Party argues the new guidance should be rescinded because it reverses the commission’s own rule that was in place in . It is also inconsistent with a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that stated voting rules should not be changed close to an election, they said. In the past, Wisconsin voters were able to cancel submitted ballots and then request a new one up to three times, for any reason. But in October , a county circuit judge ruled that this “ballot spoiling” practice was illegal. The 2nd District Court of Appeals reversed the ruling in February, finding that the lawsuit was not properly served.

stories.title: Cleo Fields Won’t Seek Reelection After Redistricting in Louisiana
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Fields’ district was at the center of the Supreme Court’s decision that largely eliminated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of .
stories.content: “I tell people all the time, the issue is not whether or not I serve another day in Congress,” Fields said. “The issue is whether or not a person like me will have the opportunity to serve in Congress." Tom Williams/AP Democratic Rep. Cleo Fields — whose Louisiana district was at the center of the Supreme Court decision gutting a key part of the Voting Rights Act — announced Tuesday that he will not seek reelection and will instead run for his old state Senate seat. Fields represents the 6th Congressional District, a majority-Black district that encompasses part of Baton Rouge and currently leans Democrat. After the Supreme Court declared the district’s existence an “unconstitutional racial gerrymander,” Louisiana lawmakers passed a new congressional map that eliminated Fields’ district to heavily favor Republicans. The new lines left intact only one of the two majority-Black districts in the state ahead of the midterms. “After a great deal of prayer and reflection, I have decided not to seek re-election to Congress, in the 6th District or any other district in Louisiana,” Fields said in a statement . “I feel my calling to serve the people is better put to use back home than here in D.C., and I intend to answer that call.” The National Republican Congressional Committee announced earlier this week that it was targeting his district to flip from blue to red. “I tell people all the time, the issue is not whether or not I serve another day in Congress,” Fields told NOTUS in May . “The issue is whether or not a person like me will have the opportunity to serve in Congress. And that’s the big focus.” He will now look to fill the unexpired term of the late state Sen. Larry Selders, a Democrat from Baton Rouge who died July 7.

stories.title: Democrats Ditch Their Old Pick in a Competitive Arizona Seat
stories.author: Christa Dutton
stories.summary: The DCCC is supporting Marlene Galán-Woods in her primary, even though she’s running against Amish Shah, the candidate it backed in the general election.
stories.content: Mike Stewart/AP Voters in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District are looking at something of a rematch in their Democratic primary. Unlike in , when House Democrats’ campaign arm let the race play out, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now has a clear preference. The group’s pick in the primary is Marlene Galán-Woods, a former broadcast journalist who has never held public office, was registered as a Republican until and came in third when she ran in . On Tuesday, she’ll off against several Democrats, including Amish Shah, an emergency-room physician and former state legislator who beat her in the primary in and competed in the general election with the DCCC’s backing. Shah narrowly lost to Republican Rep. David Schweikert in . This year, the DCCC hopes Democrats in the district will choose not to give Shah a do-over, but to go in a new direction with Galán-Woods. While the DCCC put Shah on its Red to Blue list in the general election but did not intervene in that year’s primary, now it’s Galán-Woods who’s in the DCCC’s Red to Blue program. “She’s on paper a better fit, but you're dealing with the rather uncomfortable question that she already lost a primary to him,” said a Democratic strategist and DCCC alum who has worked on previous races in the district. “So, was it a resource problem? Was there something else that has changed? No doubt that DCCC has analyzed this, weighed all of this, and still come to the conclusion that intervention enhances their odds of picking up a seat.” The candidates have few ideological differences and are running in the country’s only open toss-up seat, since Schweikert is running for governor. The Democratic race is one of several primaries the DCCC has weighed in on, along with contests in Pennsylvania and Texas battleground districts. This type of intervention in competitive primaries has prompted backlash from some corners of the party, who say the committee should let voters decide rather than putting its thumb on the scale. “It's unfair because out of respect to him for winning such a competitive primary, I think they should have either stayed out or at least waited until after the primary,” said Arizona state Sen. Flavio Bravo, who endorsed Shah. So far this year, most of the DCCC’s picks have succeeded in their primary races, but two candidates have lost: state Sen. Joe Baldacci in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District and Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains in California’s 22nd Congressional District. Those losses left some Democrats questioning the committee's use of resources and cheering the defeat of the establishment. This Arizona race has become another test for the DCCC in a primary that lacks the progressive-versus-pragmatic dynamic that has defined other races. “Unless there is a clear and obvious reason, the DCCC should not intervene in Democratic primaries, including the race in AZ-01,” said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) in a statement to NOTUS. “These resources should be focused on flipping this seat in November and winning back the House majority.” Shah was frustrated about the DCCC’s decision to weigh in. “I think they got it wrong,” he told NOTUS. “I think the Democratic Party voters do not want to see meddling from D.C. here in our district.” If he pulls off a win, he said he will “work with anybody and everybody, including the DCCC, to make sure that we do everything we can to stop this guy in the White House.” The DCCC determined that Galán-Woods has “undeniable momentum, a broad coalition, and strong fundraising,” a spokesperson said. “This designation signifies that we believe this candidate — and this campaign — are the one best positioned to flip the Republican-held district,” the spokesperson said. Galán-Woods has accumulated support from other major players in the party. She received a powerful endorsement from Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly in the final days before the primary. She also has the backing of several national Democratic groups including Planned Parenthood Action Fund, EMILYs List, the Bench and BOLD PAC. She’s proved herself to be an effective fundraiser, raising about $2.1 million as of July 1, according to Federal Election Commission filings, compared to Shah’s $1.3 million . She also has allies spending mountains of money on her behalf, far outpacing the spending on Shah’s behalf. Galán-Woods said she decided to run again because Shah, who lost the general election by 4 percentage points, underperformed Kamala Harris and Ruben Gallego in ’s presidential and Senate contests. When asked about the DCCC’s backing, Galán-Woods said she’s most proud of her local backing. “I'm happy to have the support, but I'll be honest with you, here in the district, people aren't talking about it,” she said. “People are talking about the issues that keep them up at night, and most importantly, how do we win? How do we win in November?” There’s been limited polling in the primary. HighGround, a public affairs firm that has worked on Republican campaigns, showed Shah up by 22 percentage points in a February poll. Most voters in the district are registered Republicans, but voters who did not select a party at all outnumber Democrats. “This district is a really good bellwether for how the country's going,” said Eric Chalmers, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not involved in the race. “The independents who live in this district, they went one way for three cycles voting for Dems, and then last cycle, it was almost a complete .” Some Democrats see Galán-Woods — who grew up in a Republican household with parents who emigrated from Cuba and who is the widow of Grant Woods, the former Republican state attorney general and chief of staff to John McCain — as just the right kind of Democrat to win over independents. “The appeal of a different candidate who's got a lot of support from the business community and a lot of the ‘Republican-lites’ or kind of McCain-Republican types out in CD 1, which makes up a lot of that district, led to the appeal of wanting to try Marlene,” Chalmers said. Shah, meanwhile, is pitching himself as an experienced politician. He served in the statehouse for three terms and ran in the general election before, while Galán-Woods lacks public office experience. He is known for his shoeleather campaign style and touts that he’s knocked on 28, doors in the district. But Arizona strategists said he will have to scale it up. “On paper he's just a normie Democrat with a really interesting, compelling background and compelling voice,” said DJ Quinlan, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not working on the race. “In practice on the campaign trail, he has a number of unique views.” Quinlan said one of Shah’s challenges is his apparent dislike of negative campaigning and TV ads. “He seems to have an aversion to the sort of campaign tactics that you need to be successful as you scale from a legislative race to a congressional race,” he said. Shah, however, calls that a mischaracterization. He pointed to his fundraising numbers and television ads to show that his last campaign did put up a congressional-level fight. Door-knocking helps the campaign keep an ear to the ground, he said. “We understood in that there's no way that you could run a door-knocking campaign over the course of six or eight weeks directed at , people,” Shah said. “That was nowhere in my arguments. We ran a mass communication campaign that involved mailers, that involved TV ads, that involved digital, all at the direction of the DCCC during that cycle.” The primary’s winner will advance to either former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik, business executive John Trobough, or the Trump-endorsed former NFL kicker Jay Feely.

stories.title: Will Incoming Progressives Give Hakeem Jeffries Their Support?
stories.author: Daniella Diaz
stories.summary: Brad Lander backed his New York colleague but warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.”
stories.content: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP New York’s Brad Lander said he would support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker if Democrats win back the House — an olive branch from a candidate expected to become one of Congress’ highest-profile progressives. Lander and several likely members of Congress — including Melat Kiros, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez and Chris Rabb — are part of a group of uber-progressive Democrats, many aligned with the leftist Democratic Socialists of America, who recently won competitive primaries in safe blue districts. The majority of them have not committed to supporting Jeffries if Democrats win in November. Lander’s support for Jeffries, who is a fellow New Yorker, is a tacit admission that the members are willing to give leadership a chance as they’re on the cusp of winning back the majority — but still he warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.” “I look forward to voting for Hakeem to be the speaker of the House,” Lander said in a recent interview with NOTUS. “At the same time, I want a party and party leadership that can listen to the passion and anger that voters feel and be responsive to it, and that means showing people much more clearly than leadership have so far what we're fighting for.” DSA-aligned candidates built their campaigns around a direct challenge to the Democratic Party’s “status quo,” casting themselves as insurgents willing to break with establishment leadership. Their message centered on economic populism — even when that meant taking on moderate Democrats rather than Republicans. Now that several of them are on track to easily win in November, the tug-of-war over the Democratic caucus’s center of gravity is about to grow even more pronounced. And many of the people who will be trying to pull it left will be from congressional districts in Jeffries’ backyard. Landers has previously said he plans to support Jeffries for speaker. "There will be a good opportunity for leadership to create a framework in which we can cut the line as fighters versus folders and show that it will be possible to win the majority in a strong way and to hear what voters are saying about their frustrations and the bolder posture they want to see from Democrats,” Lander, who beat incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman in a primary that attracted national attention, told NOTUS. Lander said Jeffries called to congratulate him and that the two have continued to talk, along with Jeffries' team, about how Jeffries envisions progressives working in the next Congress. When asked for comment, Jeffries team pointed to his remarks at a recent press conference. “I've talked to several of them, and we'll have more to say about it in the future,” Jeffries told reporters when asked about the winners of the competitive primaries in his home state. Building new working relationships between drastically different wings of the party isn’t an entirely new dynamic for Democratic lawmakers to navigate. In , after Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Ayanna Pressley arrived as the “Squad,” the then-new lawmakers had to establish a working relationship with then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi. They often broke with leadership on marquee votes, including when Omar and Tlaib opposed the bipartisan infrastructure bill, and several backed primary challenges against sitting Democratic incumbents in the years that followed. Pelosi, who’s retiring, said she has no concerns for Jeffries after November. “Hakeem is a very unifying force. He's eloquent. He listens,” Pelosi said in an interview. “He's very respected by the members. I was a different kind of voice, and I always had a race, except for my first time. Every single time I had a race. I don't see that for him. I think he will have a very unified caucus.” Ocasio-Cortez, who told NOTUS she’s made herself a resource for the incoming members, said she understands the candidates have to listen to their constituents who elected them for change. “Movement-based candidates don't just make individual calculations. Movement-based candidates generally try to be — especially when they're elected from their communities — I think they just conference a lot with their communities,” she said. Some centrist lawmakers, however, are already concerned that the DSA-aligned candidates will use tactics similar to those used by conservatives in the House Republican Conference, whether it be voting down a rule or refusing to back measures supported by moderate Democrats. Rep. Brad Schneider, chair of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, which has more than Democratic members, argued there should be more attention to the moderate candidates running in battleground races. He argued that candidates like the ones who have beat out incumbents are “not adding to the Democratic majority” because they’re in already-blue districts. “I am concerned about the rhetoric when [the progressives] come in and they say, ‘We are going to take down the rules, take down the speaker,’ and do these things,” Schneider said. “That just locks it up. We see that with the Republicans.” While none of the soon-to-be members of Congress have said they plan to vote against Jeffries, they’re noncommittal about supporting him. Several progressives said the fear expressed by Schneider is disconnected from reality. “I think if their fear is simply that these will be people who are more interested in division for its own sake or attention for its own sake, they've got something else coming,” said Andrew Bard Epstein, who worked on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign and Valdez’s campaign. (Mamdani backed several of the New York progressives on track to win seats in Congress.) “These are people who are smart and determined and strategic.” Lander was optimistic that in the general election, once primaries are wrapped up, Democrats will come together to win the majority. He dismissed any concerns about members of t he caucus being able to work together in that scenario. "I'm much more worried about Donald Trump and the danger that he presents to the country than I am about the divisions within the party," he said.

stories.title: Darline Graham Will Run for a Full Term in the Senate
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: “I’m in,” Darline Graham told Fox News, setting up a campaign pushed by President Trump.
stories.content: Sen. Darline Graham (R - South Carolina) said there is a "tremendous amount of pressure” surrounding her decision about whether to run for the Senate seat. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was recently appointed to temporarily serve in place of her late brother Lindsey Graham, said on Monday that she is running for a full term. “I’m in,” Darline Graham told Fox News host Sean Hannity in an interview. She said there is a "tremendous amount of pressure” surrounding her decision about whether to run for the South Carolina seat, which her brother had held for over two decades. “I have been praying a lot, talking to my family,” Graham said. “I feel like I can do it. I feel an inner peace about it. Will it be difficult? Yes. Absolutely.” Graham was sworn in July 14 after being appointed to the seat by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social encouraging her to run for a full, six-year term. “I hope Darline does this, in that there would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, Lindsey. Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement,” Trump wrote. However, some are staying out of the race for the time being. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) declined to endorse in the race, but that Graham is a “strong candidate.” “Sounds like the field is taking shape and we’ll let the voters in South Carolina decide it,” Thune said. “She obviously carries on Lindsey’s legacy, but I think she's a very accomplished person in her own right.” “I'm not endorsing anybody at the moment,” he . This story has been updated with comments from Trump and Thune.

stories.title: Republican Russell Fry Launches a Bid for Lindsey Graham’s Senate Seat
stories.author: Brett Bachman
stories.summary: The congressman may get the backing of President Donald Trump if Darline Graham opts not to run, a source previously told NOTUS.
stories.content: Bill Clark/AP Republican Rep. Russell Fry announced Monday that he was launching a campaign for the Senate seat held by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, entering a brief and potentially crowded field in South Carolina. He could be up against Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, who was appointed to hold his seat through this November’s election. President Donald Trump endorsed her last week but she has not yet officially launched her campaign for a full term. In a statement , Fry sought to position himself as a champion of Lindsey Graham’s legacy and a staunch ally of Trump’s. “There is no other way to put it: Lindsey Graham was one of a kind. There is no replacing him,” Fry said. “But I believe the best way to honor his legacy is to fight alongside the President just as steadfastly as he did.” Fry also said that he intended to focus on cost-of-living issues that he said were crushing ordinary Americans, both in his state and across the country. “Too many South Carolina families are struggling to make ends meet,” Fry said. “High gas prices and soaring grocery costs are hurting hardworking people every day.” source familiar with Trump’s thinking told NOTUS last week that the president would consider supporting Fry in the event that Darline Graham does not run for her brother’s seat. Trump met with Darline Graham on Friday at the White House, writing in a subsequent post on Truth Social that he urged her to run for the seat. “There would be nobody better to honor the legacy of her beloved brother, ” Trump wrote. “Should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina.” “RUN, DARLINE, RUN!” he . Darline Graham was appointed early last week by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster to complete her brother’s term following his death due to a heart issue last Saturday. Trump quickly decided to back her for the interim appointment and was considering backing her for the full term, NOTUS first reported last week. The window for candidates to file for the truncated Republican Senate primary opens Tuesday and is expected to include a number of boldface names including Rep. Ralph Norman, who has already announced his intention to run, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, businessman Mark Lynch and former Gov. Mark Sanford, as well as Rep. Nancy Mace. Fry’s decision to run for Senate could leave the House Republican caucus in a bind. If he — or any other member of the lower chamber — were to win the race, their seat would likely sit empty for several months. Republicans already hold a razor-thin majority in the House, one that is expected to tighten or even flip after November’s midterms. Mace appeared to call out Fry in a post on X following his announcement, pointing to the repercussions if he were to win the race: “This is an escalation that harms our country, our state and our values at such an important time in our nation’s history.”

stories.title: Maine’s Troy Jackson Is on a Path to Become Senate Nominee
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: Two contenders, Nirav Shah and Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the Democratic race after Jackson picked up a majority of delegates.
stories.content: Troy Jackson, the former Maine state Senate president, has a majority of delegates heading into Saturday’s convention to choose the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson may have effectively clinched the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine. Jackson, who is seeking to replace scandal-plagued Graham Platner on the Democratic ticket after Platner dropped out, has the backing of more than half of the delegates who will attend next weekend's nominating convention, according to an analysis by the Bangor Daily News . His position strengthened Sunday as two rivals, former state Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, withdrew from the contest. On Saturday, delegates and members of the state’s central committee are scheduled to meet in Bangor, Maine. Those delegates were being chosen this weekend. The Bangor Daily News reported that York County, which borders New Hampshire, put Jackson over the top, bringing his total of pledged delegates over . “Thank you, York County. We’re organized, we’re ready, and we’re going to win. Solidarity forever,” Jackson wrote on X. The delegates are formally unbound, meaning they are not legally required to vote for a specific candidate even if they promised to during the delegate selection process. Shah said he would withdraw from the race to put the party’s energy into defeating Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November. “Today I am stepping aside, and I am doing it for exactly the same reason that led me to get in: we must defeat Susan Collins, and the Democratic Party must be unified to do it,” Shah wrote in a statement posted to X . Shah’s and Bellows’ exit leaves former congressional staffer Jordan Wood and 10 other candidates seeking the nomination. The race to become the Democratic nominee for Senate reopened earlier this month after Platner withdrew amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied. This story has been updated to include the withdrawal of Nirav Shah from the race.

stories.title: Shenna Bellows Exits Senate Race in Maine
stories.author: Jenna Monnin
stories.summary: The Maine secretary of state’s withdrawal comes less than a week before Democrats hold a state convention to replace Graham Platner on the ballot.
stories.content: Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, who was behind on endorsements by potential delegates, said she wanted to focus on her job overseeing elections. Robert F. Bukaty/AP Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows dropped out of the race for U.S. Senate on Sunday, leaving three major candidates to off at the Democrats’ state convention this week. Bellows said she was withdrawing to focus on her role as the state’s chief election officer amid attacks on ballot integrity by President Donald Trump. “Donald Trump’s attacks are only accelerating, and the best way that I can serve our state and country at this moment is by focusing exclusively on my role as Secretary of State,” Bellows wrote in a statement posted to X. Trump addressed the nation on Thursday, arguing that recently declassified documents show rogue state actors are intent on disrupting U.S. elections and charging that hundreds of thousands of non-citizens were registered to vote, though evidence provided by the White House largely did not back up those assertions. Per the Constitution, state and local officials oversee elections. The Justice Department sent a letter to all 50 states this month threatening to prosecute election officials if any noncitizens are found to have voted in any upcoming elections. Bellows also pointed to the urgency for Democrats in this race, saying the party doesn’t “have a day to waste in unifying around” beating incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins in November. Twelve Democrats, including Bellows, have entered the race to replace Platner, the party’s nominee who dropped out this month amid sexual assault allegations, which he denied. A gathering of delegates will join the members of the state’s central committee to choose a nominee Saturday in Bangor, Maine. With Bellows’ departure, the frontrunners are considered to be former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, former Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention Director Nirav Shah and former congressional staffer Jordan Wood. Support for Jackson has surged among delegates after a televised debate last week, according to an analysis released Friday by Bangor Daily News . Among the 3, people who could fill those delegate seats, Jackson carried stated endorsements, Shah had and Bellows had 48. The delegates were being chosen this weekend at county caucuses. Jackson celebrated Bellows’ decision to leave the race, highlighting their “friendship” and “shared values.” “Defeating Susan Collins will take all of us, and I’m grateful for your commitment to bringing Democrats together around that mission,” Jackson wrote Sunday on X. “Let’s get to work.” Bellows did not immediately endorse any of the remaining Democratic contenders.

stories.title: Ralph Norman Announces Campaign to Fill Lindsey Graham’s Vacant Seat
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: The South Carolina Republican told Fox News that he was not deterred by President Donald Trump’s early endorsement of Darline Graham.
stories.content: The day before he announced his plans, Norman received nods of support from other lawmakers, including Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Rep. Ralph Norman announced on Saturday his plan to run in the special primary election to fill former South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham’s vacant seat, becoming the first major candidate to enter the race. Graham’s death on July 11 immediately spurred interest among conservatives, including Norman, in securing the GOP nomination in South Carolina Republicans’ first contested open-seat Senate primary in over two decades. “I'm running for the United States Senate because our country is at a crossroads,” Norman said in a message posted to his campaign’s website Saturday. “President Trump needs proven conservative fighters standing with him — not politicians who fold when the pressure comes. Washington doesn't need more talkers. It needs people who will do exactly what they told the voters they'd do.” By state law, candidates have from July 21 to July 28 to register their campaigns. Whoever wins the special election on Aug. 11 will Democrat Annie Andrews in the fall. The day before he announced his plans, Norman received nods of support from other lawmakers, including Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Rick Scott of Florida. But complicating Norman and other future contenders’ plans is Trump’s early backing of Graham’s sister, Sen. Darline Graham, to run for a full term. Republican Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Darline Graham to serve the remainder of her brother’s term days after his death, making her the first woman Senator in state history. She has not formally filed to run in the special election. Norman told Fox News on Saturday that Trump’s endorsement of Darline Graham did not deter his plans. “I’m in this to win,” he said. Norman said on social media that, if elected, he’d vote to pass the SAVE America Act, Trump’s priority elections bill. The president also said Lindsey Graham advocated for the bill prior to his passing.

stories.title: Democrats’ Nebraska Senate Nominee Wants Off the Ballot. The State Might Not Let Her.
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: Cindy Burbank ran for the seat in hopes of clearing a path for independent candidate Dan Osborn.
stories.content: Burbank jumped into the race to prevent Forbes from advancing in the Democratic primary, eventually securing nearly 90% of the vote in May. BRAD NORTON/AP Nebraska Senate candidate Cindy Burbank secured the Democratic nomination in May. On Friday, she submitted a request to the office of Nebraska’s secretary of state to be taken off the ballot — but a legal challenge could ensue. Burbank’s campaign website says she ran to ensure that Sen. Pete Ricketts, the incumbent Republican, could not prop up a “stooge” Democratic candidate in William Forbes, an anti-abortion pastor who voted for President Donald Trump. By announcing plans to drop out, Burbank hoped to clear a path for independent candidate Dan Osborn, who received the state Democratic party’s endorsement and has the best chance to beat Ricketts in November. But even before she sent in her official request, Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, a Republican, said he may move to keep Burbank on the ballot. “I’m going to wait and see if she wins that primary,” Evnen said at an event after Burbank publicly stated she intended to drop out. “If she submits a withdrawal, then I’m going to ask, ‘Well, what is my obligation with respect to this now? Do I have to accept it?’ So I’ve submitted this question to the attorney general to see what happens.” A spokesperson for Evnen’s office confirmed to NOTUS on Friday that they have received Burbank’s request and will write to state Attorney General Mike Hilgers’ office asking if they are required to honor it. Hilgers’ team did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “But I will be back, and I’m not going to just sit on the sidelines either,” Burbank told Courier Nebraska on Friday. “I do want to thank everybody who supported me, voted for me, and cheered me on. And it was a great, fun adventure. It reinforced to me that I grew up in a wonderful state with wonderful people.” Burbank jumped into the race to prevent Forbes from advancing in the Democratic primary, eventually securing nearly 90% of the vote in May. Since winning her primary, her campaign has been largely quiet, save for promoting nonpartisan House candidate Austin Ahlman. Limited polling suggests that Ricketts still has an edge over Osborn ahead of November. The incumbent senator raked in over three times what Osborn raised last quarter.

stories.title: Trump Is Weighing Backing Darline Graham for a Full Senate Term
stories.author: Kadia Goba, Reese Gorman
stories.summary: The late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s sister was sworn in as an interim senator and is considering running for a full term. A White House endorsement could clear the field.
stories.content: Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was sworn in to take the seat on an interim basis, but is considering running for a full term. AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite President Donald Trump is considering backing Darline Graham for the full Senate term to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsay Graham of South Carolina, two sources tell NOTUS. Darline Graham was appointed by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster last week to fill out the remainder of her late brother’s term after he unexpectedly died early Sunday morning. Trump backed her for the “interim” appointment but has not publicly endorsed her to run for a full term. In recent days, however, Darline Graham has expressed to the White House that she wants to run for the Republican nomination for the full term, sources told NOTUS, and Trump is considering backing her. Her late brother was competing for another term in November against Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a physician who ran unsuccessfully for a House seat in . Semafor first reported that Darline Graham had expressed interest in the position. One of the sources told NOTUS that she is Trump’s first choice and endorsing her would help avoid a messy Republican primary that would take place over the span of a few weeks. The special election is scheduled for Aug. 11 and a runoff, if necessary, on Aug. 25. Multiple other South Carolina Republicans have been mulling a run, including Reps. Ralph Norman, Russell Fry and Nancy Mace, but none of them have made an announcement one way or another. Darline Graham or Andrews would be the first female elected to represent South Carolina in the Senate. One source familiar with the discussion told NOTUS that Trump would consider backing Fry if Darline Graham decides not to run. The White House and Darline Graham’s office did not immediately respond to requests from NOTUS for comments. Memorials for Lindsey Graham have been scheduled for July 28 in Washington and July 29 in South Carolina, according to his office .

stories.title: Wisconsin Governor Candidate Drops Out After Reporting Financial ‘Inaccuracies’
stories.author: Brett Bachman, Elena Schneider
stories.summary: Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez’s exit from the race comes less than a month before the state’s Aug. 11 primary.
stories.content: Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, a Democratic candidate for governor in , speaks at a news conference at a food bank on Tuesday, Nov. 4, , in Sun Prairie, Wis. (AP Photo/Scott Bauer) Scott Bauer/AP Wisconsin Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez suspended her gubernatorial campaign on Friday, just days after reporting “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in campaign finance filings and accusing her former campaign manager of vastly overstating her fundraising totals. “I am deeply hurt and betrayed by what happened,” Rodriguez said in a video message posted on social media . “I cannot in good conscience let these questions become a cloud over an election that Democrats need to win. Wisconsin deserves better than that.” The Democrat’s exit from the race comes less than a month before the state’s Aug. 11 primary. decision to drop out also kickstarted a Democratic effort to convince David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, to reenter the race, one person familiar with the situation told NOTUS. Gov. Tony Evers is considering supporting the movement to get Crowley back into the race, the source said. Crowley, who endorsed Rodriguez after dropping out of the race last week, is "strongly considering" it, according to a second person directly familiar with his thinking. A crowded field remains for the party’s nomination — former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, state Rep. Francesca Hong, state Sen. Kelda Roys and former state Department of Administration Secretary Joel Brennan are all still vying for a spot on November’s ballot. Whoever wins is likely to Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is leading the Republican field. The financial misconduct allegations that roiled Rodriguez’s campaign were first revealed over the weekend, when the lieutenant governor issued a statement revealing she had fired her campaign manager, Kara Spencer, after discovering discrepancies in her campaign finance reports. Rodriguez said at a press conference Monday that she first knew something was wrong when television ads for her campaign that were supposed to air last week did not run. “I was given excuses from my campaign manager that did not make sense,” Rodriguez said after confronting Spencer about the unpaid invoices. “There was clearly a double-counting of contributions that inflated how much money we had raised,” Rodriguez said, while blaming her campaign manager for the situation. “There was also a significant failure to report certain expenses that had been paid.” The discrepancy between the reported fundraising total and the actual amount in her campaign’s coffers amounted to hundreds of thousands of dollars, Rodriguez said. As of Monday, the campaign had a total of roughly $ , on hand. A campaign lawyer for Rodriguez has reached out to the Wisconsin Ethics Commission to report the situation, the lieutenant governor . “Part of being a leader is taking swift action, doing the right thing and being as honest as possible when there’s a problem,” Rodriguez said in her video message Friday. This is a developing story and will be updated.

stories.title: Where Republicans’ Cuts to Medicaid Could Cost Them
stories.author: Zara Norman
stories.summary: The race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District tests the politics of Republicans’ social safety net cuts.
stories.content: Rep. Rob Wittman, a ten-term Republican, initially said he wouldn’t support the “One Big Beautiful Bill” because of its sweeping cuts to Medicaid. Tom Williams/AP CHESTERFIELD, Virginia — Democrats think they can flip a President Donald Trump-supporting congressional district blue. Their message: The incumbent, Virginia Rep. Rob Wittman, voted to cut Medicaid. Wittman, a ten-term Republican, told party leadership last summer that he wouldn’t support the “One Big Beautiful Bill” because of its sweeping cuts to Medicaid, a program one in eight of his constituents rely on for coverage. But ultimately, he did. Local Democratic Party committees are using Wittman’s vote to stir up their base. The official campaign arm for House Democrats says his district, the suburban and rural communities surrounding Richmond and the state’s eastern shore, “represents one of our best pick-up opportunities.” Shannon Taylor, the Democratic candidate who secured a spot on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” list , said his about- should be “the No. 1 issue” on voters’ minds as they head to the polls in November. “Wittman knew that voting for that budget bill was going to be cutting health care services and that's exactly what's happened,” Taylor, a county prosecutor, told NOTUS. “He owns that responsibility, and that's what we're out there telling people. We are letting them know that these terrible choices that they're being with day in and day out are his responsibility.” Republicans have publicly and privately fretted that their cuts to the social safety net could be a liability in battleground states. The race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District is a test of just how much. It’s a contest taking shape around the future of health care, and particularly Virginia’s rural hospitals. Three such clinics shuttered last year in Virginia, directly citing the One Big Beautiful Bill as a reason. A state legislative committee deemed that 13 more hospitals risk the same fate, though the two in Wittman’s district have no immediate plans to close . Taylor and the six other candidates vying for the Democratic nomination feel fairly confident in their odds, despite the fact that Wittman has already raised about twice the amount Taylor has, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings. Though the district voted for Trump by 5 percentage points, it also broke for Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger last year. Shannon Taylor AP- ( , AR: 1.50)“This is the first time this seat is actually up for grabs,” Elizabeth Dempsey Beggs, one Democratic candidate, told voters at a June town hall in Chesterfield. Republicans disagree. They don’t think Wittman’s vote on Medicaid is the silver bullet Democrats think it is, for his seat or for the other Republicans who voted for the bill. One House Republican strategist said they feel pretty good about securing the 1st District, citing Trump’s win. Rural hospitals struggled to stay open long before last summer’s cuts, they argue. A National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson told NOTUS they plan to “take Democrats to task” for opposing Republicans’ solution for that: a $50 billion rural health fund which was included late in budget bill negotiations to address moderate Republicans’ concerns around Medicaid cuts. “The Commonwealth of Virginia received $ million from this program, which will be used to modernize facilities, address workforce challenges, and expand life-saving services,” Wittman told NOTUS in a statement. “I was proud to advocate for this funding, and I will continue to work with our rural providers to ensure they have the resources they need to serve our communities.” Democratic lawmakers in Congress called the rural health fund a “ fig leaf ” that did little to address the budget hole the policy created. The law cut more than $ billion dollars from Medicaid over 10 years, primarily by limiting the ways states can raise revenue to cover their share of the bill, restricting noncitizen coverage and introducing new work requirements. Virginia is part of a 23-state coalition suing to stop those work requirements from being implemented. “These policy changes risk shifting care from lower-cost preventive services toward higher-cost emergency and inpatient care, which is not the best outcome for patients or the healthcare system,” a spokesperson for Augusta Health, which operated the three shuttered rural clinics, told NOTUS in a statement. Hospitals have to provide emergency care regardless of a patient's ability to pay. About 13% of Augusta Health’s patients are covered by Medicaid, meaning the company expects to see more uncompensated care. That can be make or break for rural hospitals that operate on thin profit margins, see fewer patients and have more that rely on Medicaid than their urban counterparts. Virginia’s rural health providers are waiting until later this year to assess how much damage Medicaid cuts will do, but they’re not feeling optimistic. More than , Virginians are expected to lose coverage. “The challenges facing rural healthcare are not new. In recent years, however, those headwinds have intensified,” a spokesperson from Bon Secours, which operates one of two at-risk hospitals in Wittman’s district, told NOTUS in a statement. “We are continually monitoring this shifting landscape and remain committed to addressing these challenges thoughtfully and responsibly.” The $50 billion rural health fund aimed to move rural hospitals away from reimbursement-based funding, as that model works better in urban areas with more patients. But while any funding for rural healthcare is welcome, providers said they don’t see it as a solution. “While it may help address certain needs, it is unlikely to replace the ongoing reimbursement reductions hospitals are expected to experience,” wrote the Augusta Health spokesperson. Though Virginia received $ million of the fund this year, it asked for $1 billion. To access that money, clinics must apply to the state with an innovative idea. Giving the funds without strings attached might have been preferable, Jack Hensold, a rural oncologist in Montana, told NOTUS. “All they are trying to do is keep their heads afloat. So how many of them really have a sweeping, innovative idea?” said Hensold. “That money is just going to go to waste.” In June, four of the seven Democrats running for the seat participated in a town hall where they swiped at Wittman for his record on health care. Wittman wasn’t present. Chesterfield Town Hall ( , AR: 1.33)Health care attorney Ericka Kopp said she entered the race on the back of Wittman’s vote last summer — calling it a “slap in the .” Tim Cywinski, the communications manager for the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter, said his family lost their home to medical debt. Jason Knapp, a former naval officer, said he was born to a 19-year-old single mother and they relied on Medicaid and food stamps when he was growing up. “We have seen good candidates here before, but they didn't win,” said Knapp at the town hall. “To win this seat we have to consciously get people to fire Wittman who have been voting for him all this time.” Democratic candidates hoping to oust Wittman a truncated timeline to get that message across. A statewide redistricting battle delayed Virginia’s primary elections until August 4. In the meantime, local party committees are focusing on the downstream effects of Trump’s budget bill rather than any one candidate. “There are so many parts of the Big Beautiful Bill that made things less affordable for people,” Jen Tierney, chair of the Historic Triangle Democrats, told NOTUS. “We have rural hospitals in the 1st Congressional District that are at risk because of those cuts, so it is hard to find a person who is not impacted in some way.” Republicans have known the political implications of cutting Medicaid for a while. Most adults report some kind of connection to the program, according to the health policy research organization KFF . Politico found that 11 Republicans in competitive seats represent larger-than-average Medicaid populations. “I see him gradually resented more and more,” Michael Hill, a 72-year-old retired teacher from Chesterfield, said of Wittman. “I just feel like, at this point, you might be persuaded to move in a different way.”

stories.title: Haley Stevens Is Getting Flamed Online. Will It Matter in Michigan?
stories.author: Elena Schneider, Daniella Diaz
stories.summary: The Michigan Senate primary is turning personal. “I think that we should bring the conversation back to the more substantive issues,” said an El-Sayed backer.
stories.content: "Is she the most effective communicator? The answer is no," Amanda Litman said of Rep. Haley Stevens. Kristen Norman/AP Photo/Kristen Norman A 19-second video clip of Rep. Haley Stevens — a stilted, clenched-fist pep talk with a gym-teacher affect — zinged across social media this week, triggering mockery from Democrats and Republicans of the Michigan congresswoman locked in a tight Senate primary. And on Michigan voters’ TVs this week, a pro-Stevens outside group funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee dropped another ad slamming her opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, for his “sexist attacks” on Stevens. That spot adds to the 10-to-1 advertising advantage for Stevens, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. This split screen in the Michigan Senate primary — what’s going viral online versus what’s airing on voters’ televisions — encapsulates much of what’s defined Democratic Senate campaigns throughout : debates over electability, virality, dark money spending and U.S.-Israel politics. That dynamic, now freshly injected with accusations of sexism, stands to define the closing weeks of Michigan’s Senate primary, a must-win battleground state for Democrats. Stevens’ defenders accuse El-Sayed backers of attacking Stevens’ appearance, voice and on-camera presence — of taking the “low road,” as Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), who endorsed the congresswoman this week, put it to NOTUS.
