I’ll do everything possible to continue to represent you and thank you for your grace,” Connolly said in his statement. Connolly first made public his esophageal cancer diagnosis after the election. He launched his bid last year to be the top Democrat on the Oversight committee and led a tough internal campaign against Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who lost in the final vote. The contest came to be seen as a generational battle that could yield hints about the future of the Democratic Party in the wake of its losses.

stories.title: Centrist Democrats Are Hitting the Road. Their First Stop: Arizona
stories.author: Daniella Diaz
stories.summary: The topic of the New Democrat Coalition’s first roundtable is immigration.
stories.content: Members of the New Democrat Coalition are making the battleground state of Arizona their first stop to discuss immigration and border security as part of efforts to reach voters ahead of the midterms, NOTUS has learned. The stop in Phoenix on Wednesday is slated to be the first of several the Democratic group is making in the coming weeks to address major issues and figure out how to win back voters ahead of . The New Democrat Coalition, a moderate caucus, is the largest in the House Democratic caucus at more than members. It will play a key role in deciding Democrats’ strategy to win the House in the midterms, which is crucial if they want a check on the Trump administration in Washington. Members are hoping this tour helps them identify how to reach voters in key battleground districts and on key issues, and immigration has long been seen as a weak issue for Democrats.

stories.title: The Race for Dick Durbin’s Senate Seat Has Already Begun
stories.author: Helen Huiskes
stories.summary: The senator said he’s still determining whether to run for reelection. Multiple Democrats are angling for the seat if he retires.
stories.content: Sen. Dick Durbin told NOTUS he has not yet decided whether to run for reelection. But with a potentially vacant seat and no clear successor in the wings, multiple politicians are already mulling bids. “We are pretty accustomed to bare-knuckle politics around here, so I have no doubt in my mind that an extremely consequential race will result in folks putting everything on the line,” said Tom Bowen, a longtime Illinois political consultant. “And nobody shrinks from conflict around here.” Durbin is expected to make an announcement soon over whether he’ll run for reelection in . Should he choose to retire, his seat would open up for the first time in nearly three decades. NOTUS asked all 17 members of the Illinois U.S. House delegation if they were interested in the Senate. Five members said yes, and observers expect several other federal and state figures to jump in — making for a far closer race than in , when Sen. Tammy Duckworth was the obvious Democratic frontrunner to take on Republican incumbent Mark Kirk.

stories.title: Gov. Ron DeSantis Ensures an Ally Takes Marco Rubio’s Senate Seat: State AG Ashley Moody
stories.author: Claire Heddles, Oriana González
stories.summary: Moody was an early endorser of his presidential campaign.
stories.content: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has picked Florida’s attorney general, Ashley Moody, a longtime ally who has frequently sued the Biden administration in recent years, to replace Marco Rubio if he’s confirmed as secretary of state. “Talk is cheap. We need people that have demonstrated fidelity to these principles with their actions,” DeSantis told reporters Thursday morning, pointing to her track record as the state’s top cop and her lawsuits against the Biden administration. She also has a far-reaching position DeSantis said she promised him: “She’s even taken on the United Nations, which she has pledged as a senator to defund once and for all.” Her appointment cements a strong DeSantis ally in D.C. ahead of his own ambiguous political future when he’s term-limited out as governor in early .

stories.title: Republican Senators Say Joni Ernst Would Be An ‘Easy to Confirm’ Alternative to Pete Hegseth
stories.author: John T. Seward, Em Luetkemeyer
stories.summary: “Her reputation in the Senate is impeccable,” one Republican senator told NOTUS. Ernst’s name has been floated as an alternative to President-elect Trump’s pick for secretary of defense.
stories.content: As Pete Hegseth scrambles to gather enough support to be confirmed as defense secretary, Republican senators are admitting that another nominee would have an easier path to getting confirmed. One option? A member of their own ranks: Sen. Joni Ernst. Ernst, a military veteran, previously expressed interest in the job, and she’s reportedly back in the mix as President-elect Donald Trump considers replacements for Hegseth.

stories.title: Two Florida Special Elections Will Test the Power of MAGA in Trump’s Second Term
stories.author: Em Luetkemeyer, Claire Heddles
stories.summary: The special elections in two red House districts to replace Mike Waltz and Matt Gaetz will take place shortly after Trump returns to the White House.
stories.content: Two special elections for safely Republican seats in Florida are shaping up to be races to see which candidate will be the Trumpiest. The candidates who’ve announced they’ll run — to replace Rep. Mike Waltz and former Rep. Matt Gaetz in the coming year — are already starting to flaunt their conservative records and support of President-elect Donald Trump. On Tuesday morning, Florida state Sen. Randy Fine announced his run for Congress in Florida’s 6th Congressional District in what’s gearing up to be one of two MAGA-y primaries in a state that has become a home base for much of the president-elect’s movement. The elections will take place within Trump’s first days back in office.

stories.title: Dave McCormick Is Projected to Defeat Sen. Bob Casey in Pennsylvania
stories.author: Mark Alfred
stories.summary: Casey has not conceded the race, with his campaign saying it is waiting for additional votes to be counted.
stories.content: Republican businessman Dave McCormick is projected to become the next senator from Pennsylvania after narrowly defeating incumbent Sen. Bob Casey, toppling a three-term political scion. The Associated Press called the race Thursday afternoon, marking the first time that Casey — the son of a former governor and a fixture of Pennsylvania politics for nearly three decades — has lost a statewide race. Fewer than 31, votes separated the candidates at the time the race was called. Casey has yet to concede the race, with his campaign saying the race was too close to call.

stories.title: Michigan Is Sending Democrat Elissa Slotkin to the Senate
stories.author: Amelia Benavides-Colón, Em Luetkemeyer
stories.summary: Control of the Senate is already decided, but Democrats managed to hang on to an open seat in the battleground state.
stories.content: Michigan Rep. Elissa Slotkin is projected to win Michigan’s open Senate seat, a vital win for Democrats after losing the Senate and losing the state in the presidential race. The Associated Press called the race for Slotkin on Wednesday, in a very tight race against Republican Mike Rogers. The razor-thin margin reflects Slotkin’s narrow lead before the election, where polls showed the candidates tied several times. In Michigan, Democrats lined up behind Slotkin, who currently represents a competitive House district that she won in .

stories.title: Tammy Baldwin Gives Democrats a Much-Needed Win by Pulling Off Her Reelection Bid
stories.author: Torrence Banks, Nuha Dolby
stories.summary: It was the Democratic senator’s first time running on a ballot alongside Donald Trump.
stories.content: Democratic Sen. Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin is projected to narrowly win her third-straight Senate election, defeating businessman and investor Eric Hovde in a key swing state for Democrats in her most competitive Senate race yet. It was her first time running on the same ballot as Donald Trump. Throughout Tuesday night, Democrats and the campaign told NOTUS they remained confident in her ability to win. The Associated Press called the race Wednesday afternoon. The razor-thin margin is a far cry from the margins she’s won by in the past. But it’s in line with the vast conservative shift seen nationally on Tuesday. Baldwin’s is a crucial win for Democrats, but they had already been projected to lose control of the chamber by the time her race was called.

stories.title: Jon Tester Just Lost His Seat in the Senate to Tim Sheehy
stories.author: Helen Huiskes
stories.summary: Until now, the Democrat had managed to hang on to his seat in a state Donald Trump easily won three times.
stories.content: Sen. Jon Tester couldn’t overcome the political reality that Montana is a very, very red state. Tester is projected to lose to Republican Tim Sheehy, a young former Navy SEAL backed by former President Donald Trump. The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday morning. Trump handily won the state for the third presidential election in a row. Tester, the last Democrat to hold statewide or federal office in Montana, has held on to his seat through several cycles despite Republicans gaining a clear advantage. The Senate GOP considered Tester’s seat a must-win in their quest to win back the majority (as they had in and when Tester narrowly won), and he was one of the most vulnerable incumbents running on what was a tough map for Democrats.

stories.title: Democrats Celebrate One Election Bright Spot: Two Black Women in the Senate
stories.author: Violet Jira
stories.summary: Wins by Democrats Angela Alsobrooks and Lisa Blunt Rochester mean two Black women will serve alongside each other in the Senate for the first time.
stories.content: Democrats had a tough night after projections showed they lost the Senate. But they also made history. Democrats Angela Alsobrooks in Maryland and Lisa Blunt Rochester in Delaware are projected to win their Senate races, meaning two Black women will serve in the Senate for the first time in the body’s history. Blunt Rochester, a current member of Congress, is the first woman and the first Black person to represent the state of Delaware in the Senate. She has served in the U.S. House since . Alsobrooks serves as executive of Prince George’s County; she beat Larry Hogan, the former governor of Maryland, to become the first Black person to represent Maryland in the senate.

stories.title: Sherrod Brown Loses His Seat in the Senate
stories.author: Violet Jira
stories.summary: The Democrat had been able to keep his seat in a state Donald Trump won, but Republicans managed to beat him.
stories.content: Republican Bernie Moreno is projected to beat three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown in what has been one of the most closely watched elections in the country. The race, one of a handful of battleground Senate races, is a significant blow to Democrats, both in their campaign to maintain Senate control and in their efforts to remain politically competitive in Ohio. The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday. Republicans have consistently swept statewide elections in recent years. JD Vance won the Senate race in , and former President Donald Trump took Ohio in and . Republican voters in rural areas have played a significant role in these victories. The state has also shifted demographically to favor Republicans: Ohio is whiter and has more voters without college degrees than the United States as a whole. The population has also grown older.

stories.title: A Giddy Rick Scott Moves On to His Next Campaign: Senate Republican Leader
stories.author: Claire Heddles
stories.summary: “Florida is the center of the Republican Party of this country,” Scott said in a pitch for why he should be the next GOP leader.
stories.content: BONITA SPRINGS, FL — Florida Sen. Rick Scott was riding high on election night after handily winning reelection and the state was called early for Donald Trump. But he cut the Florida-focused part of his victory speech short to talk about his next campaign: the Senate leadership race. After Tuesday’s sweeping wins for Republicans in Florida, Scott’s pitch to the room was that “Florida is the center of the Republican Party of this country,” and who better to lead the Senate party than a Floridian? “We have a great Republican Party all across this country, we need a Republican Party in D.C.” he told the crowd.

stories.title: Democrats Went ‘On Offense’ in Florida and Still Lost to Rick Scott
stories.author: Em Luetkemeyer
stories.summary: Sen. Rick Scott will return to Washington, where he’s running to replace Sen. Mitch McConnell as the top Republican in the Senate.
stories.content: Rick Scott is projected to beat former Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Mucarsel-Powell in Florida’s Senate race, despite Democrats’ hopes that ballot questions and new political vulnerabilities — including rifts with leadership in his own party — on Scott’s end would lift their candidate. The Associated Press called the race for Scott on Tuesday, and the senator’s reelection points to the party’s ever-growing influence over the state, which was once a battleground. In the land of Donald Trump, Ron DeSantis and culture wars, Democrats don’t seem to be gaining any steam. But Democrats believed this year would be Scott’s hardest reelection campaign yet, in part because he had gotten into trouble with his own party and was attacked by his opponent over his proposal in to sunset all federal legislation after five years.

stories.title: Internal Document Reveals a Quarter of House Dems Severely Behind in Dues to Campaign Arm
stories.author: Shifra Dayak
stories.summary: “The members who do and don’t step up on dues is particularly instructive in a cycle where we might actually take the majority,” said a Democratic strategist.
stories.content: The campaign arm for House Democrats has raised millions this cycle to support the party’s effort to retake the majority. But by the end of September, nearly 30% of the caucus had only paid less than half of their suggested dues to the organization, according to a spreadsheet obtained by NOTUS. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee sets dues and fundraising expectations for each member of Congress based on their seniority, committee positions and how much help they’ll need during the election cycle. Frontline candidates — the 31 Democrats who are looking to hold onto seats in competitive districts — don’t have any dues. Meanwhile, Democrats in leadership and committee chairs are expected to transfer hundreds of thousands to the DCCC. The spreadsheet shows there were 45 candidates who were less than 50% of the way to meeting their dues goals — but had paid more than $0 — with several sitting on significant amounts of cash on hand. Reps. Bill Foster, Lucy McBath and Emanuel Cleaver, for instance, all had over $1 million of cash on hand as of the end of September, per the internal document, but Foster and McBath had paid less than 20% of their required dues by then ( A spokesperson for Foster said the congressman had “fully paid on his dues for this cycle” as of the end of October. Cleaver had paid 44%. McBath isn’t considered a frontliner by the DCCC, but she’s running for reelection in a new congressional district — currently controlled by a Republican — after redistricting.)

stories.title: Two House Democrats Are Already Angling for a Leadership Spot in a Potential Majority
stories.author: Helen Huiskes
stories.summary: Kelly has already shored some up among other Illinois Democrats.
stories.content: Democrats only have a narrow shot at taking back the House and the election is still a few weeks away, but at least two members are already putting out feelers for a run at a leadership position in the caucus. Rep. Robin Kelly of Illinois and California Rep. Sara Jacobs are both planning to run for caucus vice chair in the event Democrats take the majority. With the caucus steadily behind Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the rest of the leadership team, the role of vice chair would likely be one of the few spots open for other members to rise in the ranks. A source familiar with Kelly’s thinking told NOTUS the congresswoman is talking to her colleagues already to garner support and that she’s already shored some up among other Illinois Democrats.

stories.title: Republicans Roll the Dice on Their Farm Bill
stories.author: Tyler Spence
stories.summary: With time running out, senators plow forward with their compromise, hoping Democrats come along.
stories.content: The current short-term extension of the farm bill expires at the end of September. (AP Photo/Joshua A. Bickel) The Senate Agriculture Committee will take up its version of the farm bill Thursday, with provisions meant to help farmers with financial aid, crop sales overseas and year-round sales of ethanol-blend gasoline. But the outcome is unclear, particularly without a clear bipartisan deal on parts of the measure dealing with when some states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The current short-term extension of the farm bill expires at the end of September. Chair John Boozman (R-Arkansas), after weeks of negotiations, released a compromise bill text and emphasized the need to act ahead of the August recess. “We need to act this week, or we run out of time,” Boozman said. Farm bankruptcies are at record highs largely due to several consecutive years of high input prices and extreme weather. The Senate bill attempts to help farmers on both fronts, by giving farmers more flexibility to use emergency government land and cost-sharing programs during droughts and floods. The bill also changes how conservation payments are calculated so farmers with drought- or flood-prone land receive more support. And it raises the size of loans farmers can access, puts more money into helping U.S. crops sell overseas and expands support for newer farming technology that helps producers use less fertilizer and fuel per acre. The most contentious piece remains how to handle SNAP payment error rates. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), who farms corn and soybeans with his family and has been in the Senate since , said this has been the most difficult farm bill to get bipartisan support for in his career. “I think every other farm bill that I’ve worked on in the 46 years I've been in the United States Senate has been a bipartisan bill,” Grassley told reporters . “It seems like this year, it’s very difficult to get Democratic support, mostly over a food stamp issue.” Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift to states with SNAP payment error rates above 6%, which is scheduled to start next year. Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP in a reconciliation law. Boozman’s bill met Democrats halfway, with a one-year delay. In exchange, states with higher error rates would pay a bigger share of the cost than in the original reforms passed in the reconciliation law. Boozman has acknowledged that many states simply need more time. Only nine states and the Virgin Islands have error rates below the 6% threshold, according to data gathered by the USDA. Democrats aren’t sold. Ranking member Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) hasn’t made her thoughts on the updated text public. Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) is encouraging Democrats to hold out for a better deal. “Democrats should remain united and only support a Farm Bill that includes a clean two-year delay of the SNAP cost shift to states,” Booker said in a statement. One compromise included is the bill is language authorizing permanent, nationwide year-round sales of E15, the 15%-ethanol blend corn growers have chased for years. But the provision has garnered the ire of oil producers and their representatives. A provision to approve year-round E15 in the House version of the farm bill nearly derailed the bill’s progress on the House floor, but ended up passing in a separate vote in May . Complicating all of it is the absence of Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky). Republicans and Democrats effectively enter Thursday’s markup with even numbers, raising the odds that Boozman will need Democratic votes just to move the bill out of committee.

stories.title: Maryland Lawmakers Open the Door for 2028 Redistricting
stories.author: Manuela Silva
stories.summary: The constitutional amendment would make it harder for any future redistricting efforts to be challenged in court, which had worried some Democrats.
stories.content: Maryland lawmakers deliberate in the House Chambers during a reading of a proposed constitutional amendment Tuesday, Aug. 4, , in Annapolis, Md., that would allow a redrawn congressional map. Mingson Lau/AP Photo Maryland lawmakers took a first step toward redrawing their congressional map during a special session on Tuesday, passing a constitutional amendment that could open the door for Democrats to pick up the only Republican seat in the state’s nine-member congressional delegation ahead of . Democrats in the Maryland General Assembly pushed through a constitutional amendment in both chambers that is aimed at shielding a possible redistricting effort from potential litigation. If approved by voters in November, the constitutional amendment would set a different standard for how the state draws its congressional districts compared with its assembly districts. “We have seen how the federal government has told Republican states that they should do mid- redistricting but told Democratic states to sit on our hands,” Democratic Gov. Wes Moore said at a Monday press conference ahead of the legislative special session. “We have seen how the Voting Rights Act has fallen, which we predicted would happen at the start of this year. So we are back now to be able to ensure that our elections should be in the hands of the people of Maryland. They should have the final say.” When Democrats attempted to redraw Maryland’s lines in , a Maryland state court struck down the maps, calling the proposed maps a “product of extreme partisan gerrymandering.” State Senate President Bill Ferguson has repeatedly cited the decision as evidence that any redistricting effort would not withstand a legal challenge. The new bill aims to clarify that the requirements set by the ruling only apply to General Assembly seats, making it easier to pass a congressional gerrymander. “This decision put Maryland in a very different position than many other states in this union and unless we address this uncertainty first, any other action would jeopardize our state’s current map,” Ferguson said of the ruling at a press conference on Monday before the session began. Ferguson, who had been vocally opposed to redistricting in his state for months, pointed to the Supreme Court’s Louisiana v. Callais ruling as the ultimate driving force that led him to call for legislative action. “A legal earthquake changed the landscape this spring when the Supreme Court of the United States, under Callais, eviscerated the very purpose and function of our Voting Rights Act,” Ferguson continued. “Even worse, we saw states like Tennessee, Louisiana and South Carolina act with haste to attempt to eliminate majority-minority congressional districts. These acts changed the calculus and that’s why we’re here.” Maryland is the latest Democrat-led state to consider redistricting ahead of after a whirlwind year of redistricting that began last summer when President Donald Trump called on GOP lawmakers to redraw their maps to favor Republicans ahead of this year’s midterms and intensified following the Supreme Court’s April decision. The only Democratic state that successfully redistricted was California, netting up to five seats after voters approved a ballot measure on the issue last November. The New York State Assembly advanced a constitutional amendment in June that opened up the possibility for Democrats to gain up to four House seats in . Conversations have swirled around redistricting in Maryland for months, with many Democrats urging the state to redraw their lines to oust the lone Republican representative in the seat, Rep. Andy Harris, the chair of the House Freedom Caucus who currently represents the Eastern Shore. In November, Moore created a Redistricting Advisory Commission, chaired by U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks (D-Maryland), which ultimately recommended a redrawn map in January. The state House of Delegates approved the map, but Ferguson never brought the measure to the state Senate floor during the regular session. NOTUS reported that Ferguson had begun talking with allies about how to move forward with redistricting after the Supreme Court decision, ultimately calling this summer’s special legislative session with House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk to consider the redistricting amendment.

stories.title: Big Ten, SEC Support College Sports Bill After Late Trump Pressure Campaign
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: The country’s two most powerful conferences pledged support for the bill after a series of intense negotiations, clearing the way for a Senate vote before summer recess.
stories.content: Jacquelyn Martin/AP The Big Ten Conference and the Southeastern Conference, the country’s most powerful collegiate sports conferences, have backed a bipartisan college sports bill after a flurry of intense discussions. The conferences shared their support for the Senate’s current version of the Protect College Sports Act in a joint statement Friday night, writing that they came to an agreement “following detailed and productive negotiations” with bill sponsors Ted Cruz (R-Texas), Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri). Their endorsement is a major boost to the sweeping sports bill — and came after a series of 11th-hour meetings forced this week by lawmakers eager to kill the obstacle presented by large conferences, who had opposed the bill for months over several provisions like capping power-conference membership and salary cap enforceability. Big Ten and SEC leadership had blown past other Congress-imposed deadlines this week, but they scrambled to hold meetings on revised bill text after President Donald Trump stated his intent to publicly condemn conference leadership for opposing the bill, Yahoo Sports reported Friday night. Dozens of other conferences, including the Atlantic Coast Conference and the Big 12, had vocally supported the measure since it was introduced in June because it would help close the revenue gap between themselves and the country’s two biggest power conferences. However, their endorsement could waver after the bill’s latest version more than doubles what top programs can pay their players — meaning the Big Ten and SEC’s richest members can further outpace smaller conferences. “The Big Ten Conference and Southeastern Conference support the Protect College Sports Act as currently drafted, following detailed and productive negotiations with Senators Cruz, Cantwell and Schmitt, and their respective staffs,” the short joint statement reads. “We appreciate the substantial work that has gone into this effort.” Negotiations with the conferences ran seven to eight hours a day, Schmitt told USA Today . Consensus on how a college athlete’s brand deals would impact an institution’s revenue-sharing cap was what finally got the conferences to sign off on the bill, Schmitt said. The proposal seemed unlikely to see any meaningful progress before the Senate begins its summer recess on Aug. 7, but Schmitt told Yahoo Sports on Friday that he expects a vote late next week.

stories.title: Elizabeth Warren Takes a Win on Housing to the Battleground States
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: The progressive who struck a deal with Republicans on housing affordability is rallying with Democrats in Georgia and North Carolina.
stories.content: Warren is planning to campaign alongside Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Jon Ossoff in Georgia. Bill Clark/AP Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts plans to campaign in two battleground states this weekend on the housing bill that recently became law, capitalizing on the fact that Republicans have struggled to fold it neatly into their messaging. The Democrat played a key role in negotiating the major housing bill that took effect earlier in July. On Friday, she traveled to Georgia for several events across the state alongside Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. Warren is also expected to travel to North Carolina on Saturday, where she will campaign with Roy Cooper, North Carolina’s former governor and the Democratic candidate vying for retiring Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat. That she’s able to tout legislation passed in a Republican-controlled Congress as a win is in part because of how it became law: President Donald Trump never signed the legislation and called it a “big yawn,” giving Democrats an opening to try to own it. “Donald Trump took the legs out from underneath the Republicans,” Warren told NOTUS over the phone after speaking at a roundtable event with community leaders and advocates in Georgia. “He ran for office promising to lower costs on day one, and then turned around and said affordability is a hoax when Republicans and Democrats worked together to pass this bill to lower housing costs.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Warren will be the keynote speaker at Saturday’s North Carolina Democratic Party Unity Dinner, the party’s largest annual gathering in the state. The Democrat, who was criticized during the bill negotiations by some lawmakers and stakeholders for leaving them out of the loop, is also trying to make her expertise on the bill a resource for other congressional candidates by briefing their campaigns on how to explain the housing package to voters. “This is not a heavy lift for me,” Warren said. “Democrats across the country understand that the two big issues in this race are cost and corruption.” By focusing on the housing package, particularly in states like Georgia and North Carolina, she said, lawmakers on the campaign trail can provide voters with “clear evidence that Democrats will deliver on their promises.” Democrats an uphill battle in their quest to flip control of the Senate this fall. For that to happen, Democrats need to net four seats in the chamber. Ossoff is one of the most vulnerable sitting Senate Democrats, and Cooper is running in North Carolina, one of the likeliest places for Democrats to pick up a seat. In the meantime, Republicans’ campaign message on housing has been complicated by the fact that Trump never signed the bill. Republican lawmakers in some of the most competitive districts in the country are avoiding mention of the president’s involvement as they campaign. The law is a product of the most comprehensive housing reform bill to come out of Congress in more than three decades. It includes a limit on institutional investors’ ownership of single-family homes, enforced through fines on corporations that own more than units. It also modernizes federal housing programs and overhauls quality review standards to fast-track housing development. The president had supported several versions of the bill, including the final one. In the end, however, he decided against signing it because Congress hasn’t passed the voter-ID bill that is top priority. The president criticized the housing package, calling it a “Warren-centric housing bill,” which the lawmaker downplayed and called “a family-centric housing bill.” “This new law is all about helping working families, but there's nothing in it for Donald Trump personally,” Warren said. “As a result, he's just not interested.”

stories.title: Indiana State Senate Leader Will Leave Role to Spare Colleagues From Trump’s Wrath
stories.author: Torrie Herrington
stories.summary: The president was quick to celebrate the announcement on Truth Social.
stories.content: Bray, who didn’t use Trump’s name in his announcement but referred directly to the president’s “promises,” also said that he would remain in the chamber and that he stands by his record. Michael Conroy/AP A top Republican in the Indiana state Senate said on Friday that he would not seek re-election to his leadership position in the hopes he could spare his colleagues from Donald Trump’s wrath after the president threatened to support primary challenges for any lawmakers who supported his bid. Rodric Bray, the state Senate president pro tempore, tangled with Trump last fall after Trump demanded that the state redraw its congressional maps to give Republicans a larger advantage. Bray led his colleagues in opposing the measure, which ultimately failed, and Trump quickly vowed to exact his revenge on the lawmakers who defied him. Bray, who didn’t use Trump’s name in his announcement but referred directly to the president’s “promises,” also said that he would remain in the chamber and that he stands by his record. “As the top caucus leader, the pro tem’s job is also to represent and look out for his caucus members,” Bray’s office said in a press release. “He will not put members in jeopardy from their own party simply because he is asking members to support his re-election as pro-tem.” Trump was thrilled to hear of Bray’s announcement, immediately celebrating it on Truth Social and saying that Bray should be “ashamed of himself” for costing the Republicans U.S. House seats. “I want to thank the Great State of Indiana for your support, not only in my Presidential Election, which we won with the Highest Vote in the History of the State, but also for your support in getting rid of wayward Senators, led down the Path of Destruction by a FOOL named Rodric Bray,” Trump wrote . “Better yet would be if he would resign from Office, completely, but he will be met by us at the Indiana Polls.” For much of his second term, Trump has been pushing states to redistrict in an effort to prevent Republicans losses in the midterms. In Indiana, a proposal to redraw the state’s congressional maps to give the party a 9-0 advantage in the U.S. House quickly garnered the president’s support — but Bray repeatedly insisted that it did not have enough support among his colleagues to pass the chamber. The president pro tem serves as the chamber’s elected leader, and is responsible for presiding over the state Senate, enforcing chamber rules and helping guide the chamber policy agenda. As such, he became the focus of Trump’s ire after the state’s redistricting measure failed, with 21 Republicans joining 10 Democrats to defeat it. While Bray is not up for reelection this year, several of his colleagues are. Six incumbent state senators lost to Trump-endorsed challengers , a bloodbath that Bray hopes to slow by stepping down from his leadership role. On June 4, state Senate Majority Floor Leader Chris Garten resigned from his leadership position as well, amid speculation that he may try to challenge Bray for his position. Garten supported redistricting. Bray’s announcement came as a shock to some, such as state Sen. Ron Alting, who has served in the Indiana state senate since . "What an honorable person to put the will of the caucus ahead of himself," Alting told IndyStar . "That's what you call a leader."

stories.title: Democrats Mobilize Over Fears Trump Will Deploy Troops to Polls
stories.author: Joe Gould, Kadia Goba
stories.summary: With a deep partisan split on election security, senators turn to tabletop exercises, encouraging early voting and more.
stories.content: Senate Democrats plan to use election observers at the polls to monitor and document any inappropriate activity so they can respond in the moment and inform potential action by Congress. Mike Stewart/AP President Donald Trump hasn’t ruled out deploying troops or federal agents to polling places in November. Democrats are preparing for how to respond in case that happens. Democratic lawmakers, wary of various potential disruptions to the midterm elections, conducted closed-door tabletop exercises last week that included the possibility of armed federal personnel dispatched near polling places. Sen. Alex Padilla (D-California), who participated in the exercises led by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, said Democrats are preparing to challenge the administration over any “pretext they would make for this type of deployment — because they would be lies — before those deployments even happen.” The comments reflect an atmosphere of distrust and a sharp partisan split on election security ahead of a midterm election that will determine which party controls the House and Senate — as the Trump administration has pushed aggressively on election system overhauls. Democrats have planned for their own Senate election observer program , coordination with local officials and voting rights advocates, and rapid-response legal planning. They’ve also introduced measures to prevent election interference, although such legislation has almost no chance of becoming law before the midterm elections. Padilla, who is helping lead the Senate Democrats’ Election Protection Task Force, introduced an anti-election interference bill last week that extends the statute of limitations to prosecute election interference by “troops” and “armed forces.” He said his effort is informed in part by Trump’s deployment of federalized troops to Los Angeles last year, which tested the limits of how military forces can be used domestically alongside federal law enforcement. “The deployment was unlawful, and the courts ruled that over time,” Padilla said in an interview. “The legal precedent is set, but Donald Trump disregards the rule of law far too often, so we'll have to be prepared, no matter what.” The -year-old Posse Comitatus Act generally bars military personnel from performing domestic law enforcement, and federal law makes it a crime punishable by up to five years in prison to deploy “any troops or armed men” to any location where voting is taking place. There is a narrow exception if troops are needed to protect voters or respond to an armed threat — which some Democrats fear Trump could claim. Senate Democrats plan to use election observers at the polls to monitor and document any inappropriate activity so they can respond in the moment and inform potential action by Congress. In the meantime, Padilla said Democrats are encouraging early voting. “If you cast your ballot by mail, you don’t have to worry about federal agents at the polls on Election Day,” Padilla said. “We’re reminding people of those options, but nonetheless standing up for people’s right to vote free of intimidation on Election Day, if that’s their choice.” The Democratic National Committee filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department, Pentagon and Department of Homeland Security seeking any records that reveal whether the agencies have planned deployments of federal agents or troops around polling places, ballot drop boxes or election offices. A judge has directed the agencies to begin producing records Friday. In the wake of inquiries from Democrats to those three departments, the Department of Homeland Security has said the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency is not planning an aggressive campaign at voting sites during the midterms. Schumer and 11 Senate Democrats sent a letter this week demanding information about the administration’s possible plans. Democrats already have pointed to a range of recent actions by Trump to justify their fears. He has pushed federal election directives on states , threatened local election officials with prosecution , sought detailed voter and election-worker records , and tied federal funding to changes in state voting practices . Trump announced in May that he would launch an "Election Integrity Army" and did not rule out sending National Guard or ICE to voting locations. In January, he said he regrets not sending the National Guard to seize election equipment during the election . Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) introduced legislation last month that would require the president to get Congress’s approval before deploying uniformed troops or federal law enforcement. When she asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at a hearing in April whether he would deploy troops to polls, he dismissed it as a “gotcha hypothetical.” Slotkin, who took part in Schumer’s tabletop exercise last week, said participants considered a scenario out of the “authoritarian playbook,” in which a cyberattack, allegations of widespread noncitizen voting or another security incident could be used to justify sending federal forces to polling places. Having troops or federal agents handle ballots or voting machines could cast doubt on whether the votes remained secure, opening the door to challenges over whether they should be counted. “What we see, for instance, in Hungary,” Slotkin said, “is a security incident that only federal forces can somehow respond to.” Slotkin argued that even if troops and agents did not handle voting machines — which could break the chain of custody and call the votes into question — a visible presence could deter people from voting. “If you tell me that a ton of ICE agents are going to be surrounding polls and that voters have to go run the gauntlet of masked ICE agents, % that’s intimidating,” she said. Republican lawmakers asked by NOTUS to respond to Democratic concerns were largely dismissive, and several on the Senate Armed Services Committee said they had not heard of any such plans from the administration. “I think the Democrats are fearmongering and trying to create a scenario where people are more concerned than they should be,” said Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), a former state attorney general. “It’s a political game more than anything.” Partisan distrust and splintering over election administration predates Trump’s return to office. For decades, House Democrats and Republicans jointly dispatched staff to observe ballot counting in potentially contested elections. But Republicans broke with that tradition in , deploying their own observers during voting instead of participating in the bipartisan effort that takes place during counting. House Administration Committee Chair Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin) said he plans to continue that approach this year, citing the reelection of Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) by a paper-thin margin. “What we learned from the race of Mariannette Miller-Meeks was that it would be beneficial to be deployed at the time of the election,” Steil said. “So we began that policy when I became chairman.” Democrats argue the move reflects the broader erosion of trust over election administration. Rep. Joe Morelle (D-New York), the panel’s ranking member, said Republicans’ abandonment of the joint election observer program “breaks 50 years of tradition and precedent.” “Honestly, there’s not too many Republicans I trust anymore on election security, on making sure that we're committed to the administration of our elections, and who aren't willing to allow the president to subvert the process,” Morelle said. Some of the warnings about the potential use of federal forces during the election are coming from a nonpartisan group of former military lawyers. Retired Maj. Gen. Steven Lepper, of the Former Judge Advocates General Working Group, said the organization has held discussions with multiple congressional offices about the threat and possible legislative safeguards. But Lepper said that with congressional action to restrict the use of troops at polling places unlikely before the election, the decision to carry out an order to deploy in the midst of an election would ultimately fall on military commanders. “The unwillingness of Congress to do its job has now placed the burden on military members, on military commanders, to have to either stand up to the president and refuse to obey unlawful orders, or obey unlawful orders and essentially put our military in a position where they're committing crimes,” Lepper said. “It’s just a shameful situation for our military to be put in.”

stories.title: Senate Considering a Delay in SNAP Cost Shift to States
stories.author: Tyler Spence
stories.summary: “I think what we’re looking at is possibly a short-term extension,” Sen. John Boozman said.
stories.content: Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift to states with SNAP payment error rates above 6%. (AP Photo/Allison Dinner, File) The chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee said Thursday he is considering some respite for states that must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) told NOTUS the issue is part of negotiations with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), the panel’s ranking member, on a way forward on the Senate’s version of a farm bill. Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift to states with SNAP payment error rates above 6%, an increase scheduled to start next year. Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP in a reconciliation law. “I think what we’re looking at is possibly a short-term extension,” Boozman told NOTUS. “We’ve been talking to Sen. Klobuchar, talking to the administration, seeing if the time we’ve given is adequate. Nothing has been finalized,” he said. Boozman didn’t specify how long a delay could be, only referring to it as “short-term.” Boozman has said the committee will mark up the farm bill late next week. Boozman’s office said the final version of the Senate farm bill is still being worked through but will be released soon. Klobuchar previously said she was having “productive negotiations” on the farm bill. Her office said Thursday there was nothing to add, but that “there is a lot of work left to do.” Only 9 states and the Virgin Islands had error rates below the 6% threshold . The changes in the reconciliation law require states to pay for a portion of the implementation of SNAP if their error rate exceeds that level. “What we want to do is make sure that we have rules that states can actually get. I think the states understand, and they are working really hard to get their error rates down,” Boozman said. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia), a member of the committee, welcomed the potential delay. West Virginia’s error rate in was just above 6%. “There are states that are going to be so impacted, it’s unbelievable. And West Virginia is going to get hit to the tune of tens of millions,” Justice told NOTUS. “I think what we need is a graduated runway. But working together and having some form of extension, with all the other stuff that we want on our side, I think that’s the way to go.” West Virginia is just one of many Republican states facing high payments for their error rates. Boozman’s home state of Arkansas sits at above 8%, and several mayors in the state have called on Boozman to provide an extension and protect SNAP more broadly. Other Republicans on the committee weren’t immediately sold by the idea. Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota) told NOTUS that the idea would land in the “we’ll see column.”

stories.title: Defense Hawks Challenge the White House Push for a Narrow Reconciliation Bill
stories.author: Joe Gould, Avani Kalra
stories.summary: The Senate Armed Services chair says roughly $ billion is needed for “this generational investment.”
stories.content: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon need an influx of funding for an Iran war that is again escalating. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP Images Senate defense hawks are pushing back on the White House plan for a narrowly tailored reconciliation bill, warning that Republicans may have only one opportunity to finance President Donald Trump’s military buildup and demanding far more than the House’s $60 billion defense proposal. The fight is complicating Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s effort to cobble together 50 Republican votes before the Senate adjourns next week until mid-September. Republicans broadly agree the Pentagon needs significantly more money, but they are divided over whether the next reconciliation bill should cover only immediate needs or finance a sweeping military buildup. Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi) said the package should include roughly $ billion for defense — roughly five times the House instruction — while other hawks urged Republican leaders to increase the number substantially. “We need something close to $ billion for this generational investment, to defend ourselves in the world against the axis of aggression,” Wicker said. The push runs counter to fiscally conservative Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought’s pitch for a narrow bill, with the remainder of Trump’s $1.5 trillion military budget request deferred to a later reconciliation package . “It should be tight,” Vought told reporters after meeting with Senate Republicans this week. “It should be for the defense needs that we need now, for the [agriculture] needs that we need now, and to get this as straight a shot to the president's desk as possible.”House Speaker Mike Johnson, along these lines, sent the Senate the House’s $95 billion reconciliation bill by striking a delicate balance between defense hawks in his conference and fiscal conservatives wary of adding billions to the deficit. Offsetting the new spending could require politically painful spending cuts just ahead of November’s elections. Thune has signaled that the House’s defense number is likely to be too low for his members. He told reporters he would “prefer doubling” it as Republican leaders search for enough votes to advance the measure. But Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), a fiscal hawk whose committee would spearhead the reconciliation bill, poured cold water on the defense increase. He said Thune had not mentioned it to him. “White House is trying to skinny it down for passage, so we’ll see,” Johnson said. “I know there's a desire on the part of many to increase those numbers. Again, we'll have to figure out what the conference wants to do here.” The unresolved questions come amid growing alarm over the Iran war’s toll on U.S. munitions stockpiles, which are being further depleted because of Trump’s fresh escalation in the conflict. The Pentagon on Wednesday signed a $56 billion contract with Lockheed Martin for Patriot interceptors, but the money for that and other budget priorities, such as Golden Dome missile defenses, requires congressional approval. “You look at munitions — you look at Golden Dome — that are in reconciliation; time is running out,” said Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

stories.title: Let RFK Jr. Cook
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visits University of Utah to discuss Utah's new fluoride ban and food additives legislation. Melissa Majchrzak/AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 29, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST President Donald Trump could pull Todd Blanche’s nomination until after Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) leave office — even though Senate Republicans are not guaranteed a favorable midterms cycle this year. Cornyn said today that at least a few of his colleagues also share concerns about Trump’s IRS settlement. “The president’s not winning on this issue,” Tillis said . “It is killing some of our candidates because they can’t explain it. And now it looks like they weren’t being honest when they said it was inoperative.” John Thune still thinks there’s “a way” to confirm Blanche this year, but told reporters he’d “defer to whatever the White House” wants to do. THE HILL Thune plans to bring a continuing resolution to the Senate floor next week, emphasizing that “appropriators are working in good faith to produce a clean, bipartisan product, free of poison pills.” The Senate advanced three nominees out of committee today: Erica Schwartz for CDC director, Sean Kaufman for an HHS assistant secretary role, and Keith Sonderling for labor secretary. HELP Committee Chair Bill Cassidy reversed some of his positions to support all three. The Senate also defeated Democrats’ latest Iran war powers resolution 49-50. THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL Mandela Barnes suspended his Wisconsin gubernatorial campaign this afternoon. The decision came just as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel was preparing a story detailing sexual impropriety allegations involving the Democratic candidate. Elon Musk authorized his super PAC to spend up to $ million on a new field program aimed at electing Republicans in at least eight states, The New York Times reports . THE ADMINISTRATION RFK Jr. revealed an online cooking show mixing “healthy” recipes with MAHA talking points. The “Freedom Haulers” initiative launched today. The program would boost veteran hiring within the trucking industry in the White House’s effort to replace non-citizen drivers. A U.S. government map of Africa — likely made with AI tools — mislabeled every country during a State Department presentation abroad this week. CONCACAF rejected today FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s plans to allow private investors to buy stakes in the World Cup. The organization, which represents the U.S. and 40 other member associations, joins the powerful European governing body in denouncing the proposal. THE COURTS The DOJ awakened a terrorist deportation court for the first case in its 30-year existence. Palestinian authorities are petitioning the Supreme Court to stave off a $ million penalty that they argue would destabilize critical government services in the West Bank. IVORY ‘COAST’ THANK YOU FOR READING Today’s newsletter was produced by Brett Bachman, Kate Nocera and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: Democrats Want to Avoid an Election Season Shutdown
stories.author: Stephen Neukam, Igor Bobic
stories.summary: “No one wants a shutdown in October,” said Sen. Patty Murray, Democrats’ top appropriator.
stories.content: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., right and Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., left, listen during a news conference on IVF, Thursday, July 23, , in Washington. (AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib) Mariam Zuhaib/AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib Democrats only have one major leverage point left against the Trump administration — and they're not about to use it. With Congress approaching a government funding cliff at the end of September, key Senate Democrats signaled they want to take the threat of a government shutdown off the table. Several told NOTUS this week that they are open to a short-term stopgap spending measure to get through the election. “If we can come up with a good bipartisan [continuing resolution], that would be great,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told NOTUS. Last year, Democrats forced a record-breaking 43-day government shutdown over expiring Obamacare tax credits, and earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security was shut down for months due to a fight over immigration enforcement and Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding. But on the verge of an election in which Democrats hope to retake power in the Capitol, they seem ready to punt the issue. “We certainly want to avoid a government shutdown, and Democrats have been very clear about that,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), a member of the Senate Appropriations Committee, told NOTUS on Wednesday. Van Hollen was one of the Democrats last year who blocked GOP attempts to reopen the government during the record-breaking shutdown. “We hope that Republicans will negotiate in good faith.” Democrats in both chambers bristled at the opening salvo in funding negotiations from the GOP last week. House Republicans passed a short-term funding package that would kick the shutdown deadline to December. Democrats have panned the bill, arguing it doesn’t include adequate restrictions on how Trump administration officials could move funding around. Democrats have also laid out a red line that they will not approve additional funding for ICE without concessions on reforms from the White House. Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), the top Democrat on the Appropriations panel, said Wednesday that she is working with Senate Republicans to draft a short-term funding measure into December that would “fix the problems with the bill that the House Republicans drafted.” Republicans need the support of at least seven Senate Democrats to pass any government funding package to avoid a filibuster. “No one wants a shutdown in October,” Murray said. Sen. Katie Britt (R-Alabama), another member of the Appropriations Committee, told NOTUS this week that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the status of government funding talks. “I appreciate at this point people engaging in a meaningful way, which truly seems to be what's occurring,” Britt said. Murray said Wednesday that a short-term deal would give lawmakers time to negotiate full spending bills for . The government will shut down at the end of September without the passage of spending bills or a stopgap measure. Progressive grassroots groups have heavily criticized congressional Democrats for failing to stand up to the Trump administration, urging them to get more aggressive in opposing the president’s budget. "Democrats should use every ounce of leverage they have to protect their constituents and lower costs for working families — including continuing to hold the line against any additional funding for ICE or Border Patrol without ironclad guardrails,” Andrew O’Neill, director of advocacy at the progressive group Indivisible, said in a statement. Pushing some Democrats toward a bipartisan compromise is the threat from Republican leaders to use the budget reconciliation process to fund the government. Reconciliation requires just a majority vote for passage and skips a potential filibuster in the Senate. Republicans earlier this year used that process to fund ICE and Border Protection, despite Democratic objections. That move would cut Democrats out of the funding talks altogether. “It’s a bit of a pick-your-poison moment,” said Minnesota Sen. Tina Smith, acknowledging concerns about another Republican reconciliation package. But other Democrats are still grappling with how to proceed on government funding given the Trump administration’s recent admission in court that it canceled grants for clean energy programs that Congress approved solely based on whether states voted for Trump in the election. “We now know this unequivocally, that the president of the United States is withholding money from states for purely political reasons, not any other reason, and New Jersey is being shortchanged significantly,” said New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker. “This is unconscionable what’s happening right now.”

stories.title: Boozman Plans Senate Farm Bill Markup Without Clear Bipartisan Deal
stories.author: Tyler Spence
stories.summary: The Agriculture Committee chair says he is working “to see if we can get a path forward.”
stories.content: Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) also said he is still unsure whether Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will be present for a committee markup. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) The chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee said Wednesday that the panel will take up the farm bill late next week, despite what has been a partisan deadlock on the measure. Sen. John Boozman (R-Arkansas) told reporters he is working closely with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), the committee’s ranking member, “to see if we can get a path forward” and that details are still being worked out. “We've got a good bill. I think lots of our members and both sides want to support it,” Boozman said. But Klobuchar, in a statement from her office, said there is still plenty of ground to cover. "We're continuing to have productive negotiations, but there is a lot of work left to do. Senate Ag Democrats have been clear that a Farm Bill must meet the needs of both farmers and families across America,” Klobuchar said in a statement. Boozman did not go into details of the negotiations, but any deal is likely to include some compromise on when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a change Republicans put in a previous law. Democrats have asked for a two-year delay in the cost shift for states with error rates above 6%, with one calling the request a “ deal-maker and a deal-breaker. ” Republicans have preferred to leave the changes made to SNAP from the “one big, beautiful bill” last year. Boozman also said he is still unsure whether Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will be present for the committee's markup. McConnell has been recovering from an illness and unable to participate, leaving the committee tied with 11 Republican and Democratic members each. “We're going to go forward regardless. I've always said for a farm to be successful it needs to be bipartisan,” Boozman said. “So that’s what we’re working on getting done.” Even if Republicans can advance the farm bill from the committee without Democratic support, it does not appear to have enough support to overcome the 60-vote threshold needed to advance on the Senate floor, since Democrats say they would not support the bill without a SNAP cost-shift delay. A markup, which would be the first time the committee has voted on a farm bill since , is tied to a hard deadline.The current extension of the farm bill runs through Sept. 30. The House passed its version of the farm bill on April 30.

stories.title: F-Bombs
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and Chief Medical Advisor to the President, claimed his right to not answer questions under the 5th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution during his testimony before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on July 29, in Washington, D.C. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 29, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Todd Blanche was given a 4 p.m. deadline to convince GOP Sens. John Cornyn and Thom Tillis that he was on track to kill Donald Trump ’s “anti-weaponization” fund and narrow the scope of the president’s tax audit immunity settlement — and thus secure support for his nomination. The Texas Republican is currently meeting with Tillis and Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley about the IRS immunity portion of the agreement. It’s unclear if tomorrow’s confirmation vote will move forward as planned. The White House still wants the Senate to move on Reconciliation 3.0 before August recess. But its push to add SAVE America Act provisions raised objections at today’s GOP lunch — including from John Thune — because including elections language would open up the bill to multiple committees outside of Rules, Punchbowl reports . Several Republicans are concerned the vote-a-rama process involved will force members to take politically damaging votes before the midterms. OMB Director Russ Vought said an increase in the debt limit would not be part of the pre-recess bill. “We believe that is something that should come later in Reconciliation 4.0,” he said. Is Thune still the man for the job, a reporter asked Donald Trump later in the afternoon? “We’re going to find out,” he replied. “I’ll let you know.” THE HILL After Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment during a COVID-19 hearing led by Sen. Rand Paul , the Kentucky Republican announced a vote next week to hold Fauci in contempt. The hearing prompted a rare congressional F-bomb: “Who the fuck do you think you were for doing that?” Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) asked Fauci, questioning his enforcement of strict policies during the pandemic. The Senate passed by unanimous consent a resolution opposing presidential clemency for Ghislaine Maxwell . Chuck Schumer said he met with Maine Senate hopeful Troy Jackson this morning, and that they are “working together to win the seat. THE ADMINISTRATION Trump promised the U.S. would “beat the fucking shit” out of Iran after the country conducted a ballistic missile attack on American forces in the region. The attack was intercepted. The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady today, again forgoing a cut that the White House would prefer. The White House is asking for $10 million in additional funding for events held by Freedom . Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu called their meeting yesterday a success. But the summit did little to resolve central issues in the U.S.-Israel relationship, NOTUS’ Akbar Shahid Ahmed reports . THE COURTS James Comey’s attorneys argue DOJ officials intentionally misled judges in their quest to charge the former FBI director with threatening to kill the president. ‘I NEED JHELP’ THANK YOU FOR READING Today’s newsletter was produced by Brett Bachman and Erik Schutz. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: Signal Sent. Now What?
stories.author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walks with Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Roger Wicker and Jim Risch as he arrives for a meeting at the U.S. Capitol on July 28, . Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Today’s notice: What comes next after last night’s Senate vote. Slotkin weighs in on “Ogre-gate.” An uncomfortably timed pardon for Pennsylvania’s 7th. Wasserman Schultz’s redistricting problem. One woman’s quest to claw back Platner donations. And: federal workers vs. the EEOC. THE LATEST The Senate sent a message: We stand with Ukraine. By a vote of 86-12 last night, the Senate advanced a Russia sanctions package that was in part a tribute to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who had long championed the issue, and in part a strong rebuke of a movement to dial back U.S. support for Ukraine in the country’s long war countering Vladimir Putin ’s invasion. The bill had languished before Graham’s death, NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Hamed Ahmadi write , but got moving again in part due to a provision by Graham’s replacement — his sister, Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina). The new language would extend existing sanctions authority over Iran’s energy and weapons sectors through , as demanded by Donald Trump . Sanctions supporters say the cloture vote was all anyone needs to know about where the president stands now, despite his administration’s initial skepticism of ongoing support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . The Ukrainian leader watched the vote from the Senate gallery last night, calling it “a big signal to Europe, a big signal to Ukraine, big support of our people.” It’s still, though, just a signal. The bill still needs final passage in the Senate and in the House, which isn’t back until Aug. 31 and where the sanctions measure’s chances are less than assured. Some Democrats see the bill as a shadow endorsement of Trump’s tariff powers. “I don’t know that we have much evidence that he’s going to use it to do what we need him to do,” said Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Georgia), one of those 12 “no” votes. Plenty of people from MAGAworld remain skeptical of Ukraine, and are not interested in continuing support for the war. Yesterday, however, Politico reported on Trump ally Laura Loomer ’s conversion to a Ukraine backer. But that high-profile shift may not be enough. “The idea that there’s been some sea change in opinion amongst the base as it relates to Ukraine isn’t accurate,” a Republican strategist close to the White House told NOTUS’ Jasmine Wright. “The Republican establishment has always had Zelenskyy’s back. Hopefully they’ll learn how to have America’s before November.” Open tabs: Federal Immigration Agents Called Latinos Racial Slurs While Conducting Stops, Video Shows (NOTUS); Senate Confirms Jay Clayton as Director of National Intelligence (NOTUS); ICE Arrests Surge at Airports, Opening New Front in Deportation Drive (NYT); US thwarts Iranian missile attack and launches strikes with Saudi Arabia against militias in Iraq (AP) From the campaign trail Elissa Slotkin comes off the sidelines in the Michigan primary. “All leaders should be thoughtful about their language and not use language about hurting people,” the Democratic senator from Michigan told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic when asked about the recent “Ogre-gate” controversy in the hotly contested Senate primary between Rep. Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed . Slotkin is one of the few remaining Democratic electeds in the state not to take a side in the primary. Her language was couched but suggested she’s joining the chorus condemning El-Sayed for using the term, which some thought was aimed at Stevens. El-Sayed said it was actually about Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania). Department of Awkward Timing. On June 30, Republican megadonor Adam Kidan , a key figure in the Jack Abramoff fraud and lobbying scandal, donated $2, to the leadership PAC for Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-Pennsylvania). On July 3, Trump pardoned Kidan, wiping away a guilty plea to fraud charges and likely vacating significant restitution payments. NOTUS’ Avani Kalra reports that Mackenzie’s office said the congressman didn’t talk to the White House or Trump about the pardon before it happened, and declined to say whether he’ll keep the campaign donation. Mackenzie might have just been the last stop on the donation gravy train. Kidan has been a prolific donor this cycle, particularly in Pennsylvania, giving to GOP Reps. Rob Bresnahan , Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry . Scenes from redistricting: Florida’s 20th. “The greatest civil rights threat that’s facing us today” is how rapper Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell , formerly of 2 Live Crew, described Democratic Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz ’s decision to run in the Fort Lauderdale district. Campbell is one of several Black candidates running in the district’s Democratic primary, and has assailed the veteran white congresswoman for jumping into a district that, until state Republicans redrew the lines this year, was majority Black. NOTUS’ Oriana González reports on how fears of diluted Black political power are playing out in the primary. THE BIG ONE Refund, please! There’s an effort afoot to help Graham Platner donors recoup their money to the now defunct Maine campaign. The only question is whether those who gave money will actually do it. Activist and lawyer Cheyenne Hunt is deploying her organization, Reckoning Action, to mass text the donors directly and walk them through how to get their money back, NOTUS’ Oriana González reports . It’s a move Hunt took after seeing former Rep. Eric Swalwell use campaign funds to pay legal fees after multiple sexual assault allegations. Automated texts were sent with this message: “If you donated to Graham Platner and feel betrayed, you’re not alone. You signed up to help elect a champion for freedom and equality and take back the Senate — not to fund a predator.” FEC reports showed Platner had $1.7 million in cash on hand at the end of last month. NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Sports desk: As Training Camp Begins, Commanders Say They Are ‘Happy’ With Receivers , by Martenzie Johnson ON NOTUS PODCAST From your favorite podcast app: On today’s episode of On NOTUS , Rep. Nanette Barragán (D-California) said Latino voters who backed Trump in have “buyer’s remorse.” “They’re looking at what’s happening and saying, ‘This is not what we voted for,’” Barragán told NOTUS’ Oriana González. Barragán also talked about her vote to end all U.S. aid to Israel, the future of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus and her recruiting pitch to former MLB players to bolster the Democratic lineup in the Congressional Baseball Game. NOTUS PERSPECTIVES Last week’s arrival of a new season of “King of the Hill” is good news for America, says Matt K. Lewis, because the show is a roadmap to a better conservatism . NEW ON NOTUS EEOC pauses class actions by employees against federal agencies. That’s the allegation from a new lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees, which has asked a judge to compel the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to resume processing class-action complaints, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports . The upshot of the pause is federal employees alleging sexual harassment or other forms of discrimination are currently blocked from collectively seeking relief, he writes. The EEOC did not respond to a request for comment. Eric notes that Project suggested that the EEOC should no longer hear complaints from federal employees, and that those responsibilities should be transferred to the Merit Systems Protection Board. stories.title: Mike Lee’s Threats to Nix August Recess Are Infuriate His Colleagues
stories.author: Al Weaver
stories.summary: How would canceling recess go over with Senate Republicans? “A total nonstarter,” one senior GOP aide said.
stories.content: Sources said that outside of his social media postings, Lee has done little to try to sway skeptical colleagues. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) Bill Clark/AP Senate Republican leaders are used to headaches from Utah Sen. Mike Lee, but the battle is reaching an apex as Lee attempts to derail the August recess and force another vote on President Donald Trump’s priority voting bill. Lee said that he planned to object to the upper chamber’s planned five-week August recess “until such a time as the Senate has passed the SAVE America Act.” On Monday, Trump joined Lee’s call and demanded that the Senate cancel recess to push through the bill. Those loud, and very online, efforts are part of a deepening rift between Trump and members of Senate leadership, who have little interest in keeping the conference in town to take a perilous vote only months before the midterm elections. Top Senate Republicans not only believe those votes would be a waste of time, but they would be politically problematic. Staying in session would preclude incumbent senators from campaigning back home, though senators who vote to give themselves a long summer break might have a difficult time explaining themselves to constituents. "If I thought there was a path to getting a result, I'm all for it,” said Senate Majority Leader John Thune. “But if we are going to be sitting here and in endless quorum calls, I don't know if that's in anybody's best interest.” Thune also noted that versions of the SAVE America Act have failed on five occasions to win simple majority support. Not only does it not have the requisite Democratic support to overcome a filibuster, there are not enough votes to weaken the 60-vote threshold in favor of a “talking” filibuster that Lee and Trump have repeatedly hailed. “It’s an act of futility,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said of Trump’s call to cancel recess. When asked how canceling recess to work on the voting bill would go over with members, one senior Senate GOP aide was blunt. “A total nonstarter,” the aide said, adding that the “math doesn’t math.” The Senate’s much-cherished August break is set to run from Aug. 7 until Sept. 13. House lawmakers fled Washington last week and are set to return the week before Labor Day. As for Thune allies, much of the frustration since the start of the year has centered on Lee, who has led the messaging effort almost entirely through his rapid-fire X account. A Lee-forced tally would force Republicans to take a difficult vote and, effectively, open them up to an uptick in criticism from conservative activists with massive followings and, potentially, the president. “Of course,” Cornyn said when asked if Lee is putting members in a bad spot. “He’s demoralizing our base of voters we’re depending on in 99 days to elect Republicans. What possible rationale could there be for that other than self-aggrandizement.” A pair of sources noted that outside of his social media postings, Lee has done little to try to sway skeptical colleagues — and is largely quiet during weekly Senate GOP lunches. “The worst threat to a GOP majority: Mike Lee’s continued SAVE Act antics,” a second senior Senate GOP aide told NOTUS. The second aide also noted that colleagues have frequently observed him scrolling through X on his phone and view his SAVE Act actions “as a ploy to become a social media star” rather than a serious legislative effort. "I think it's snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. I think what we need to do is get out of here,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina). “Staying here longer and just assuming that because we're here, we're going to bridge some profound differences between people, is a catastrophic political miscalculation and shows that we're tone to the fact that we have a real threat ahead of us with respect to losing the majority.” “I want the Senate members home doing that, not doing the performative politics up here that people like Mike Lee want to do,” Tillis . Lee is not without allies: Sens. Rick Scott (R-Florida) and Ashley Moody (R-Florida) have joined his cause. “While the Spartans said ‘come back with your shield, or on it,’ my demand is a lot easier: only return home if we carry the SAVE America Act as a prize for the whole country,” Lee said, defending his position, in a statement to NOTUS. The timing of Lee’s pressure campaign could not be worse in the eyes of some in the conference, as Election Day is coming increasingly in view for members. Democrats need to pick off four seats in November in order to take back the majority, and the road for them requires toppling a number of incumbent Republicans — with Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) at the top of the list. “People want to campaign,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), a member of Republican leadership. “I just came from inspecting floods and damage in my state. Staying connected is really important.” Threats and calls to cancel the August break have become something of a tradition over the years. Then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell canceled the first week of the break in for Republicans to work on health care after the late Sen. John McCain blocked the party’s “skinny repeal” effort. Only a year later, the Kentucky Republican canceled more than two weeks of the break. The move kept a number of Senate Democrats at the Capitol and away from campaigning in their home states. Republicans are expected to discuss how to handle recess in the coming days, including during conference-wide luncheons. “It’ll be a week,” Capito said.

stories.title: ‘I’ve Done More for You Than Your Parents’
stories.author: Kelly Poe, Manuela Silva
stories.content: President Donald Trump speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground Monday, July 27, , in Milford, Mich. Paul Sancya/AP Photo Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 27, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Donald Trump spoke this afternoon in Michigan, touting his economic agenda and blasting former administrations for actions he said have hurt the auto industry in this key swing state. “I’ve done more for you than your parents, OK? Your parents are good, I’m not gonna knock your parents, but I have been better to you than your parents,” Trump told the audience. Former Michigan GOP Rep.
