Mike Rogers is expected to a tough Senate race against either Rep. Haley Stevens or Abdul El-Sayed , who will debate tonight ahead of the Aug. 4 primary. Trump thinks the Senate should delay its planned August recess until it passes the SAVE America Act, he posted on Truth Social this morning. John Thune has repeatedly insisted that the voting bill doesn’t have the votes. “He’s got to get his job done. It’s fine. I have a good relationship with John Thune ,” Trump told reporters later today. Trump that he’s never thought about replacing Thune. THE HILL Sen. Mitch McConnell is not yet medically cleared to return to work after his June 14 fall, he said in a press release that included a new photo of the senator. The House Ethics Committee announced it is looking into Rep. Lance Gooden (R-Texas), saying it would announce next steps by Nov. 9. THE ADMINISTRATION Trump said the U.S. had paused strikes on Iran at Tehran’s request in a renewed attempt at diplomacy. Trump told Axios that the two countries were in “very deep talks,” but threatened “very strong military action” if they don’t move quickly. ICE has made plans to target and detain Haitian immigrants as hundreds of thousands of Haitians prepare for their Temporary Protected Status to expire, CBS reports . Asylum applicants could see their cases funneled directly to immigration courts following a rule change this morning, allowing USCIS officers to potentially skip interviewing those applying for asylum and instead send them to immigration judges. THE COURTS James Comey asked a judge Monday to dismiss the federal charges against him for posting a photo of seashells spelling out “86 47” last year. THE STATES The investigation of Pete Buttigeig that separated him from his twins last month stemmed from an unsubstantiated allegation from someone authorities later deemed possibly “mentally unstable,” The Washington Post reported . TO TUCK OR NOT TO TUCK? THANK YOU FOR READINGToday’s newsletter was produced by Matt Berman and Jonann Brady. If you like it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: Trump Tells the Senate to Delay Recess Until His Voting Bill Passes
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: At least four Republican senators have signed on to the effort.
stories.content: Alex Brandon/AP President Donald Trump said Monday that Senate Majority Leader John Thune should keep the Senate in session until his signature voting legislation clears the upper chamber — something he’s been repeatedly told is on arrival. “John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to ‘leave town’ until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER” the president posted on Truth Social. Trump has been relentless in calling on the Senate to pass the Republican-backed election bill that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to show proof of U.S. citizenship. But Thune and other Republican senators have said they simply don’t have the votes, leaving them at an impasse with the White House. While many Republicans support the bill, some — including Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine — have voted against the measure. Trump also said that terminating the filibuster — another no-go in the Senate — would allow it to address the “looming debt ceiling.” Some senators have called to cancel the recess to pass the election bill. “I hereby object to any effort to put the Senate into recess in August—at least until such time as the Senate has passed the SAVE America Act—and hereby request a roll call vote,” Sen. Mike Lee of Utah posted on X on Sunday. He suggested he would attempt to block the recess, which could complicate the matter but would not necessarily prevent it. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida replied to Lee to say he supported the effort. “I will vote to stay in session unless we have passed the SAVE America Act,” he wrote on X. Sens. Ashley Moody of Florida and Jim Banks of Indiana similarly called for the Senate to stay in session until the SAVE Act is passed.

stories.title: Potential Presidential 2028 Democrats Split Over Russia Sanctions
stories.author: Igor Bobic
stories.summary: Imposing new sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine is broadly bipartisan, but some Democrats warn President Trump will go too far with new authority.
stories.content: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff said he had questions about how to go about implementing the bill. Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images A bipartisan bill aiming to penalize Moscow's war in Ukraine has exposed a fissure among potential Democratic presidential contenders, some of whom worry the measure would turbocharge President Donald Trump’s power to impose tariffs and harm the economy. The bill, titled the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of ,” could get a vote in the Senate as early as next week. It would authorize tariffs of up to % on the top five foreign purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, which is a key source of revenue for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. The long-stalled bill gained fresh momentum after the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, its champion and original Republican sponsor. But critics argue the legislation is written too broadly and would hand Trump unprecedented, broad authority to impose geopolitical tariffs on U.S. trading partners. They point out the legislation allows him to go even further than the second round of global tariffs he imposed on many U.S. imports last week, which could exacerbate inflation and raise prices for consumers. “Trump has shown himself to abuse tariff authority in a really reckless way that's causing harm to our economy,” New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said. “I know that we've been working to narrow that, so that's what I'm going to be looking at.” The debate over the bill has extended to other Senate Democrats eyeing a run for the White House who are supportive of Ukraine and its fight for survival but also wary of voting to give Trump a blank check that could come back to bite them in a Democratic presidential primary. “I've been fairly consistent that what is happening in Ukraine — and making sure Ukraine wins this war — is in direct national interest of the United States,” said Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego. “There's been a bipartisan effort for almost a year and a half now to pass this bill, and I think that we should pass it and not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.” Another Arizona Democrat and potential candidate, Sen. Mark Kelly, is one of the bill’s 62 co-sponsors, and he said he’d have preferred imposing even higher tariffs on purchasers of Russian oil and gas. The original legislation would have authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to %, but that was reduced to attract more support in the Senate. “They narrowed it, which was good,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), another co-sponsor. Other Democratic senators who have been mentioned as potential Democratic contenders are taking a wait-and-see approach on the bill. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is “still looking at,” the bill, referring to “interesting” questions about its tariff provisions. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff said he had questions about how to go about implementing the bill, while his fellow Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, another potential Democratic candidate, said that giving Trump additional tariff authorities would be “deeply concerning.” “I would like to see if we can get to a better version of the bill,” Warnock said. “I certainly support the notion of checking Putin, and I'm deeply concerned about the implications of his ambitions, not only with respect to Ukraine, but where he might go next.” Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations who has also made moves fueling speculation about a bid, said he hasn’t yet made up his mind on the bill. Supporters of the bill are working to address concerns about its tariff provisions. As it stands, it would give the president authority to impose sanctions on three groups of countries: top five importers of Russian oil, top five natural gas importers and top five Russia sanctions evaders. It does not specify which countries would apply specifically, which critics argue opens the door to tariffs on U.S. allies, some of whom also purchase Russian oil. Senate Majority Leader John Thune is hoping to secure an agreement from Democrats to fast-track the bill, which requires the consent of all senators. Without that, it would take the Senate days to consider the bill — time that Thune cannot spare given a laundry list of legislation and confirmations he wants to plow through before the Senate leaves town early next month for its annual August recess. Democrats could use their leverage to demand votes on amendments in exchange for agreeing to fast-track the bill. But there’s no guarantee that Thune would agree, or that those amendments would succeed. Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, a supporter of sanctioning Russia who has raised objections about the bill’s tariff provisions, declined to answer when asked if he would object to speeding it along on the Senate floor. “I'm going to continue to make the case to my colleagues that, after all of this work on something that is absolutely right and correct and the smart thing to do, doing something that is going to undermine the affordability agenda doesn't make any sense to me,” Wyden said. Booker is hoping to see more changes before he supports the bill. “Especially with Ukraine's increasing reach [in Russia], it's really time to do everything we can to support them,” he said. “But the details are really important to me.”

stories.title: A House Republican’s Final ‘Mission’
stories.author: Paul Kane
stories.summary: As he battles terminal heart disease, Neal Dunn is taking on Big Auto and hoping his Trump connection helps.
stories.content: The Florida Republican wants to see right-to-repair legislation passed as his final act in Congress. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Rep. Neal Dunn shows up for votes these days in a scooter that helps get him to the House floor. A sign is taped to the front of it, allowing him to serve as a one-man mobile lobbying shop: “Get the REPAIR ACT Dunn!!!” The Florida Republican, who is retiring at the end of this term, has made the bill — which would defend the rights of independent auto repair shops — his legislative swan song. Dunn, 73, almost resigned earlier this year after a terminal heart disease diagnosis. But after working with doctors at Walter Reed Medical Center, he has committed to serving out the remainder of his term. “I do what I do because it's a mission, really, a mission,” Dunn told NOTUS in an interview Tuesday. “You run for office, and it's kind of like joining the Army. You do a mission, and you can't leave the mission.” Dunn’s proposal was slated to be part of the federal highway bill, but support for it fell apart just before the House Energy and Commerce Committee took up the provision amid pushback from powerful auto lobbying forces. Dunn’s new strategy has now largely focused on trying to win over an audience of one: President Donald Trump. He talks more frequently with the president than most rank-and-file lawmakers, in part because of Trump’s role in giving Dunn a little more of a lease on life. In the late winter, as his diagnosis grew bleak, Dunn drew up a plan with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis to “sneak out the back door” into retirement. He would announce his resignation set to some point in July, and the Republican governor could call a special election for then. Dunn intended to serve right up until that time, if his health allowed, so that his replacement in the heavily Republican district could be selected and House Speaker Mike Johnson would not lose a reliable GOP vote for any length of time. Then Trump called Dunn from the golf course with DeSantis and told him not to retire. "I've got the best doctors in the world. They're big. They're beautiful. They're on their way. Don't go anywhere,” Trump said, as Dunn recalled. That stint at Walter Reed bought Dunn more time, but it didn’t heal him. “No question, my prognosis is better than it was,” he said. “You know, I'm still on a glide path.” At a March news conference, Trump blurted out that Dunn would have been “ by June” if not for his intervention, something the lawmaker was trying to keep private. “Obviously Trump kind of outed me there,” he told NOTUS, smiling. Ever since, he’s pledged to be on hand for Johnson and Trump anytime an important, close vote is scheduled. He flew up from Florida for crucial votes on Tuesday and Wednesday on national defense policy, but he did not attend Thursday’s less consequential votes on other matters. Rep_Dunn_Edits/_C0A4778 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Rank-and-file Republicans applaud Dunn’s perseverance as other perfectly healthy members skip key votes to campaign for higher office. In a different congressional era, lawmakers facing their own mortality were granted a last favor. Just before he died in , Rep. Joe Moakley (D-Massachusetts), who had chaired the House Rules Committee for years, asked Democratic leaders for a final wish: install his former aide, Rep. Jim McGovern, to the rules panel. McGovern got the nod and now serves as the committee’s top Democrat. So far, Dunn has received no such reward for his loyalty, but the president did voice support for independent repair shops at an Oval Office event last month, a day after he met with top car manufacturer CEOs. “They don’t want people to fix their car. I said, ‘That’s strange, I’d never heard of that.’ They have a thing — nobody’s allowed to fix their car,” Trump told reporters . “We’ll get it all straightened away,” he . Dunn, an Army-trained surgeon, served his residency at Walter Reed and eventually ran a large urology practice in Florida. Given his background, his passion for the Right to Equitable and Professional Auto Industry Repair Act is perhaps a surprising coda to his congressional career. But Dunn fought (and won) a similar battle with medical devices, and dove in when he found out the same debate was happening in the auto industry. But Dunn is up against a very powerful duo of lobbying forces: large auto manufacturers and car dealers. “The basic moral question is: If I buy a car, truck, a motorcycle, whatever, from you, is it mine or is it yours? It's mine,” he said. “I buy it, and you know who owns it, and then I should be able to control it. If I want to put a torch to the thing, I can do that — but I can't repair it? That's crazy.” Dunn says the bigger corporations are trying to force car owners into pricier repairs, freezing out the usually cheaper independent operators. This comes as new cars have soared in cost and Americans are holding on to their old cars longer than ever, making the auto repair market more lucrative than ever. “Ford, GM, Toyota — they all dug in, and they made it really, really, really difficult to allow the secondary market to continue,” he said. The lead opponent to the REPAIR Act is the National Automobile Dealers Association, which has accused the car insurance industry of trying to gain access to sensitive “vehicle data.” “Insurers are pursuing controversial provisions to lower their costs and limit consumer choice by expanding the use of cheaper, non-original and recycled parts for vehicle repairs,” Kerry Feehery, a senior lobbyist for NADA, wrote in a memo last month after the a compromise deal on the bill collapsed. The Dunn-related compromise would have greatly expanded the amount of auto technology shared with independent repair shops beyond the deal they reached in . Cars have advanced so much technologically over the past that repair shops need more information from auto makers and dealers to fix cars. Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Kentucky), chair of the Energy and Commerce Committee, acknowledged Thursday that the deal fell apart because the car dealers are very powerful and turned members against the proposal. “They're in everybody's district. I mean, that's people listening to their constituents, and so that's what you hear,” he told NOTUS, pledging to try to find more support for Dunn’s original ideas. “We're still working.” Dunn came in with the class of , along with a low-profile Louisiana Republican who would go on to become House speaker. But his friendship with Johnson has thus far been unable to overcome the more powerful lobbying forces. Mike Johnson ( , AR: 1.50)“The speaker has a lot of pressures from different directions, and I don't know all those pressures. I'm sure that GM and Ford are two of them,” he said. So far in , GM has spent more on federal lobbying ($11.4 million) than any individual company in America . Only a few major associations like the Chamber of Commerce have a bigger budget. Time is running short both for the House — it’s scheduled for just 16 days in session over the next three-and-a-half months — and for Dunn’s tenure on Capitol Hill. Private polling shows overwhelming support for the independent repair shops. So Dunn said he’s hopeful Trump could throw his full support behind the REPAIR Act and get it attached to one of several must-pass bills at the end of the year. “There's just not that many issues that are 85 percent. So, you know, I feel good about it,” he said. Dunn paused to consider the forces he is up against. “I'm not — I'm not betting my soul on it.”

stories.title: Mike Johnson is ‘Sick of This Shit’ (But Sorry He Said So)
stories.author: Reese Gorman
stories.summary: Most House Republicans are frustrated that a small band of conservatives are upending the party’s agenda, yet they few consequences.
stories.content: House Speaker Mike Johnson continues to struggle with his own members for control of his party's agenda. J. Scott Applewhite/AP Speaker Mike Johnson was at his wit’s end. For months, he had been dealing with one rebellion after another, and now members were about to tank a bipartisan veterans bill. The House was scheduled to quickly approve the bill that Thursday morning and head out for the weekend. Trying to salvage another priority for his party, Johnson brought a handful of members, including those threatening to block the bill, into his “ceremonial room” across from the House chamber. Reps. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida), who opposed the bill, and Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), who supported it, started yelling at each other. Luna then pointed her anger toward Johnson. Fed up, the speaker snapped and replied, “I’m sick of this shit,” according to multiple sources in the room. Witnesses were shocked that the typically even-keeled Johnson had lost his cool. Almost immediately, he apologized to Luna for his outburst. He then walked over to the elementary-school-aged son of Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado), who had witnessed the interaction, and got down on one knee and apologized for cursing in front of him, the sources said. Johnson left the room and did what he’s been forced to do repeatedly this Congress: pull the bill because a few Republicans wouldn't agree to vote for it. NOTUS spoke with more than a dozen lawmakers and aides for a broader view of how the speaker’s daily crises — often brought about by his own members — continue to derail his party’s agenda. Most rank-and-file Republican members are upset with the handful who regularly make the House look like a hot mess. Some lawmakers refuse to be team players, and the incentive structure that rewards them makes governing impossible, they say. (Proposals that would punish those who step out of line are even being considered, sources told NOTUS.) “It creates anger and resentment,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska) said. “We want to get things done, and dysfunction’s not good.” Republicans have shut down the House floor, tanked rules, cursed at one another on the floor and gotten in each other's faces — and those are just the fights that have happened in public. In private, members have grown increasingly incensed at the state of the House of Representatives. And the episode between Luna and Johnson off of the House floor encapsulated that. Johnson and House Republicans have managed, with a razor-thin majority, to pass significant legislation, but it hasn’t been easy or pretty. This week the conference passed three marquee bills — the annual defense authorization bill, a budget resolution for defense and farm aid and a bill curbing lawmakers from trading individual stocks. But even these items came with significant hand-wringing and last-minute agita. A handful of members — particularly those on the far right — have learned they can use their votes as leverage to get what they want. Johnson has frequently placated most of their demands, much to the dismay of the rest of the conference. “The Republican conference is a diverse gathering of people, some of whom are really effective at getting things done and others who are more interested in knocking things down,” Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-South Dakota) told NOTUS. As the House starts its annual August recess, members are fed up that the rebels are being rewarded for their bad behavior. Mike Johnson ( , AR: 1.50)“The vast majority of members are team players who do not appreciate the minority, the small minority, that does that,” Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Florida) said of the members who block legislation. “I don’t appreciate it, but we live in that reality that they can leverage it. So there are the vast majority of us who don’t like that. We're team players.” But the group that’s spent this year holding things up view themselves as fighting for conservative principles. “It’s the hardcore conservatives against everybody else,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee) said. “Matt Gaetz told me, I remember, he said that, ‘We'll have more power if we don't have a supermajority; it gives us more opportunity because if we did, we’d just get run over,’” referring to the former House Republican who regularly clashed with top leaders. Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland), the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, said “the only measure is whether we are successful in delivering for the American people.” Members across the Republican conference agree on one thing: Johnson has the hardest job in Washington. Gimenez described Johnson as being in a “very difficult situation” and said, "It's tough to herd cats.” “So while some of us may be frustrated by some of the actions, it's not by his actions. It's merely by the actions of those few,” Gimenez . Bacon agreed, noting that with just a two-seat majority, “there's not a lot of leeway.” “They should be adults and be responsible. So it's really the individuals versus Mike. I mean, Mike can only do so much,” he said. Anna Paulina Luna ( , AR: 1.50)Earlier in the summer, Luna and a handful of other members shut down the House floor for more than two weeks over President Donald Trump’s priority voting bill that’s going nowhere in the Senate. Johnson eventually gave Luna a commitment the House would attach the bill to must-pass legislation in an attempt to force the Senate’s hand. In the past, lawmakers who rebelled against the speaker were punished; they lost a plum committee assignment or leaders refused to advance their bills. Now, with such a narrow majority, members believe there’s not much leadership can really do. “You have a chicken-and-egg situation,” one GOP member said. “There's really no ability to lay consequences on someone's feet when you need them again next week.” This House Republican said the way it typically plays out is unfair to everyone else. “You’ve seen the speaker and the leadership spend a wildly disproportionate amount of time with a narrow band of members. And, you know, that hasn't necessarily sat well with the couple that come here, work together, work hard and are trying to move their own objectives forward,” they said. But some members told NOTUS that Johnson is being an enabler by agreeing to almost every demand. “They get accommodated a lot, and we don't like it,” Bacon said. The constant cycle of rebels getting away with stalling Republican bills is prompting some members to come up with ways to punish them, sources tell NOTUS. When then-Speaker Paul Ryan challenges from those in the Freedom Caucus, Rep. Austin Scott (R-Georgia) proposed a rule that if any Republican voted procedurally with the Democrats and blocked legislation from coming to the floor, then the GOP-led steering committee — a panel that doles out committee assignments — could take action against the member by removing them from a committee or stripping them of a gavel. Rep. Austin Scott ( , AR: 1.50)Ryan ultimately rebuffed the plan. But now, Scott has revived the idea as a measure of accountability and is pitching his colleagues on it, two members with knowledge of the discussions told NOTUS. “It’s clear these guys are no longer representing their districts,” one of those Republican members told NOTUS. “So this would provide more to be put [on] the steering committee, not a speaker who effectively has a gun to his head every time he makes a decision.” Without any real ability to penalize lawmakers, Johnson has had to find different ways to keep his members in line. One strategy has been to make promises he can’t always keep. Back in June, Johnson promised hard-line conservatives a vote on a controversial immigration bill known as “HR 2” before the July 4 recess, but that upset more moderate members who didn’t want to vote on the bill in an election year. In turn, Johnson ended up not putting the bill up for a vote, which caused a ripple effect of drama. The speaker has also promised to include members’ wish lists in subsequent reconciliation packages as a way to punt fights to a later time. In , when members were upset that their priorities weren’t in the first reconciliation bill, Johnson assured them they would be included in the second party-line package the conference was planning to vote on in . When that bill became narrowly focused on funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol, the speaker promised those same members that their issues would be addressed in a third reconciliation bill. Mike Johnson ( , AR: 1.50)But the White House has instead commandeered that package to be for Iran war funding, aid for farmers and portions of the SAVE America Act. “Unfortunately, the call has been made,” said Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), who was the top Republican pushing for a larger reconciliation package that could have included policies tackling prescription-drug costs, energy affordability and fraud prevention. Burchett said the promise of another party-line bill is “a moving target” and that “it’s frustrating” when the goal keeps moving. One senior GOP member said Johsnon is acting as “a military tactician” when it comes to lining up legislation. “In order to hold the front line together, the speaker has been strategically retreating across the calendar,” the senior Republican said. But at some point, the speaker will have to the political realities of making members potentially vote for another sprawling reconciliation package, and that could impact his own future. “Will the great political battle come in September or after the November general election? I cannot say,” the member said. “But it is coming.”

stories.title: John Thune and the White House Are Openly Fighting Over the SAVE Act
stories.author: Al Weaver
stories.summary: “John’s doing the best he can, but John can’t put a gun to people’s head and make them vote a particular way,” Sen. John Kennedy said.
stories.content: Senate Majority Leader John Thune is left taking the intra-party arrows every time he admits there is little that can be done to move the bill along. Aaron Schwartz/Sipa USA via AP The battle over the SAVE America Act ratcheted up a few notches Thursday as the White House and Senate Majority Leader John Thune traded barbs over the lack of progress on the voting bill that President Donald Trump considers his top priority. Trump’s frustrations about the stalled legislation have simmered for months but took a sharp turn Wednesday. At a rally in Georgia, he panned the upper chamber as “a place you send things when you want them to die.” But it was a back-and-forth between White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt and Thune that really gas to the fire. When Leavitt was pressed about the Republican leader, she told reporters that the president's “patience is running out” — comments that did not sit well with Thune. “She or somebody else ought to get on the phone and get the votes, right?” the mild-mannered Thune shot back. “So instead of pointing the finger at Republicans, they might think about going after the people who are stopping it on the floor, which is the Democrats. And if there are Republicans that they think are gettable, get on the phone. Let’s get them to ‘yes.’” The exchange marked the latest crescendo in a battle that has lasted for much of the year, with Trump loyalists pounding the table to get the bill to the president’s desk despite the fact it can’t pass the Senate. The measure not only doesn’t have Democratic support to overcome a filibuster, it does not have the needed votes to weaken the 60-vote threshold in favor of a “talking” filibuster that Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) has championed. Even if that did happen, the bill has previously failed to win simple majority support. “We just don’t have the votes, and so there’s nothing that Senator Thune can do to change that. This idea that he can just command members of the Republican Conference to get in line is just a fantasy, so I think it’s unfair,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) told reporters. Thune is left taking the intra-party arrows every time he admits there is little that can be done to move the bill along. Republicans are left frustrated over what they believe are unrealistic expectations by Trump and conservative activists over the bill’s future. Cornyn blamed people misleading the White House. “I don’t know who it was that sold the president on this idea that this was attainable, but it’s creating a circular firing squad for Republicans,” Cornyn said. “Here we are, what, days before the midterm elections, and this is not a great place for us to be.” The bill would require voters to present a photo ID to vote and proof of citizenship for voter registration, and would severely curtail the use of mail-in balloting. Trump has insisted that as much of the SAVE America Act as possible has to advance before the August recess. The House took a step of its own before it departed for a weekslong recess by green-lighting $10 billion in incentives for states to pass portions of the voting measure. However, the Senate isn’t in lockstep. Thune announced this week that he won’t move the House’s budget resolution before the August break. He explained this was a strategy to preserve a third reconciliation bill if one is needed to pass a government spending measure before the Sept. 30 funding deadline. He has also been loathe to allow another vote-a-rama, required under reconciliation rules, before November to keep from exposing vulnerable incumbents to tough votes. A number of other Republicans also took issue with Leavitt’s characterization of Thune and indicated they believed he was dealing with the math. “Everybody wants to talk about 60 votes — we don’t have 51 votes,” Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota) said. Others believe Thune has few options at his disposal. “I don’t think it’s a news flash. John’s doing the best he can, but John can’t put a gun to people’s head and make them vote a particular way,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana). “When you’re majority leader, you take a lot of the spears and the arrows. That’s his job.” “I think John is generally for the [SAVE America Act.] It’s just that we have some people that aren’t,” he continued. Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Thom TIllis of North Carolina and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska have voted against versions of the voting bill. Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida), who has at times been a thorn in Thune’s side and has been a preeminent supporter of the measure, indicated he’s sympathetic to both sides in the spat. “It’s hard being leader. … I think he’s working hard,” Scott said of Thune. “I’m sure if I was the president of the United States, I’d be frustrated if everything I wanted didn’t get done. So that is probably pretty common.” Trump has recently attempted to use the voting proposal as a cudgel, further complicating matters for the Republican leader. Last month he said he wouldn’t sign a reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act unless SAVE America was approved as well. At this point, Trump’s maneuvers have left members exasperated as they readily acknowledge the situation is basically at an impasse. “Nobody said it was going to be easy,” Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) said about the bill before criticizing Leavitt’s remarks. “I can’t imagine that she knows what it’s like to be a leader in the Senate with 53 very strong-minded people that have different opinions.” “If [the president’s] going to be an immovable force, I don’t know why they can’t be an immovable force too,” she said of Republicans opposing the SAVE America Act. “That’s what we’re seeing here — immovable forces coming up against one another.”

stories.title: House Republicans Focus on Democrats' Plans, Not Their Own Wins
stories.author: Kadia Goba
stories.summary: Republicans admit messaging on their own tax bill has been challenging, so they are warning voters about what Democrats would mean to their pocketbooks.
stories.content: “What’s really important as relates to the tax code is to contrast what we’ve done to help make life more affordable for families and put more money in their pocket versus what the Democrats would do,” Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) told reporters on Thursday ahead of a weekslong summer recess. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP House Republican leaders are kicking off their summer campaign blitz warning voters about how Democrats’ policies will increase their taxes instead of touting their own signature tax cut bill. The strategy highlights the difficulties GOP lawmakers when it comes to voters feeling the economic benefits of their policies. “What’s really important as relates to the tax code is to contrast what we’ve done to help make life more affordable for families and put more money in their pocket versus what the Democrats would do,” Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-Louisiana) told reporters on Thursday ahead of a weekslong summer recess. Republicans passed a party-line package to extend and make permanent President Donald Trump’s tax cuts. Since then, they have struggled to make the marquee legislation an effective pitch to voters as they look to retain their slim majority. “Do we communicate our ideas great all the time? That's been a fault of the Republican Party,” Scalise acknowledged. Instead, Republicans are highlighting the far-left insurgence within the Democratic Party, often referring to Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates as “communists.” And in many cases working to paint the entire party as extreme leftist. This approach differs from what some members competing in purple districts say they’d prefer to emphasize, even as top leaders fan out to those contests this summer. “We’ll focus exclusively on the issues that matter to people, from affordability and the cost of living, and what we’ve done on taxes and housing. Obviously, energy costs, and not just gas, but utilities,” Rep. Mike Lawler, (R-New York), who represents a district Kamala Harris won in , told NOTUS. Lawler faces Cait Conley, a military veteran who Democrats note is running slightly ahead of Lawler in polling. Republicans have seized on recent primaries in New York City where voters voted for Mayor Zohran Mamdani and a handful of democratic socialist who beat out Democrats who were viewed as establishment candidates. Speaker Mike Johnson and Scalise have plans to visit New York state in August. Rep. Derrick Van Orden, whose Wisconsin district became more competitive this cycle, according to Cook Political Report’s rating, said he’ll be traveling the district on his Harley talking about “gas, groceries and grandkids” and hopes leadership does the same. Another Republican in a tight race, Pennsylvania Rep. John Bresnahan, said leaders should focus on affordability but also speak to issues important to northeast Pennsylvania such as eradicating an Obama-era storm water management fee levied on homeowners. “Absolutely, we could talk about no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security,” Bresnahan said. “These are all incredible things that we could take back home.” When asked if Democrats’ proposals should be part of their talking points, he indicated yes. “He could certainly talk about some of the communism ideology that seems to be infiltrating the Democrat Party right now,” Bresnahan said about Scalise. Democrats, meanwhile, accused Republicans of making them the scapegoat for rising living costs. They’re planning their own campaign pitch to voters starting this Sunday. “The do nothing Republican Congress has been a complete and total disaster. Costs haven’t gone down. Costs have gone up. Gas prices are out of control. The war in Iran is spiraling, and they continue to try to divert blame onto us,” Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told NOTUS. “The American people aren’t buying it .”

stories.title: Democrats See an Opening on Trade — If They Can Agree
stories.author: Jade Lozada, Violet Jira
stories.summary: Democrats see the Trump administration’s renegotiations of USMCA as a political opportunity.
stories.content: Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, led a letter to Trump in November advocating for “significant renegotiations” of the USMCA. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Democrats say they have an opportunity to stand up to President Donald Trump on trade. They just haven't reached a consensus on what their trade agenda is. The Trump administration opened the door to a renegotiation of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. In a hearing with senators this week , United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he wanted interim agreements with both countries by the end of the year, and to tackle thornier issues in . Those talks, according to Rep. Jimmy Panetta (D-California), are Democrats’ chance to “take back trade” from Republicans, who he says have conceded to the president’s aggressive tariff regime. But Democrats, he said, need to get to work smoothing out their policy differences. “The consensus isn't developed yet,” Panetta said. “But I think now more than ever we should be.” Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, led a letter to Trump in November advocating for “significant renegotiations,” primarily to address Mexican wage issues, create new labor and environmental protections and enforce existing ones. That letter was signed by other House Democrats. Panetta was not one of them. The New Democrat Coalition wrote a letter , led by Panetta, last November advocating for more of a fine-tuning of the agreement. Only a handful of Democrats like Reps. Darren Soto (D-Florida), Tom Suozzi (D-New York) and Steven Horsford (D-Nevada) signed both letters. “I would say 90% of the congressional Democrats, House and Senate, have a particular position, which is pretty much reflected in DeLauro’s letter, which lays out at a high level the whole kit and the caboodle,” Lori Wallach, director of the Rethink Trade program and an expert on congressional trade battles, told NOTUS. “However, there are outliers.” These are the big-picture ideas Democrats agree on: they don’t want to exit the deal entirely as Trump has threatened to, they want certainty for businesses and, broadly, they want to strengthen labor and environmental protections. The disagreements come down to the specifics. For example, DeLauro called for stronger rules of origin — the guidelines that specify a product’s nationality — whereas Rep. Linda Sánchez of California, the top Democrat on the Ways and Means trade subcommittee, instead argued that existing rules just needed clarification. DeLauro’s letter panned USMCA as a failure that offshored U.S. manufacturing jobs. The New Democrats’ letter makes no mention of offshoring, and the coalition called the trade agreement a “cornerstone of North American competitiveness” in a letter Monday. Rep. Val Hoyle (D-Oregon) said her Democratic colleagues who supported the North American Free Trade Agreement, which USMCA replaced, are engaging in talks on strategically deploying tariffs to protect American jobs from offshoring. “What we have seen in Mexico is that wages are lower, environmental standards are not the same as we have here, and it's not fair that we offshore issues like underpayment of workers or environmental degradation to another country. We can't be blind to that,” Hoyle said. “They are open to that conversation, and I'm talking to people who come from very, very different places on what tariffs should be, and I feel like we're in a really good place,” she . As they find their footing, multiple Democrats signaled frustration over communication between the Trump administration and Congress on USMCA. “I’ve been surprised that there has not been consultation,” Rep. Richard Neal (D-Massachusetts) told NOTUS last week of the White House’s communication with Congress. Democrats said there’s been a more open line of communication with Greer. DeLauro told NOTUS that she and others met with Greer recently to discuss their interests. So far, Democrats’ efforts to exert influence over USMCA have been limited to letters and statements, hampered by the fact that they are in the minority. But they could find themselves in a position of real leverage and influence should they take the House in the midterms. After Democrats won back the House in , the new majority forced the Trump administration to redo USMCA negotiations to secure members’ votes. Unlike in , however, approval from Congress is not required unless the Trump administration negotiates changes to the USMCA that are significant enough to require legislation to be changed or updated. Already the administration has signaled it does not want the agreement to go to Congress. “If Dems take back the House they, have substantial oversight capabilities, which is a really important tool to drive the narrative through hearings and engaging with the administration,” said Allison Smith, a vice president at communications and lobbying firm Lot Sixteen and a former deputy assistant U.S. trade representative. Democrats are prioritizing trade on the campaign trail. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee cited tariffs as one of Republicans’ biggest vulnerabilities heading into the crucial elections. In the interim, Panetta and DeLauro told NOTUS they think the differences are surmountable. “We voted for it the first time around. Now we're talking about what are the changes that need to be made, and you know where we are on digital trade, wages and offshoring. You know, the environmental piece,” she said. “The rapid-response mechanisms work, but it's got to be better. We’ve got to focus on making the agreement more worker-centric.” “I think the discussions are beginning. I think we can come out in the same place.” Panetta, however, did raise another possible complication. Some congressional Democrats are just not up to speed on the issue. “There are different levels of understanding of trade by different levels of members,” Panetta told NOTUS. “There are members who aren't really as on trade, yet they're politically driven rather than policy driven.”

stories.title: McConnell’s Absence is Grinding Some Senate Business to a Halt
stories.author: Avani Kalra, Al Weaver
stories.summary: Farm bill and government funding negotiations are at a standstill without Sen. Mitch McConnell, with just 10 legislative weeks left this year.
stories.content: Sen. Mitch McConnell has been away from the Senate for more than a month. Jacquelyn Martin/AP Sen. Mitch McConnell’s extended absence has thrown a number of the Senate’s top priorities into limbo. McConnell has not voted since he was hospitalized following a fall on June 14, and it’s still unclear when the Kentucky Republican will return to the upper chamber. His absence has complicated the math for leadership on several key votes as Republicans continue to grapple with a slim majority and only 10 legislative weeks before the end of the year. “We’re at 52” Republican votes, Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS, versus the 53 seats the party holds in the Senate. “This is the reality.” McConnell’s absence is a particular problem for committees trying to negotiate urgent matters such as government funding and the farm bill. The Appropriations Committee has been at a standstill for about a month on talks to avoid a government shutdown. Without McConnell, who chairs the subcommittee on defense, the Appropriations Committee is split 14-14 between Democrats and Republicans, making it impossible to advance legislation that doesn’t have bipartisan support. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), who serves on the committee, told NOTUS that losing McConnell’s vote in such partisan negotiations has made those conversations “impossible.” “We miss not just his vote, we miss him,” Capito said. “But it definitely has an impact on approps –– it’s probably the most deeply felt.” Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins said she’s hopeful that McConnell will return before the committee has to vote on any kind of funding bill. “I believe he will be back in September, so I am very optimistic about that,” said Collins, a Republican from Maine. Talks over the farm bill are also at a standstill without McConnell , the second-ranking Republican on the Agriculture Committee. Democrats want to delay when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a provision that Republicans are staunchly opposed to. McConnell’s absence leaves the committee at 11-11, giving Democrats a new leg up in those negotiations. Sen. Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) told NOTUS that every day the bill is delayed is difficult for farmers in his home state. “Let’s just pray that he gets back really, really soon and gets back in a good, healthy way where we can move this along,” Justice said. Justice said Congress should pass a bill to prevent these sorts of absences from causing legislative impasses in the future. He suggested that if a lawmaker’s absence stretched beyond 30 days, their party could be allowed to select someone to fill their place on committees. “That completely is so reasonable it’s unbelievable to me,” Justice said. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) told NOTUS that repeated Republican absences are causing consistent problems for committee work and other legislative business in the upper chamber. “Basically, we’ve been unable to do stuff today in committees,” Hawley said. “All the committees I was in today had to be canceled or couldn’t do business because Republicans weren’t there. And I’m like, wow, we’ve got two weeks to go.” Hawley that the issue extends to the Senate floor. On Thursday, Senate Republicans shot down a resolution limiting the Trump administration’s war powers in Iran, but any absence can make those kinds of votes all the more difficult. “There’s only 53 votes,” Hawley said. “When you have multiple people gone at a time, it's like, well, you can't even control the floor. It’s got to be frustrating to be the leader.” But other Senate Republicans said they aren’t taking issue with McConnell’s extended absence just yet. Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) noted that other senators have also taken time off from legislating for medical reasons. Fischer pointed to former Sen. Mark Kirk (R-Illinois), who was absent for a full year after suffering a stroke in , and former Sen. Tim Johnson (D-South Dakota), who missed nine months after a brain hemorrhage in . “I would say there wasn't the deep interest that Sen. McConnell has been under,” Fischer said of those previous absences. “He's doing some rehabilitation. He wants to come back, that's his choice.” Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said simply: “I have not missed a vote since I've been here. … I just can only control myself.”

stories.title: The Senate Is Struggling to Pass Lindsey Graham’s Last Bill
stories.author: Igor Bobic, Joe Gould
stories.summary: Lawmakers are running out of time to pass a Russia sanctions bill before recess.
stories.content: The late Sen. Lindsey Graham said he had reached a deal with the White House on a Russia sanctions bill. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Supporters of a long-stalled Russian sanctions bill hoped it would gain momentum in the Senate after the sudden death of its top champion : Sen. Lindsey Graham. Initially, at least, it seemed like the bill was on track to pass before the August recess. Graham, a South Carolina Republican, announced before his death that he had reached a deal with the White House to move forward. The bill surpassed 60 co-sponsors, giving it a filibuster-proof majority. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother’s seat, also signed on, fueling optimism it would finally succeed. Instead, the measure is once again at risk of stalling out. “We're going to screw around here and lose this bill if we don't go vote,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) told NOTUS. “We just pissed away two weeks. Now we got a week and a half left, and I don’t know if a vote is scheduled.” Some Democrats are concerned the bill could harm U.S. allies. The White House has warned it wouldn’t have enough flexibility to waive sanctions. And President Donald Trump has demanded the bill include fresh sanctions on Iran, throwing another wrench into the carefully negotiated legislation. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday that he hopes to get the bill “teed up” next week. He said lawmakers were “homing in on” including Iran sanctions — which Darline Graham is championing. But Thune has not yet secured an agreement from Democrats to fast-track the bill, which would need all senators to agree. Without that, it would take the Senate days to consider the bill under its arcane rules — time that Thune cannot spare given a laundry list of legislation and confirmations he wants to plow through before they leave Aug. 6, including Jay Clayton for director of national intelligence and Todd Blanche for attorney general. The bill, titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of , would penalize countries that continue to import Russian oil and natural gas. The idea has been to choke off a revenue stream Russia uses to fund its war against Ukraine more than four years after its full-scale invasion. The revamped bill more narrowly applies sanctions to the top five purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas while reducing the tariff from a blanket % to %. It would grant exceptions for countries weaning themselves off Russian supplies. Some of the Democrats who haven’t signed onto the bill argue the tariff provisions are still too broad, however, and worry it would give Trump unprecedented power to sanction any country he sees fit, including European allies. “Giving Trump additional authorities to act on tariffs in a reckless way that he's been doing is deeply concerning,” Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock said. Vermont Sen. Peter Welch said the bill’s broad language “gives the executive carte blanche to do what he wants for whatever reason he wants.” “That actually is in conflict with every conversation I had with Lindsey about how the tariffs should be targeted to achieve the specific goal of squeezing Russia's revenue,” Welch continued. Backers of the revised Russia sanctions bill worked this week to maintain momentum. One of the lead Democratic negotiators, New Hampshire Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, said she wasn’t opposed to adding Iran sanctions, noting they were in an earlier version of the bill and echo language Congress passed before. “I’d like the Senate to add Iran back in to address the service members being killed by Iran, myself, but those discussions are still ongoing,” she said. Lindsey Graham’s lead co-sponsor, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), said Darline Graham requested personally that Iran sanctions be included, so he is inclined to try. However, his preference is to proceed with the deal already reached with Trump. Meanwhile, Blumenthal has been trying to tamp down concerns from both parties, including the Democrats who are worried about handing Trump more tariff authority. “What we're finding is that some of those concerns are based on a fictional notion of the bill, without an understanding of the real constraints on Trump's authority under the bill,” he said. Democrats are discussing tweaks to address the tariff provisions. But Blumenthal pushed back on suggestions that negotiators are preparing substantial revisions to win over skeptics. “This bill was the result of very painstaking, often painful negotiations involving the U.S. trade representative, White House, colleagues and leadership,” he said. “My hope is it will be passed as-is. But I'm not the only one who has a say in this process. And my objective, first and foremost, is to get the bill to be law.” With the August recess quickly approaching, the Senate is staring at the possibility of bungling its best chance yet to pass the bill. Failing to move ahead would deal a blow to Ukraine’s fight against Russia — and to Graham’s legacy. “We should all remember the press conference we had on a bipartisan basis last week about remembering Graham's legacy,” Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said. “Anybody that says they'd oppose it because it doesn't go far enough — everything that we can drop, every straw we can drop on the camel's back for Putin counts, and we should pass it. That should be one thing that we get done.”

stories.title: House Votes to Rein In Trump’s Iran War
stories.author: Hamed Ahmadi
stories.summary: Four Republicans voted for the measure.
stories.content: "After 60 days of hostilities, you’ve got to come to us” for authorization, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick said. Graeme Sloan/Sipa USA via AP The House voted Thursday to limit President Donald Trump’s authority to expand the war with Iran, its first war powers action since a temporary agreement with Tehran collapsed and fighting resumed. The resolution, led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), passed - . Four Republicans — Reps. Tom Barrett, Brian Fitzpatrick, Thomas Massie and Warren Davidson — joined Democrats as renewed fighting raised fears of a wider conflict. “The president is once again showing his contempt for Congress and for the Constitution, continuing this destructive, deadly, and costly war despite Congress having already passed a War Powers Resolution that has the force of law,” Jayapal said Wednesday. This was the House’s second vote to end the war. Like the first, which happened in early June, this vote cannot legally force Trump to stop the fighting. But the vote adds to signs of bipartisan concern over his decision to continue the war without congressional authorization as the conflict intensifies. Four U.S. service members were killed in the latest escalation, bringing the American death toll to 18. More than troops have been wounded since the war began. U.S. strikes against Iran have continued for 12 consecutive nights. One of the Republican backers of the House war powers resolution, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, said the collapse of peace negotiations and the troop deaths might be driving GOP support. He said he has been supporting the resolutions to assert Congress’ powers over the executive branch. “I follow the law,” Fitzpatrick said. “Under the War Powers Act of , it says you’ve got to give a 48-hour notification, and after 60 days of hostilities, you’ve got to come to us” for authorization. The administration says Trump has sufficient authority under the Constitution’s Article II to continue the campaign. “We have all the authorities necessary at this moment,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Tuesday at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing. Trump told Congress in a July 10 letter that hostilities had resumed July 7 after the administration accused Tehran of violating a memorandum of understanding that had paused the fighting. The administration says the renewed campaign started a new 60-day period under the War Powers Resolution, a position lawmakers in both parties have questioned. Republicans opposed to the resolution argued that limiting Trump during active hostilities would undermine U.S. forces and benefit Iran.

stories.title: House Committee Advances Bill Limiting D.C.’s Ability to Raise Taxes
stories.author: Martin Austermuhle
stories.summary: City officials say the measure would “straightjacket” their ability to govern D.C., while DoorDash faces criticism for supporting the bill.
stories.content: House Oversight Committee Chair James Comer. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP A House committee approved a bill Wednesday that would broadly restrict D.C.’s ability to increase or decrease local taxes and fees , again highlighting Republicans’ aggressive interest in managing how the city runs — down to the dollars and cents it collects. The bill passed the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform on a party-line vote, sending it next to the full House for consideration. It faces much steeper odds if it gets to the Senate, though. Speaking during a brief debate, committee Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky), who introduced the measure, said it would benefit residents and businesses and make the city more economically vibrant. “Radical D.C. Democrats want to solve their spending problem by reaching deeper into taxpayers’ pockets and driving further on the path to socialism,” he said. “Actions like these only serve to hurt small businesses and the District’s already vulnerable residents. These are just more examples of bad policies that disincentivize investment, drive residents out and undermine the economic competitiveness of the city.” But Comer also conceded that the bill is meant as a preemptive attack on a new class of elected officials who are expected to take office next year, including Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George, a democratic socialist who overwhelmingly won the city’s Democratic Party primary in June and is expected to cruise to victory in November’s general election. “This bill enhances Congress’s constitutional oversight authority over D.C. to restrain irresponsible policies pursued by future socialist and ultra-progressive D.C. Democrats,” he said. Lewis George has said D.C. should consider raising taxes on certain businesses and wealthy residents to collect new revenue as the city faces a sluggish economy, and the D.C. Council is expected to hold a hearing in the fall on possible revenue-raising options. Comer and other Republicans said Wednesday that city lawmakers should instead focus on cutting spending. But congressional Democrats and city officials alike pushed back on Comer’s bill, calling it an unnecessary and unwelcome intrusion into plainly local affairs. “D.C.’s locally elected leaders are accountable to D.C. residents, and local leaders should be empowered to address local matters without congressional interference,” said Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California). “If Donald Trump or congressional Republicans want to run D.C., they should run for mayor and D.C. Council.” Congress has a significant amount of say in D.C.’s local affairs. Every bill passed by the council undergoes a 30-day review on Capitol Hill (or 60 days when a bill changes criminal law), during which time members of Congress have the power to stop any measure from becoming law. That has happened rarely since D.C. gained home rule more than 50 years ago, though more recently, Republicans have increasingly wielded the power — including a vote that rejected a sweeping rewrite of the city’s criminal code. But city officials warned that Comer’s bill would effectively flip the existing process on its head, allowing council bills touching on taxes or fees to become law only if Congress proactively approved them. “The bill would straightjacket the District because it would paralyze our tax code,” Council Chair Phil Mendelson wrote in a letter to Comer, noting that D.C. Superior Court consistently faces a shortage of judges because confirmation votes are delayed in the Senate. In her own statement, Mayor Muriel Bowser told Comer — with whom she has otherwise had a friendly relationship — that Congress could take other steps to help the city’s economy, which has been hit by President Donald Trump’s aggressive effort to trim the size of the federal workforce. “While the federal government should not touch the District's ability to raise and spend its local dollars, they can and should help us replace the economic activity lost through reductions to the federal workforce and a shrinking federal footprint,” she wrote. Democrats on the House Oversight Committee, including Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Florida), highlighted what they said was an inherent hypocrisy in the bill: Congress giving itself more responsibility over D.C. while facing persistent challenges passing an annual federal budget. “We can’t even pass our own bills. Now you want to add to that and pass the bills of D.C.?” Frost asked. “You want to run the D.C. budget? Why don’t we run our own budget?” While D.C. officials largely criticized Republicans for approving the bill, a second (and unexpected) target also emerged: DoorDash. Comer said during the debate that the food-delivery platform supported his bill, which DoorDash confirmed to NOTUS. John Horton, the platform’s head of North American policy, said its decision was motivated by the council’s recent approval of a 20-cent fee on all third-party deliveries in the city. "We've said from the start that taxes like this fall hardest on the people D.C. says it wants to protect, and nothing has changed. We have always supported home rule for D.C., but will continue to do everything we can to defend D.C.’s small businesses, local economy, and underserved residents,” Horton wrote in a statement. DoorDash’s decision prompted outrage from some local advocacy groups, including Free D.C., which called on residents to boycott the app. Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker similarly expressed his anger on social media. “Every District resident should know that @DoorDash doesn't support DC Home Rule and is actively working to undermine it by lobbying for the GOP’s efforts to control DC tax policies,” he wrote on X . “Govern yourselves accordingly, neighbors.”

stories.title: House Republicans Ram Through Reconciliation 3.0 Despite Little Senate Buy-in
stories.author: Stephen Neukam
stories.summary: The framework includes money for defense, farm assistance and changes to voting laws.
stories.content: House Speaker Mike Johnson urged conservatives pushing to add more items to the budget bill to hold off and put them in another package after the November midterms. Francis Chung/POLITICO via AP Images Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP House Republicans on Wednesday muscled through a $95 billion budget framework that includes President Donald Trump’s request to fund the Iran war, farm aid and grants for states to encourage voter ID requirements. The resolution’s slim - passage comes after the White House and House GOP leaders for weeks worked to corral rank-and-file Republicans in support of the measure. Lawmakers voiced concerns about various components of the third package. Republican leaders are using the budget reconciliation process to get around a Democratic filibuster in the Senate. The budget resolution includes $73 billion for defense and intelligence, $12 billion for farm assistance and $10 billion for the voter ID grant programs. “Here we are, reconciliation 3.0, supporting our troops in their time of need … bullets and bombs to finish the job,” Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), the chair of the House Budget Committee, said on the House floor ahead of the vote. “Strengthen our food supply and ultimately, we want to safeguard the integrity of our elections.” Before the vote, House Republicans across the ideological spectrum criticized the budget resolution, some arguing that it was too narrow and some complaining it did not contain enough conservative priorities or spending cuts to offset the cost. Speaker Mike Johnson previously pledged to lawmakers that the party’s third reconciliation bill would be a broader package. Part of the pitch from Johnson and the White House this week was that Republicans would instead shift some conservative priorities to a fourth reconciliation package — after the November midterms. Ultimately, conservatives, moderates and fiscal hawks backed the nearly $ billion budget blueprint that did not include offsets for the new spending. Two House Republicans, Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio and Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, broke with their leaders and opposed the package. Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California also voted against it. The vote is the opening salvo in what is expected to be an extended back-and-forth between Republicans in the House and Senate over how to pass the party’s third reconciliation package this Congress. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters this week that he would hold the House’s budget resolution until lawmakers can sort out government funding, which is set to expire at the end of September. The House separately approved a bill largely along party lines that would punt the government funding fight until after the midterms, funding the government into December. That plan faces an uncertain future in the Senate, where GOP leaders will need the support of at least seven Democrats to pass any government funding measure. Senate Democrats have been hesitant to vote to fund the government over the past year and a half without concessions from Republicans. Thune indicated if Senate Democrats fail to negotiate a bill to avoid a shutdown he could decide to add it to the party-line package. House and Senate Republican leaders are working against a ticking clock to negotiate agreement on a package that can pass both chambers. Thune has repeatedly said the SAVE Act provisions, focused on Trump’s priority bill requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote, do not have the votes to pass in the Senate. House lawmakers are scheduled to leave Washington on Thursday for a monthlong August recess and return with just four more weeks in session before the November midterms. Senators are in Washington until the end of July, and will return in September with just three weeks of session left.

stories.title: Stock Block
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: A United States flag is reflected in the window of the Nasdaq studio, which displays indices and stocks down, in Times Square, New York, Monday, March 16, . (AP Photo/Seth Wenig) Seth Wenig/AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 22, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST The House just passed the National Defense Authorization Act, with six Democrats voting in favor and seven Republicans voting against the measure. They will soon take up Reconciliation 3.0, which includes billions in Iran war funding and farm aid — and faces opposition from a handful of Republican holdouts. A majority of Democrats opposed both measures over a slate of conservative amendments and tacked-on SAVE America Act language. John Thune said it’s possible the Senate will “hold” the House’s budget framework if needed as a backup vehicle to avoid a government shutdown in September. Lawmakers also approved the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prevent Congress members and their families from buying individual stocks, but the measure is likely DOA in the Senate. THE HILL Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyoming) released new CLARITY Act text today. It would ban all elected officials — including the president and members of Congress — from issuing digital assets in a White House-approved ethics agreement that sunsets in January . As written, Trump’s existing crypto businesses — central to Democrats’ concerns — would be grandfathered in. “It’s a non-starter over here,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren , the Banking Committee’s top Democrat, told NOTUS’ Avani Kalra. “Someone can call it an ethics provision, but if it doesn’t stop the president from profiting off crypto and using it as a way to take bribes right out in public, then it’s not really an ethics provision.” Sen. Mitch McConnell’s absence from the Agriculture Committee has put farm bill negotiations into a standstill. Election deniers swept Arizona’s Republican primaries last night. Trump says he’s pleased . THE ADMINISTRATION Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz sets a “dangerous precedent” for other parts of the world, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said today during a summit in the Philippines. Trump attended four deceased soldiers’ dignified transfers in Dover, Delaware, today: “All of them said, very strongly, that we can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon, so we’re going to honor them.” America’s trade strategy will continue to include import taxes, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Congress today — foreshadowing a barrage of new tariffs the White House plans to introduce. The EPA must fund the Biden-era Environmental and Climate Justice Grants it illegally canceled last year, a federal judge ruled today. The administration has moved to stop collecting workplace demographic data. THE COURTS Nicolás Maduro’s criminal trial will start next June , a judge announced Wednesday, a timeline that reflects the mountain of classified evidence involved. MONEY TALKS Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: House Lawmakers Pass Bill Restricting Congressional Stock Trading
stories.author: Taylor Giorno, Avani Kalra
stories.summary: But it’s likely on arrival in the Senate.
stories.content: Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin) sponsored the Stop Insider Trading Act, which passed the U.S. House on July 22, . Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP The House on Wednesday passed legislation that would prevent members of Congress, their spouses and their children from buying individual stocks. But the bill is likely on arrival in the Senate , where Republican leadership has shown little interest in the matter. And some lawmakers in both chambers say the House bill does not go far enough to mitigate potential conflicts of interest between lawmakers’ official actions and their personal finances. The Stop Insider Trading Act, which passed on a - vote with 13 Democrats joining Republicans, allows lawmakers and their immediate family members to retain, and eventually sell, individual stocks they already hold. Lawmakers would be required under the bill to publicly disclose their plans to sell stock holdings between seven and 14 days in advance of a sale. The legislation also imposes a fine of $2, or 10% of a transaction — whichever is greater — for disclosure and trading violations. House Republicans combined the measure with language from another bill that would require voters to present photo ID to cast a ballot — President Donald Trump’s top priority ahead of the midterm elections. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), who has worked on several stock-ban bills this , said on the House floor Wednesday afternoon before the vote that he would have preferred a standalone vote on the stock-trade language. But, Roy , he was “proud of the legislation.” “This is a giant step forward. I wish my colleagues on this side of the aisle and my colleagues on this side of the aisle would recognize that and praise it,” Roy said. Republican lawmakers lined up alongside Roy to express their support. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) said he supported ending stock trading by members of Congress because “trust in our democracy cannot be a luxury item.” “It must be the everyday expectation of every American,” Lawler . House Democrats largely opposed the bill, characterizing it as a watered-down version of other bipartisan bills that would go further by barring members of Congress and their families from owning stocks altogether and apply the same standards to the president and vice president. “Two things can be true at the same time. I can support voter ID requirements, which I do, and I can support banning members of Congress from trading stocks, which I do,” Rep. Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pennsylvania) said during debate on the House floor Wednesday afternoon. “I can also oppose this bill because it is not in that honest attempt to do either.” But Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin) criticized his colleagues for making “Goldilocks arguments” claiming the bill went too far or did not go far enough. “I believe this is our opportunity where we can simply stop members of Congress from trading individual stocks. Period. Full stop,” Steil said during remarks on the House floor. “Doing so removes even the appearance of wrongdoing. Americans should be confident that individuals working here are working on their behalf, not on behalf of their own financial interests.” Democrats worked alongside Republicans on other stock-trade ban proposals this year, including the Restore Trust in Congress Act . A bipartisan group of lawmakers including Roy and Reps. Seth Magaziner (D-Rhode Island), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida) negotiated the Restore Trust in Congress Act for months before unveiling the legislation last September . The bill would have barred members of Congress and their families from trading and owning individual stocks and forced them to divest from any stock holdings, allowing them to defer paying taxes on the sale if they reinvest in a mutual fund. But unlike the Stop Insider Trading Act, the Restore Trust in Congress Act and other similar measures failed to generate enough support in the current Congress to advance to the full House for a vote. Ethics watchdogs including Common Cause, Campaign Legal Center, Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, Public Citizen and the Project on Government Oversight supported the Restore Trust in Congress Act . They expressed serious concerns about the Stop Insider Trading Act allowing lawmakers to continue to own or sell stocks. The Senate is unlikely to take up the Stop Insider Trading Act –– the measure is not likely to overcome the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster, especially with the voter ID provisions , and previous stock-ban bills have stalled in the upper chamber . A much stronger stock-ban bill championed by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) advanced out of a Senate committee in July with the help of the committee’s Democratic members. But the bill has languished since then and Senate leadership hasn’t scheduled a vote on it. Hawley’s bill, called the Halting Ownership and Non-Ethical Stock Transactions Act, or HONEST Act , would require members of Congress, the president and vice president, along with their spouses and dependent children, to sell their existing individual stocks and prevent them from buying new ones. While Hawley said the Stop Insider Trading Act is “not nearly as robust as I would like,” he didn’t outright oppose it, saying something is better than nothing. Momentum has been building for Congress to advance a stock-trading ban after a series of high-profile controversies, such as lawmakers making a flurry of stock trades immediately before and after the initial COVID-19 pandemic shutdowns of early . NOTUS and other news organizations have also identified dozens of members of Congress this who’ve violated the disclosure provisions of the existing Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, or STOCK Act, of . Barring members of Congress from trading individual stocks has high public support among Republican, Democratic and independent voters alike, according to polls . The STOCK Act of was the last major piece of legislation that regulated congressional stock trading and prohibited conflicts of interest. The bill clarified that insider-trading laws apply to Congress and expanded financial-disclosure requirements, but did not place limits on lawmakers’ ability to buy, sell and own individual stocks.

stories.title: House OKs a $1 Trillion Defense Bill in a Tight Vote
stories.author: Joe Gould
stories.summary: Democrats largely opposed the bill over the Iran war, the price tag and anti-trans language.
stories.content: “We are giving industry the certainty it needs to invest, expand and produce faster,” said Rep. Mike Rogers, the top Republican on the on the House Armed Services Committee. Alex Brandon/AP The House narrowly approved sweeping defense policy legislation that codifies President Donald Trump’s Pentagon plans, including his “Department of War” rebrand and push to deny coverage for health care to transgender troops. Just six Democrats voted for the $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, while all but seven Republicans backed the bill. The final vote was - . The NDAA’s passage was a win for House Speaker Mike Johnson, who agreed this month to merge the SAVE America Act with the defense policy bill in order to quell a rebellion from his hard-right members, led by Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna. The SAVE America Act, a top priority for Trump, would require proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and showing an ID to cast a ballot. Democrats largely rejected the NDAA as a referendum on the Iran war and Trump’s budget request, which seeks $1.5 trillion for defense while slashing social programs. “Whatever else may be said about the NDAA — there’s a lot of positive aspects to it — it will continue to support the Department of Defense that the president is using to wage this war, this incredibly disastrous, terrible decision of a war,” said Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee. The panel’s top Republican, Rep. Mike Rogers of Alabama, has argued the bill is necessary to support troops, foster innovation and strengthen an eroding defense industrial base in the of China’s growing might. “We are giving industry the certainty it needs to invest, expand and produce faster,” he said. House Republicans on Tuesday crossed a red line for many Democrats when they a provision to ban gender-affirming care for service members and their dependents through Tricare, the military’s health care plan. They also included an amendment barring transgender girls from participating in girls’ sports at Defense Department schools for military families. Other hard-right amendments included language to approve the default when qualified service members and Pentagon civilian employees ask commanders for permission to carry personal firearms on military installations. Lawmakers also some measures opposing divisive Pentagon policies, including one that would restore collective bargaining at the Defense Department.
