Others include a mandate to restore military base names selected by Congress’ bipartisan renaming commission, new reporting requirements when senior military officers are fired and restrictions on the construction of the Navy’s proposed “Trump-class” battleship. The bill is not in its final form. Democrats and Republicans typically reconcile separate versions from the House and Senate with final passage expected in December. The NDAA is considered must-pass legislation, and Congress has drafted and passed a version each year for decades. The most controversial provisions in the House-passed bill have little chance of clearing the Senate, where bipartisan support is needed to advance legislation. The views of the president, who holds veto power, will also be a factor in composing any final bill. Senate Democrats will “robustly” oppose any GOP anti-trans provisions, said Sen. Jack Reed (D-Rhode Island), the Senate Armed Services Committee’s ranking member. “I mean, getting into the medical diagnoses and all those things, it's an issue that is more to appease their supporters, not to help personnel or to make the military better.” Last week, Senate Democrats blocked Republicans from bringing their chamber’s version of the bill to the floor to protest the Trump administration’s Iran war and attempt to gain leverage in negotiations over next year’s federal budget. House and Senate negotiators have in the past reconciled a House-passed and Senate Armed Services Committee-passed bill. This week, Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the panel chair, did not rule out that strategy. “That's not an ideal process, but we'll get it done at some point, the sooner the better,” Wicker said. “But it speaks volumes that our Democratic colleagues were not even willing to proceed to the bill.”

stories.title: Senate Farm Bill Negotiations Are Stuck During McConnell’s Absence
stories.author: Tyler Spence
stories.summary: Democrats want a delay in when states must start sharing SNAP costs, and have leverage with McConnell away.
stories.content: Sen. John Boozman acknowledged the setback on farm bill work without the Kentucky Republican’s presence. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) Sen. Mitch McConnell’s absence from the Agriculture Committee has put farm bill negotiations into a standstill. Democrats want to delay when states must start sharing costs under the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, a change Republicans put in a previous law. Committee Chair John Boozman (R-Arkansas) has wanted to keep that potential delay out of negotiations. But with McConnell, the second-ranking Republican on the panel, away from the Senate for more than a month for medical reasons , Democrats have more leverage over the process. The committee is currently split 11-11, making it impossible to advance legislation without bipartisan support. The stalemate over SNAP has dimmed Boozman’s hope of marking up the Senate version of the farm bill at the end of July. Boozman acknowledged the setback without the Kentucky Republican’s presence. “We're in a situation where we are trying to get Sen. McConnell back. He's progressing well, so hopefully we'll get him back soon,” he said. The Senate is set to leave soon for a break that lasts until mid-September, which leaves Congress with a steep challenge to pass the farm bill before the current version expires at the end of September. The potential expiration is a pressure point on both parties, as farmers record-high bankruptcies and surging input costs. The multi-year bill addresses an array of agricultural and food programs, and the last farm bill’s economic assumptions have largely become outdated. Democrats have demanded a two-year delay in shifting SNAP benefit costs under last year's reconciliation law, which requires states to start covering 5% to 15% of SNAP benefit costs beginning in October , based on their payment error rates. The error rate measures overpayments and underpayments to recipients, not fraud. “We want a two-year delay on SNAP provisions,” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), a member of the committee, told NOTUS. “It's a deal-maker and a deal-breaker.” Democrats point to an exception that the worst-performing states already received in last year’s negotiation process for the reconciliation bill. States with error rates of 20% or higher got a two-year delay in the law as part of a deal that secured the vote of Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) for the broader reconciliation package; Alaska's error rate is among the highest in the country. Democrats are asking for the same delay for every state. Boozman has acknowledged states have had more trouble than expected getting under the 6% error-rate threshold that triggers the cost share: Only nine states achieved full compliance in fiscal , while the national average of the error rate was 10.62%. Boozman said he would rather not touch SNAP in the Senate version of the farm bill, but he hasn’t ruled it out either. Other Republicans say they aren’t ready to budge. “I think at some point they [Democrats] come to a realization that they get to keep pushing their social program, and they will,” Sen. John Hoeven (R-North Dakota), a member of the committee, told NOTUS. “We get that, but it's time to move on and get something done.” Hoeven also noted elements of the farm bill that Democrats do heavily support, and said he thinks that going without a bill would be a bridge too far. For now though, Democrats seem resolved not to back down from their demand. “I think it’s too important,” Sen. Adam Schiff (D-California), a member of the committee, told NOTUS. Schiff said farm bills are traditionally bipartisan, and this one’s pathway for consensus resides with a delay in the SNAP cost shift. “We desperately want a farm bill on both sides of the aisle. There is a path forward, but it will require some mitigation of the harm from the SNAP cuts,” he said. Republicans say deadline pressure could be alleviated somewhat when farm-related provisions included in the reconciliation bill come online in October. The farm bill has been overdue since the last five-year authorization, the Agriculture Improvement Act, expired in . Congress has spent the years since patching it together with extensions.

stories.title: ‘Beautifully Messy’
stories.author: Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Gold-colored presidential seals are seen on a fireplace in the Oval Office as President Donald Trump meets with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House, Tuesday, July 21, , in Washington. Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo Today’s notice: Big day in the House for big bills. A must-read civics lesson. Don’t put too much stock in the stock-banning push. DHS has a contract to buy body-worn cameras. And: A top DHS official investing like a Democrat. THE LATEST What the president’s watching: House Republicans are about to bolt for August recess, and thus have a make-it-or-break-it day to push through a litany of White House priorities they can deploy as fodder on the campaign trail. Donald Trump put on a charm offensive in the Oval Office last night, a source familiar with the meeting told NOTUS’ Kadia Goba, sending a dozen of his allies back to the Capitol with signed baseball hats and a nudge to deliver on his agenda. The remaining question is whether the House GOP conference will be able to get it all done before members depart this week, and if the Senate, which is sticking around for at least another week, will go along — or if they’ll all go home empty-handed. “We’re set on fulfilling our role in this partnership with our president,” Rep. Clay Higgins (R-Louisiana) told Manuela, calling the final legislative lift and Senate negotiations “beautifully messy right now.” Already done: The House passed the government funding stopgap - last night. Left on the plate: A must-pass defense policy bill, as well as the $95 billion budget blueprint for the Iran war, farm aid and parts of Trump’s voting-restrictions bill. The problem for House members is twofold. First, they don’t know what the Senate will do with these bills — especially the supplemental measure with portions of the SAVE America Act that are DOA in the upper chamber right now. (Senate Majority Leader John Thune also said yesterday that the White House has a different plan for the stopgap than the House’s.) And second, spending large sums of money and the war with Iran aren’t popular talking points back home. Adding it all up: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth finally offered a preliminary price tag for the war in a tense back-and-forth with senators yesterday. Hegseth said the war will cost taxpayers nearly $38 billion by the end of September — though experts last month had already estimated its cost to be roughly $40 billion, and that’s before the ceasefire collapsed and daily strikes resumed, NOTUS’ Joe Gould and Hamed Ahmadi report . Open tabs: A Houthi Blockade Could Worsen an Already Fragile Oil Market (NYT); Software Glitch Put Thousands of Noncitizens on New Jersey Voter Rolls (NOTUS); Zelensky ousts Ukraine’s military commander as major shake-up continues (WaPo); Trump Approves Landmark Nuclear Deal With Saudi Arabia (WSJ) THE BIG ONE A civics lesson: Aangad Singh and his family left Washington in June with no trophy but a lot of questions. They believe Aangad correctly answered nearly every single question in the Presidential Award civics competition, and yet he didn’t even finish in the top three. “It doesn’t make sense,” his mother, Ramandeep Singh , told NOTUS’ Sam Fortier for a dizzying, spellbinding story about doubts and distrust in our age of suspicion. The prospect that the Department of Education may have fixed the competition and a chorus of validation from Aangad’s fellow contestants shook his immigrant family, who strongly believe in American ideals, to the core. So they went searching for answers, and recourse, not knowing what they might find. From the campaign trail Michigan money: Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ’s campaign raised $3.3 million in just three weeks, with 68% of donors giving to his camp for the first time, according to numbers his campaign shared exclusively with NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz. El-Sayed will off against Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Aug. 4 Democratic primary. From the Hill What ban? After an exhausting few months of legislative sausage making, the House is finally set to vote today on a bill that would restrict stock trading by members of Congress. Curtailing lawmakers’ ability to profit off of individual stock has been a longtime priority for some members. However, it’s not a safe bet it’ll make it through the Senate, NOTUS’ Avani Kalra and Taylor Giorno report . House Republicans have tied the stock-trading ban to a bill that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter identification to cast a ballot — two issues the Senate lacks the votes to pass. A second reason? The Senate hasn’t even scheduled it. “We have a whole list of things that we’re going to talk about on how to prioritize, because it takes a lot more time in the Senate to get things done,” Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming), the Republican whip, told reporters. From the administration Body-worn cameras on the way? The Department of Homeland Security ordered more than $30 million in body cameras from Axon Enterprise after recent fatal shootings by federal immigration agents, NOTUS’ Jackie Llanos reports — from contracts awarded just days ago. DHS has already spent millions on body cameras, but immigration agents weren’t wearing them at the time of the shootings in Maine and Texas. Not moving: The Department of Agriculture announced in July that it was reorganizing, a mammoth project that would relocate more than half of its D.C. workforce and other employees around the country. Critics argued it could be a sneaky way to lay people off. Now a year later, workers say they don’t want to move and the shake-up would severely hurt the department, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence, Eric Katz and Natalie Alms report . Employees are sounding the alarm: policy rollouts, damage research, wildfire response and getting money out the door will all be delayed, they say, if the workforce is significantly diminished. ON NOTUS PODCAST From your favorite podcast app: On today’s episode of On NOTUS , Rep. Jim Himes (D-Connecticut) warned that Trump could interfere in November’s midterm elections and urged Americans to think through the president’s election claims. “If an individual citizen can’t exercise the critical faculties involved in seeing the president’s lies for what they are, if 50% of America believes lies that are easily disprovable, we’re done,” Himes told NOTUS’ Kadia Goba, though he that he wasn’t pessimistic about voters. He also discussed the fight over FISA, his belief in a “big tent” Democratic Party, his beekeeping hobby and what Congress has in common with a jar of bees. NOTUS METRO NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter! Local news: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend , by Torrie Herrington From Cycling to Fishing, Concerns About East Potomac’s Future Go Beyond Golf , by Shamira Muhammad NOTUS PERSPECTIVES The secretary of defense is offering hormone replacement therapy for warfighters with low testosterone. But his Senate testimony yesterday left Dana Milbank wondering : Does Pete Hegseth have too much? NEW ON NOTUS Stocking up: A top DHS official is intentionally investing his money like a congressional Democrat, according to his federal financial disclosures reviewed by NOTUS’ Dave Levinthal . Pedro M. Allende , a department under secretary, recently purchased between $15, and $50, worth of shares in an exchange-traded fund that mimics moves made by Democratic members of Congress. Dan Weiskopf , the senior portfolio manager for the group that oversees the ETF, told Dave it is an “inherent conflict of interest” for someone in Allende’s role to invest in the fund. More: Trump Lifts the Ban on Direct U.S. Flights to Lebanon , by Jenna Monnin Cleo Fields Won’t Seek Reelection After Redistricting in Louisiana , by Torrie Herrington Mamdani Says He Can’t Arrest Netanyahu if He Comes to New York , by Manuela Silva Wisconsin Dems Ask Elections Commission to Allow Voters to Recast Absentee Ballots , by Torrie Herrington NOT US The Secretary of Homeland , by Nick Miroff for The Atlantic The New York Young Republican Club Has an Antisemitism Problem , by Nathan Taylor Pemberton for New York magazine How the G.O.P. Turned Olive Garden Into a Voter ID Talking Point , by Michael Gold for The New York Times Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS Newsletter, please forward it to a friend.
