stories.title: Jim Himes Sounds the Alarm on Potential Trump Interference in the Midterms
stories.author: Kadia Goba, Ed Demaria
stories.summary: The top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee warns against how that interference could play out.
stories.content: Himes’ warning comes days after Trump claimed vulnerabilities in America’s election system during a primetime address. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP Images) Rep. Jim Himes said President Donald Trump will deny the results of the midterm elections if Democrats take control of the House or Senate and warned the president could interfere with the results by using the same tactics he used in the aftermath of the presidential election. “All it takes is for the president to say ‘The election was corrupt, and you need to go to the Capitol to fight, fight, fight,’” Himes said on the latest episode of the On NOTUS podcast. “This time it'll be you need to show up at polling places in Michigan and North Carolina and Georgia.” “Don't tell me this is not possible, we saw what was possible on Jan. 6,” Himes said. Himes, the ranking member on the House Intelligence Committee, said his Democratic colleagues are mobilizing ahead of the election, including running tabletop exercises for potential scenarios under the supervision of the House Administration Committee ranking member, Rep. Joe Morelle. “It's not the Democrats' job to make sure that our elections are not compromised,” Himes said. “It's the American people's job, it's civil society. But obviously, since we know that it will be weaponized against us, we're very, very active on this right now.” said Americans must do their own research about Trump’s false claims on foreign interference in elections for the good of American democracy. “If an individual citizen can't exercise the critical faculties involved in seeing the president's lies for what they are, if 50% of America believes lies that are easily disprovable, we're done,” Himes said, adding that he wasn’t pessimistic about voters. “The real obligation lies with the American citizens.” Himes’ warning comes days after Trump claimed vulnerabilities in America’s election system during a primetime address Himes said was a “pratfall.” “It was a big nothing burger, pretty much everybody acknowledged that,” Himes said. “I've looked at all the intelligence and, by the way, you don't need to trust me, you can go look at the… intelligence community assessment around the election of .” Himes also urged Congress to reauthorize Section of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a controversial surveillance tool that lets the federal government collect communications of foreigners overseas. “Congress doesn't act very well unless the unabstract pain of not acting is right in your ,” Himes said. “Heaven forbid, but if we had an attack because didn't allow us to follow, connect the dots, all of a sudden we'd get called back here and would be passed in a millisecond.” Authorization for Section expired in June, but Himes said it is still operational while companies continue to cooperate with government requests. Himes said that he was “pained” by Director of National Intelligence nominee Jay Clayton’s testimony at his confirmation hearing before the Senate Intelligence Committee, but said he expected Clayton to be “law-oriented” and a better choice than the acting DNI head, Bill Pulte. “Bill Pulte has shown that he will very happily break the law,” Himes said. “Choose Jay Clayton every single day and twice on Sunday, in terms of the likelihood that that individual is gonna be profoundly corrupted.” Himes brushed aside questions of division inside the Democratic Party over Israel and socialism by praising his party’s “big tent” and the potential success it could yield at the ballot box. “You don't need to be a mathematical genius to know that the party that gets the biggest tent, that has the most people in it, is going to have majorities in the House and the Senate and probably win the presidency,” Himes said. “That's just third-grade math.” Still, Himes urged his fellow Democrats to avoid vilifying the ultra-rich and other groups while pushing for increased taxation. “When you start getting into the business of vilifying billionaires, there's not that many billionaires, but now all of a sudden if you're vilifying corporations and the management class, and you're vilifying white men because they're toxic, pretty soon you're vilifying a good chunk of the American population that you desperately want supporting you,” Himes said. On NOTUS is a weekly podcast where NOTUS reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here .

stories.title: CR Conundrum
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: House Speaker Mike Johnson speaks with reporters as he departs a vote at the U.S. Capitol. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 21, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST The House will vote later this evening on a short-term measure to fund the government through after the midterms. As with other GOP proposals on the table this week, the continuing resolution’s details put Democrats between a rock and a hard place on messaging: It’s technically free of policy riders, but many will likely block it over “unchecked” immigration enforcement funding language. “Drafting errors” and other exclusions are signs the bill is not “a serious proposal,” Pete Aguilar said during a news conference. THE ADMINISTRATION Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Dan Caine asked Senate appropriators for more Iran war funding today, in their first in-depth public comments about the conflict in months. Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) criticized the pair over dozens of female and Black officers being sidelined: “The U.S. military is one of the greatest meritocracies in the free world. We need to make sure that it stays that way.” Until Iran is “ready to meet in a meaningful way, we have no interest in meeting,” Trump told reporters today. The president also threatened military action against Yemen’s Houthis if they disrupt Saudi shipping. The administration will withhold more than $1 billion in Medicaid payments to California and Minnesota in a new round of fraud-related freezes. THE STATES Thousands of noncitizens were to New Jersey’s voter rolls due to a software error, Gov. Mikie Sherill said. Fewer than cast ballots in elections since . THE HILL House Republicans grilled National Museum of American History director Anthea Hartig today, categorizing the Smithsonian museum as an “ideological” political organization. Senate Intelligence advanced Jay Clayton ’s nomination for director of national intelligence by a 9-8 party-line vote this afternoon. THE COURTS A federal appeals court unanimously upheld Trump adviser Peter Navarro ’s criminal conviction, handed down after he refused to testify or provide documents in connection to a congressional Jan. 6 probe. Another federal appeals court denied former President Joe Biden ’s bid to block release of recordings and transcripts from interviews with a ghostwriter. INNIT? Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: A House Stock-Trade Ban May Finally Advance. The Senate Might Squash It.
stories.author: Avani Kalra, Taylor Giorno
stories.summary: The bill doesn’t go as far as some lawmakers would like and faces a tough path forward in the upper chamber.
stories.content: House Speaker Mike Johnson supports a House bill that would ban congressional stock trading, but the legislation's prospects in the Senate are dim. Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call via AP The House is expected to vote Wednesday on a bill that would place restrictions on stock trading by members of Congress after clearing a key procedural hurdle Tuesday afternoon. This would be the first time the full House has voted on legislation to limit lawmakers’ ability to trade individual stocks — House Democrats torpedoed a promising effort in — although the legislation doesn’t go as far as some lawmakers and advocates would like. House Republicans have tied the vote to a bill that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and mandatory voter identification to cast a ballot, one of President Donald Trump’s top legislative priorities. Even if the House passes the stock-trading bill, the legislation faces dim prospects in the Senate, which has not yet scheduled a vote on a separate bill that would prevent members of Congress and their families — as well as the president and vice president — from owning and trading individual stocks altogether. “We have a whole list of things that we’re going to talk about on how to prioritize, because it takes a lot more time in the Senate to get things done,” Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyoming), the Senate Republican whip, told reporters. The House bill, called the Stop Insider Trading Act , would prevent members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from buying new individual stocks. But, critically, it does not prevent lawmakers or their families from owning them. Instead, the Stop Insider Trading Act allows lawmakers to continue to hold their existing stock and would require them to publicly disclose plans to sell their stock at least between seven and 14 days in advance. The bill also increases fines for lawmakers who run afoul of the law to $2, or 10% of the offending transaction, whichever is greater. House Speaker Mike Johnson has personally backed it. Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Wisconsin), who chairs the committee that advanced the bill in January, told the House Rules Committee on Monday that the bill “ensures that lawmakers cannot use their position to profit off insider information they may garner while serving in Congress.” BryanSteil ( , AR: 1.48)“The legislation, I believe, is critical to restoring public trust in this institution,” Steil said. Public disclosures filed under the existing Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act, which became law in , “lacked detail” and can be filed one month after the transaction, Steil . (And, as NOTUS has reported, lawmakers frequently fail to disclose stock trades within that timeline .) But critics say the bill does nothing to limit lawmakers’ ability to take official actions that might benefit the stocks they already own, thus failing to reduce public perception that lawmakers are profiting off their position. “When lawmakers own stock in companies impacted by their official decisions or committee assignments, people naturally question whether policy choices are being made for the public good or to increase the value of private holdings,” Eric Kashdan, the director of federal advocacy at Campaign Legal Center, wrote in a letter to House members Monday. “Even if financial gain is not a specific member’s motivation, the appearance of the conflict will persist until reforms are enacted.” Campaign Legal Center and other ethics watchdogs supported a bipartisan bill introduced last fall by lawmakers including Reps. Seth Magaziner (D-Rhode Island), Chip Roy (R-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington) and Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida). The bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act, would have barred members of Congress and their families from trading stocks. The authors of the original bipartisan compromise are less than thrilled with the Stop Insider Trading Act. “House Republicans are pushing a voter suppression bill that will upend mail-in-voting and throw the elections into chaos, and are trying to trick members into supporting it by linking it to a partial stock trading ban that falls short of the full Congressional stock trading ban that the American people want,” Magaziner wrote in a statement to NOTUS. Seth Magaziner AP- ( , AR: 1.50)Roy told reporters Monday that although he would prefer stronger protections around stock trading, the Stop Insider Trading Act still represents significant progress in holding lawmakers accountable. “I worked in good faith with Bryan Steil to put that together as an approach that we thought we could rally around,” Roy said. “It would be a giant step forward to say that you can literally not buy any equities whatsoever. I think that's a huge deal.” Nearly a year ago, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee advanced its own bipartisan bill sponsored by Sen. Josh Hawley (D-Missouri). But the bill , called the Halting Ownership and Non-Ethical Stock Transactions Act, or HONEST Act, has languished, and leadership has yet to schedule a vote on it. Barrasso said that Hawley’s bill is on leadership’s radar, but he that the upper chamber has a number of other priorities ahead of the August recess. The stock-ban bill is “always something [Hawley] has been pushing,” Barrasso said. Hawley told NOTUS that although he prefers his own bill to the House measure, he’s open to supporting any legislation that could help curb stock trading in Congress –– especially if it has better odds in the Senate. Sen. Josh Hawley ( , AR: 1.50)“The House bill is not nearly as robust as I would like it, but something is better than nothing,” Hawley said. “I think that’s moving the ball forward –– I hope they’ll pass it. It’s just a matter of what we can get passed.” Sen. Rand Paul (R-Kentucky) who chairs the Senate’s homeland security committee and opposed Hawley’s bill, told NOTUS he hasn’t reviewed the House measure to see if he’d support it. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Michigan), the top Democrat on the committee, also told NOTUS he hasn’t looked closely at how the House stock-ban bill compares to Hawley’s Senate bill. But Peters said he thinks any movement on a stock-trading bill is good. Senate Democrats are still trying to move the HONEST Act, Peters , but continue to struggle with the legislative calendar. The Senate has just about 10 weeks worth of session left this year amid the midterm elections on Nov. 3. Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Nebraska), who is sponsoring the Stop Insider Trading Act in the Senate, told NOTUS that although he feels good about the legislation’s chances in the upper chamber, he’s aware the Senate’s legislative calendar “will be part of the challenge.” “It's a commonsense piece of legislation that will help restore people's faith in the Senate. So I believe we can get the votes,” Ricketts said.

stories.title: Tax Cuffs
stories.author: Zara Norman, Jenny Gathright
stories.content: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform Chairman Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., arrives for a hearing with former Goldman Sachs senior counsel Kathryn Ruemmler and her ties to Jeffrey Epstein, on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, July 15, , in Washington. Rod Lamkey/AP Photo Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A consequential tax code vote, continued weather woes and the dismantling of the D.C. streatery. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST The House is set to vote tomorrow on a bill that would prevent the D.C. Council from making changes to the city tax code without explicit congressional approval. House Oversight Chair James Comer (R-Kentucky) said he introduced the measure because he wants to prevent city lawmakers from raising taxes, a step D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson has said they may take to confront a budget crunch in the coming year, Jenny reports. The twist? The bill could also prevent the city from decreasing existing taxes or fees. If it passes, any change to Title 47 of the D.C. code could go into effect only if both chambers of Congress approve. Comer said in a statement that tax increases are the true target of the policy. "Congress must have stronger oversight tools to prevent these job-killing tax hikes, which will drive employers, investment, and residents out of the city," he told NOTUS. "And if pigs ever fly and the DC Council approves tax cuts instead, I'll be the first to lead the charge for Congress to approve them immediately.” The bill would an uphill battle to overcome the filibuster if it makes it to the Senate. It’s the latest in a series of attempts by Republicans to undermine the D.C. government’s ability to dictate local policy — and it underscores just how much some watchful eyes on Capitol Hill are scrutinizing the D.C. Council. Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton said “the entire Committee, Republicans included, should be offended by this reckless waste of their time.” FROM THE DISTRICT D.C.’s weather woes continue this afternoon, with severe storms likely and “a tornado or two” possible, Capital Weather reports . The city is ordering restaurants to dismantle their streateries, Axios D.C. reports . These outdoor dining areas were a lifeline for restaurants during COVID, but an onerous permitting process to make them permanent has spelled their doom. FROM VIRGINIA Ratepayers would be on the hook for a proposed -mile transmission line traversing rural Virginia, WTOP reports . It would power the northern part of the state, which is home to the world’s densest concentration of data centers. FROM MARYLAND National Harbor’s “Sphere” will be taller than the U.S. Capitol and almost exactly the height of the Washington National Cathedral — or 45 AJ Dybantsas , per City Cast DC . GUESS THE LISTING pool1 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) Listed for $1, , , this three-bedroom brick Cape Cod is a party in the back with a stone patio, in-ground pool and custom-built pool house. Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer: Maryland Virginia D.C. We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right. SPORTS With the battle over the future of college sports heating up in the Senate, a major question is whether senators pushing the Protect College Sports Act can get the SEC and Big Ten conferences on board. As NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty reports , one potential tweak to the bill has to do with conference realignment and expansion, as the initial text would have halted any future expansion for leagues making more than $ million (which includes the SEC and Big Ten). The change the various factions are kicking around: capping conferences at 19 programs instead and making it so any school that wants to jump from one power league to another has to first go independent for five years. Nationals infielder Luis García Jr., a surprise slugger this season, has received interest from multiple teams on the trade market, The Athletic reports . The MLB trade deadline is Aug. 3. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Rockies, 8:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Garland Gay. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) John Quincy Adams. A special shout-out to Susan Stonesifer, who answered first.

stories.title: Fetterman's Ultimatum Giving Some Democrats Anxiety He’ll Switch Parties
stories.author: Igor Bobic
stories.summary: The Pennsylvania Democrat warns he will leave the party if it officially changes its platform regarding its stance toward Israel.
stories.content: Sen. John Fetterman is warning that he may leave the Democratic Party if it officially changes it's platform on support for Israel. Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call via AP Images Bill Clark/AP Sen. John Fetterman’s increasingly independent political moves are raising eyebrows among his Senate colleagues and giving fodder to his progressive critics, fueling speculation about whether he might leave the Democratic Party. Fetterman said last week he would formally switch his affiliation if Democrats make opposition to Israel part of their official platform. It’s the first time the Pennsylvania senator has laid out a scenario in which he would jump ship. Fetterman’s colleagues have doubts about his ability to win a Democratic primary. One Democratic senator, who requested anonymity to speak freely, expressed anxiety over the prospect of an unexpected party switch by Fetterman. “I am concerned,” the senator told NOTUS. Fetterman has pointed to recent contested primaries as evidence that the party is changing. “Look at the kinds of people that are winning our primaries. Not just, ‘I'm pro-Palestinian,’ but, ‘I'm intensely anti-Israel.’ That's a significant difference,” Fetterman told NOTUS. His decision to set up a joint fundraising committee with Republican Sen. Dave McCormick, his Pennsylvania colleague with whom he shares a uniquely close bipartisan friendship, is also raising questions. Joint fundraising committees are a common way to bulk up one’s coffers, but it’s highly unusual for participants to be affiliated with different political parties, a move that didn’t go unnoticed by his colleagues in the Senate. “I've never seen it before. Yes, I'm struck by it,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), who served as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NOTUS. Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pennsylvania), a progressive who has left the door open to a potential challenge to Fetterman once his term expires in , called Fetterman’s decision to team up with McCormick on fundraising “crazy stuff.” “We have battleground races in Pennsylvania that we are trying to flip, and now we’ve got John Fetterman helping the Republicans to raise money to beat Democrats,” Deluzio told MeidasTouch last week. Asked to respond to Deluzio, Fetterman told NOTUS the congressman “shouldn’t criticize” because he donated money to “an accused rapist,” referring to Graham Platner, who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault, something Platner denied. Deluzio’s political action committee, Yinzer PAC, gave $ to Platner’s campaign in March, before the allegations against Platner were made public. Fetterman downplayed the joint fundraising committee with McCormick, telling the the Washington Examiner, “It’s nothing sinister.” “It’s just — people have joint interest in the things that we happen to agree on, if we both represent Pennsylvania,” he told the outlet. Fetterman has increasingly found himself isolated in the Democratic Party. Although he votes with Democrats on most bills and nominations, his staunch support for Israel, the Iran war and border security has irked some in his party. He seems to relish attacking Democrats, most recently lambasting progressives for their decision to back Platner in Maine’s Senate race. Last month, Fetterman expressed regret for calling to eliminate the filibuster during his Senate run and praised former Democratic Sens. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema for defending the Senate’s long-standing supermajority requirement under President Joe Biden’s tenure. “If we lose the filibuster, then the rights of the minority, whether that will be Democrat or Republican minority, would have effectively little to no voice,” Fetterman said in an interview with conservative podcast host Katie Miller, the wife of White House adviser Stephen Miller. “And if we become a smaller version of the House, that would have profound ramifications for the United States, and that would be dangerous. I'll be the first to say that our entire Democratic Party was wrong about that in that cycle." Fetterman’s approval ratings in Pennsylvania have fallen to 19% among Democrats, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released last week. The same survey found that 52% of voters want Fetterman to leave the party. The senator told CNN he couldn’t explain how “a guy that votes 90% on the Democratic line [has] 80% GOP approval. He : “If I'm becoming more unpopular with Democrats, that's a strong correlation of being a proud Israel supporter.” Asked if he thought he could win a Democratic primary, Fetterman said, “I guess we’ll see.” He hasn’t announced whether he will seek another term. Adam Jentleson, Fetterman’s former chief of staff and founder of the Searchlight Institute, a Democratic think tank, said he believed the senator might leave the party “in order to stay relevant,” particularly in a scenario where Democrats win a Senate majority by a single seat in November. “I think, if he is the majority-maker, he will flip, because it would give him a massive amount of attention,” Jentleson, who last year expressed concerns about his former boss’ mental health, said in an interview with NOTUS. Jentleson said the real risk for Democrats is if a vacancy opens up on the Supreme Court. Fetterman recently voted to confirm former Sen. Markwayne Mullin as Trump’s Homeland Security secretary, so he could cross the aisle again to back a future Trump Supreme Court nomination. “I would be the first to say that Senate seats are invaluable, but Democrats should not debase themselves by trying to negotiate with him,” Jentleson . “If he switches, it’s containable — it will be a problem for two years but we can recoup it in .” Other Democrats were skeptical about the idea of Fetterman becoming a Republican, noting he maintains progressive policy positions on key social issues including abortion, marijuana and LGBTQ+ rights. “He votes Democratic all the time. I mean, he'd be a bad Republican,” Vermont Sen. Peter Welch, who is friendly with Fetterman, told NOTUS. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich urged Fetterman not to leave the party. “I would just encourage him to stay,” Heinrich said. “I think you can have policy differences, but on balance, with the exception of one or two issues, when you look at what he cares about, I think that looks a lot more like the Democratic Party than the Republican Party. He's always, always welcome in our caucus.” Maine Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the “water’s OK” on charting a different path in the Senate. “The Democratic Party has been very good to me, allowing me to develop seniority on committees, work on the committees I’m interested in,” King said. Sen. Steve Daines (R-Montana), the former head of his party’s Senate campaign arm, said he found Fetterman joining the Republican conference “unlikely,” but he agreed it would be tough for him to win reelection in Pennsylvania as a Democrat. “I applaud his moral clarity and his courage, and that's greatly respected by voters on both sides. But it would be hard to run in a Democrat primary now,” Daines said. History wouldn’t be on Fetterman’s side if he does decide to leave the party. When then-Pennsylvania Sen. Arlen Specter, a moderate, left the Republican Party ahead of anticipated GOP primary loss in , he provided Democrats a crucial 60th vote in the Senate, allowing them to ultimately pass the Affordable Care Act, the landmark health care law. But Specter’s party switch and his vote for Obamacare didn’t save him in the end. He went on to lose in the Democratic primary against then-Rep. Joe Sestak. Berwood Yost, director of the Floyd Institute for Public Policy at Franklin & Marshall College, said Fetterman is listening to voters in a battleground state like Pennsylvania who want their elected officials to reach across the aisle. But Yost said the strategy might backfire in the current partisan political environment. “He’s had appeal with voters many Democrats are interested in winning back,” Yost said in an interview with NOTUS. “His political brand has always been snarky — cynical in some ways. Some people read him as progressive, but he’s always been his own brand.” “I think it’s more likely he would become —declare himself an independent — but that hasn’t worked in Pennsylvania,” Yost . “He finds himself in a place of his own making.”

stories.title: House Judiciary Panel Gives Border-Enforcement Legislation Another Try
stories.author: Jackie Llanos
stories.summary: The new proposal keeps many immigration provisions from a bill House Republicans passed in .
stories.content: The new proposal, titled the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act, includes provisions that would add penalties for immigrants who overstay their visa by more than 10 days, and expands the Homeland Security secretary’s authority over third-country deportations and the asylum process. Charlie Riedel/AP More than three years after House Republicans passed a major tough-on-immigration bill, the House Judiciary Committee is set to consider a proposal Tuesday with many of the same provisions on asylum, visas and other border policies. The text of the bill , released ahead of the panel meeting, reflects a shift after President Donald Trump took office and Congress, via reconciliation bills, gave Trump billions for border wall construction and his campaign promise of mass deportations. Some House Republicans, including Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), have insisted on following through with campaign promises for tougher immigration proposals in the remaining six months of the current congressional session. In a letter to colleagues this month, Roy called on the House to pass the immigration policies reflected in the bill, which stalled in the Senate. Last month, Roy introduced a bill similar to the effort that shares the same title as the new proposal slated for markup. The newest version doesn’t include a section on border wall construction, or a requirement for all companies to use E-Verify to ensure their new employees can legally work. That provision caused conflict with Republicans worried about reducing the unauthorized agriculture workforce. The new proposal, titled the Permanent Trump Secure Border Act, includes provisions that would add penalties for immigrants who overstay their visa by more than 10 days, and expands the Homeland Security secretary’s authority over third-country deportations and the asylum process. The bill would allow Mullin to deport people to countries they’re not from without a contract with the other governments. Rarely used in previous administrations, the federal government now has 35 agreements with other countries to accept deportees who are not their citizens, according to a tracker from Refugees International and Human Rights First. Under the bill, migrants seeking asylum would also have to prove they didn’t go through other countries they could’ve requested protection from before reaching the U.S., or that other countries denied their request for asylum. Immigration courts are already denying asylum for nearly all applicants. Denials have sharply increased since the end of last year. Immigration judges, who are Justice Department employees, denied nearly 80% of asylum cases in December, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse . In May, they denied almost 94%. The immigration-enforcement bill is getting traction after Speaker Mike Johnson leveraged a vote on it to gain support from Roy for a reconciliation bill to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, Punchbowl reported. Agriculture-minded Republicans didn’t get to add an expansion to the H-2A visa program for temporary farmworkers.

stories.title: Trump Undercut Republicans’ Campaign Message on Housing
stories.author: Raymond Fernández
stories.summary: “You could talk about the policy,” said one Republican operative. “You don’t have to talk about how it became law.”
stories.content: Bill Clark/AP President Donald Trump’s refusal to sign the housing bill passed by Congress has turned into a complicated political question for Republicans: How do you campaign on a legislative win that was rejected by the head of your party? The legislation, which is the most significant housing package to come out of Congress in more than three decades and represents one of the biggest legislative victories of the year for Republicans, became law this month despite the president’s inaction. It’s making for some hard conversations with the voters, who are very attuned to the cost of living. “[Housing is] one of the number one asks I have in my district,” Rep. Zach Nunn (R- Iowa) told NOTUS of issues constituents asked Congress to work on. “If the president didn’t want to sign it, that’s over to the president.” “I’m glad that we stood firm and we had a veto-proof majority. And sometimes Republicans have to stand up to the president and say, ‘This is what our districts need.’” The president endorsed several versions of the bill, including its final form. But he ultimately refused to sign it, saying instead that the Save America Act was the administration’s top priority and should be Congress’ too. “I don’t speak for the president,” Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R- Pennsylvania), who represents a swing district that could help determine control of the House next year, told NOTUS when asked whether he believed voters would credit Republicans for the policy despite Trump’s calling the bill “a big yawn” relative to election security. “I know my voters, my constituents. My electors are super excited about the package,” Bresnahan said. The housing bill is aimed at fast-tracking housing development across the nation by removing some environmental and construction review standards and expanding how existing federal programs administered by the Department of Housing and Urban Development use funds for construction. It also limits the number of single-family homes institutional investors can own. Every step of passing the bill was a headache for Republicans . It got caught up in a monthslong standoff between the House and Senate . Some Republicans griped about the outsize role Democrats took in negotiating the package, which in the end passed with broad bipartisan support. And Trump oscillated in his support for at least one of the provisions in the bill. Now, the careful dance Republicans have to do around it on the campaign trail has become another in a long line of headaches, when they’d widely expected an easy-to-sell legislative feat. “Every House Republican can claim that they fought to have this bill passed because they voted for it, and so you know they’re the ones running, not President Trump,” a Republican operative told NOTUS, adding that the package is not the only affordability policy Republicans should message on. “You could talk about the policy. You don't have to talk about how it became law.” Some Republicans running for reelection are doing exactly that. Sarah Chamberlain, president of the Republican Main Street Partnership — a conservative nonprofit that nearly a hundred sitting lawmakers are part of — told NOTUS that Republicans' messaging on the package should be “localized” and that lawmakers should keep talking about “the fact that they voted, they passed the bill, and it became law.” “The members of Main Street are back in their districts talking about the importance of this legislation and how it affects your day-to-day life. They’re not mentioning what the president said,” Chamberlain said. Both Republican operatives told NOTUS that they believed people outside of D.C. are not aware of the president’s comments or his refusal to sign the bill. Asked about Republican messaging on the legislation and Trump’s refusal to sign it, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pennsylvania) said the bill was a “huge” bipartisan policy win “on probably the most important aspect of affordability, which is housing.” Pressed about the president’s role, Fitzpatrick — who holds another key seat the Republicans are trying to hold on to in order to keep the majority — said the president’s opinions were “his.” “Overwhelming numbers of Democrats, Republicans in the House and Senate voted for it. Everybody’s got to be accountable for our actions,” Fitzpatrick said. The White House did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment. Housing is a key part of the affordability conversation both parties say they want to address. The U.S. is currently facing a shortage of more than 5 million homes, according to Pew Research Center. A Gallup poll conducted in May found that only 25% of non-homeowners believe they will be able to buy a home in the next five years — the lowest percentage in more than a . In the fight for control of the lower chamber, Democrats have also been campaigning on the bill. The day the president canceled the signing ceremony, more than 20 Democratic lawmakers held a rally outside the Capitol to demand the president to sign the legislation and accused him of holding it hostage. Now, vulnerable House Republicans are downplaying that the bill became law without Trump’s signature. “I’m less worried about the process and more about the actual specifics of the bill,” Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York), who is running in a district won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the presidential election, told NOTUS. He touted the bill as a Republican-led effort. Some Republicans are even choosing not to speak about the package at all. When asked about the bill and the president, Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado) said: “Oh, well, let’s back up even before that. Let’s go back to the Working Families Tax Cut.”

stories.title: The Senate Is Working More on Party-Line Nominations — and Less on Legislation
stories.author: Avani Kalra
stories.summary: The decades-long Senate trend toward less legislating is the result of extreme partisanship.
stories.content: Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vermont) speaks out against attorney general nominee Todd Blanche, an increasingly common trend in a polarized Senate. Mattie Neretin/Sipa USA via AP The Senate is known as the world’s greatest deliberative body, but lately it’s not debating much and is largely holding party-line votes on nominees for the administration and the judiciary, a NOTUS review of Senate voting patterns shows. NOTUS examined hundreds of roll-call votes taken in and under a Democratic trifecta and in and in Republican-controlled Washington and found that the Senate is voting more frequently on Cabinet and judicial appointments than on legislation, regardless of the party in power. from the Congressional Research Service shows that nominations made up less than 20% of the total roll-call votes prior to , when the Senate lowered the threshold to a simple majority for most federal judges and executive branch nominations. By the end of , that number topped 60%. “There has been a decades-long transformation of [the Senate],” Casey Burgat, a politics professor at George Washington University, said. “There's been a huge atrophying of the lawmaking power of individual senators and of the Senate as a whole.” Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), the Democratic whip who has served in the Senate for nearly 30 years, told NOTUS that the increased focus on nominations has detracted from legislating. “It’s gotten to the point where we spend most of our time talking about nominations,” Durbin said. Gregory Koger, a political scientist who studies the Senate’s 60-vote voting threshold, the filibuster, said that greater polarization is responsible for the meltdown in the Senate’s ability to pass laws. The number of competitive seats across the country has shrunk to historic lows, according to the Cook Political Report . Lawmakers no longer have to compete as aggressively for moderate voters or members of the opposing party, and bipartisan collaboration has become a liability rather than an asset in tenuous primaries, Koger . “Increasingly there's a downside risk from an angry, disappointed partisan base, on both sides, for compromising,” he said. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), who chairs the Senate Republican Policy Committee, agreed, telling NOTUS that bipartisanship has declined throughout her nearly 12 years in the upper chamber. “There’s certain issues that we can go bipartisan, but most recently, even those are getting shut down. Everything is about a political advantage,” Capito said. Senators are instead spending more time voting on partisan proposals offered by the minority party. The NOTUS review of roll-call votes found that Senate Democrats have forced more than 30% of the roll-call votes in –– up from under 20% in , which was similar to the number of Republican-forced votes under Democratic control. “Your whole goal is to make them look bad,” Burgat said. “To not help, to obstruct, because that's what your voters want. It helps you as a party maintain a better electoral strategy heading into campaign season, and it's always campaign season.” on bipartisan legislation has been steadily decreasing since . Republicans, then led by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky), decided it would be politically advantageous to block any legislation and nominees proposed by then-President Barack Obama. That strategy was followed by a change in the Senate’s nomination process, lowering the 60-vote threshold to a simple majority vote for most federal judicial nominees. Later, Republicans eliminated the filibuster for nominees to the Supreme Court. In , Senate Republicans voted to make it easier to confirm executive branch nominees in groups under a simple majority. Senate Majority Leader John Thune announced in April that the Senate had nearly cleared President Donald Trump’s nominations backlog and that leadership was set to begin a four-week push to confirm more before summer recess in August. “It’s not like that then makes the Senate more efficient so it has more time to legislate,” Koger said. “It’s mostly so they can approve more nominations.” Donald Trump,John Thune ( , AR: 1.50)A decline in bipartisanship has also led to both Democratic and Republican majorities legislating more aggressively through the budget reconciliation process over the past two decades. The maneuver allows leadership to bypass the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster and pass tax and spending priorities primarily along partisan lines. The Senate has voted on five approved reconciliation bills since and 12 in total since , including two so far this year alone. The upper chamber passed its first major party-line bill in and passed only nine over the following two decades, according to the Senate’s list of “vote-a-ramas.” Steven Smith, a political scientist who studies the Senate, told NOTUS that today’s expanded use of the reconciliation tool began back in , when congressional Republicans employed the process to pass the first wave of tax cuts under then-President George W. Bush. “It's gradually blossomed into one or more reconciliation bills carrying the bulk of a president's agenda,” Smith said. “Between reconciliation, appropriations and nominations, you get a very big chunk of the roll-call voting record in the Senate.” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire), a moderate Democrat who has led bipartisan negotiations on issues like infrastructure, health care and foreign policy since she joined the Senate in , told NOTUS that she’s seen a breakdown in good-faith talks on Capitol Hill because of the uptick in party-line bills. “It is not a good way to approach getting things done around here,” Shaheen said. “It becomes very, by design, partisan. It doesn’t allow for debate and for working together.” The expanded use of party-line legislating has contributed to the declining power of the Senate’s committees. In years past, individual senators from both parties negotiated legislation in groups behind closed doors. Now, Senate leadership drives bills forward, injecting a more partisan lens to the process. “Ultimately the [outcome] of these monster reconciliation bills, that try to impose as much of the president's program as possible, is that it limits the number of members who have a meaningful role in designing public policy,” Smith said. Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), the president pro tempore of the Senate, where he has served for more than 45 years, pushed back on the assertion that the number of party-line bills has increased. He said reconciliation has always been the go-to when it doesn’t seem like a bill can get to 60 votes. “As far as reconciliation, it hasn’t changed much,” Grassley told NOTUS. “I think we've had ‘vote-a-ramas’ ever since I can remember." Vote-a-ramas are a long series of amendment votes tied to reconciliation bills. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), who is in line to take over as chair of the Senate Budget Committee following the death of Lindsey Graham, said that he expects the upper chamber will continue to use the maneuver. U.S. Congress ( , AR: 1.50)“It’s probably going to be the only tool because Democrats are completely obstructionist and being obnoxious and not doing what’s in the best interests of the nation,” Johnson said. But the scope of what is included in those spending bills has expanded. For example, Senate Republicans funded the Department of Homeland Security using reconciliation after bipartisan negotiations to fund the agency fell apart. According to the Congressional Research Service , it was the first time senators replaced the traditional appropriations process with a party-line bill after they couldn’t secure funding for certain government agencies. The unraveling of the appropriations process followed two of the longest government shutdowns in history and could drive majorities even further toward partisan funding efforts. Appropriations measures are still considered some of the few must-pass bipartisan bills and are negotiated in committee. “That is not how it works,” Durbin said about bypassing committees for party-line bills. “We’ve ended up with a situation virtually where it’s used for everything. We’ve pushed the lever way too much.”

stories.title: Regional Fights Stall Daylight Saving Time Bill's Senate Chances
stories.author: Al Weaver
stories.summary: “It’s got a lot of opposition,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) told NOTUS.
stories.content: While many issues fall along party lines, the fault lines in the fight over daylight saving vs. standard time are largely geographic. Charlie Riedel/AP There’s a whole lot of daylight between the House and the Senate — literally. The House voted last week to make daylight saving time permanent, marking the latest congressional foray into the decades-old battle over whether the U.S. should change the clocks twice a year. But despite the sizable bipartisan vote, the bill — known as the Sunshine Protection Act — is showing few signs of making headway across the Capitol, with scores of senators representing Midwestern and northern states lining up against it. “I think it’s pretty strong,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) said of the level of opposition, adding that the bill’s prospect of passage is dim. While many issues fall along party lines, the fault lines in the fight over daylight saving vs. standard time are largely geographic. While coastal states would be the beneficiaries of a full year with more daylight later in the day, midwestern and mountain states would feel more impacts. The lack of sun in the early morning hours when children are leaving for school in the morning is a chief concern. Under permanent daylight saving time, cities along the westernmost parts of the eastern, central and mountain time zones would not see the sun rise in the winter until later in the morning. Some cities, including Pierre, S.D., and South Bend, Ind., would not see the sun until after 9 a.m. on some days. “Have you ever seen any issue that people are more passionate about and that divides the country more by region than that one?” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS about changing the current system. “It’s got a lot of opposition.” Leading the charge is Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, the No. 3 Senate Republican, who has made clear he would block any attempt to pass the House bill via unanimous consent. The effort to lock the clock in favor of daylight saving has been a windy road in recent years. A bill backed by former Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Florida) passed somewhat surprisingly with a unanimous vote in . Cotton revealed in a floor speech last year that he did not object at that time because there was a “miscommunication,” as he expected another senator to do so. He also said he had not “adequately communicated to my staff the depth of my opposition” to the measure. The bill died in the House. Proponents of daylight saving once tried again to pass it unanimously last year, but Cotton blocked it, arguing they were trying to put “a sunny ” on the proposal. More than a dozen senators from both parties have voted against the daylight saving shift recently in the Senate Commerce Committee: Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware), Ted Budd (R-North Carolina), Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois), Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), Gary Peters (D-Michigan), Jacky Rosen (D-Nevada), Tim Sheehy (R-Montana), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Todd Young (R-Indiana), Thune and Wicker. Even proponents of the measure don’t see a path at present. “No, Tom Cotton’s going to block that,” Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama) said. Tuberville also quipped that more daylight would give him more time on the golf course. When asked how many more rounds he’d get in, Tuberville laughed and conceded: “Quite a few.” Also dooming the bill is that it would not allow individual states to opt out of permanent daylight time. They would have already needed to pass a bill to observe permanent standard time. The only two states to do that are Arizona and Hawaii. “I just don’t think we want a mandate,” Thune said. The push to lock the clock one way or another stems from the unpopularity of the pair of clock changes during the year. According to an AP-NORC poll taken in October, only 12 percent support the current system compared to 47 percent in opposition. Forty percent were neutral. Congress passed a law establishing permanent daylight saving in the 1970s, but it was repealed less than a year later due to the dark mornings. “In Minnesota, Michigan and the Dakotas, you’re going to have schoolchildren getting mowed over waiting for the school bus in the dark,” Wicker said. “I’m surprised the House passed it by such an overwhelming majority.” Another thing standing in the way is the crowded to-do list on the Senate floor. Ahead of the August recess alone, the chamber is expected to deal with the nominations of acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department, Jay Clayton to become Director of National Intelligence and acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling to head the department full-time. Passing a larger package of lower-level nominations is also in the works. The Senate is also hoping to move other items, including a reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a Russia sanctions package and a cryptocurrency regulatory bill. Further complicating the calendar is that memorial services for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-South Carolina) in Washington and his home state are slated for the end of July. Amid the spirited debate, there are also members who simply don’t care one way or another. “I don’t wake up or go to bed thinking about it. I know it’s religion for everybody … but it’s not religion for me,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina). “Just tell me what time to set my clock.”

stories.title: Trump’s Election-Tampering Claims Fall Flat, Including With Republicans
stories.author: Angie Orellana Hernandez
stories.summary: Some lawmakers expressed concern that the president’s speech could jeopardize the GOP’s chances in November.
stories.content: President Donald Trump is seen speaking from the East Room on a television in the West Wing of the White House, Thursday, July 16, , in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo President Donald Trump laid out dramatic plans in a Thursday night speech to unveil evidence of widespread election vulnerabilities within the U.S. Some congressional Republicans are still skeptical. Democrats immediately panned the speech, which contained myriad falsehoods about foreign interference in American elections. Many Republican lawmakers have been largely silent about the speech a day later, seemingly disinterested in engaging with the president’s claims. Republican leadership across the House and Senate did not amplify the president’s speech on X, nor did the official congressional GOP accounts. A handful of lawmakers used the night to promote passage of Trump’s priority elections bill or the Homeland Security Department’s announcement to ramp up efforts to root out noncitizen voting , an extremely rare occurrence. But those leaving or already outside the president’s influence had more to say. Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Kentucky), a Trump critic, said Republicans are “wasting our opportunity that the voters gave to us” and that they will receive an “absolute shellacking” in the November midterms if the party doesn’t “wake up.” “We won all the damn elections, and we’re in charge,” Massie said in a video posted to X . “And what are we doing with it? We’re bankrupting the country. We’re starting new wars. We’re violating the Constitution.” At least one Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about Trump’s speech and only saw clips of the address, told NOTUS that Trump’s China election-interference evidence "begs an investigation." The White House published heavily redacted documents on its website after the speech that appeared to contradict Trump’s claims of foreign interference, such as an unclassified email from a senior FBI official that expressed concerns over lending credibility to the claim that China tried to sway election results. “It was a little complicated for a prime-time address," the Republican said, noting that they did not think the earlier parts of Trump’s speech on tax cuts would land with voters weighing midterm candidates. The member said they expect briefings on the matter but lauded Trump for providing a website and actual data to convey his message about election-integrity concerns. Outgoing Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), a member of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said “there wasn’t a whole lot new” within Trump’s Thursday speech. "We have days until the midterm elections,” Cornyn said at the Aspen Security Forum the next day. “I don't understand talking about what happened six years ago in light of these upcoming elections." Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana), who joined Cornyn at the forum and will also exit Congress next year, said Republicans should be honing in on affordability instead of election security ahead of the midterms. “My concern is that it's setting up a Democratic wave election,” Cassidy said. “We should be talking about what matters to the people around the kitchen table, and right now they can't afford their health care, their housing, their groceries or their gasoline." Sean Spicer, who served as press secretary during the first Trump administration, said in an appearance on NewsNation that the reactions to the speech were a “mixed bag” in conservative circles. He called election integrity an issue that resonates with members of the MAGA movement, but that Trump should have detailed more concrete action in his address. “We need to have more of a call to action, more of a to-do list,” Spicer said. “I saw a lot of negative comments online last night from the MAGA faithful saying, ‘What else can we be doing? What else are we doing?’ Raising an issue and then not having a solution is a little bit of a problem.” John Solomon, a special government employee hired by the White House to review election documents, told CBS News on Thursday that Trump did not overstate any of the information provided to him by intelligence agencies during his address. When Solomon was asked outside the White House if there was evidence to prove Trump actually won the election, he said, “Not yet.”

stories.title: Blame Canada
stories.author: Marissa Martinez
stories.content: National Guardsmen patrol the Lincoln Memorial as the sun, obscured by wildfire smoke, rises above the Washington Monument and the Reflecting Pool on Friday, July 17, . Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 17, . You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free! THE LATEST Donald Trump is backing Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) for a full Senate term ahead of the Aug. 11 special election. Will this prevent a messy primary? Reps. Ralph Norman , Russell Fry and Nancy Mace are all considering running, but none have made announcements one way or the other. Lindsay Graham’s memorial services will be held July 28 in D.C. and July 29 in South Carolina. Election officials who don’t follow the Trump administration’s election integrity efforts may heavy fines — or prison time, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced today. The agency wants to mandate systemic “enhancements” across states by withholding federal grants. House Republicans released a short-term proposal to extend government funding until Dec. 4 — a month past the midterm elections. THE HILL Republican lawmakers are trying to punish Canada for the country’s wildfire smoke. Trump said the country’s “willful negligence” is costing the U.S. billions — a cost that “must of necessity” be to Canada’s tariffs. The House Judiciary Committee won’t take up an H-2A visa bill, bucking Republicans who sought a quick path to help the agriculture industry expand the temporary farm worker program. Rep. Randy Fine has squashed his with outside Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz , meaning the Florida Republican will no longer vote against House rules. A Florida judge dismissed a lawsuit to keep embattled GOP Rep. Cory Mills off the primary ballot. But the legal battle may continue. Alan Dershowitz, who negotiated Epstein’s plea deal, canceled his scheduled House Oversight hearing appearance for Monday. THE ADMINISTRATION The U.S. has conducted nearly a week of consecutive strikes against Iran — raising risk of return to a larger war. The Trump administration improperly fired the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s CFO, a federal judge ruled today. While the Supreme Court has expanded the president’s power to dismiss officials within the executive branch, justices never overruled rules for lower-ranking employees, wrote Judge Michael Nachmanoff, a Joe Biden appointee. THE STATES Sara Rodriguez suspended her gubernatorial campaign after the Wisconsin lieutenant governor reported “serious mismanagement and inaccuracies” in campaign finance filings. Democrat Cindy Burbank dropped her Nebraska Senate campaign, clearing the field for nonpartisan candidate Dan Osborn to challenge Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts . FOLKS … Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Kelly Poe and Erik Schutz. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at finalnotus@notus.com .

stories.title: House Judiciary Panel Won’t Include Farmworker Visa Changes in Immigration Package
stories.author: Jackie Llanos, Tyler Spence
stories.summary: “I expect there will be major heartburn from producers across the country,” Rep. Glenn Thompson said.
stories.content: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) said any changes to include H-2A visa legislation in an immigration package would have to be considered “down the road.” (AP Photo/Nathan Howard) Chair Jim Jordan said the House Judiciary Committee won’t take up legislation next week to expand a visa program for temporary farm workers, bucking Republicans who sought a quick path to help the agriculture industry. The bipartisan bill, spearheaded by House Agriculture Committee Chair Glenn Thompson (R-Pennsylvania), would eliminate the seasonal work requirement and make other changes to the H-2A visa program, allowing for temporary workers in dairy, mushroom, ranching and greenhouse operations. Thompson had said he believed the bill had a path forward when he introduced it last month. “I think part of it is the border is under control, part of it is the fact that food security clearly is national security, and workforce is a main factor,” Thompson said. But Jordan (R-Ohio) told NOTUS on Thursday he wants to pass an immigration enforcement package that resembles as close as possible the committee's proposal from . He said that proposal is slated for markup next week, and any changes to include H-2A legislation in it would have to be considered “down the road,” maybe on the House floor. “Secure the border, step one; enforcement, step two; step three, look at all that,” Jordan said, referencing visa programs. “I think you have to go in that sequence.” Jordan’s stance on the Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act of is a setback for Thompson and agriculture industry groups, who hoped that a stronger border would be enough to get immigration-minded Republicans on board with the bill. “I expect there will be major heartburn from producers across the country if enforcement measures move forward without addressing the needs of the agriculture industry,” Thompson said in a statement to NOTUS, “and I remain confident in my belief that the Securing Agriculture's Workforce Act of is the best farm labor solution put forth in years.” The H-2A agricultural guest worker program hasn’t changed in decades. The agriculture industry considers the changes long overdue and has waited patiently for a chance at reform. Use of the H2-A program has increased dramatically over the past , reaching nearly ,00 workers in due to the lack of American workers willing to work in the industry. According to data from the Farm Bureau, only of over , advertised positions received a domestic applicant in fiscal year . “Our need is not covered by the rules that we have today,” Mark Currie, CEO of The Giorgi Companies Inc., a company that grows and distributes mushrooms nationwide, told NOTUS at the bill’s introduction in June. “We’re never fully staffed ever.” Currie said his company is often forced to pay overtime to harvest the crop, which creates high additional costs for producers. The Trump administration issued guidance in June that dairy farmers could use the H-2A program as long as the jobs they were trying to fill were seasonal, but the impetus has been on Congress to solidify changes. The bill would also rewrite wage rules and let eligible undocumented farmworkers access the visa program. “If lawmakers are serious about food security and affordability, we need to add SAWA to HR2,” said James O’Neill, director of legislative affairs for the American Business Immigration Coalition. “Enforcement only without legal pathways for long-term skilled immigrants only drives up cost of food and threatens our national security.” While promoting the bill, Thompson boasted support from more than industry groups. However, farmworker labor unions and groups that oppose more foreign workers rejected expanding the H-2A visa program . Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Washington), one of 51 co-sponsors of the bill, said at the bill’s introduction in June that many growers turn to the H2-A program when they struggle to find the workers they need in the communities. “The cost of that program truly is putting very big hardship on our farmers, on their bottom lines,” Newhouse said.

stories.title: Ballot Bluster
stories.author: Evan McMorris-Santoro, Jasmine Wright, Manuela Silva
stories.content: Saul Loeb/Pool AFP via AP Today’s notice: After-address reviews. Campaign trail reporting on Medicaid, Michigan and where the abortion issue went. Members and SpaceX stock. And: Staying elected in Maine. THE LATEST What comes after that speech? The message from Donald Trump was not subtle last night: “These disclosures reveal an election system so broken and vulnerable that no one can possibly defend it.” The president’s address veered from campaign speech to list of grievances to complaints about the media to repackaging of long-standing MAGA conspiracy theories. There’s no doubt people will be digging through the documents he released, though initial reads show them to be heavily redacted and missing context. Trump reinvigorated those ready to blow up the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act. “Tonight’s revelations in @POTUS’ speech were truly shocking,” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Florida) posted. “We need the SAVE America Act NOW.” But there’s no sign this speech changed the legislative math, which shows passage of the bill is simply impossible. The speech was not the subject of real-time chatter like the White House — which billed it as a major address and “breaking news” — may have expected. Two broadcast networks — ABC and NBC — didn’t carry it live, and CBS picked it up late. Fox News carried it live but quickly moved on to the Iran war after. NOTUS’ Kadia Goba told us she sent dozens of texts about the speech to lawmakers and similarly plugged-in types and received mostly radio silence back. The message Trump delivered was old, and that may have been the problem. Two GOP strategists close with the White House, supportive of Trump and the SAVE America Act both told Jasmine they were unsure why the president chose five months before the midterm elections to rehash . “Sounds like this is a speech of someone who thinks they’re going to lose in November,” one of the strategists said. When the second strategist got a look at one of the heavily redacted documents on China accessing voter files, they simply replied, “You’ve got to be kidding me.” Democrats had a similar response. Rep. Joe Morelle (D-New York) told C-SPAN right after the speech, “It’s the ranting of a pathetic and unserious person.” But also, a person with a lot of power. The documents are there, and some pointed out that what comes next could be not more words, but actions. Before the speech was over, one lawmaker texted Kadia their summation: “Setting the stage to meddle with the midterms.” The NOTUS team has more details on what was in the speech and what it means. Open tabs: ICE officer in Maine shooting has history of violent behavior, family and records say (AP); Smoke Floating Far From Canada’s Wildfires Will Darken Skies Again on Thursday (NYT); Fetterman Lays Out ‘Red Line’ That Would Lead Him to Ditch Democrats (NOTUS); Trump’s Teleprompter Operator Is Accused of Betting on the President’s Speeches (NOTUS) From the campaign trail Medicaid cuts on the trail: Democrats say the steep cuts to the program in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill are an albatross around the neck of any Republican incumbent. NOTUS’ Zara Norman traveled to Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, a Trump +5, where Democrats say the cuts give them what they need to oust Republican Rep. Rob Wittman , who criticized the cuts before voting for them. Wittman allies say he knows the district and its politics better than any Democrat. But one Republican seems very concerned about this issue. In Maine, Sen. Susan Collins is currently running a TV ad that touts her vote against the OBBB, specifically because it made cuts to Medicaid. The ad really could not be stronger evidence that this particular Republican is very worried about being associated with these cuts: “Shady, out-of-state groups are falsely attacking Susan,” the narrator says, “but independent fact-checkers have proven those attacks are false.” The two Democratic Senate primaries in Michigan: The establishment candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens , is outspending the progressive, Abdul El-Sayed , 10-1 in paid advertising. But as anyone who has a social media account knows, El-Sayed supporters are out-dunking on Stevens conservatively 1 million-1. Which matters more? NOTUS’ Elena Schneider and Daniella Diaz detail a particularly split-screen week in this race. Abortion moves to the backburner: Four summers ago, the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, inciting Democratic voters to overcome conventional midterm turnout and effectively thwart a Republican wave that November. That same fury about abortion rights appears to have vanished, reports NOTUS’ Oriana González , who tracked how the lightning-rod issue for Dems in and has receded ahead of these midterms. Lawmakers are making adjustments. Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nevada) told Oriana that abortion would definitely play a part in her race because Nevada is one of multiple states with a constitutional measure to protect abortion rights on the ballot. But, she said, “I think the economy is a far bigger issue for people on a day-to-day basis.” From the Hill “Buy” rating: A bipartisan moment in the House: Four members who sit on committees that directly regulate SpaceX have shares of the company’s stock in their family holdings, NOTUS’ Samuel Larreal reports . Rep. Gil Cisneros (D-California) and family members of Reps. John McGuire (R-Virginia), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania) and John James (R-Michigan) have together purchased up to $ , of the hot stock, which only IPO’d in June. Cisneros, McGuire and Meuser did not respond to requests for comment. A spokesperson for James said: “The James children are excited about space exploration and Liz purchased stock for them through a brokerage firm, like other members of the public were welcome to do.” Liz is James’ wife. NOTUS METRO Sign up for our local newsletter. NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for all the latest , launching Monday! Local news: New House Bill Would Block D.C. From Raising Taxes , by Jenny Gathright In an Age of ‘Takeovers,’ D.C. Gives Teens Another Place to Party , by Shamira Muhammad NEW ON NOTUS A good path to job security is to get yourself elected to statewide office in Maine, NOTUS’ Paul Kane writes . The last incumbent Maine senator to lose reelection was in , when Republican Bill Cohen won his first of three terms. And it’s been 60 years since a Maine governor sought reelection and lost. That Made It a Trump Target. By Rebecca Davis O’Brien and Kim Bhasin for The New York Times Trump made $1.4bn from crypto in one year. Is Justin Sun the man who helped him do it?
